result1: the impact of cover crops on available water stored in the soils depended on the soil depth considered. in the upper soil layers changes produced by the introduction of cover crops in the rotations had both positive and negative effects but in deep soil layers this trend was clearly negative.
result2: NA
general_conclusion: the impact of cover crops on available water stored in the soils depended on the soil depth considered.

search_strategy: data used in this study came from a global soil health database known as soilhealthdb (jian et al., 2020a), and included responses of 38 soil health indicators to cover crop usage. in total, 4024 comparisons were collected from 269 individual studies . literature were compiled from: the soil health institute “research landscape tool”; cover crop meta-analyses focused on south america (alvarez et al., 2017), africa (sileshi, 2009) and global-scale responses (gattinger et al., 2012; poeplau and don, 2015); and a literature search using isi web of science, google scholar, and the china national knowledge infrastructure.
selection_criteria: not specified
data_analysis: the results suggested that many rrs did not have normal distributions. for these indicators, we used a bootstrapping method to estimate the mean and 95 % confidence interval; however, the bootstrapping results were found to be very similar as the results from one sample t-tests. therefore, the t-test results were used directly without further modification. for the one sample t-tests, the null hypothesis was that the mean rr is zero, indicating no difference between cover crop treatments and no cover controls. an indicator therefore had a significant response to cover cropping if its 95 % confidence interval excluded zero (p < 0.05).
background: Many producers use cover crops as a means to increase soil health and agricultural productivity, yet benefits of this practice vary depending on environmental and management conditions. In an effort to objectively evaluate how cover crops affect soil properties and crop production across climates and systems, we compiled data from 269 studies that compared cover crop treatments versus no cover crop controls.
objective: (1) analyze response of soil health/productivity indicators to cover crop usage across a range of climates, soil types, and cropping systems; and (2) develop a predictive calculator that estimates cover crop effects on 13 key parameters associated with soil health and crop productivity. the results from this study provide a valuable tool for farmers, planners, and regulators to evaluate potential benefits from including cover crops within rotations.
result1: cover crops did not affect soil water content.
result2: NA
general_conclusion: cover crops did not affect soil water content.

search_strategy: using the web of science database and the china national knowledge infrastructure, we searched journal articles published from july 1987 to march 2020 that reported ground cover in orchards. the search terms included ‘ground cover’, ‘cover crop’, ‘mulch’, ‘green manure’, ‘catch crop’, or ‘sod cultivation’ and ‘orchard’, ‘fruit tree’, or ‘fruit’.
selection_criteria: (a) at least one of the targeted fruit tree variables (yield and quality indicators) was reported under both ground cover management and clean tillage (bare soil) management; (b) only field studies were chosen; (c) only the latest observations were taken to meet the standard of independence of samples, when variables were measured at multiple time points; (d) multiple ground cover management types, cover crop species, fruit tree species, cultivation durations, and tree ages in one study were considered as independent observations.
data_analysis: natural logarithm transformation was conducted to improve the statistical power by lowering the estimated bias and normalizing the sample distribution. a weight factor (ω) was estimated for each study. if the variance of the mean value was not reported in some studies, the weight factor was estimated. the mean effect size of each given variable was calculated. the percentage of changes (c%) of the investigated variables induced by ground cover were calculated. a normality test of rr for each variable was conducted using the kolmogorov-smirnov test. we found that most variables did not follow a normal distribution. the nonparametric bootstrap analysis (resampling n = 10,000 iterations) was calculated by spss v20.0 (ibm, chicago, usa).
background: An important management strategy for the development of sustainable agriculture in orchards is the management of ground cover. However, there is a knowledge gap regarding the effects of ground cover on fruit yield and quality.
objective: the objectives of this study were to quantitatively evaluate: (a) the overall effectiveness of ground cover management on fruit yield and quality indicators; and (b) the effectiveness of ground cover management based on climatic condition, fruit tree species and ground cover types. the aim of this study was to provide evidence-based means to improve fruit yield and quality using more sustainable management practices.
result1: legume cover crops significantly increase soil moisture content. non-legume cover crops had no significant effect.
result2: NA
general_conclusion: legume cover crops significantly increase soil moisture content. non-legume cover crops had no significant effect.

search_strategy: the authors conducted a systematic literature search in two major databases, scopus and web of science (wos) core collection database (sci-expanded index), for studies that compared es or biodiversity with different vegetation management (initial database query 25 january 2016; detailed search terms in appendix s1). this resulted in a total number of 1,429 publications.
selection_criteria: 1) less than three spatially independent replicates per treatment level, (2) vineyards under plastic or in greenhouses, and (3) treatments not directly manipulating soil or vegetation management in the vineyards (e.g. application of synthetic or external mulches or the use of different fungicide or insecticide treatments) were excluded. in addition, only studies, which reported means and any dispersion measure of the dependent variable (e.g. sd or sem), were used. we contacted the authors of recently published papers with missing data of variance or additional information like irrigation regime of the treatments.
data_analysis: the results are reported as the back-transformed values of the relative percentage of increase (positive values) or decrease (negative values) in comparison to the control treatment. we chose to analyse data with hierarchical mixed-effects meta-analysis models that allow incorporating fixed (moderators), true random effects as well as a nesting factor for effect sizes in the respective sources or articles. as several data points were extracted from a single article, we used the article id as a nesting factor to avoid violating the assumption that effect sizes are independent from each other. we used the rma.mv function of the metafor package (viechtbauer, 2010) for r (r development core team, 2017) to fit mixed-effects models to incorporate the true variation in the effect size variation across studies and the fixed effects by adding moderators (borenstein et al., 2009). the effects of treatment are significant, if the confidence interval (ci) did not overlap with zero.
scale: global. major wine producing regions world-wide except asian countries, new zealand and argentina
background: At the global scale, vineyards are usually managed intensively to optimize wine production without considering possible negative impacts on biodiversity and ecosystem services (ES) such as high soil erosion rates, degradation of soil fertility or contamination of groundwater. Winegrowers regulate competition for water and nutrients between the vines and inter-row vegetation by tilling, mulching and/or herbicide application. Strategies for more sustainable viticulture recommend maintaining vegetation cover in inter-rows, however, there is a lack of knowledge as to what extent this less intensive inter-row management affects biodiversity and associated ES.
objective: the main objective of this study was to perform a meta-analysis to identify, whether extensive vineyard vegetation management practices have consequences on biodiversity and associated es across viticultural regions world-wide. the supposed trade-off between provisioning services of wine yield and quality with other es and biodiversity is of central interest for this study. therefore, we addressed the following research questions: (1) does extensive vineyard vegetation management increase biodiversity and es provision in comparison to conventional practices? (2) which es categories or biodiversity parameters respond positively and which respond negatively to extensive vineyard vegetation management? (3) which environmental parameters alter the response to vineyard management? the outcomes of this study will help to formulate agricultural policy recommendations in order to benefit service-providing biodiversity and associated es.
result1: soil water budget parameters showed no significant responses to extensive vegetation management in the mixed-effect model.
result2: NA
general_conclusion: soil water budget parameters (water stress integral, water loss, volumetric soil water content) showed no significant responses to extensive natural vegetation management in the mixed-effect model.

search_strategy: the ebsco discovery service (https://www.ebscohost. com/discovery/content) was the primary search engine used to compile the database for this analysis. the search terms included were: water retention or field capacity or moisture retention or porosity and perennial w1 grass* or cover crop* or agroforest* or forest*. these keyword terms found >400 studies, of which 25 ultimately fit our criteria. to supplement the ebsco discovery service search, the usda–nrcs soil health literature database (usda– nrcs, 2016) was used to find additional research papers. this database is an ongoing effort of the nrcs soil health division to categorize the impact of conservation practices on soil properties and uses large search databases (including google scholar) to find papers.
selection_criteria: (i) studies compared land managed with continuous plant growth (including cases of actively restored perennial landscapes) versus annual crop systems that did not include continuous plant cover and (ii) studies measured at least one of two indicators of soil hydrology: water retained at field capacity (the maximum level of plant available soil water, hereafter referred to as field capacity) or total porosity (the maximum volume of water that soil can hold).
data_analysis: the ebsco discovery service (https://www.ebscohost. com/discovery/content) was the primary search engine used to compile the database for this analysis. it searches a comprehensive collection of titles, including more than 23,000 publications from databases such as jstor and publishers such as wiley, elsevier, springer–nature, iop, royal society, oxford, cambridge, thomson reuters, aaas, and the american society of agronomy. the ebsco discovery service matches on subject headings, keywords, and abstracts, making it an ideal search engine for building a database targeted to the highly specific question in this analysis. the keyword search included descriptors of the soil properties (given the multiple terms that might be used to describe field capacity) as well as the different continuous living cover practices. the search terms included were: water retention or field capacity or moisture retention or porosity and perennial w1 grass* or cover crop* or agroforest* or forest*. these keyword terms found >400 studies, of which 25 ultimately fit our criteria. to supplement the ebsco discovery service search, the usda–nrcs soil health literature database (usda– nrcs, 2016) was used to find additional research papers.
background: Increased rainfall variability due to climate change threatens the efficacy of critical soil ecosystem services. One strategy to negate effects of too much or not enough rainfall is to improve soil water properties. Practices that offer “continuous living cover” can enhance soil water storage and other soil hydrologic properties relative to annual crop systems, but to what extent such benefits can accrue, under different conditions, remains under-quantified.
objective: provide a quantitative summary of how practices that promote continuous living cover including cover crops, perennial crops, agroforestry and managed forestry, improve two key soil hydrologic properties that relate to water storage.
result1: there was evidence of improvements in both hydrologic properties analyzed (however, no statistical analysis is provided).
result2: NA
general_conclusion: there was evidence of improvements in both hydrologic properties analyzed (however, no statistical analysis is provided).

search_strategy: peer-reviewed research articles published between 1980 and 2020 were searched in web of science, google scholar, and china national knowledge infrastructure database to determine the cover crop effects on swsp, pse, succeeding crop yields, et, and wue. keywords included soil water, precipitation storage efficiency, crop yield, water use efficiency, cover crop, catch crop, and green manure. the search provided 485 publications including both rainfed and irrigated systems.
selection_criteria:
i. field studies that reported soil water content, cover crops grown between the harvesting of a previous cash crop and planting of a succeeding cash crop, and cash crops with similar management practices, such as irrigation, fertilization, and tillage, were selected for the study. studies conducted on greenhouse and pot experiments were excluded. studies that included cover crop as an intercrop with other crops were also excluded.
ii. data included comparison of cover crops vs. no cover crop (fallow) in a region with similar soil and climatic conditions. studies with the no control treatment were discarded.
iii. treatments were replicated at least three times, and mean values were shown with standard deviation (sd) or standard error (se).
iv. in humid and subhumid regions, two to three crops could be grown in a year. in such cases, only data for those crops that were exclusively stated as cover crops were used for analysis. data for crops used as supplemental cash crops in a year were excluded.
subjected to these criteria, 117 studies from 99 publications from studies conducted across the world were selected for the meta-analysis
data_analysis: to determine the cover crop effect on pse, swsp, succeeding crop yield, et, and wue, mean effect size and 95% bootstrapped confidence intervals (cis) were computed by using a random model analysis with metawin 2.1 software (sinaure associate inc., sunderland, usa). the effect was not significant when cis crossed zero.
background: Cover cropping is practiced to enhance soil health and sustain succeeding crop yield; however, the effect of cover crop on soil water storage, succeeding crop yield, and water-use efficiency (WUE) may not be consistent in all regions.
objective: (1) evaluate how cover crop species and management impact pse, swsp, succeeding crop yields, et, and wue under various soil and climatic conditions, and (2) determine if cover crop biomass and termination date relate to these parameters.
result1: data for succeeding crop et and wue (188 and 148 paired observations). 129 paired observations for pse, 465 for swspt and 152 for swsp30, respectively.
result2: cover crop significantly increased wue of succeeding crop by 5.0% compared to no cover crop. the increase was contributed primarily by legume cover crop, with limited effect of nonlegume and mixture of legume and nonlegume cover crops. cover crop decreased evapotranspiration of the succeeding cash crop by 6.2%.
result3: cover crop, overall, decreased pse by 33.4% compared to no cover crop. this was true for legume, nonlegume, and legume and nonlegume cover crop mixture.
result4: all cover crop species and mixtures also exhibited lower swspt, with an overall decline of 13.2% for cover crop compared to no cover crop. in contrast, cover crop overall increased swsp30 by 6.0% compared to no cover crop, especially for nonlegumes and legumes, but not for the mixture
general_conclusion: cover crop increased water use efficiency of the succeding cash crop by 5.0% (p < 0.05) compared to no cover crop.
knowledge_gaps: although no publication bias was found in this meta-analysis (supplementary table s3), limited data available for pse, swsp, succeeding crop yield, et, and wue in certain climatic zones and soil texture as well as residue management practices may have resulted in inconclusive results. for example, rr of cover crop for pse was greater in loam, but lower in all other soil textures. residue removal increased pse, but reduced swspt and swsp30. similarly, succeeding crop yield and et in response to cover crop compared to no cover crop were lower, but wue was greater for silty clay loam soil (fig. 5). this resulted in the reduced reliability of interpretation for certain parameters in some soil and climatic conditions and residue management practices. increased data availability, however, will enhance the meta-analysis of these data in the future.

search_strategy: the authors performed extensive keyword searches of several databases (web of science (isi), scopus, cab abstracts (isi), academic search complete (ebsco) and google scholar), and the reference list of cited references. the keywords used in the search included ammonia/nh3 emission; volatilization; loss and/or mitigation; management practice; fertiliser n source; rate; time; place; split application; irrigation; urease inhibitors; controlled release fertilisers; nitrification inhibitors; name of the inhibitors such as nbpt; dcd; dmpp; agriculture; cropping; pastures; and their combinations.
selection_criteria: 1) the sample sizes and means of nh3 volatilization had to be reported for control and treatment plots; 2) details on experimental location; year; design and conditions must be provided to enable the cross checking of duplicate publication; 3) multiple observations from the same experimental site over sampling time or year of study were averaged.
data_analysis: effect sizes were weighted by a function of sample size. the meta-analysis was conducted using metawin version 2.1. mean effect sizes and 95% confidence intervals were generated by bootstrapping (4999 iterations). a fixed-effects model or a mixed-effects model is technically not applicable for non-parametric meta-analytic procedures based on weighting by replication. however, to perform a correct bootstrapping using metawin, a fixed-effects model had to be selected. the effects of the mitigation strategies were considered significant if the 95% confidence intervals did not overlap with zero.
background: Ammonia (NH3) volatilization is a major pathway of nitrogen (N) loss in agricultural systems worldwide, and is conducive to low fertiliser N use efficiency, environmental and health issues, and indirect nitrous oxide emission. While mitigating NH3 volatilization is urgently needed, a quantitative synthesis is lacking to evaluate the effectiveness of mitigation strategies for NH3 volatilization from synthetic fertilisers applied in agricultural systems.
objective: the authors report the results of a quantitative synthesis of the current literature on the mitigation strategies of nh3 volatilization to provide critical information on how to minimize n loss as nh3 in agricultural systems.
result1: residue retention significantly increased nh3 volatilization by 25.5%.
result2: NA
general_conclusion: crop residue retention significantly increased nh3 volatilization by 25.5%.

search_strategy: peer-review scientific literature published between january 1, 1980 and march 31, 2021 were searched using a combination of keywords (such as “nh3 volatilization” or “nh3 emission”) from the web of science and china knowledge resource integrated databases.
selection_criteria: 1) only experiments conducted in china were included; 2) studies must have reported a mean value of cumulative soil nh3 volatilization after fertilisation; 3) field, in-situ pot or lysimeter studies were included.
data_analysis: a random-effect model was employed to calculate the mean effect size of each improved farming practice, and it's 95 % confidence interval (ci) was obtained using a bootstrapping procedure with 4999 iterations (rosenberg et al., 2000). a categorical random-effect model was used to determine the mean effect size of different groups among the improved farming practices and to derive impact factors of specific improved farming practices. calculations were performed using metawin 2.1. the improved farming practice was deemed to have a significant impact on av or ysav when the 95 % ci did not overlap with the zero line. categorical groups were deemed significantly different where the 95 % cis did not overlap with each other.
background: High ammonia (NH3) emissions from fertilized soil in China have led to various concerns regarding environmental safety and public health.
objective: select effective measures based on absolute (av) and yield-scaled (ysav) nh3 volatilization reduction potential, with the aim of establishing a comprehensive nh3 mitigation framework covering various crop production sectors, and offering a range of potential solutions.
result1: significant ammonia volatilisation reductions were associated with applying straw to neutral or alkaline soils with low soil organic matter content, adopting maize or cash crops as crop type, or by applying added n fertiliser to the soil subsurface.
result2: NA
general_conclusion: no effect of straw return on ammonia volatilisation reduction.

search_strategy: peer-reviewed publications were collected by searching web of science (http://apps.webofknowledge.com) and china national knowledge infrastructure database (https://www.cnki.net) with various combinations of keywords “nitrous oxide” or “n2o,” “nitric oxide” or “no,” and “agricultural soils.”
selection_criteria: (i) the n2o and no emissions were simultaneously measured during at least a whole growing season; (ii) only the field measurements were included, without considering incubation, pot and lysimeter experiments or modelling results; (iii) the experiments on upland soils and paddy soils during the non-waterlogging period were included, without considering those on the flooded paddy soils; and (iv) the spatial replicates and standard deviation of each treatment were clearly recorded.
data_analysis: mean effect size and the 95 % confidence intervals were generated by a bootstrapping procedure with 999 iterations using metawin 2.1 (rosenberg et al., 2000). the management effects were back-transformed and reported as percentage changes ([rr-1] × 100). the effects were considered significant if the 95 % confidence intervals did not overlap with zero.
background: The development of management strategies that mitigate N2O and NO emissions without crop productivity penalties remains a great challenge.
objective: quantify the effects of various management practices on n2o and no emissions and crop yields by performing a pairwise meta-analysis.
result1: returning crop residues decreased no emissions (by −32.1 %), which supports the initial hypothesis, i.e., fresh crop residues promote denitrification by releasing labile organic carbon substrates and generating anaerobic conditions through decomposition.
result2: NA
general_conclusion: crop residue return reduces no emissions compared with crop residue removal.

search_strategy: we used several databases such as web of science, google scholar, china national knowledge infrastructure database, china wanfang data, current contents connect (isi), academic search complete (ebsco), scopus, and cab abstracts to search peer‐reviewed publi- cations (before august 2018) related to the effects of straw return on various nr losses, crop productivity, and soil c sequestration. the keywords used in the search included “crop straw or crop residue or crop stubble,”“nr losses (nh3 emissions, n2o emissions, n leaching, and runoff), soc content, crop productivities (crop yield, crop n uptake, and n use efficiency (nue)) and/or other soil properties.”
selection_criteria: 1) the control (mineral n fertilisation) and straw treatment (mineral n fertilisation plus straw return) received equal mineral n fertilisation rates, which indicated that the straw treatment provided additional straw n supply to soils; 2) publications needed to report on at least one of the target variables and sample sizes for the con- trol and treatment plots. multiple observations that were conducted at the same experimental site over several sampling years were aver- aged; 3) the observation duration of the experiment must have covered the main discharge period of various nr losses.
data_analysis: mean effect sizes and the 95% confidence intervals (cis) were generated by a bootstrapping procedure with 4,999 iterations, using metawin 2.1. effects of straw return were considered significant if the 95% cis did not overlap with zero. the means of the categorical variables were consid- ered significantly different from each other if their 95% cis did not overlap.
background: It is widely recommended that crop straw be returned to croplands to maintain or increase soil carbon (C) storage in arable soils. However, because C and nitrogen (N) biogeochemical cycles are closely coupled, straw return may also affect soil reactive N (Nr) losses, but these effects remain uncertain, especially in terms of the interac- tions between soil C sequestration and Nr losses under straw addition.
objective: this paper is aimed to: 1) evaluate the overall effects of straw return on various nr loss pathways (nh3 emissions, n2o emissions, n leaching, and runoff), crop productivity and soil c sequestration in agroecosystems under different environ- mental and management conditions (straw quality and quantity, soil properties, agricultural management, and climate conditions); 2) explore the interactions between various nr losses and soc sequestration following straw return; 3) estimate how straw return has affected nr losses from global croplands and the overall cropland nr balance for the period 2005−2015.
result1: on average, straw return significantly increased nh3 emissions by 17.0% (n = 116); the positive effect was smaller for rice paddies (11.4%, n = 35) than for upland crops (20.3%, n = 81).
result2: NA
general_conclusion: on average, straw return significantly increased nh3 emissions by 17.0% (n = 116).

search_strategy: the data for the present meta-analysis were collected from published peer-reviewed experimental studies that reported changes in soil quality, environmental impacts, and crop production indicators responding to rr compared with residues removed in china's croplands from the web of science (before the year of 2017, http://apps.webofknowledge.com.proxy.insermbiblio.inist.fr/) and the china knowledge resource integrated database (before the year of 2017, http://www.cnki.net/) with the key words of 'residue or straw,' 'retain or retention or return or mulch or incorporation,' and 'china.'
selection_criteria: (a) the experiment was designed as side-by-side paired-plot field studies with well-defined control composing of crop residues removal treatment as rr in china's croplands (mainland china); (b) other field managements that were clearly stated or described as 'similar field managements were conducted involving both controls and treatments' (e.g., the same cropping intensity, irrigation, and fertilisation); (c) one or more variables of soil quality, crop production, and environmental impacts parameters were obtainable with the same sampling and measuring methods under rr and residues removed treatments; and (d) location for each field experiment was provided.
data_analysis: a random-effect meta-analysis was conducted to assess crop residues removal(rr)-induced changes for all compiled indicators of soil carbon sequestration (active organic carbon; dissolved organic carbon; light fraction organic carbon; liable organic carbon; particulate organic carbon; soil organic carbon). the weighted mean effect size (lnr++) and 95% confidence interval were generated by bootstrapping through 4,999 iterations.
background: Crop residue retention (RR) is a recommended practice in China and globally. However, comprehensive assessment of changes and mechanisms affecting crop production and soil processes with RR and thus identifying systems of sustainable residues management are not widely studied.
objective: the objectives of the present study were to (a) compile a national dataset of published literatures and conduct a national meta-analysis on the positive and negative responses of soil quality, environmental impacts, and crop production under rr; (b) identify the combined effects of different farming practices with rr; (c) determine the interactive relationships among these indicators; and finally (d) hypothesize possible mechanisms on how rr affects crop production and soil processes.
result1: soil organoc carbon (soc) had a significant increase by 12.3% with adoption of crop residues retention in china's croplands (p < .05). the active fractions of soc pool were relatively more sensitive to crop residues retention (rr). magnitude of active organic carbon, dissolved organic carbon, light fraction organic carbon, particulate organic carbon,  and labile organic carbon responded positively to rr and was significantly increased by 21.5%, 18.8%, 26.0%, 36.4%, and 16.5%, respectively (p < .05).
result2: the data presented herein also demonstrated alterations in responses of soc pool to rr among crop species and different farming practices.
general_conclusion: residue retention significantly increased soil organic carbon (soc) by 12.3% and active soc fractions by 16.5–36.8%, with variations among crop types, farming practices, and environmental factors.

search_strategy: we collected data from relevant peer-reviewed publications. the publications were identified using the online database isi web of science, within the period 1997–2017. publications were searched using the keywords “organic amendment” and the results were refined using additional words—“long-term”, “yield”, “manure”, “compost”, “olsen p”, and “microbial biomass”. additionally, articles cited in review papers which had analysed data from long-term agricultural studies (≥ 10 years)  were also included in the dataset.
selection_criteria: 1) studies that reported crop yield, soil organic carbon, microbial biomass (mb) and/or plant-available p data for at least two types of treatments: (a) those that did not receive any fertiliser (‘nil control’); or (b) those where only inorganic npk fertiliser (if, ‘standard control’) was applied, and (c) where organic amendments (oa) with or without supplemental if was used. we defined oa as raw or composted materials derived from animals (e.g., manure), plant (e.g., straw) and municipal waste (e.g., sludge). the standard control did not always receive equivalent nutrient rates to those in oa and oa + if treatments; 2) crop yield data were included only for wheat, barley, corn, and rice grain in order to minimise differences in nutrient needs and rooting systems.
data_analysis: the meta-analysis was performed according to hedges et al. (1999) and cayuela et al. (2014) using metawin 2.0 software. the effect sizes (responses) of soil oc, mb, and olsen p were calculated  using a categorical random effects model, where the effect size is weighted by the inverse of the variance.
background: In recent years there has been a renewed interest in using organic amendments (OA) to agricultural soils as partial or full substitutes for inorganic fertilisers (IF) in order to manage nutrients more cost effectively, decrease our dependence on non-renewable resources (for example, P from phosphate rock), reduce and recycle waste that would otherwise be disposed to landfill, and increase soil organic matter.
objective: the present work aims to investigate the effect of oa and oa + if additions on soil nutrient fertility by carrying out a meta-analysis based on results from 132 long-lasting fertility trials (≥ 10 years) worldwide. in this study, the responses of crop yield—along with those of soil organic carbon (oc), size of mb, and plant-available p (i.e., olsen p)—to oa and oa + if relative to if alone (standard control) and no fertilisation (nil control) are determined. here results of the effect of oa and oa + if additions on soil organic carbon are reported.
result1: the straw amendment with mineral fertilisation has a positive effect compared bott to no fertilisation and mineral fertilisation.
result2: NA
general_conclusion: straw amendment with mineral fertiliser has a positive effect on soil organic carbon compared both to straw removal with mineral fertilisation.

search_strategy: published peer-reviewed journal articles from 1990 to 2016 were identified using isi web of science and the china knowledge resource integrated database, with the keywords ‘‘microbial activity’’, ‘‘enzyme’’, ‘‘fertilisation’’, ‘‘manure’’, or ‘‘straw’’.
selection_criteria: 1)  studies were carried out in the territory of mainland china. six fertilisation practices were primarily focused on, including unbalanced application of one or two types of chemical fertiliser (ucf); balanced chemical fertilisation with n, p and k (cf); straw residue retention combined with the application of chemical fertilisers (cfs); straw residue retention only (s); application of manure and chemical fertilisers (cfm); and manure application only (m). 2) the mean and standard deviation (sd) or standard error (se) of the enzyme activities were provided either as part of the experimental design or in figure captions. 3) if an individual study had more than one treatment type (e.g. inorganic fertiliser, straw residue, manure), measurements from different treatment types were considered as independent observations to evaluate the effects of fertiliser management on soil enzymes; 4) studies were based on field trials, with an experimental duration lasting 3 years as a minimum; 5) studies had clear specifications of the experimental design and a minimum of three replications (or blocks); 6) if results were from multiple soil depths, measurements from the uppermost soil layer (0–100, 0–150, 0–200 and 100–200 mm in 15, 9, 70 and 6% of studies, respectively) were used for comparison; 7) published general methodologies were used to measure enzyme activities; 8) experiments had at least one control (no fertilisation) and one fertilisation treatment.
data_analysis: the variance, weighted response ratio (rr++), standard error of rr++ and 95% confidence interval (ci), were calculated using routine statistical methods. a random-effect-model was applied. in addition, meta-regression analysis was performed using the metafor package to investigate whether the activities of urease, phosphatase, invertase and peroxidase under different fertiliser management practices, were influenced by site-specific factor variables (map, mat, initial soil ph, initial soc and experimental duration).
background: The effects of fertilisation and residue retention practices on enhancing crop yield and soil productivity, have been extensively investigated in various cropping system studies. However, various potential interactions exist among system components (soil, plant, microbial).
objective: using a meta-analysis of 85 peer-reviewed articles published in the past three decades, we synthesized the eeas of four major soil enzymes (urease, phosphatase, invertase, and peroxidase), which are affected by various fertilisation and residue management practices used in cropping systems of china.
result1: straw induced significantly positive effects on soc concentrations.
result2: NA
general_conclusion: straw residue retention had strong positive effects on the improvement of soil organic carbon.
knowledge_gaps: this analysis largely ignored the interactions with other management-related factors such as irrigation and tillage; larger confidence interval was present due to insufficient data for s treatment condition and more studies that would incorporate these practices will be needed to draw more precise conclusions;

search_strategy: comprehensive search of relevant peer-reviewed articles and dissertations in the web of science® and proquest databases using com- binations of the following search string: (“litter remov- al” or “no litter” or “decreased litter” or “clipping” or “mowing” or “straw harvesting” or “thinning” or “bare fallow” or “litter manipulation” or “litterfall manipulation” or “leaf litter manipulation” or “organic matter manipulation” or “detritus manip- ulation” or “carbon input manipulation” or “altered aboveground litter inputs” or “alterations in forest detritus inputs” or “increased litter” or “litter addi- tion” or “double litter” or “straw incorporation”) and (“soil carbon” or “soil organic carbon” or “soil characteristics”). we further classified straw harvesting and residue removal in crop- land as “litter removal”, straw mulching with the equiv- alent of annual aboveground litter production as controls, but straw mulching in excess of the annual aboveground litter production as “litter addition”.
selection_criteria: xe only included results for crop residue man- agement that were comparable with litter manipulation treatments in other ecosystems. we thus excluded the results of manure, fertiliser or plastic mulch applica- tions, as well as studies focusing only on the effect of crop rotations or the type of cover crops on soil c storage.
data_analysis: we conducted a metaanalysis using the “metafor” package (viechtbauer 2010). the data were analyzed using effect sizes for each observation calculated as the natural log of the response ratio (rr): rr=ln(xt/xc), where xc is the control mean, i.e. data from plots receiving natural litterfall, and xt is the treatment mean, i.e. data from plots receiving no litter inputs or added litter inputs. effect sizes and variances were calculated using random-effects models with re- stricted maximum-likelihood estimators (viechtbauer 2005), which allows for sampling error and cross-study variability in true effect sizes. we then ran standard meta-analyses to test the total heterogeneity of effect sizes within each model whereby p values <0.05 indicated heterogeneity in effects between studies when accounting for sampling error (koricheva et al. 2013). to identify differences in the magnitude of effects among ecosystem types, we subsequently conducted a subgroup analysis for each parameter. the publication bias was estimated by the dnorm function (fig. s1 in the supplement a), and the frequency distributions of all rr values for the target variables followed a normal distribution, indicating an absence of publication bias in our study
background: Aboveground plant inputs, such as leaf litter, are an important source of carbon (C) for soils. There is still much uncertainty in our understanding of how changes in aboveground plant litter inputs will affect soil C storage. Importantly, we know very little about how soil C content is affected at different soil depths across ecosystems and whether the impact of treatments increases or attenuates over time.
objective: meta- analysis of 237 studies, in which aboveground litter inputs were experimentally manipulated or altered by management practices. we assessed the influence of litter manipulation on soil c storage at multiple soil depths across ecosystems.
result1: overall, there was a significant decline in soil c content and stocks with litter removal at all measured depth increments (0–5 cm, 5–20 cm, 0–10 cm, 0–20 cm and 20– 100 cm) and a significant increase in soil c content with litter addition at all measured depth increments but there was no response of soil c stocks to litter addition at any soil depth across all ecosystems.
result2: litter removal had no significant effect on soil c content at some specific the soil depths in grassland.
result3: in croplands there was no effect of bare fallow at 0–5 cm but lower soil c content at 5–20 cm, 0– 10 cm, 0–20 cm and 20–100 cm.
result4: in cropland, soil c content at 20–100 cm was significantly higher with litter addition but there was no effect of litter addition on soil c content at other depths.
general_conclusion: crop residue retention has either positive or no effect on soil carbon content depending on soil depth.  additional straw application has a positive effect in the 0-5 cm soil profile and no effect in 0-20 cm profile in grassland. additional straw application has no effect in the 0-20 cm soil profile and a positive effect in 20-100 cm profile in cropland.

search_strategy: the authors searched the institute for scientific information (isi) web of science database for keywords related to ‘bacterial/microbial community,’ ‘bacterial/microbial alpha-diversity,’ and ‘mineral nitrogen/ straw/manure/fertiliser types’ for papers published from january 2008 to february 2020. studies
selection_criteria: studies were selected according to the following criteria: 1) included mineral nitrogen, straw, or manure addition; 2) field trial duration ≥ 1 year; 3) reported bacterial alpha-diversity (shannon or chao1) and/or sensitive bacterial phyla for mineral nitrogen, straw or manure addition and non-fertilized (i.e., control) treatments.
data_analysis: a mixed-effects model was used to determine whether mineral nitrogen, straw, or manure addition significantly affected soil physicochemical properties and soil bacterial alpha-diversity and composition using metawin 2.1. if the 95% confi- dence interval (95% ci) values for effect size did not overlap zero, then the effect of the mineral nitrogen, straw, or manure addition on soil bacterial alpha-diversity and composition was considered significant; otherwise, it was not significant. conventional heterogeneity statistics (q-statistics) were used to test between-group heterogeneity (qm). structural equation modeling (sem) was used to describe the relationship between environmental factors and bacterial alpha-diversity.
background: Different types of fertiliser can significantly change soil fertility. The response of soil bacterial communities to different fertilisation regimes has been studied widely, but the inconsistent results urged us to systematically study the effect of multiple environmental factors on bacterial diversity and composition under different fertilisation regimes.
objective: the study evaluated the 1) general trend in bacterial community diversity under different fertilisation regimes; 2) changes in sensitive bacterial phyla under different fertilisation regimes; 3) factors with the greatest effect on soil bacterial alpha-diversity and phyla under mineral nitrogen, straw, and/or manure addition.
result1: soc increased with straw addition (soc: 27.84%).
result2: NA

search_strategy: a literature search focusing on publications reporting pairwise comparisons between conventional management and scs practices in vineyards was conducted in october 2019. the search covered the electronic databases of isi web of knowledge and scopus, using the keywords “soil organic carbon”, “soil organic matter” or “soil carbon sequestration” and “vineyard” or “vitis vinifera”. seeking complete coverage, a second search of the same databases used the keywords “cover crop”, “no-tillage”, “amendment”, “biochar”, “hedge”, “agroforestry”, “pruning”, “soil erosion” or “ph” in com- bination with “vineyard” or “vitis vinifera”. these keywords corre- spond to scs practices applicable to viticultural soils, to soil properties playing a role in soc sequestration, or to phenomena affecting soc sequestration.
selection_criteria: (i) they included experiments measuring soc or som levels within existing vine- yards or through experimental manipulation of vineyard manage- ment practices; (ii) they were performed under field conditions (laboratory studies and pot experiments were excluded) for a minimum period of three years; and (iii) they were published in or after 2000. when several studies contained data from the same field experiment, only the longest study was selected to avoid redundancy in the data.
data_analysis: the collected data harmonised to a depth of 0.3 m was used to calculate three effect sizes for soc stock comparisons: (i) the soc stock response ratio (rr), to estimate the change in soc stocks under scs practices relative to conventional management, (ii) the soc stock rate of change (r), as a measure of the annual growth rate in soc stocks under scs management relative to conventional management, and (iii) the raw difference in means of soc stocks for soc sequestration rate comparisons. weighted mean effect sizes of each category of scs practices, bioclimatic zones and study length were calculated. the studies were weighted by sample size. bias-corrected 95% confidence intervals were generated for each weighted mean effect size by bootstrapping procedure with 10,000 iterations.
background: Vineyards are usually cultivated in soils characterised by low soil organic carbon (SOC) content and have high risks of soil erosion and degradation. Increasing SOC stocks in these cropping systems has the potential to contribute to climate change mitigation through SOC sequestration and to enhance soil quality.
objective: compare the soc stock response ratio, the soc stock rate of change, and the soc sequestration rate in vineyards under different soc sequestration (scs) practices relative to conventional management. we focus on pruning residue management here.
result1: soil organic carbon stock was significantly increased when pruning residues were returned to the soild
result2: this practice had a positive effect on soc stock change rate relative to conventional management.
general_conclusion: postive effect of returning pruning residues to the soil on soil organic carbon

search_strategy: the authors collected peer-reviewed publications by searching the isi web of science and chinese national knowledge infrastructure (cnki). the publication time set was from january 1946 to december 2021. the search key-words and their combinations used to identify proper studies were: (soil mineral-associated organic carbon or soil mineral-associated organic matter or maoc or maom or mom) and (straw or litter or glucose or labile carbon or exogenous carbon) and (addition or application or input or amend) and (decomposition or respiration or mineralization).
selection_criteria: 1) the study included the control without sub- strate containing c input and the treatment with substrate containing c input; 2) all experimental conditions were equal between control and treatment; 3) the studies reported soil maoc content or poc content or maoc decomposition under control and treatment; 4) means, standard deviations (sds) or standard errors (ses), and the number of replicates for control and treatment can be obtained from text, tables or digitized graphs.
data_analysis: the standard mean effect size and its corresponding 95%confidence interval (ci) were employed to indicate the effect of c input on maoc content, poc content, and maoc decomposition. heterogeneity in effect size among observations was assessed using the q statistic and quantified using the i2 statistic. random effect model was used if i2 was above 50% and p value was below 0.1, otherwise fixed effect model was used. if the observations had different units, then the value should be standardized as standard mean difference (smd). the effect (promotion or inhi- bition) was statistically significant if the corresponding 95%ci was greater than zero. subgroup analysis was performed to explore the source ofheterogeneity and the impacts of variates (such as soil properties) when heterogeneity was observed. all statistical analyses were performed using review manager and stata software. in addition, potential publication bias was ex- plored by using funnel plots, trim and fill method, and egger's test.
background: Aminor change ofsoil organic carbon (SOC) greatly influences atmospheric carbon dioxide concentration and climate change. Exogenous carbon (C) input into soils can induce SOC decomposition or sequestration. The response of SOC to C input can be better understood when SOC is separated into mineral-associated (MAOC) and particulate (POC) organic carbon.
objective: the study aims to determine 1) howpoc and maoc respond to exogenous c input, 2) explore the key controlling factors of their responses to exoge- nous c input.
result1: c input from straw had a significantly positive effect on maoc content.
result2: straw input had the largest effect on poc content than other substrates input.
general_conclusion: exogenous carbon input from straw increases maoc and poc content.

search_strategy: literature was searched using the “web of science” search engine that published before 2021. specifically, we used the “web of science core collection” to search using the keywords “soil carbon” and “soil nitrogen” and “agricultur* or farmland or upland or padd*”.
selection_criteria: i) three ca practices (minimal soil disturbance, crop rotation/diversification, residue return) must be compared with con- trol using conventional tillage; ii) experimentation must have taken place in the field; iii) the experiments on fertiliser inputs need to have the types of nitrogen inputs used well defined (manure, inorganic or mixed); iv) experiments on tillage must have compared tillage operations (no-till, tillage, tillage with residue) and their association with cropping systems must be clear; v) all studies must report both soc and tn content; vi) the control and treatment must be well defined and the number of replications reported.
data_analysis: a random-effect model was used to determine each crop and soil management practice's effect on the initial soc and tn conditions. the effect of treatment on control is considered significant (p < 0.05) only when the 95 % ci value did not overlap with 0. statistical processing of the data through the random effects model was done with metawin. bootstrapping (4999 iterations) was used to obtain 95 % confidence intervals (ci) and between-group variance (qb) of categorical variance.
background: Conservation agriculture (CA) can be an important strategy for improving soil organic carbon (SOC) and total nitrogen (TN). Numerous studies have examined SOC and TN dynamics in different cropping systems. However, there is some uncertainty regarding the relative impacts of some CA practices, and it is not always clear how other agricultural man- agement, particularly nitrogen addition, interacts with these practices to influence SOC and TN sequestration.
objective: the authors hypothesized that (1) ca system and each of its components would increase soc and tn content; (2) the utilization of manure and mineral fertiliser would increase the accumulation the soc and tn compared to no-fertiliser; and (3) crop rotations with legumes and cover crops would decrease in the c/n ratio. the main objectives were to (i) identify the impact of conservation agriculture and its components on soc and tn storage in different environments; (ii) deter- mine the impact of fertilisation and fertiliser type on soc and tn content; (iii) assess the impact of crops systems on the c/n ratio.
result1: residue retention significantly increased soc content at 0–15 and 0–30 cm compared to no residue retention. the highest increase in soc (37.60 %) was at the depth of 0–30 cm.
result2: residue retention combined with no-tillage resulted in a significant increase (p<0.05) in soc (32.39%) compared to no residue retention.
result3: in contrast, conventional tillage combined with residue retention caused a smaller increase in soc of 10.05 %.
general_conclusion: residue retention increased soil organic carbon compared to residue removal.
knowledge_gaps: the adoption and application of conservation agriculture (ca) are difficult in several regions of the world. the primary constraints are the lack of knowledge regarding how best to manage a ca system and the lack of resources and adequate techniques to simultaneously implement all three ca system principles.

background: Conservation tillage, defined as no-till with/without straw stubble covering, reduced tillage, or minimum tillage in this study, is widely used to mitigate the negative effects of intensive tillage.
objective: the authors hypothesized that: 1) conservation tillage can increase the om, oc, tc, nutrients (n, p, and k), and their available contents; 2) conservation tillage can increase metal cation contents (ca2+, mg2+, na+) and cec, thereby increasing the amount of bases and balancing the ph. to test this hypothesis, this global-scale meta-analysis was designed to determine the direction and magnitude of changes in soil chemical properties in response to conservation tillage practices.

search_strategy: systematic literature review using “isi web of science (core database)”. the search term was “(soil organic matter or c sequestration) and manure”.
selection_criteria: studies were included if they were performed under field conditions and if the effect and control size was expressed as content of total organic carbon (toc) or quantified as soc or toc stocks. if som rather than soc information were given in a study, we calculated soc as som multiplied by 0.58. all treatments with a duration of≤3 years were removed to exclude short-term effects and the influence of the cultivated crops.
data_analysis: we calculated the response ratio (r), which is the mean of the manure treatment divided by the mean of the control group (all the same but without manure application) and we calculated the soc stock mean dif- ference (∆soc). considering the fact that only a few of the analyzed studies provided sufficient infor- mation on statistical measures and replicates, we decided to use un-weighted meta-analysis, to include as many treatments as possible.
background: Manure application to agricultural soils is widely considered as a source of nutrients and a method of maintaining levels of soil organic carbon (SOC) to mitigate climate change. At present, it is still unclear which factors are responsible for the SOC stock dynamics.
objective: analyze the relationship between soc stock changes and site characteristics, soil properties, experiment characteristics and manure characteristics (including straw).
result1: the application of straw had a significantly positive response on soc stocks
result2: NA
general_conclusion: the application of straw type had a significantly positive response on soil orcanic carbon stocks

search_strategy: a search for literature was conducted in google, google scholar, science direct, springerlink, scopus, scifinder, and web of science platforms using key words and terms such as “soil”, “soil erosion”, “soil organic carbon loss”, “surface runoff”,and “factors controlling soil erosion”
selection_criteria: the published papers considered for the current analysis reported on (i) field experiments under natural rainfall conditions at plot scale, (ii) soil and/or soil carbon losses (mass per unit area per unit time), (iii) specific land use or land uses where experimentswere carried out, and (iv) experiments that lasted at least one full rainfall season. in addition, preferred papers were those that published results of experiments carried out in the last 25 years; this choice wasmade to limit the potential impact of climate change on the results. moreover, it was assumed that these reports most likely used closely similar methods for analyses.
data_analysis: descriptive statistics were computed for climaticfactors, soil factors, and soil erosion variables. box plots were used to descriptively illustrate the impacts of land use and soil surface cover on the soil erosion variables. all data were analysed using genstat (14th edition) software. the significance of difference between means was tested using tukey’s multiple comparisons. significant differences are at p < 0.05, unless specified.

Many site-specific stover removal experiments report accrual rates and SOC stock effects, but a quantitative, global synthesis is needed to provide a scientific base for long-term energy policy decisions.
objective: the objectives were to: (a) assess the overall effects (direction and magnitude) of stover removal on global final experimental soc stocks and accrual rates over time and (b) identify factors driving the observed soc changes.
result1: soil organic carbon loss (socl) was significantly higher in bare soils than in crop residue covered soils, with the greatest 25th to 75th range.
result2: NA
general_conclusion: soil organic carbon loss was significantly higher in bare soils than in crop residue covered soils

search_strategy: we used several databases such as web of science, google scholar, china national knowledge infrastructure database, china wanfang data, current contents connect (isi), academic search complete (ebsco), scopus, and cab abstracts to search peer‐reviewed publi- cations (before august 2018) related to the effects of straw return on various nr losses, crop productivity, and soil c sequestration. the keywords used in the search included “crop straw or crop residue or crop stubble,”“nr losses (nh3 emissions, n2o emissions, n leaching, and runoff), soc content, crop productivities (crop yield, crop n uptake, and n use efficiency (nue)) and/or other soil properties.”
selection_criteria: 1) the control (mineral n fertilisation) and straw treatment (mineral n fertilisation plus straw return) received equal mineral n fertilisation rates, which indicated that the straw treatment provided additional straw n supply to soils; 2) publications needed to report on at least one of the target variables and sample sizes for the con- trol and treatment plots. multiple observations that were conducted at the same experimental site over several sampling years were aver- aged; 3) the observation duration of the experiment must have covered the main discharge period of various nr losses.
data_analysis: mean effect sizes and the 95% confidence intervals (cis) were generated by a bootstrapping procedure with 4,999 iterations, using metawin 2.1. effects of straw return were considered significant if the 95% cis did not overlap with zero. the means of the categorical variables were consid- ered significantly different from each other if their 95% cis did not overlap.
background: It is widely recommended that crop straw be returned to croplands to maintain or increase soil carbon (C) storage in arable soils. However, because C and nitrogen (N) biogeochemical cycles are closely coupled, straw return may also affect soil reactive N (Nr) losses, but these effects remain uncertain, especially in terms of the interac- tions between soil C sequestration and Nr losses under straw addition.
objective: this paper is aimed to: 1) evaluate the overall effects of straw return on various nr loss pathways (nh3 emissions, n2o emissions, n leaching, and runoff), crop productivity and soil c sequestration in agroecosystems under different environ- mental and management conditions (straw quality and quantity, soil properties, agricultural management, and climate conditions); 2) explore the interactions between various nr losses and soc sequestration following straw return; 3) estimate how straw return has affected nr losses from global croplands and the overall cropland nr balance for the period 2005−2015.
result1: across all studies, straw return significantly increased soc content by 14.9% (0−15 cm soil layer; n = 246; figure 1), with an increase in 11.4% (n = 86) for rice paddies and 17.0% (n = 160) for upland fields.
result2: the soc content increased significantly with an increasing straw addition rate (p < 0.001) and straw c input rate. for straw quality, the increase in soc content is greater with a straw c/n ratio larger than 30 (e.g., cereal straws; 15.1%, n = 219), compared to a smaller ratio (c/n ratio <30, e.g., legume straws; 10.3%, n = 25).
result3: for straw quality, the increase in soc content is greater with a straw c/n ratio larger than 30 (e.g., cereal straws; 15.1%, n = 219), compared to a smaller ratio (c/n ratio <30, e.g., legume straws; 10.3%, n = 25.
result4: with regard to agricultural management, the effect of straw return on soc content is similar for different mineral n fertilisation rates and application methods (surface application vs. incorporated), but a long‐term (≥4 years) straw addition resulted in significantly higher c sequestration (27.7%, n = 28) than a short‐term addition (13.4%, n = 213).
result5: for soil texture and clay content, straw return resulted in the highest c sequestration in silt loamy soils (21.0%, n = 59) or soils with clay content between 20% and 40% (18.2%, n = 127). climate conditions (temperature, precipitation, and climate zones) had no significant impact on the responses of soc content to straw return.
general_conclusion: across all studies, straw return significantly increased soil organic carbon content by 14.9% in the 0−15 cm soil layer.

search_strategy: the review was limited to 3,380 peer-reviewed publications included in the web of science as of june 2018. keywords for the review were developed by combining typical phrases associated with web of science literature searches. keywords: ("corn" or "maize" or "zea mays") and ("soil carbon" or "soil c" or "organic carbon" or "organic c" or "soil organic matter" or "carbon sequestration" or "soil health" or "soil quality") and ("residue" or "stover" or "straw" or "tillage" or "manure" or "irrigation" or "irrigated" or "cover crop")
selection_criteria: (a) corn was the predominant rotational crop (e.g., continuous corn, corn–soybean, corn–wheat, and corn–millet); both corn grain (48) and corn silage studies were included in the database. partial corn silage removal studies and sweet corn cultivars were excluded from this analysis. (b) measurements or experiments were conducted 3 years or longer. (c) the study had to be field experiments. (d) modeling, simulation studies, and laboratory incubations were excluded. (e) soil organic carbon was measured. (f) defined corn stover (residue) removal treatments were included in the experiment. (g) the experimental design included both control (non-removal) and treatment (removal) groups.
data_analysis: meta-analysis was used to quantitatively determine mean soc responses to different crop residue management practices and to compute confidence limits around those means. in each experiment, mean, standard deviation (sd), and sample size (replicates) of soc measurement were extracted to weight each study by variation (sd) and sample size (n). heterogeneity tests and meta-regression were also employed to identify the magnitude and sources of variations in the soc responses. to identify predominant drivers associated with the variations among observations, subgroup analysis was conducted by grouping paired observations into different groups based on biophysical (e.g., soc sampling depth) and management practices (e.g., tillage system). to investigate potential drivers associated with the observed soc differences, a random-effects meta-regression model was used.
scale: usa, mexico, spain, france, equatorial africa, india, china
background: Corn (Zea mays L.) stover is a global resource used for livestock, fuel, and bioenergy feedstock, but excessive stover removal can decrease soil organic C (SOC) stocks and deteriorate soil health. Many site-specific stover removal experiments report accrual rates and SOC stock effects, but a quantitative, global synthesis is needed to provide a scientific base for long-term energy policy decisions.
objective: the objectives were to: (a) assess the overall effects (direction and magnitude) of stover removal on global final experimental soc stocks and accrual rates over time and (b) identify factors driving the observed soc changes.
result1: stover removal generally reduced final soc stocks by 8% in the upper 0–15 or 0–30 cm, compared to stover retained, irrespective of soil properties and tillage practices. a more sensitive meta-regression analysis showed that retention increased soc stocks within the 30–150 cm depth by another 5%.
result2: meta-regression analysis suggested that end soc stock, soc reporting method (esm or fixed-depth), sampling depth, duration of studies, and crop rotation were the five most significant variables explaining the variation in response ratios. tillage, n fertiliser rate, irrigation status (rainfed or irrigated), and climate (mean annual precipitation and mean temperature) were not significant variables.
result3: for plots with stover returned rather than removed, soc accrual rate calculated from experimental baseline (initial soc level) tended to be positive (mean = 0.41 mg c ha−1 year−1, ci = 0.25, 0.58)
general_conclusion: stover removal generally reduced soil organic carbon stocks by about 8% in the 0–15 or 0–30 cm profile, compared to when stover was returned, irrespective of soil properties and tillage system.
knowledge_gaps: 1) for a more accurate and confident soil organic carbon (soc) change assessment, more observations measuring deep (>30 cm) soil profiles are clearly needed. 2) for future studies, reporting soc changes based on a standard calculation protocol would assist in distinguishing soc changes from soil volume changes, which would be particularly important for long-term studies; 3) further analysis on the effects of stover removal along with key conservation practices like cover crop or manure addition would deepen our understanding of soc changes in current farming practices. 4) to guide sustainable utilization of crop residue resources at a relevant scale, a spatially explicit database regarding soc and farm management practices, including stover removal, is necessary.

data_analysis: we defined 4 datasets in this study: the soc response to a straw application compared with an unfertilised control and a mineral fertilisation treatment (s-z and sm-m; s – straw application; z – unfertilised control; sm – straw application and mineral fertilisation treatment; m – mineral fertilisation treatment); a straw application compared with a mineral fertilisation treatment (s-m); and a mineral fertilisation treatment compared with an unfertilised control (m-z). meta-analyses were conducted by review manager (ver. 5.3, copenhagen: nordic cochrane centre, cochrane collaboration) and the r 3.2.2 software (r development core team, auckland, new zealand). the heterogeneity of the effect size distribution was examined using the higgins method as well as the p-value and i2 statistics (de la cruz et al. 2017). when heterogeneity was found, the random effect model was used, whereas the fixed effects model was selected for non-heterogeneity.
background: Straw return is considered an effective way to improve the soil organic carbon (SOC) content of farmland. background: In recent years there has been a renewed interest in using organic amendments (OA) to agricultural soils as partial or full substitutes for inorganic fertilisers (IF) in order to manage nutrients more cost effectively, decrease our dependence on non-renewable resources (for example, P from phosphate rock), reduce and recycle waste that would otherwise be disposed to landfill, and increase soil organic matter.
objective: the present work aims to investigate the effect of oa and oa + if additions on soil nutrient fertility by carrying out a meta-analysis based on results from 132 long-lasting fertility trials (≥ 10 years) worldwide. in this study, the responses of crop yield—along with those of soil organic carbon (oc), size of mb, and plant-available p (i.e., olsen p)—to oa and oa + if relative to if alone (standard control) and no fertilisation (nil control) are determined. here results of the effect of oa and oa + if additions on crop yield are reported.
result1: the straw amendment caused a mean yield increase >160% compared to no fertilisation.
result2: the straw amendment with mineral fertiliser compared to mineral fertilisation has no effect on crop yield.
result3: the straw amendment with mineral fertiliser compared both to no fertilisation and mineral fertilisation has no effect on crop yield of the final year of experiment.
general_conclusion: straw amendment with mineral fertiliser has a positive effect on crop yield compared to straw removal mineral fertilisation. it has no effect on crop yield at the end of the experiment compared to straw removal with mineral fertilisation.

search_strategy: the authors conducted a review of peer-reviewed scientific journal articles on water productivity in maize production published from january 2000 to march 2018 using the china national knowledge infrastructure and web of science databases. the different combinations of search terms included “irrigation” and “maize” or “corn” and “yield” and “water use efficiency” or “water productivity” and “china” were used for article selection.
selection_criteria: same data, the older study was excluded.
data_analysis: the authors used a linear mixed-effects model with yield (ln-transformed), water supply (ln-transformed), and water productivity (wp) (ln-transformed) as response variables and experimental year (continuous, transformed), study agro-ecological zones (categorical, three levels), maize cultivars (categorical), seasonal average temperature (st) (continuous, ln-transformed), seasonal average precipitation (sp) (continuous, ln-transformed), seasonal irrigation depth (continuous, ln-transformed),  vapor pressure deficit (vpd) (continuous, ln-transformed), seasonal n application amount (continuous, ln-transformed), soil organic matter (som) (continuous, ln-transformed), latitude (continuous, ln-transformed) and plant density (continuous, ln-transformed) at the study locations as independent variables. the authors included interaction terms for some factors (sp * irrigation depth) in the model. finally, they included a random intercept term for the experimental sites of studies data from previous studies (i.e., chinese provinces). to identify effective crop management practices for improving maize wp and yield, authors pooled studies that included side-by-side comparisons of different crop management practices (i.e., the treatment was the same as the control in all aspects except for the each crop management practice) and calculated effect sizes for pairwise comparisons: optimal irrigation vs. farmer’ irrigation; plastic mulch vs. no mulch; straw re-incorporation vs. no straw re-incorporation; deep tillage/deep ripping vs. rotary tillage; no tillage vs. rotary tillage; ridge planting vs. flat planting; and polymer application vs. no polymer application.
background: Understanding water productivity (WP) on a regional scale is useful for identifying and managing inefficiencies in irrigated crop production systems. However, relevant WP analyses are not available for maize production systems in China.
objective: the authors conducted a meta-analysis of maize yield and water use data presented in peer-reviewed studies in northern china (2354 observations from 282 studies) to: 1) investigate the current state of irrigated maize wp and influencing factors, 2) evaluate management practices to improve wp, and 3) estimate the boundary function for wp within different maize-production regions.
result1: straw re-incorporation significantly improved yield compared to straw removal.
result2: NA
