result2: overall, ui application significantly increased nue by 20.1% (ci: 13.1 to 28.1%). positive effect of ui on nue was found when nbpt (17.2%, ci: 0.3 to 24.7%) or limus (20.9%, ci: 6.2 to 40.5%) were applied, but not when hq was applied. ui application significantly increased nue when mean annual temperature was higher than 20°c (55.3%, ci: 18.5 to 103.4%). the positive effect of ui on nue was found in acidic soils (28.4%, ci: 18.5 to 39.1%), but not in neutral or alkaline soils (no significant effect).
result3: overall, di increased nue by 22.1% (ci: 15.3 to 29.6%). di effect was lower for the mixture of dcd and nbpt (mean effect: 19.0%, ci: 12.3 to 26.0%) compared to other di forms (61.9%, ci: 32.3 to 97.4%). but this last estimate is based on a lower of observations (n = 3), compared to the one for dcd + nbpt (n = 52). di effect was significant when rainfall was comprised between 800 and 1200 mm (29.7%, ci: 22.1 to 39.1%), while di effect was not significant when rainfall was lower than 800 mm. di effect was significant for coarse textured soils (27.1%, ci: 19.7 to 33.6%) and for medium textured soils (17.4%, ci: 4.1 to 35.0%), but was not significant for fine textured soils. di application increased nue in acidic soils (37.7%, ci: 31.0 to 46.2%) but not in neutral soils. the effect of di was stronger when applied with manure (34.2%, ci: 27.5 to 41.9%) than with synthetic fertilizer (13.0%, ci: 3.5 to 23.8%).
result4: overall, ni increased nue by 32% (ci: 15 to 54%). dcd application significantly increased nue by 34.4% (17.4 to 59.0%), while the effect of dmpp on nue was not significant. ni impact on nue differed according to crops. there was no significant effect of ni on vegetables and wheat and maize, while ni effect on crop yield varied for 11% (4 to 20%) for paddy to 48% (23 to 86%) for grassland. climatic factors: lower annual average temperature appeared to enhance the impact of ni on increasing nue, 30% (17 to 45%) higher in areas of <10°c, compared to 12% otherwise. the positive effects of ni on nue depended on temperature and rainfall. it was not significant in areas of high rainfall (>1200 mm). ni increased yield by 19% (8 to 30%) and 9% (4 to 16%) in areas of moderate (800-1200 mm) and low rainfall, respectively (<800 mm). soil ph influenced ni effect on nue. ni effect was not significant in alkaline soils. applied in neutral or acidic soils, ni increased nue by 15 (5 to 28%) or 57% (21 to 116%), respectively. furthermore, ni was apparently more effective in enhancing nue in irrigated compared to rainfed systems (no quantitative results reported).
general_conclusion: polimer coated fertilisers, fertilisers amended with urease inhibitors, and fertilisers amended with double inhibitors application significantly increased nue. nitrification inhibitors are a viable option to increase nue across all conditions tested.

search_strategy: published peer-review studies were identified from several databases (included google scholar, web of science, and china knowledge resource integrated) by using the key search terms “urease inhibitor”, “nitrification inhibitor”, “double inhibitor”, “nitrogen stabilizer”, “nitrogen recovery”, “15n recovery”.
selection_criteria: 1)field, pot or lysimeter studies; 2) 15n tracer method had to be used to determine fertilizer nitrogen uptake by the crop or retained in the soil ; 3) n derived from fertilizer (ndff) or fertilizer n recovery in the crop and the soil have to be reported; 4) control (fertilizer without inhibitors) and treatments (fertilizer with inhibitors) have to be subjected to the same management (such as fertilizer type and application rate, irrigation, or micro-plot size).
data_analysis: the mean effect size of each group was calculated by a categorical random-effect model and its 95 % confidence intervals (cis) were generated using a bootstrapping procedure with 4999 iterations. the heterogeneity in different categorical groups (qbetween/qtotal) for each explanatory variable is also reported in table s1. the potential impact of study methods (field or pot) and sampling procedures (premature or mature harvest) were tested. for further analysis of the importance of the explanatory variables to the effects of n-stabilizers on n recovery, boosted regression tree (brt) analysis was used to rank their contribution for different recovery n pools (crop recovery, soil retention and total recovery).
background: Nitrogen (N) fertilizer stabilizers (including urease inhibitors, i.e. UI, nitrification inhibitors, and double inhibitors, i.e. DI) are promising tools to mitigate N pollution from agricultural production. A better understanding is required on how N stabilizers impact the fate of fertilizer-N and which factors (such as soil properties and management conditions) have a major contribution to the efficacy of the N stabilizers.
objective: the aim of this study was to assess the efficacy of n stabilizers (ui and di) in improving agronomic and environmental management of nitrogenous fertilizers and enable the provision of advice on the application of n stabilizers for sustainable agricultural production. here the results of ui effect and di effect on soil retention are reported.
result1: use of urease inhibitors increased fertiliser-n retention in the soil by 5.8%. amendment with nbpt and ppd increased fertilizer-n retention in the soil by 6.9 and 8.9 %, respectively, and the efficacy of ppd was significantly greater than that of hq.
result2: the greatest soil n retention was associated, for ui, with a higher n application rate (above 100 kg n ha−1), multiple application timings, and neutral coarse textured soils. with ui, amendment to paddy fields increased soil retention of fertilizer-n but there was no significant effect on dry land. increasing soil ph improved soil retention of fertilizer-n under ui amendment.
result3: the use of di did not significantly impacted soil n retention.
result4: fertilizers amended with ni significantly enhanced fertilizer-n retention in the soil by 10.2%. nitrapyrin and dcd enhanced fertilizer-n retention in the soil by 22.3 and 19.1 %, respectively. the impact of dmpp application on fertilizer-n retention in soil was not significant.
result5: higher soil retention was measured after multiple n application. the greatest soil n retention was associated with a higher n application rate (above 100 kg n ha−1), multiple application timings, and neutral coarse textured soils.
general_conclusion: the use of fertilisers amended with urease inhibitors significantly increased soil fertilizer-derived n content, while the use of fertilisers amended with double inhibitors did not significantly impacted it. fertilisers amended with nitrification inhibitors application significantly enhanced fertiliser-n retention in the soil.

search_strategy: search was conducted in the isi web of science for publications in english and the cinii (scholarly and academic information navigator) for publications in japanese. different combinations of 3 keywords were used: either abandon∗ or fallow; either biodiversity, animal, plant, bird, mammal, amphibian, reptile, fish, vertebrate, insect, or spider; and japan. we translated the above search string into japanese for cinii. we found additional studies through cited references. to minimize publication bias, we included grey literature (e.g., reports, conference proceedings, and books) as well as peer-reviewed articles.
selection_criteria: 1) reports data on species richness or abundance in any 2 of 3 rice-field management states: cultivated, fallow (or recently abandoned field: tilled or mowed once every 1–3 years), and abandoned; 2) only abundance data for nonpest species was acepted.
data_analysis: authors calculated the mean effect size and 95% cis. the effect size was weighted by the inverse of a simplified estimate of the variance:  w = (nt × nc)/(nt + nc), where nt and nc are the treatment (fallow fields in this case) and control (cultivated fields in this case) sample sizes, respectively. a mixed-effects null model was used as a general statistical approach for the meta-analysis with the effect size (log response ratio) as the dependent variable and the study being examined as the random factor. a q-test was used for the heterogeneity analysis. publication bias was explored by illustrating the funnel-shaped distribution of the data points when plotted against the sample size, as well as by conducting an egger regression test. the sample coverage to check for possible bias in species richness due to unequal sample sizes was also estimated.
background: Rice fields have become substitutes for natural wetland ecosystems. The abandonment of rice fields is thus likely to have strong negative impacts on biodiversity of species dependent on wetland ecosystems. In addittion, management of rice fields often includes the maintenance of seminatural grasslands on levees and edges of surrounding forests. Thus, abandonment of rice fields may also cause loss of grassland organisms.
objective: to examine how rice-field abandonment affects species richness and abundance and how the impact of rice-field abandonment on biodiversity is affected by multiscale factors, such as management state, climate, and topography. finally, to consider how the influence of these factors varies by taxon or ecological niche of organisms. here, only results on the effect of recently abandoned lands (fallows) are reported.
result1: there was no significant effect on organisims of rice-field fallowing compared to cultivation.
result2: NA
general_conclusion: fallow fields supported an equal level of biodiversity than cultivated rice fields. these results suggest rewilding will not necessarily be achieved by rice-field abandonment. moreover, wetland species are particularly prone to being negatively affected by abandonment.

search_strategy: search was conducted in three electronic databases (agricola 1970 through 2002, agris 1981 to june 2002, and biosis 1990 to june 2003) for publications containing terms associated with agricultural set-aside land (agri-environment, conservation reserve program, field* and margin*, flower* and strip∗, permanent cover program, set∗ and aside∗). a few papers were discovered by consulting reference lists in other published studies.
selection_criteria: 1) studies contained identifiable replicates of at least two treatments or land-use types, one conventional agriculture and the other set-aside land. conventional fields included row crops, grains, and intensively managed meadows; 2) the studies presented means and some measure of variation among replicates for either population density or the number of species of at least one plant or animal taxon, defined narrowly or broadly (e.g., skylarks or birds); 3) studies monitored farmland managed under locally accepted standards for set-aside and conventional agriculture. set-aside parcels in about 11% of the studies were established at unnaturally small spatial scales for experimental purposes but were included because they enabled to evaluate biodiversity responses across a broad range of field sizes.
data_analysis: effect sizes were combined across studies with a mixed- effects model implemented in metawin. heterogeneity in effect size among taxa or types of set-aside land was tested using qb, which is chi-squared distributed.
background: Agricultural set-aside schemes were originally established to reduce overproduction of crops and to combat soil erosion. More recently, there has been widespread hope that they might halt or reverse decades-long declines in farmland biodiversity. A thorough review of the literature on set-aside land is needed to synthesize information on the quantity and quality of plants and animals within set-aside land. If the results are positive, they may help ensure political acceptance and continuation of these programs, whereas negative results could guide recommendations for alternative methods of biodiversity conservation in farmland.
objective: to synthesize information on the quantity and quality of plants and animals within set-aside land. here, results on bird species richness and population density for birds, spiders and plants are reported.
result1: the number of species of birds was significantly higher on set-aside land than on nearby control areas under conventional agriculture.
result2: the population densities of birds were higher on set-aside land.
result3: the population densities of plants were higher on set-aside land.
result4: the population densities of birds, spiders and plants were higher on set-aside land.
result5: funnel plots depicting the relationship between effect size and sample size indicated that the data set was only modestly biased by selective reporting.
general_conclusion: land withdrawn from conventional production unequivocally enhances biodiversity in north america and europe.

search_strategy: compilation of data from publications in english, russian and german language via key words, including: soc, sequestration, carbon stocks, humus, land-use change, abandonment, organic matter recovery, ex-arable land, old field succession, no-till and agro-ecosystems. key word searching also allowed to widen the database to the “grey” literature.
selection_criteria: 1) restricted to terrestrial mineral soils of the temperate zone such as retisols, luvisols, cambisols, phaeozems, chernozems and kastanozems; 2) every study used in the dataset had to provide at least two carbon values for different land-use types measured in one or several soil depths.
data_analysis: because most studies did not provide error estimates, an un-weighted meta-analysis was conducted. mean effect sizes were calculated with bootstrapped 95% confidence intervals based on 1000 bootstrap replications using the package ‘boot’ in r3.0.2 software. publication bias was explored by graphical inspection of funnel plots. moreover, a spearman rank correlation test revealed no significant correlation between response ratio and sample size (rho =−0.05, p = 0.42).
background: Restoring depleted soil organic carbon (SOC) stocks of arable land to remove carbon from the atmosphere and offset fossil fuel emissions is a promising strategy for the mitigation of climate change.
objective: to investigate if soil organic carbon sequestration in the top-soil of ex-arable grasslands and under conservational tillage regime is significantly affected by edaphic and climatic conditions. speciffic questions addressed: (i) how do soc stocks change after longstanding arable land is converted to managed or unmanaged grasslands (ex-arable land) or if ancient grassland is converted into arable land, (ii) how do soc stocks of ancient grassland and ex-arable land differ, (iii) how do soc stocks develop after conversion to conservational tillage, and iv) what are the effects of time since abandonment, climate and initial soc stock on the variability of soil carbon change in ex-arable land and arable land with conservational tillage management. here, only results on the effect of short time since abandonment (0-4 years) are reported, as equivalent to the effect of fallowing.
result1: soil carbon change (t/ha) in ex-arable lands recently abandoned (0-4 years) compared to arable lands was 2.8± 2.3, but such an increase was not significant according to the effect size 95% ci.
result2: NA
general_conclusion: soc sequestration in recently (0-4 years) abandoned arable lands was not significantly higher than in arable lands.

search_strategy: the studies included were located by searching through computer library databases. however, this alone does not provide a comprehensive search. therefore, it was supplemented with checking the references of published studies and manual searching through conference abstracts, published proceedings, book chapters, monographs and direct contacts based on the authors' extensive knowledge on studies conducted in the sub-saharan africa.
selection_criteria: 1) have been published in a refereed journal, book chapter or peer-reviewed proceeding; 2) have originated from sub-saharan africa; 3) have reported maize yield from at least one legume species used for green manure or improved fallow (treatment) and a corresponding maize yield from an unfertilized plot (control); 4) be a well designed, randomized and replicated experiment either on a research station or on farmers’ fields; 5) have reported the mean (and if possible the standard deviation or variance) as numerical or graphical data or this was available by personal communication.
data_analysis: computation of the variance (vi) for each ith study was done following miguez and bollero (2005). effect sizes were weighted by the reciprocal of their variances. a mixed modelling approach was adopted in this analysis. the akaike information criterion was used as measure of parsimony in deciding on the linear mixed model that gives the correct estimate of the 95% ci. publication bias and normality in the data were assessed using descriptive statistics and normal quantile–quantile (q–q) plots.
background:
In parts of West, Central, East and southern Africa, where the fallow periods have been shortened and cultivation has been extended for more than 2 years, maize yields generally decline rapidly. Promising alternatives include the use of nitrogen-
fixing and weed-suppressing legumes planted as improved fallows.
objective: assessing whether or not there is a consistent evidence for yield benefits using green manure from herbaceous and woody legumes in sub-saharan africa. the specific objectives of this analysis were to (1) provide a comprehensive, quantitative synthesis of published reports on the effect of woody and herbaceous green manure legumes on maize yield, (2) conduct parametric estimation of the magnitude of yield response and (3) determine the factors that moderate the response.
result1: natural fallows had yields equal to the control in 27% of the cases. however, overall yield difference (d) between natural fallows and control fully fertilised maize crops was positive (0.3 t ha-1) and significant. the 95% confidence intervals of response ratio (rr) from the natural fallow included 1, indicating a lack of difference between the unfertilized maize and maize grown after natural fallows.
result2: the 95% confidence interval of mean response ratio (rr) in herbaceous fallows (1.49–1.90) did not overlap 1, indicating a significant positive effect on yields after improved fallows compared to control continuously cropped unfertilized maize monocultures. the 95% confidence interval of mean yield difference (d) after herbaceous fallows compared to continuously cropped unfertilized maize monoculture (0.8–1.2 t ha−1) did not overlap 0, indicating a significant positive effect on yields after improved fallows.
result3: the 95% confidence interval of mean response ratio (rr) in fallows with coppicing species did not overlap 1, indicating a significant positive effect on yields after improved fallows compared to control continuously cropped unfertilized maize monocultures. the 95% confidence interval of mean yield difference (d) after fallows with coppicing species compared to continuously cropped unfertilized maize monoculturedid not overlap 0, indicating a significant positive effect on yields after improved fallows.
result4: the 95% confidence interval of mean response ratio (rr) in fallows with non-coppicing species (1.27–1.43) did not overlap 1, indicating a significant positive effect on yields after improved fallows compared to control continuously cropped unfertilized maize monocultures. the 95% confidence interval of mean yield difference (d) after fallows with non-coppicing species compared to continuously cropped unfertilized maize monoculture (0.88–1.41 t ha−1) did not overlap 0, indicating a significant positive effect on yields after improved fallows.
result5: the normal q–q plots also indicate the presence of asymmetry and publication bias. in the q–q plot of the yield difference, the curve is slightly u-shaped, indicating that the data are skewed to the right.
general_conclusion: the global maize yield response to improved fallows with legume species is significantly positive and higher than unfertilized maize and natural vegetation fallows.

search_strategy: the search was conducted in multiple electronic databases and the internet using different combinations of boolean search terms. the databases used were dogpile, google, google scholar, web of science, and scirus. authors used the following search terms in various combinations: (plantation* or ‘‘planted forest*” or afforestation or ‘‘production forest*”) and (agricult* or meadow* or crop* or farm* or grass* or pastur* or paddock* or graz* or field* or range*) and (biodiversity or diversity or richness or abundance or species or bird* or mammal* or reptile* or amphibian* or frog* or invertebrate* or insect* or arthropod* or plant* or flora or fauna). search terms were run in separate or limited combinations depending on the requirements or limitations of the database used. authors also obtained papers from colleagues and through reference lists from published studies including major review articles and books on plantations. furthermore, information from some government studies and reports was also included.
selection_criteria: 1)  studies comparing the species richness and abundance of plantations and pasture lands for five taxonomic groups: plants, invertebrates, reptiles/amphibians, mammals, and birds; 2) studies that provided estimates of mean species richness and/or abundance, and the corresponding estimates of standard deviations and sample sizes.
data_analysis: the effect sizes were analyzed using linear mixed models. fixed and random effects were estimated using residual maximum likelihood (reml) estimation. for each response variable, simplified model was selected using backwards stepwise selection. the significance of fixed effects was assessed by computing scaled wald statistics which were treated as having an approximate f distribution. the significance of variance components (random effects) was assessed using likelihood ratio test statistics. these were treated as being distributed approximately as chi-squared random variables. the fit of the final model for species richness and abundance for each taxonomic group was assessed by checking diagnostic plots of residuals for normality, constant variance and outliers. each study was given equal weight. authors accounted for heterogeneity by fitting available study-level covariates as fixed effects and study and division within study random effects to account for the effect of unreported factors. analyses were conducted using standard statistical software. the functions available in genstat were used to fit the models.
background: Most of the world’s new plantations are generally established on former agricultural lands, that are often of declining economic value for grazing or cropping.
objective: to review existing evidence of how plantations and pasture lands influence species richness and abundance by summarizing the data from the literature using meta-analysis techniques. specifically, to assess for different taxonomic groups of flora and fauna whether: 1) plantations support higher species richness than pasture lands; 2) plantations support a higher abundance of organisms than pasture lands
result1: for birds, the estimated average effect sizes were not significantly different from zero (average effect size = -0.45, 95% ci: -1.20, 0.31, p = 0.27) and (average effect size = 0.95, 95% ci: -0.80, 2.70, p = 0.32) indicating that there was not a significant difference between plantations and pastures in bird species richness and abundance, respectively. for the subset of studies where it was reported whether or not pastures included remnant vegetation, there was a significant effect of presence or absence of remnant vegetation on bird species richness (p = 0.001).
result2: for reptiles/amphibians, the estimated average effect size was significantly different from zero (-1.24, 95% ci: -1.73, -0.72, p < 0.001) indicating that the species richness was 1.24 standard deviations lower in pastures than in plantations. for the subset of studies where it was reported whether or not pastures included remnant vegetation, there was a significant effect of presence or absence of remnant vegetation (p = 0.002). the estimated average effect size  for abundnace (-1.96, 95% ci: -3.95, 0.03) was not significantly different from zero (p = 0.14) indicating that there was no significant difference in reptile/amphibian abundance between pastures and plantations.
result3: for mammals, the estimated average effect sizes for species richness (-0.75, 95% ci; -1.98, 0.49, p = 0.29) and abundance (-0.16, 95% ci: -2.18, -0.13, p = 0.06) were not significantly different from zero, indicating that there was not a significant difference in mammal species richness nor abundance between pastures and plantations. for the subset of studies where it was reported whether or not pastures included remnant vegetation, there was a significant effect of presence or absence of remnant vegetation (p < 0.05) on mammals abundance.
result4: for invertebrates, the estimated average effect sizes for species richness (-0.02, 95% ci: -1.10, 1.06, p = 0.97) and abundance (1.54, 95% ci: -0.62, 3.70, p = 0.2) were not significantly different from zero indicating that there were not significant differences in invertebrate species richness nor abundnace between pastures and plantations.
result5: for plants, the estimated average effect sizes for species richness (-0.43, 95% ci: -1.45, 0.59, p = 0.42) and abundance (-1.00, 95% ci: -3.47, 1.47, p = 0.46) were not significantly different from zero indicating that there were not significant differences in plant species richness nor abundance between pastures and plantations.
general_conclusion: birds and reptile/amphibians exhibited significantly higher species richness, and mammals exhibited significantly lower abundance in pasture lands which lacked remnant vegetation than in plantations. reptile/amphibian species richness was significantly higher in plantations in general. no significant differences in species richness were found for mammals, plants, or invertebrates, and no significant differences in abundance were found for birds, reptiles/amphibians, invertebrates, or plants. it is only within the presence of taxonomic caveats (i.e. reptiles/amphibians), or specific landscape features (i.e. absence of remnant vegetation within pasture), that it can be concluded that plantations support higher species richness or abundance than pasture land.

search_strategy: literature search of peer-reviewed journal articles in the web of science database using the advanced search function to identify articles published from 1 january 1900 to 14 november 2018 that fit the following topic search (ts) criteria (i.e., terms found in titles, abstracts, and keywords): ts = (savanna* or grassland* or woodland* or pine or pinus or eucalypt* or cerrado or prairie or veld* or steppe) and ts = (herb* or grass* or forb* or understor*) and ts = (richness or diversity) and ts = (“old growth” or secondary or succession* or remnant* or “old field” or restor* or reference or abandon* or “post agric*” or “woody encroach*” or mine or mining or degrad* or pasture or plantation or afforest*).
selection_criteria: 1) study sites were grasslands, broadly defined to include savannas and open-canopy grassy woodlands. as such, the studies in this analysis encompass herbaceous-dominated ecosystems with scattered trees that are often called “forests” or “woodlands”. 2) studies included old-growth grasslands that were either clearly described in the article or that we were able to verify through correspondence with the authors. 3) studies included secondary grasslands on sites previously occupied by old-growth grasslands that had been destroyed by tillage agriculture, tree plantations, or other intensive land uses. 4) studies reported data for herbaceous plant species richness for both old-growth and secondary grasslands. 5) study plots were not treated with nutrient additions (e.g., nitrogen or phosphorous fertilizers). 6) studies were conducted in a unique location. 7) studies on “actively restored” grasslands (i.e., restoration treatments such as sowing seed mixtures, soil, or hay transfer) were only included if they had a control treatment of “passive restoration” (i.e., secondary grassland communities assembling without propagule additions). for such studies, only data from the passively restored secondary grasslands and the paired old-growth grasslands were extracted.
data_analysis: the variance of the logarithm of the response ratio (lnrr) was calculated based upon reported sample sizes and the weight by the inverse variance. openmee was used to perform the meta-analysis, including tests for heterogeneity, publication bias, and sensitivity. the weighted overall mean effect size was calculated using a random-effects model, with between-study variance estimated using the restriction maximum likelihood (reml) approach. reml was also used to calculate effects by subgroups using moderator variables. to test if there was significant heterogeneity associated with the effect sizes, the q statistic was computed and tested this against a x2 distribution. authors also report heterogeneity with the i2 statistic. three sentitive analyses were performed to verify that the meta-analysis results were robust. the effect of secondary grassland age on lnrr was tested using a metaregression mixed-effects model with study as a random effect. to understand the proportion of variance explained by the regression model, r2 was calculated as qm/(qm + qe). metaregression was performed using the metafor package in r (v 3.6.3). to assess publication bias, first nonparametric correlation tests were performed. second, a cumulative meta- analysis (cma) to assess publication bias with publications sorted by year and using a random-effects model was performed. last, the rosenberg’s fail-safe number was calculated.
background: Emerging research suggests that old-growth grasslands support substantial biodiversity and are slow to recover if destroyed by human land uses (e.g., tillage agriculture, plantation forestry). But despite growing interest in grassland conservation, there has been no global test of whether old-growth grasslands support greater plant species diversity than secondary grasslands (i.e., herbaceous communities that assemble after destruction of old-growth grasslands).
objective: 1) to test the relevance of the old-growth grassland concept to our understanding of global patterns of herbaceous plant diversity; 2) to determine the rate at which secondary grasslands recover the species richness of old-growth grasslands.
result1: secondary grasslands supported 37% fewer plant species than old-growth grasslands (log response ratio = −0.46).
result2: secondary grasslands support 63% of the species richness of old-growth grasslands (95% confidence interval: 53%, 76%; global weighted mean lnrr: −0.46, 95%  ci: −0.64, −0.28).
general_conclusion: evidence of the slow assembly of old-growth grasslands underscores recent calls to move away from the view of most grasslands as a successional stage, toward recognition that endogenous disturbances can sustain species-diverse grasslands for very long periods of time in climatic zones that can also support forests.

search_strategy: authors sourced published literature relating to arthropods in agricultural landscapes up to september 2007 using the internet-based scientific literature search engine scopus, searching the data base using a series of keywords. keywords were divided into 35 taxonomic terms representing the target taxa and 14 land-use/management-related terms. finally, authors undertook further searches in general internet search engines to locate ‘grey literature’.
selection_criteria: not provided
data_analysis: the pooled standard deviation for each comparison was calculated following the methods in bengtsson et al. (2005). fixed-effects and random-effects models were conducted as appropriate. to assess the average effect size across the studies, the effect sizes for each individual study were combined in a fixed-effects model. the fixed-effect model also calculated a homogeneity test statistic q. where q was significant, the effect sizes comprising e ++ were heterogeneous, differing among the studies. in this event, the average effect size e ++ was recalculated using a random-effects model that assumes random variation among studies in a class. all meta-analytical calculations were conducted using metawin.
background: Although many individual studies show that biodiversity declines with agricultural expansion and intensification, this paper aims at establishing whether this pattern was evident across a range of regions, habitats, agricultural systems and taxa.
objective: to determine whether arthropod richness and abundance for combined taxa, feeding guilds and broad taxonomic groups respond in a globally consistent manner to a range of agricultural land-use and management intensification scenarios. the paper aims to address the following questions relating to both broad scale land use and cropping management: 1) is arthropod richness and abundance greater in native vegetation than in agricultural production land? 2) is there a general trend in arthropod richness and abundance along a land-use intensification/anthropogenic disturbance gradient from native vegetation to intensive cropping? 3) do patterns of richness and abundance among land uses differ among different feeding guilds and taxonomic groups? 4) are the identified patterns in richness and abundance consistent between meta-analytical techniques of differing robustness and sophistication? here, results for the comparison between improved pastures and natural grasslands or croplands are reported.
result1: authors found a greater richness in the systems with less intensive land use. however, there was no significant difference in predator richness between improved/introduced pasture and cropping.
result2: results for arthropod abundance were not significant.
general_conclusion: arthropod richness was significantly higher in areas of less intensive land use; that is, in natural grassland compared to improved pasture and in improved pasture compared to cropland.

search_strategy: standard systematic review methodologies were followed to collate empirical studies from temperate regions that measured soc or ghgs in ‘treatment’ bioenergy plantations, relative to ‘control’ existing common land uses - arable, grassland and forests.
selection_criteria: 1) appropriate response metrics must be measured in the publications: soc measures as c (carbon) in units of t ha-1 y-1 (or a convertible figure) and ghg emissions for crop life cycle, partitioned into co2, n2o, ch4 or ‘all’ measured as carbon dioxide equivalents (co2e) in units of t ha-1 y-1 (or convertible figures); 2) studies featured transitions of interest; 3) studies had to report both pre-existing (control) and post-conversion land-use (treatment) values for the response metric(s) of interest. studies were also eligible if they documented a land conversion not strictly for use as bioenergy, but used similar land management practices as would be used for bioenergy cultivation; 4) study locations were relevant to a temperate climate i.e. within the 23.5º and 66.5º latitudinal band; and 5) the species were inclusive of first and second generation bioenergy crops, but only those able to be cultivated in a temperate region.
data_analysis: random-effects models were applied to calculate overall effect sizes. the meta-analysis was weighted in that each study-wise effect size was weighted by the inverse of its variance. all models used the restricted maximum-likelihood estimation (reml) estimate. heterogeneity was examined using a heterogeneity measure (q), calculated by weighting the sum of squared differences between individual effects and the pooled effect, tested against a chi-square distribution. restricted maximum-likelihood estimation was used to estimate t2. all statistical analyses and calculations were performed in r version 3.0.2 using the metafor package 1.9-3. publication bias was tested by assessing funnel plots of effect size vs. standard error of the effect size using the metafor package. weighted regression with multiplicative dispersion using standard error as the predictor did not detect funnel plot asymmetry, indicating no evidence of publication bias.
background: The carbon and GHG balance associated with dedicated bioenergy crops has been the subject of considerable debate in recent years. Empirical measurements on the direct impacts of land use change to bioenergy are only just starting to emerge, with the indirect impacts of land-use change remaining difficult to quantify. There are also conflicting messages from a fragmented literature regarding land use changes, as these effects can vary depending on the starting land use, the initial carbon stocks, the management regime and the climatic region where the land exists. Quantitative syntheses are lacking which are able to bring this body of research together in a succinct analysis.
objective: to assess the current state of knowledge and quantify the effects of land use change (luc) to second generation (2g), non-food bioenergy crops on soil organic carbon (soc) and greenhouse gas (ghg) emissions of relevance to temperate zone agriculture. here, results on soc for luc from arable land to perennial grasses or from grasslands to perennial grasses are reported.
result1: transitions from arable to perennial grasses (mostly miscanthus or switchgrass) resulted in increased soc (25.7 ± 6.7%). transitions from grassland to perennial grass showed a decrease in soc (-10.9 ± 4.3%).
result2: NA
general_conclusion: transitions from arable to perennial grasses resulted in increased soil organic carbon (soc), whilst transitions from grassland to perennial grass showed a decrease in soc.
knowledge_gaps: this review has revealed a knowledge gap concerning the existence of robust, empirical studies investigating both the short-term and long-term consequences of luc to bioenergy on soc and ghg emissions in temperate regions.

search_strategy: the authors searched for studies that reported effects of land-use change (plowing of ancient grassland, abandonment of cropland) and different tillage techniques on soil carbon stocks. the search was restricted to terrestrial mineral soils of the temperate zone such as retisols, luvisols, cambisols, phaeozems, chernozems and kastanozems. data was compiled from publications in english, russian and german language via key words, including: soc, sequestration, carbon stocks, humus, land-use change, abandonment, organic matter recovery, ex-arable land, old field succession, no-till and agro-ecosystems. key word searching allowed to widen the database to the “grey” literature as well, to ensure maximum retrieval of edaphic and climatic data necessary for the present soc study.
selection_criteria: 1) every study in the dataset had to provide at least two carbon values for different land-use types measured in one or several soil depths. these two values were used as paired values for the calculation of effect sizes. 2) the paired values were comparable because the chosen case studies selected paired sampling locations with similar soil conditions, slope and aspect. to avoid the comparison of carbon stocks from sites with contrasting environmental conditions, effect sizes were only calculated from the comparison between different studies but not from different publications.
data_analysis: the authors calculated mean effect sizes with bootstrapped 95% confidence intervals based on 1000 bootstrap replications using the package ‘boot’ in r3.0.2 software.
background: Depleted arable soils have the potential to remove some carbon from the atmosphere by restoring carbon stocks in arable and ex-arable land.
objective: the authors address the following questions: 1) how do soc stocks change after longstanding arable land is converted to managed or unmanaged grasslands (ex-arable land) or if ancient grassland is converted into arable land; 2) how do soc stocks of ancient grassland and ex-arable land differ, 3) how do soc stocks develop after conversion to conservational tillage, and 4) what are the effects of time since abandonment, climate and initial soc stock on the variability of soil carbon change in ex-arable land and arable land with conservational tillage management.
result1: all analyzed changes in land use resulted in significantly higher soc stocks in the less intensively used soil. however, in most cases mean effect sizes were small and did not exceed 0.3.
result2: in soils of ex-arable grasslands (average abandonment time: 14 years) soc stocks were on average only 7.4 t ha−1 lower than in ancient grassland soils.
general_conclusion: all analyzed changes in land use resulted in significantly higher soc stocks in the less intensively used soil.

search_strategy: literature searches were performed using electronic databases: cab abstracts, biological abstracts and web of science.
selection_criteria: 1) studies had to report soil carbon concentrations or stocks per unit land area both before and after land use change with means and number of replicates from specific experiment designs (mainly paired-site studies); 2) reporting of standard deviations was preferred but not essential; 3) any study lacking replication was not considered.
data_analysis: an unweighted meta analysis was used. mean effect size for each study was calculated, with bias-corrected 95% confidence intervals (cis) generated by a bootstrapping procedure (5000 iterations) using meta-win software. in a procedure analogous to the partitioning of variance in analysis of variance, the total heterogeneity for a group of comparisons (qt) is partitioned into within-class heterogeneity (qw) and between-class heterogeneity (qb). the q statistic follows a chi-square distribution, with k±1 degrees of freedom. for analyses of land use change effects, between-group heterogeneity (qb) was examined across all data for a given response variable and the overall mean and confidence interval (ci) were presented.
background: The effects of land use change on soil carbon stocks are of concern in the context of international policy agendas on greenhouse gas emissions mitigation.
objective: to review the effects of various land use changes on soil carbon stocks and to summarize the data from the literature using meta analysis. here, results for transitions from crops to pastures are reported.
result1: soil carbon stocks increase after land use changes from crop to pasture (+19%).
result2: NA
general_conclusion: when cropland is placed under pasture, soil carbon stocks increase to below 100 cm depth but the fractional increase decreases with depth.

search_strategy: authors collected data from peer-reviewed studies until 1 may 2020 through the institute for scientific information web of science and china national knowledge infrastructure databases. the search terms included (“land use” or deforestation or degradation or afforestation or restoration or revegetation) and (methane or ch4) and (oxidation or uptake or flux or emission).
selection_criteria: 1) studies should be carried out in the uplands; 2) only field studies were selected; 3) the measurement duration of soil ch4 uptake rate should be at least one growing season or an entire year; 4) the standard deviation about the data had to be reported or could be calculated from the information provided.
data_analysis: the overall effect size was calculated with a categorical random effects model using the metawin 2.1 software. confidence intervals (95%; cis) were generated by the bootstrapping (9,999 iterations). between-group q statistical test was applied to compare the heterogeneity of the weighted effects size of different groups for each categorical variable.
background: Land degradation and restoration profoundly affect soil CH4 uptake capacity in terrestrial ecosystems. However, a comprehensive assessment of the response of soil CH4 uptake to land degradation and restoration at global scale is not available.
objective: to identify the general patterns of the effects of land degradation and restoration on soil ch4 uptake rate. to quantify the differential response of soil ch4 uptake to different environmental variables (e.g., time since land use change, climate zone, mean annual precipitation, ph, and soil texture) under land degradation and restoration, and explore their drivers. here, results for the conversion of cropland to pasture are reported.
result1: the ch4 uptake rate was significantly increased when the cropland converted to pasture, with hedges' d value of 1.38.
result2: NA
general_conclusion: all types of land restoration significantly increased the capacity of soil methane (ch4) uptake. interestingly, the response of soil ch4 uptake rate to land degradation and restoration was asymmetric: the increased soil ch4 uptake rate in response to the land restoration was smaller compared to the decrease in ch4 uptake rate induced by the land degradation.

search_strategy: extensive keyword searches from web of science, scopus, cab abstracts, academic search complete, and google scholar, and the reference list of cited references were conducted. the keywords used in the search were: ammonium/nh4+ immobilization; ammonium/nh4+ nitrification; n/nitrogen immobilization; and nitrification and their combinations.
selection_criteria: 1) gross nitrification and immobilization rates were reported simultaneously; 2) details on experimental design and conditions were given to enable cross-checking for duplicate publication.
data_analysis: replication-based weight was adopted in this study. the meta-analysis was conducted by metawin version 2.1. a fixed-effect model with 4999 iterations bootstrapping was used to generate the mean effect size and the 95% confidence intervals (cis).
background: Nitrogen in soil is an important plant nutrient, but its loss to the environment is ecologically and economically undesirable. Nitrate (NO3−) is readily lost via leaching or transformation into gaseous nitrogen during nitrification and denitrification; which leads to eutrophication and water contamination. Only a handful of studies reported nitrification rates on a global scale; a comprehensive global-scale assessment of the N/I ratio is lacking to reflect the potential risk of nitrogen loss from soils.
objective: to assess the effects of different management practices on the potential risk of nitrogen loss. this study aimed to 1) reveal the global pattern of the soil n/i ratio as an indicator of the potential risk of soil nitrogen loss worldwide; 2) test the relationships between the soil n/i ratio and climatic factors and soil properties; and 3) evaluate the effect of management practices on the potential risk of nitrogen loss. here, results for objective 3 and in particular for the conversion of cropland to grassland are reported.
result1: converting cropland to grassland decreased the soil n/i ratio by 45%.
result2: in general, the soil immobilization rate was higher in natural ecosystems than that in agricultural systems because of the higher carbon/nitrogen ratio of natural soils.
general_conclusion: converting cropland to grassland significantly reduced nitrification and the n/i ratio.
knowledge_gaps: soil gross immobilization and nitrification rates included in this study were mostly measured under controlled conditions in laboratory experiments. this may lead to potential bias of prediction in the extrapolation to field conditions.

search_strategy: to identify relevant studies, authors conducted a search on web of science on april 12, 2019 using the following key terms “prairie restor* and (pollinat* abundance or pollinat* richness or pollinat* diversity or bee abundance or butterfly abundance or moth abundance)”, “savannah restor* and pollinat*”, “prairie restor* and bird pollinat*”, “meadow restor* and pollinat*”, “grassland restor* and pollinat*. haphazard searches were also conducted in google scholar with similar keywords. in addition, authors searched the reference lists of the papers selected to include studies not found by database searches.
selection_criteria: studies were excluded if: 1) focused on land remediation of coal mines or quarries; 2) were small-scale studies that took place within a larger agricultural or urban context, such as wildflower strips or pollinator gardens; 3) focused on floral resources within the plant community and did not measure pollinator responses directly; 4) used small-scale experiments (plots only a few meters in size).
data_analysis: effect sizes along with the variation for each study were calculated to assess restoration treatment significance using the r package metafor. to compare effect size means across the different groups, randomized effect models were carried out in r (version 3.6.0) also with the metafor package.
background: While grassland restoration efforts typically improve plant communities, it is still unclear whether such restorations are as successful in restoring pollinator communities.
objective: to assess the overall impact of grassland restorations on pollinator communities. specifically: 1) do grassland restorations improve pollinator communities compared to degraded sites? 2) do these restorations restore the pollinator communities to remnant conditions?
result1: both pollinator richness and abundance responded positively to grassland restorations when compared to degraded sites (abundance: d = 1.31, p = 0.015; richness: d = 0.894, p = 0.045).
result2: when restored grasslands were compared to remnant grasslands, pollinator communities were not significantly different, indicating that restorations were effective at restoring pollinators to target conditions (abundance: d = − 0.366, p = 0.167, richness: d = − 0.411, p = 0.253).
general_conclusion: grassland restorations significantly improved both pollinator abundance and richness as compared to degraded grasslands. additionally, pollinator abundance and richness did not significantly differ from remnant sites, indicating a near full recovery.

search_strategy: peer-reviewed literature was searched using common keywords related to soil phosphorus, agriculture, and land-use history in isi web of science, scopus, and google scholar up to march 2011.
selection_criteria: 1) studies had to report labile or total p measurements for non-agricultural sites previously used for arable cropping, grazing, or forage grass production (at least 1 year since cessation of use), as well as a comparable reference site that best represented pre-agriculture soil or late-succession ecosystem conditions for a given location (e.g., ‘primary forest’) and had no reported agricultural history or minimal disturbance. also studies that reported soil p measurements for both contemporary and former agricultural sites that had comparable land use and management histories. 2) all studies had to contain the following methodological information: soil sampling depths and p measurement methods that were equivalent between the reference/current agriculture and abandoned agriculture sites; the dominant type of agriculture practiced prior to abandonment; the approximate time since cessation and vegetation type established after abandonment; as well as the number of study sites, replicates, and soil samples collected. 3) studies reporting fertilization, experimental manipulation of soils or extensive forest harvest after cessation of agriculture were omitted.
data_analysis: the overall mean effect size was calculated for each former land use as well as separate means for each vegetation transition category. bootstrap bias-corrected accelerated 95% confidence intervals based on 10000 random simulations were used. because there was no systematic publication bias according to sample size, equal weight was given to all effect size observations in each of the meta-analyses. all statistical analyses were performed in r v.2.13.1, using the ‘boot’ package for bootstrapping.
background: Agriculturally driven changes in soil phosphorus (P) are known to have persistent effects on local ecosystem structure and function. Yet there has been little synthesis to understand broad patterns of soil P after cessation of agriculture or the factors that affect this.
objective: to assess evidence of land-use legacies throughout the world by comparing soil labile and total p content in abandoned agricultural areas to that of reference ecosystems or sites remaining in agriculture. the following specific questions for labile and total p are addressed: 1) do broad categories of past agricultural land use result in any generalizable legacies for current soil p across regions? 2) what factors contribute most to soil p dynamics following cessation of agriculture? 3) do land-use legacies on soil p differ over time since cessation of agriculture, and are these patterns consistent across regions? here, results on the comparison of non-agricultural grasslands established after agricultural use cessation and nearby areas with agricultural use are reported.
result1: croplands becoming non-agricultural grassland had lower mean labile and total p compared to sites still used for agriculture.
result2: NA
general_conclusion: abandoned agricultural sites typically had lower mean labile and total p compared to sites still used for agriculture.

search_strategy: data were acquired by searching existing refereed literature (1971–2010) and through personal communication with individual data owners, if necessary.
selection_criteria: not specified
data_analysis: authors categorize the measures in three groups: decrease, no effect, increase of nh3 loss (the majority of the measures indicate an increase of nh3 loss). they identify factors related to nh3 loss (some soil types are associated with strong loss, and other with lower loss) using a simple meta-regression model.
background: Nitrification inhibitors (NI) can reduce production of the greenhouse gas nitrous oxide by inhibiting nitrification and subsequent denitrification processes. However, this extended retention of N in the NH4+ form in the soils treated with NI can increase ammonia (NH3) emission.
objective: the objectives of this paper is to summarize findings regarding impact of ni on nh3 emissions by categorizing reported results from peer-reviewed papers, to explore what may cause difference between results, and to discuss how to mitigate the negative impact of ni. here we report results regarding the impact of ni on nh3 emissions.
result1: significant increase in loss of nh3 in ni application was seen in 6 out of 12 grassland trials.
result2: no significant change in loss of nh3 in ni application was seen in 5 out of 12 grassland trials.
result3: significant decrease loss of nh3 emissions in ni application was seen in 1 out of 12 grassland trials.
general_conclusion: results suggest that nh3 loss significantly increases with ni application, depending on soil properties such as soil ph and cation exchange capacity. reviewers’ note: we labelled the results as uncertain due to the lack of statistical testing.

search_strategy: in october 2015, studies in any language, comparing different mowing frequencies were searched for using the databases scopus, biological sciences, biological abstracts and agricola. the search terms used were mow*, hay*, scythe*, harvest* or cut*; and frequenc*, intensit*, regime*, month*, “every other”, “every second”, “every third”, “mow* time”, “mow* date”, “harvest* date”, “harvest time”, “hay* date”, “hay* time”, “cut* date”, “cut* time”, season*, or interval*; and grassland*, meadow*, fen*, heath*, wetland*, marsh*, bog* or reed*; and management (where * indicates a wildcard). only studies performed in europe were included as we expected european grasslands to have a similar history of formation and agricultural policies compared to grasslands outside of europe. the exclusion of non-european studies was specified by including the search terms not “north america”, australia*, or chin*. from the list of articles resulting from the literature search, four highly relevant and well performed studies were chosen as sources of additional articles suitable for inclusion. all articles found in the reference lists of these articles and lists of papers citing these articles were added in the article list.
selection_criteria: 1) studies has to compare at least two different mowing frequencies. studies comparing the timing of different mowing events during the same year (e.g., beginning and end of summer) were excluded. mowing once per year was chosen as the reference treatment and therefore had to be used as a treatment in all included studies. 2) studies had to examine a relevant outcome for the conservation of semi-natural grasslands. 3) only studies where the desired outcome was clear from a conservation viewpoint, e.g. a higher mean species richness, were included. 4) studies had to contain data in the form of estimates with a measure of variation (e.g. means and variance). 5) studies where fertilizers were used during the study period were excluded, as well as studies where grasslands were grazed before or after mowing.
data_analysis: in all analyses, ln(rr) was calculated using random effects models. to avoid bias in ln(rr) due to small sample sizes, lajeunesse’s method of calculating ln(rr) and the variance of ln(rr) was used. analyses were made using the software comprehensive meta- analysis 2. sensitivity analyses were performed. first, analyses were run while removing one study at a time to examine the impact of that study. second, analyses were run while removing one response variable at a time to examine the impact of that response variable. third, analyses were run with only one response variable per study site (randomly selected when there was more than one response per site), to test if the results were influenced by non-independence between response variables from the same study. if the results were robust, only small differences were expected between the results of the original analyses and the sensitivity analyses, and only modest differences between studies within the analysis of specific explanatory variables. the presence of publication bias in the studies included in the meta-analysis was investigated by means of egger’s regression asymmetry test.
background: Both agricultural intensification and abandonment have led to the loss of European semi-natural grasslands. Nature conservation management measures like mowing are essential for preserving the biodiversity of remaining grasslands. However, there are no conclusive results from studies examining effects of different mowing frequencies across Europe.
objective: to determine which mowing frequency is the most effective for preserving the biodiversity of plant and animal species in semi-natural grasslands.
result1: overall, mowing once per year was marginally more positive than mowing less frequently, while mowing more frequently than once per year had a more positive effect.
result2: mowing every second and fifth year had effects similar to mowing once per year, while mowing every third year was marginally worse.
result3: mowing three times per year did not significantly differ from mowing once per year while mowing two times per year was significantly, but only slightly, better than mowing once per year (ln(rr) = 0.125
result4: there was no evidence of publication bias (bias = 1.260, p = 0.152).
general_conclusion: overall, authors found similar effects of the different mowing frequencies on the biodiversity of flora and fauna. more frequent mowing generally had a more positive effect, but differences between frequencies were small. these results suggest that in most european semi-natural grasslands, mowing less frequently is a way of using the limited funds available for management more efficiently while still maintaining grassland conservation values.

search_strategy: in october 2014 studies, in any language, comparing grazing and mowing were searched for in the databases scopus, biological sciences and biological abstract. the search terms used were mow* or scythe*; graz*; grassland*, meadow*, pasture*, fen* or heath* (where * indicates a wild card). in addition we used agricola, a database containing literature citations relating to all aspects of agriculture, using the search terms mow* and graz*.
selection_criteria: articles eligible for inclusion in the meta-analysis had to 1) compare grazing vs. mowing or grazing vs. mowing with aftermath grazing. only studies where mowing was performed once a year were included.  2) the goal of the sutudy was to preserve the high conservation value of grasslands, e.g. management for high species richness. therefore, studies which only reported e.g. annual yield were excluded from further analysis. 3) the management had to be considered to directly affect the effect measures e.g. studies only measuring soil nutrients were excluded but not e.g. studies reporting species richness. 4) studies had to contain data in the form of estimates with a measure of variation (e.g. means and variance) and sample size.
data_analysis: before the analysis, the explanatory variables were grouped into four categories: (i) geography and habitat type; (ii) study design; (iii) management; and (iv) other. for all analyses the standard difference in means (d), using random effects models was calculated.  analyses were made using the software comprehensive meta- analysis 2.
background: To maintain the high biodiversity of semi-natural grasslands, management by grazing or mowing is needed. Given the limited resources and few remaining areas, the best management method should be used. However, only a few studies comparing the effects of mowing and grazing on grassland biodiversity exists.
objective: to determine whether grazing or annual mowing is more effective in preserving the biodiversity of semi-natural grasslands, by reviewing the literature, and evaluate as much as possible of the available data in meta-analyses. the authors aimed to determine the best available management method and give direct recommendations for the management of semi-natural grasslands.
result1: the analysis of all studies together revealed an overall positive but no significant effect of grazing compared to mowing (d = -0.145).
result2: results revealed that the effect of grazing and mowing differed for different continents and grassland types.
result4: effects of grazing and mowing differed for mowing date.
result5: the effects of grazing and mowing differed for different historical and recent management practices.
general_conclusion: grazing generally had a more positive effect on the conservation value of semi-natural grasslands compared to mowing, but effect sizes were generally small to moderate for most contrasts. furthermore, effects varied across some grassland characteristics.

search_strategy: authors used a combination of terms in web of science and examined the title, keywords and abstract to assess the potential eligibility of the study. references from these studies were also used to locate relevant articles.
selection_criteria: only field studies were included in this analysis.
data_analysis: meta-analyses were conducted in r. random effects models generated with the “rma.mv” function of themetaphor package. metaregressions were run on all response variables. to account for non-independence of observations made on the same experimental plots, all models included observation number and publication as random variables. to select models that best explain the heterogeneity in effect sizes, the glmulti package was used. authors used a candidate set of models with only first-level variable combinations (no interactions) for model averaging. relevant variables were narrowed using automated model selection and selected variables for further analyses when the variable importance was 0.8 and above. using the selected variables from this model, authors fitted metaregression models with interactions with the metaphor package using all possible combinations of a single continuous and a single categorical variable. authors used variance inflation factors using the function “vif” in the metaphor package to determine multicollinearity and fit only combinations of variables that were determined to be non-collinear. model fit was compared to the no-interaction model using akaike’s information criterion corrected for small sample size (aicc). marginal and conditional coefficients of determination (r2) and pseudo-r2 were also calculated as metrics of model explanatory power.
background: Biosolids are a source of nutrient-rich organic material that can be used to improve degraded or disturbed soils. Research on vegetation responses to the land application of biosolids has increased in the past 20 years, but there is no consensus on how plant communities respond to biosolids applications.
objective: to explore how the application of biosolids impacts ecosystem processes, including above-ground productivity, total vegetative cover, and plant community responses (species richness, shannon diversity and exotic species success) on reclaimed land. specifically, this study explores how application rates of biosolids or biosolids mixtures (e.g., biosolids mixed with ash, wood chips, lime, etc.) may affect productivity and plant community responses and if these factors impact how long the effect of biosolids persists following its application. here, results for the effects on plant species richness are reported.
result1: biosolids were not found to have an overall effect on species richness (p = 0.15, lrr = 0.27 [−0.10, 0.65], k = 159).
result2: NA
general_conclusion: the land application of biosolids had no significant overall effect on species richness on degraded lands restored into grasslands.

search_strategy: the following web databases were searched for documents: isi web of science, science direct, jstor, google (100 first hits) and google scholar (100 first hits). a high-sensitivity and low-specificity approach was used to ensure that all important relevant information was found. the databases searches were carried out between september 2012 and january 2013. any apparently relevant citations or links were followed one step away from the original hit. in addition, national and international experts on the subject were asked for any related literature and unpublished data
selection_criteria: 1) relevant subjects: natural or seminatural grasslands in temperate mountain zones. mediterranean, subtropical and arid climates that occur within the temperate latitudes were excluded; 2) types of intervention: addition of nitrogen (alone or in combination with other nutrients); 3) types of comparator: non fertilized control plots (experimental studies) or suitable reference areas that have not been fertilized (observational studies). control plots had to be managed in the same way as treatment plots with the exception; types of outcome: species richness or shannon index of diversity (h0) of at least one taxonomic group. changes in biomass production or absolute abundance of functional groups were also recorded if provided. the authors limit this review to vascular plants.
data_analysis: random- and mixed-effects meta-analytical models were used. here, the q test and i2 statistic were used to assess heterogeneity among studies. in addition to the weighted mas that utilized variances among replicates, unweighted meta-analyses were applied to a larger data set that included effect sizes without associated variances. publication bias was assessed using funnel plots, by applying a regression test for funnel plot asymmetry. all statistics were performed using r version 3.1.2.
background: Although the influence of nitrogen (N) addition on grassland plant communities has been widely studied, it is still unclear whether observed patterns and underlying mechanisms are constant across biomes.
objective: this systematic review thus focuses on temperate mountain ecosystems including montane, subalpine and alpine grasslands. it aims at assessing the available evidence regarding the effects of n addition upon biodiversity and productivity of temperate zone mountain grasslands. in particular, it investigates how abiotic factors that potentially interact with n addition drive the variable plant community responses that are commonly observed in nature. the term n addition refers here to n from anthropogenic origin, either in the form of agricultural fertilization (sometimes in combination with other nutrients) or atmospheric deposition.
result1: species richness was reduced by n addition in weighted and unweighted mas.
result2: NA
general_conclusion: overall, this systematic review indicates that n addition generally reduces plant species richness.

search_strategy: the authors systematically searched for published field studies that reported effects of organic amendments on one or more ecosystem properties. they first performed a web of science search and then identified additional studies by screening cited references in papers obtained. gray literature cited by a peer-reviewed paper was considered eligible if it met all other criteria.
selection_criteria: 1) field experiment with control [no amendment) and treatment [amendment) plots; 2) non forested ecosystem with sufficient plant biomass to support livestock grazing; 3) carbon-based amendment to which synthetic nutrients had not been added; 4) soil not subjected to “severe disturbance” within the 20-year period prior to experiment initiation [as reported by the paper's authors). the authors considered severe disturbance to include activities such as mining, roadcuts, and agricultural tillage; 5) arid, semiarid, or mediterranean köppen–geiger climate zone; 6) reported effect of amendment addition on at least one of 20 prospective response variables.
data_analysis: all analyses were conducted in r. the authors chose five predictors—climate zone, days between amendment application and measurement, amount of amendment applied, amendment total n concentration, and [for soil outcomes) soil sample depth—that were reported for 91%–100% of observations.
background: Interest in land application of organic amendments—such as biosolids, composts, and manures—is growing due to their potential to increase soil carbon and help mitigate climate change, as well as to support soil health and regenerative agriculture. While organic amendments are predominantly applied to croplands, their application is increasingly proposed on relatively arid rangelands that do not typically receive fertilizers or other inputs, creating unique concerns for outcomes such as native plant diversity and water quality.
objective: the authors present a meta‐analysis of organic amendment additions to rangelands in arid, semiarid, and mediterranean climates, synthesizing amendment effects on a suite of ecosystem outcomes. specifically, they analyzed 11 ecosystem outcomes that had sufficient published data: soil organic carbon concentration, soil water holding capacity, aboveground net primary productivity (anpp), plant species diversity, plant tissue nitrogen (n) concentration, soil co2 emissions, soil lead (pb) concentration, plant tissue pb concentration, runoff quantity, runoff phosphorus, and runoff nitrate. here, results for plant species diversity are provided.
result1: impacts on plant species biodiversity were essentially neutral (mean = 0.98×).
result2: NA
general_conclusion: amendment addition to rangeland has no effect on plant species diversity.

search_strategy: in april 2018, the scopus and web of science databases were used to collect primary studies. the search strings were composed of “or” and “and” statements combining terms related to n‐addition experiments and different dimensions of plant species diversity, for example (“nitrogen fertilization” or “nitrogen addition”) and (“abundance” or “composition” or “number” or “richness”).
selection_criteria: 1) data from plots where n addition was performed together with watering, temperature increase, litter removal, grazing or fire manipulation or where n was added in combination with other nutrients were excluded. 2) selection was limited to experiments conducted on natural or semi‐natural vegetation, excluding studies conducted on crops, mono‐cultures or where species were artificially introduced in plots. 3) studies that reported the same data as other studies already included in the database were excluded.
data_analysis: a meta‐analysis using multilevel mixed‐effect models was performed to control for non‐independence in the data owing to multiple effect sizes per study and species. first, authors fitted single meta-regression models using yearly n addition as the only moderator, in order to compare changes among the metrics for a given amount of n applied. then, authors fitted multiple meta‐regression models by including other moderators and interaction terms between the amount of n addition and these other moderators. stepwise backward selection based on the bayesian information criterion (bic) was performed, whereby a moderator was excluded only if it was also dropped from the interaction term. the amount of heterogeneity reduced was estimated in the best models selected and by each moderator using the omnibus wald‐type test of moderators. because of non‐independence of the effect sizes, the variance–covariance matrix based on lajeunesse (2011) was computed. for species richness and individual abundance, the models were fitted with the rma.mv function of the r package “metafor”. observations were weighted by the inverse of the sampling variance. missing standard deviations were imputed using the coefficient of variation from all complete cases with the impute_sd function of the r package “metagear”. for mean species abundance and geometric mean abundance, the number of replicates in each experiment was used to weight the observations. multi‐level linear mixed‐effect models were fitted for these two response variables with the lme function of the r package “nlme”. finally, null models were used to estimate the weighted mean pooled effect size, namely the overall amount of plant diversity change across all experiments, independently from the amount of n addition. based on these models, publication bias was also investigated with visual estimation of the funnel plots. the significance of asymmetry of the funnel plots was tested with the egger’s test. all analyses were performed in the r environment.
background: Experimental nitrogen (N) addition (fertilization) studies are commonly used to quantify the impacts of increased N inputs on plant biodiversity. However, given that plant community responses can vary considerably among individual studies, there is a clear need to synthesize and generalize findings with meta‐analytical approaches.
objective: to reveal the overall effects of n addition on various metrics of local plant biodiversity and explore the role of potential experimental (amount of yearly n applied, experimental duration, type of fertilizer and plot size) and environmental (temperature, precipitation, soil ph, soil cation exchange capacity (cec) and atmospheric n deposition) moderators. here, results for temperate grasslands are reported.
result1: all metrics of plant diversity responded negatively to increasing yearly n addition.
result2: NA
general_conclusion: n enrichment decreases both species richness and abundance of plants in n‐addition experiments in grasslands.

search_strategy: the authors searched for peer-reviewed journal articles published up to 7 february 2020 and catalogued in the isi web of science using the search terms “fertilization” or “fertilisation” or “nutrients” or “nutrient addition” or “micronutrient” or “nitrogen” or “phosphorus” or “potassium” or “npk” and “arthropods” or “insects” and “prairie” or “grassland” or “pasture” or “savannah” or “savanna” or “steppe” or “old field”. to provide a more adequate representation of fertilization effects and help reduce publication bias, the authors additionally searched the lter (long term ecological research) database for raw experimental data.
selection_criteria: the authors included only those studies that were non-cage field experiments in non-agricultural grassland ecosystems (although the experimental area could be mowed, grazed, or have been previously used for agriculture). additionally, the authors selected only studies that included both a fertilization treatment and a control (no fertilization) treatment, and from which they were able to obtain either raw arthropod abundances or both means and standard deviations of arthropod abundances in treatment and control plots.
data_analysis: to identify which fertilizer predictor variables best estimated arthropod responses to fertilization (effect sizes), the authors used an akaike information criterion (aic) framework. to test how both the underlying gradients and responses of plant biomass and plant nutrient content to fertilization mediated arthropod response to fertilization the authors used linear models within an aic framework. the authors used egger’s regression test in the r package metafor  and a funnel plot to test for publication bias effects and found none.
background: Ongoing alterations to Earth’s biogeochemical cycles are expected to impact plants, plant consumers and all subsequent trophic levels. While fertilization experiments often reveal arthropod nutrient limitation by nitrogen and phosphorus via effects on plant nutrient density and biomass, these macronutrients are only two of many nutrients important to arthropod fitness. Micronutrients are key to osmoregulation and enzyme function and can interact synergistically with macronutrients to shape the geography of arthropod abundance.
objective: the primary goal was to test for the ubiquity of n, p, k and micronutrient limitation – or some combination of the above – on total arthropod abundance and the abundance of six common feeding guilds: chewing herbivores, sucking herbivores, omnivores, predators, pollinators and detritivores.
result1: arthropod abundance varied widely with fertilizer type, from low abundance with k + micronutrients fertilization (effect size: −0.1) to high abundance with the addition of npk fertiliser + micronutrients (effect size: +1.3).
result2: NA
general_conclusion: total arthropods response to fertilization showed a positive response for p, np, npk, npk+micronutrients, while it showed no effect for n, nk + micronutrients, pk + micronutrients. negative results were reported for k + micronutrients.

search_strategy: the search for data concerning n addition experiments focused on peer-reviewed articles that studied the impact of n addition on biomass, the number of species per unit area (species richness) or both variables at the community level. relevant studies were identiﬁed through searches of the bibliographic database of the isi web of knowledge and the references therein (1955 to 2009). the search terms nitrogen, addition, vegetation and experiment* were used, singly and in various combinations.
