selection_criteria: 1) only data from in situ n addition experiments were incorporated into the database. ex situ n addition experiments or papers considering vegetation change as a consequence of atmospheric depositions were not considered; 2) the authors included studies performed in terrestrial ecosystems and classiﬁed them into forest understoreys, heathlands, grasslands and three types of wetland. grassland studies were only included if the area had been continuously grassland for the last 20 years. 3) only experiments in which inorganic n was added (to be comparable with n additions through atmospheric depositions) were included. simultaneous additions of phosphorus or potassium were omitted, as the impact of these nutrients may interfere with the effect of n. 4) to unravel the relative impact of n addition from all other environmental variables being randomly assigned to treatments, only studies reporting results for both n-treated and control plots were selected. 5) the authors focused on articles reporting data on the impact of n addition on biomass or species richness or on both variables.
data_analysis: the authors calculated the effect size and a 95% bootstrapping conﬁdence interval (ci) with n = 1000 iterations using resampling stats v.4.0. due to a lack of standard deviation or error estimates in some studies, the bootstrapping approach used was more appropriate than the standard meta-analytical procedures.
background: Elevated inputs of biologically reactive nitrogen (N) are considered to be one of the most substantial threats to biodiversity in terrestrial ecosystems. Several attempts have been made to scrutinize the factors driving species loss following excess N input, but generalizations across sites or vegetation types cannot yet be made.
objective: the authors conducted a large-scale meta-analysis of in situ n addition experiments, focusing on the effects on the vegetation’s biomass and species richness. here, results for species richness are reported.
result1: species richness signiﬁcantly decreased with n addition in grassland.
result2: NA
general_conclusion: n addition showed a negative effect on species richness in grassland.

search_strategy: web databases were searched for relevant documents: isi web of science, science direct, jstor, google (100 first hits), google scholar (100 first hits). searches were conducted in english, french and german using translations of the following logical search string: (mowing or cutting) and (meadow or grassland) and (biodiversity or richness). any apparently relevant citations or links were followed one step away from the original hit. in addition, national and international experts on the subject were asked for any relevant literature and unpublished data.
selection_criteria: 1) relevant subjects: semi-natural grasslands that are mown annually, including conventionally managed grasslands, agri-environmental schemes meadows, hay or litter meadows. 2) types of intervention: first mowing date delayed (treatment). 3) types of comparator: comparison with similar meadows or plots that are first mown on an earlier date (control). treatment and control plots must be similar in all management respects, except the date of the first cut, and must be located in the same habitat type. 3) types of outcome: species richness and/or abundance (any taxa). 4) both experimental and observational studies to be included, but excluded studies that provided only qualitative evidence.
data_analysis: random- and mixed-effects models were chosen. first, the null model was generated. then all univariate models including the following moderators (effect modifiers) were tested: ordinal day, time lapse (in days) between the early and the delayed cuts, study duration (in years), meadow type and plot size of the vegetation relevés. multivariate models (various combinations of the above mentioned variables) were also explored. further subgroup analyses were conducted to investigate the influence of key moderators separately. models were ranked based on their aic values (akaike information criterion) and on the level of significance of the estimates. permutation tests were not always possible due to an insufficient number of data points, which limits the number of possible iterations. therefore test statistics of the effect sizes and corresponding confidence intervals referred to the normal distribution (z test). the q test and i2 statistic were used to assess heterogeneity between studies. publication bias was assessed using funnel plots, by applying a regression test for funnel plot asymmetry. all statistics were performed using r version 2.13.0.
background: Meadows are regularly mown in order to provide fodder or litter for livestock and to prevent vegetation succession. However, the time of year at which meadows should be first mown in order to maximize biological diversity remains controversial and may vary with respect to context and focal taxa
objective: to answer the following question: does delaying the first mowing date increase biodiversity in european farmland meadows?
result1: no overall significant effect of delaying the first mowing date was supported as regards plant species richness (mean hedges’d= 0.017 with 95% ci −0.237 – 0.2716, z= 0.134, p= 0.882).
result2: a significant positive effect of delaying the first mowing date on invertebrate species richness was found (mean hedges’d= 0.511 with 95% ci 0.129 – 0.893, z= 2.6217, p= 0.009).
result3: delaying the first mowing date had no significant effect on invertebrate abundance (mean hedges’d= −0.053 with 95% ci −0.889 – 0.783, z= −0.1249, p= 0.901).
result4: overall, there was strong between-study heterogeneity.
general_conclusion: in general, delaying the first mowing date in european meadowlands has either positive or neutral effects on plant and invertebrate biodiversity (except for plant species richness when delaying from spring to fall or from early summer to later).
knowledge_gaps: the low number of data points stemming from an even lower number of studies precluded investigations on specific invertebrate taxa, and on the influence of several moderators.

search_strategy: all peer-reviewed publications that investigated the effects of plant diversity on carbon pools and fluxes in grasslands using the isi web of science, google scholar, and the china national knowledge infrastructure through december 31, 2019. authors used different keyword combinations for the search, including grassland, biomass, production/productivity, aboveground, below-ground, root, soc, rs, rh, carbon pool, carbon flux, diversity, mixtures, pure, monoculture, and richness.
selection_criteria: 1) experiments had at least one pair of data at the same temporal and spatial scales (under monoculture and mixtures), including carbon pools and fluxes; 2) the effect of diversity was clearly described, including diversity level (species richness) and experimental duration; 3) the means, standard deviations/errors and samples size of variables in the monoculture and mixtures groups could be extracted directly from the context, tables, or digitized graphs.
data_analysis: random effects models were used to analyze the weighted average response ratio and meta-regression in the study and the between-sampling variability was estimated by the rma function based on restricted maximum likelihood estimation (reml) with the lme4 package in r 3.5.1. the weights for studies was estimated by sampling standard deviations and the between-sampling variability. to prevent overfitting, the most parsimonious model was selected among all alternatives as long as plant diversity and experimental duration were retained, because they were part of the core hypotheses to be tested. random-effects meta-regression were used to evaluate the relationships among the response ratio of carbon attributes, plant diversity, and experimental duration.
background: Positive relationships between plant species diversity and carbon attributes have been observed in grasslands, but synthesis studies of how plant diversity affects the carbon balance of grasslands and how the response ratio changes over time both remain limited.
objective: to examine the effects of plant diversity loss on natural and manipulated grasslands, measured as the ratio of the main carbon inputs (aboveground biomass, belowground biomass, and total biomass), outputs (soil respiration and heterotrophic respiration), and balance (soil organic carbon) in plant mixtures to the average of those in monocultures. specifically authors tested whether: 1) plant mixtures showed a greater carbon sink than monocultures in grasslands; 2) the positive effects of plant diversity on six carbon attributes increased with experimental duration; and 3) the reduction in carbon sequestration of grassland ecosystems following plant diversity loss would be exacerbated over time.
result1: soil organic carbon increased significantly by an average of 10.7% in plant mixtures compared with the average of those in monocultures.
result2: NA
general_conclusion: this meta-analysis revealed that plant diversity loss has ubiquitous negative impacts on multiple carbon attributes in grasslands, underlined the interactive effects of plant diversity loss and experimental duration on carbon attributes, and suggested that the reduction of carbon storage in grasslands following biodiversity loss will be greater in the future.

search_strategy: from february to june in 2020, authors conducted a comprehensive search of relevant peer-reviewed articles and dissertations published from the year of 1990 to 2020 in the web of science and proquest databases using combinations of the following search string: (plant ‘diversity’ or ‘biodiversity’ or ‘tree diversity’ or ‘species diversity’ or ‘plant species richness’ or ‘species mixture’ or ‘plant community composition’) and (‘plant growth’ or ‘plant productivity’ or ‘plant biomass’ or ‘basal area’) and (‘soil microbial*’ or ‘soil biota’ or ‘soil bac- terial and fungal*’) and (‘soil carbon’ or ‘soil organic carbon’). authors then cross-checked the references of the relevant articles to identify other relevant book chapters and peer-reviewed reports.
selection_criteria: papers were excluded if were 1) natural diversity gradient studies, 2) controlled global change experiments, in which plant diversity has been altered by global change factors, but not having a direct diversity treatment, 3) meta-analysis studies or review studies, 4) papers not including c storage and other variables that were in the focus of this study. authors kept the papers from biodiversity-ecosystem functioning experiments and experiments that had one-species and mixed-species plantations.
data_analysis: effect sizes and variances were calculated using random-effects models (with restricted maximum-likelihood estimators). to control for the existing non-independence, the factors ‘study’ and ‘site’ were used as random factors in the analyses to account for the non-independence of data coming from the same study. the total heterogeneity of effect sizes was tested within each model. the publication bias was estimated by the dnorm function. all statistical analyses were conducted with the ‘metafor’ package in r.
background: Plant diversity has a strong impact on a plethora of ecosystem functions and services, especially ecosystem carbon (C) storage. However, the potential context-dependency of biodiversity effects across ecosystem types, environmental conditions and carbon pools remains largely unknown.
objective: to explore the effects of plant diversity on different c pools, including aboveground and below- ground plant biomass, soil microbial biomass c and soil c content across different ecosystem types. here, results for grasslands are reported.
result1: no differences were found in the soil c content to increased plant diversity in grasslands.
result2: NA
general_conclusion: plant species richness has no effect on soil carbon content.

search_strategy: peer-reviewed publications published prior to june 2019 which investigated the effects of plant diversity on soil organi carbon (soc) and soil microbial biomass carbon (smbc) using the isi web of science and google scholar with the search term: ’soil organic carbon or microbial biomass carbon or soil microbial quotient and diversity or richness or mixture or pure or polyculture or monoculture or overyielding’, and also authors searched references within these papers.
selection_criteria: 1) papers were purposely designed to test the effects of plant diversity on soc content, soc stock, and smbc in mineral soils; 2) they had at least one species mixture treatment and corresponding monocultures; 3) they had the same initial climatic and soil properties in the monoculture and mixture treatment plots.
data_analysis: the number of replications was used for weighting effect sizes. models were tested using the restricted maximum likelihood estimation with the lme4 package. to prevent overfitting, authors selected the most parsimonious model among all alternatives with the condition to retain species richness, as it was intrinsic to the purpose of the study to assess the effect of the species richness in mixtures. the model selection was accomplished by using the ’dredge’ function of the mumin package. in order to assess whether results were biased by the relatively few data points with higher species richness (e.g. a species richness of 60 in some experiments), authors conducted the same analysis for the data set after removing observations with 60 species. they compared the estimates and species-richness trends for the data sets with and without a species richness of 60, and found that both data sets yielded qualitatively similar estimates and trends. all statistical analyses were performed in r 3.5.2.
background: Soil organic carbon (SOC) is a valuable resource for mediating global climate change and securing food production. Despite an alarming rate of global plant diversity loss, uncertainties concerning the effects of plant diversity on SOC remain, because plant diversity not only stimulates litter inputs via increased productivity, thus enhancing SOC, but also stimulates microbial respiration, thus reducing SOC.
objective: to examine the overall effects of species mixture on soil organic carbon (soc) content and stock, soil microbial biomass carbon (smbc), and smbc/soc in mineral soils. furthermore, to test whether these effects increase with species richness (or functional group richness) in mixtures and with stand age, and whether these effects differ across a wide range of ecosystem types, mean annual temperatures, and annual aridity indices at the study sites, and across soil depths. here, results on grassland ecosystems are reported.
result1: plant species mixtures did not change soc content and stock in grasslands.
result2: NA
general_conclusion: plant species mixtures did not change soc content and stock  in grasslands.

search_strategy: the authors systematically searched for published field studies that reported effects of organic amendments on one or more ecosystem properties. they first performed a web of science search and then identified additional studies by screening cited references in papers obtained. gray literature cited by a peer-reviewed paper was considered eligible if it met all other criteria.
selection_criteria: 1) field experiment with control (no amendment) and treatment (amendment) plots; 2) non forested ecosystem with sufficient plant biomass to support livestock grazing; 3) carbon-based amendment to which synthetic nutrients had not been added; 4) soil not subjected to “severe disturbance” within the 20-year period prior to experiment initiation (as reported by the paper's authors). the authors considered severe disturbance to include activities such as mining, roadcuts, and agricultural tillage; 5) arid, semiarid, or mediterranean köppen–geiger climate zone; 6) reported effect of amendment addition on at least one of 20 prospective response variables.
data_analysis: all analyses were conducted in r. the authors chose five predictors—climate zone, days between amendment application and measurement, amount of amendment applied, amendment total n concentration, and (for soil outcomes) soil sample depth—that were reported for 91%–100% of observations.
background: Interest in land application of organic amendments—such as biosolids, composts, and manures—is growing due to their potential to increase soil carbon and help mitigate climate change, as well as to support soil health and regenerative agriculture. While organic amendments are predominantly applied to croplands, their application is increasingly proposed on relatively arid rangelands that do not typically receive fertilizers or other inputs, creating unique concerns for outcomes such as native plant diversity and water quality.
objective: the authors present a meta‐analysis of organic amendment additions to rangelands in arid, semiarid, and mediterranean climates, synthesizing amendment effects on a suite of ecosystem outcomes. specifically, they analyzed 11 ecosystem outcomes that had sufficient published data: soil organic carbon concentration, soil water holding capacity, aboveground net primary productivity (anpp), plant species diversity, plant tissue nitrogen (n) concentration, soil co2 emissions, soil lead (pb) concentration, plant tissue pb concentration, runoff quantity, runoff phosphorus, and runoff nitrate. here, results for soil organic carbon are provided.
result1: amendment addition increased soil organic carbon concentration (mean = 1.34×).
result2: NA
general_conclusion: amendment addition to rangeland increased soil organic carbon.

search_strategy: an exhaustive literature survey of peer-reviewed publications was carried out using web of science for articles published before december 2014.
selection_criteria: 1) measurements have to be made under field conditions; laboratory incubation and soil column experiments were excluded. 2) the reported results had to include emissions for the treatment with and without nitrification inhibitors (ni) for the inhibitor efficiency determination, or the control and treatment with ni for determination of the emission factor, or both. 3) environmental conditions and management (e.g., fertiliser application rates) were equal for the treatments with/without ni.
data_analysis: a regression analysis was carried out to determine if fertiliser application rate, the number of measurement days or the inhibitor application rate had an impact on the emission factors and the effect of the inhibitor. a meta-analysis was carried out using genstat to estimate ni effect according to soil, fertiliser and inhibitor type and land use. analysis of the correlations between variables was carried out using pairwise correlations and tests to estimate the correlation between the ef and the inhibitory effect with all the variables.
background: The main sources of nitrous oxide (N2O) emissions are nitrogen fertilizer and manure applications to agricultural fields. Many field studies have tested the effectiveness of nitrification inhibitors (NI) to reduce N2O emissions but results varied considerably because the studies were carried out under different climate and soil conditions.
objective: the objectives of this study are to analyse the new peer-reviewed literature to determine the variability in the efficiency of nitrification inhibitors (ni) and the effect of environmental parameters on this efficiency and to develop n2o emission factors for chemical fertilizers and animal excreta used with ni.
result1: large inhibitor effect was found for grassland systems (40.8% +/-5.4, 95% confidence interval (ci) 29.0% to 52.9%)
result2: NA
general_conclusion: fertilisation inhibitors have a positive effect on n2o emissions in grassland in all type of soil, with exception for the combination of sandy loam-sandy clay loam with ammonium–nitrate based fertiliser and 3,4-dimethyl pyrazole phosphate.

search_strategy: data were compiled from the literature on the effects of n fertilization on soil denitrification for the period 1982 through september 2016. an exhaustive literature survey of publications was identified using the isi web of science with the search terms “denitrification and soil and nitrogen.” additional searches using the same keywords were also conducted via google scholar and china national knowledge infrastructure. these searches were expanded by including all studies cited in key review papers.
selection_criteria: 1) only focused on studies that were conducted on agricultural soils; 2) to better represent the response of soil denitrification to n fertilization under natural conditions, only those studies that were performed under field conditions or used undisturbed soil cores in the laboratory were included; 3) the plant species and soil types between the treatment and control plots had to be identical.
data_analysis: the authors used a random-effects model and the restricted maximum likelihood approach to pool and compare the effect sizes in this meta-analysis. the impact of n fertilization on soil denitrification was considered significant if the 95% confidence intervals (ci) did not overlapwith zero. the between-group heterogeneity test (qb) was used to assess whether different groups among each categorical variable showed different responses to n fertilization, with a significant qb indicating that the groups differed. with the exception of n application rate, a random-effects meta-regression was used to explore the relationships between lnrrs and environmental and forcing factors. the publication bias in the studies where variances were reported was evaluated by the funnel plot and egger regression.
background: Terrestrial soil denitrification is of great importance for closing the nitrogen (N) cycle, yet the current understanding of soil denitrification response to N fertilization remains uncertain. While there has been a focus on factors controlling N2O fluxes from agricultural soils because of its global warming effect, much less is known about factors controlling total denitrification losses, yet these can be sufficiently large to affect N use efficiency.
objective: the authors collated field observations of soil denitrification (n2o+n2) based on the ait from cropland and grassland ecosystems and conducted a global-scale meta-analysis 1) to quantitatively examine the general patterns of n fertilization effects on denitrification and the n2o:n2 ratio; 2) to assess how environmental and experimental factors affect the response of soil denitrification to n fertilization; 3) to explore the relationship between the change in soil denitrification to n input and the rate of n application.
result1: grasslands showed a higher increase in denitrification (271%) than that of croplands (147%; qb=12.97, pb 0.001).
result2: NA
general_conclusion: n fertisation has a negative effect on n2o emissions.

search_strategy: the authors searched the relevant journal articles published before september 2020 in the datasets of the web of science and the china knowledge resource integrated database, with the keywords “ch4” or “methane” or “ghg” or “greenhouse gas” and “n” or “nitrogen” or “nh4” or “nh3” or “ammonium” or “nitrate” and “addition” or “deposition” or “input” or “application” or “fertilization” or “amendment” or “enrichment”.
selection_criteria: 1) both control and treatment experiments are included; (2) n addition experiments are conducted in the field, rather than in laboratory incubation; 3) the means, standard errors (se) or standard deviations (sd), and sample sizes are clearly reported or can be determined arbitrarily; 4) n addition duration is longer than a growing season or a full year; 5) the data obtained under different n addition levels, durations, forms, and experimental locations are independent.
data_analysis: the percentage change (%) transformed from the weighted response ratio (rr++) is used to quantify the magnitude of the impacts of n addition. if the 95% ci of rr++ for a selected variable does not overlap zero, the impact of n addition on this variable is considered to be significant at p < 0.05. furthermore, between-group heterogeneity tests (qb tests) are conducted to analyze whether there is a statistical difference among the impacts ofn addition in different groups.
background: Elevated nitrogen (N) addition from anthropogenic activities has great impacts on soil methane (CH4) uptake, which could interrupt the existing global CH4 balance and cause feedbacks to climate and biogeochemical processes. Previous studies have come to inconsistent conclusions on both the quantification of the response of CH4 uptake to N addition and understanding of its underlying mechanisms, probably due to the lack of experimental data.
objective: the aims of the meta-analysis was to quantify the response of ch4 uptake to n addition, and further reveal its underlying mechanisms, based on the most recent papers published before september 2020. specifically, the following questions are addressed: what are the differences in the responses of ch4 uptake to n addition in different ecosystems? how do experimental conditions (n addition level, duration, and forms) affect the ch4 uptake response? based on previous experimental and synthesis studies, the authors hypothesize that: 1) the upland soil ch4 uptake could be reduced on average under n addition; and 2) there exists a threshold of n addition (level and/or duration) which indicates a shift of the effects of n addition on soil ch4 uptake to an opposite trend.
result1: grassland has a slightly smaller rr of−0.17 (−0.09 to −0.24), with an absolute response of −15.29% (95%ci: −8.95 to −21.17%), indicating that the decreases in ch4 uptake is significant and with small uncertainty.
result2: NA
general_conclusion: n fertilisation has a negative effect on ch4 uptake in upland grassland.

search_strategy: a literature survey of peer-reviewed publications was performed using web of science and google scholar, with the keywords of ‘n2o’, ‘no3−leaching’, ‘n uptake’ or ‘plant yield’and ‘urine’or ‘dung’and ‘soil’or ‘grassland’in combination with ‘ni’, ‘ui’, or ‘biochar’, before february 2016.
selection_criteria: the inhibitor types considered for the analysis were dcd (a ni), pyrazole derivatives (pd, a ni), and n-(n-butyl) thiophosphoric triamide (nbpt, a ui). only direct measurements were included and no data were obtained from modeling studies. studies performed under laboratory, greenhouse, and field conditions were all included. only studies with a measurement period that lasted longer than 30 days were considered.
data_analysis: the effect sizes were calculated for each grouping using a categorical random effects model. the mean effect size for each category and the bias-corrected 95% confidential intervals (cis) were generated by a bootstrapping procedure (9999 iterations). the meta-analysis was conducted using meta-win version 2.0. publication bias was analyzed by rank correlation test using meta-win version 2.0.
background: Excreta (urine and dung) patches on grazed grasslands are significant sources of nitrogen (N) trace gas emissions and leaching. Nitrification inhibitors (NIs), urease inhibitors (UIs) and biochar have been tested to reduce N losses and increase N utilization in various agro-ecosystems. Although the effectiveness of NIs, UIs or biochar on N losses or N utilization for chemical N fertilizers and manures have been evaluated in previous studies, there has been no comprehensive assessment on their effectiveness for excreta patches of grazing animals on grassland.
objective: the authors conducted a comprehensive meta-analysis of their effects on n2o emissions, no3−leaching, plant n uptake, and plant yields  to better understand the effects of inhibitors and biochar on the major n dynamics in excreta patches. the following two main objectives were addressed: 1) evaluating the effects of inhibitors and biochar on n losses or uptake; 2) investigating the main factors that affect the efficacy of inhibitors and biochar in grazed grassland ecosystems.
result1: significant decreases in n2o emissions from urine patches were found after the application of dcd(l) (mean: −52%, bias-corrected 95% ci: −56% to −47%), dcd(z) (−39%, −44% to −33%), nbpt + dcd(l) (−47%, −53% to −41%), and nbpt + dcd(z) (−52%, −56% to −46%).
result2: non-significant effects were found for pd (8%, −11% to 34%), biochar (−15%, −39%to 19%), and nbpt (−23%, −53% to 4%).
result3: there were significant differences in the responses between dcd(l) and dcd(z), as well as between dcd(z) and nbpt+dcd(z).
result4: on average, nbpt + dcd significantly reduced n2o emissions by 48% (−53% to −43%).
general_conclusion: overall, dcd inhibitors have a positive effect in reducing n2o emissions with excption of pyrazole derivatives in liquid form (pd) and n-(n-butyl) thiophosphoric triamide in liquid form (nbpt). biochar has no effect in reducing n2o emissions.

search_strategy: the authors collected publications by searching for “nitrogen and phosphorus”, “methane”, “grassland” and “upland” in google scholar in july 2016, and later updated in september 2018.
selection_criteria: 1) manipulation experiments with either external n and/or p addition; 2) the ﬁeld measurements must cover at least one full growing season, which makes the estimation of annual budget more reliable; 3) the studies report clear information for the ﬁeld site that is useful when extracting edaphic and meteorological data from global datasets.
data_analysis: the authors used a one-way anova analysis (anova; r package) followed by duncan’s post hoc test to examine the n and p impacts on annual ch4 uptake rate, soil nh4+ and no3-, and plant n content. a stepwise multivariate analysis was adopted to evaluate the response of the soil plant and microbial communities to environmental factors as well as their correlations with each other.
background: Grasslands cover more than 20% of the Earth’s land surface and typically serve as a net sink for atmospheric CH4. However, this CH4 sink may be altered by the growing input of nutrients, particularly nitrogen (N), due to anthropogenic activities.
objective: the authors integrated a 4-year field manipulation experiment, a meta-analysis and an empirical modelling approach to investigate the effects of n + p additions on ch4 flux in grasslands and the underlying mechanisms.
result1: n addition and concurrent n + p additions cause signiﬁcant declines in annual ch4 uptake: -27% (p < 0.01) and -14% (p < 0.01) respectively.
result2: NA
general_conclusion: n fertilisation and n+p fertilisation reduced ch4 uptake, while p fertilisation showed no effect.

search_strategy: the authors conducted a detailed review of literature published in peer-reviewed journals through 2008 and identified field studies that compared n2o and no emissions from plots to which nitrification inhibitors (nis), polymer-coated fertilizers (pcfs), or urease inhibitors (uis) were applied with those from plots to which conventional fertilizers were applied.
selection_criteria: 1) only field experiment data were included; small-scale experiments such as incubation or soil column experiments were excluded; 2) papers those emission data with the same total nitrogen application rate for treatment and control; 3) studies with no replication or no reported number of replications were excluded from the analysis.
data_analysis: to conduct a meta-analysis, the mean n2o and no emissions, stardard deviation (sd), and number of replicates from the treatment and control are needed. when no sd was reported, the authors assigned the average sd derived from other sd reported datasets – that is, 23% of means for n2o emissions – to include as many studies as possible in the analysis. if outlying data points were not obvious artifacts, outliers were included in the analysis to illustrate variability. using rrs, the authors conducted a weighted meta-analysis. mean effect size for each category was calculated, with bias-corrected 95% confidential intervals (cis), using a bootstrapping procedure (9999 iterations). the meta analysis was conducted using meta-win version 2.
background: Agricultural fields are an important anthropogenic source of atmospheric nitrous oxide (N2O) and nitric oxide (NO). Although many field studies have tested the effectiveness of possible mitigation options, including the application of nitrification inhibitors (NI) on N2O and NO emissions, the effectiveness of each option varies across sites due to environmental factors and field management.
objective: the aim of this study was to integrate results of field measurements to evaluate quantitatively the effect of nitrification inhibitors on no emissions from agricultural fields, using meta analysis.
result1: effects of nis on n2o emissions in grassland were −54%, ranging from −60% to −43%.
result2: the mean effect of pcfs for grassland showed a very significant reduction (−77%, −88% to −58%) compared with conventional fertilizers. note that all studies for grassland were conducted on gleysols in scotland.
general_conclusion: fertilisation with nis and pcfs in grassland has a positive effect on n2o emissions.

search_strategy: review of the biodiversity–ecosystem functioning literature through march 2018.
selection_criteria: authors collected data sets from an experimental species richness gradient greater than four species in a field or large controlled environment facility (ecotron) context with typical grassland species (including both grasses and forbs).
data_analysis: prior to conducting the meta-analysis, linear mixed-effects models using the package lme4 were fitted, with the package lmertest to calculate satterthwaite approximations of denominator degrees of freedom for each individual data set. for each site, the model was fitted with the dependent and independent variables and random effects and transformations that were relevant. then, authors extracted pearson’s correlation coefficient r for each question for each data set (using the package mumin), standard error, and sample size. the package metafor was then used to calculate fisher’s z-transformed correlation coefficients (rz). the rz were used as the model input in mixed-effects meta-models with a nested random effect of site within experiment to control for the uneven distribution of the data sets among the sites and the sites within broader experimental units. all data analyses were performed with r statistical computing software version 3.5.1.
background: Locally, plant species richness supports many ecosystem functions. Yet, the mechanisms driving these often-positive biodiversity–ecosystem functioning relationships are not well understood.
objective: authors present a meta-analysis of spatial resource partitioning across vertical resource gradients in grassland biodiversity– ecosystem functioning experiments. they assess 1) as a prerequisite, if plant species richness enhances community biomass production or resource uptake at these sites. then, they test 2) if there is evidence of spatial resource partitioning along vertical resource gradients, and 3) if this evidence of spatial resource partitioning is positively correlated with community biomass production or resource uptake. here, results for objective 1 are reported.
result1: species richness enhanced aboveground biomass production overall (aboveground biomass only set, rz = 0.462, p < 0.0001)
result2: NA
general_conclusion: plant species richness enhances ecosystem functioning especially in terms of total community biomass aboveground and belowground at the majority of the sites included in this meta-analysis.

search_strategy:
the authors searched peer-reviewed journal articles published before december 2017 from the web of science and google scholar. the search terms were ‘either n addition, n enrichment, n fertilization or n deposition; either p addition, p enrichment, p fertilization or p limitation;
either n and p additions, n and p fertilization or nutrient limitation’.
selection_criteria: 1) observations were only compiled from field manipulative experiments that conducted in natural terrestrial ecosystems; 2) at least one 2 × 2 full-factorial experimental design was applied to evaluate the effects of fertilizer applications; 3) at least one of the selected target variables (e.g., agb) was examined; 4) initial environmental conditions, vegetation types, and soil properties were the same in the treated and control plots; 5) measurements of the target variables in the experimental and control groups were performed at the same temporal and spatial scales; 6) n and p application form/rate, and experimental duration were clearly stated; 7) the means, standard deviations, and samples sizes of the target variables were reported or can be estimated from the reported results; 8) for multiple measurements at different time, only the last values were used to satisfy the assumption of statistical independence among observations.
data_analysis: anova was used to examine whether the rr++ of a specific variable related to plant growth differed significantly among n, p or np addition. the rr++ was transformed into the net percentage change in the treatment relative the control (%), and was calculated using the equation of × 100%. the rr++ and its bias-corrected 95% bootstrap ci were calculated by the meta-analytical software metawin 2.1. the publication bias in the dataset was identified by the funnel-plot method using metawin 2.1.
background: Co-limitation of ecosystem productivity by nitrogen (N) and phosphorus (P) is gaining increasing recognition, but how co-limitation through N and P inter actions differs among different terrestrial ecosystems remains unclear.
objective: the authors conducted a meta-analysis to quantify the interactive responses of plant growth-related variables [i.e., agb, bgb, leaf n and p concentrations, leaf n: p ratios, root n and p concentrations, soil mineral n and ap] to n and p additions. based on the previous studies, we hypothesize that the interactive effects of n and p additions on plant growth in terrestrial ecosystems are synergistic for the biomass production, but vary with ecosystem type for the other growth-related variables.
result1: all fertilisation types have a positve effect on aboveground biomass in grassland.
result2: the interaction among fertilisers is synergistic.
general_conclusion: n, p and np fertilisations have an positive effect on aboveground biomass in grassland.

search_strategy: peer-reviewed journal articles were searched using web of science and china national knowledge to compile a database, which included the responses of agb, agbgrass, agbforb, soil available n and p, soil water content, and soil ph to n addition. the following key words were used to identify studies: n addition/deposition/enrichment, n + p addition, n + water (w) addition, biomass production, agb, aboveground net primary production, soil available n and p, and grasslands.
selection_criteria: 1) the experimental data must be collected from field experiments involving n addition and conducted in natural grasslands; 2) experiments must include n-addition treatments and a control treatment; if the field experiment only had n addition as a treatment, the original experimental control was used to estimate the response ratio of only n addition for agb, agbgrass and agbforb; if the n-addition treatments were combined with p or w, the treatments with only p or w addition were regarded as the control treatments to eliminate the effects of other factors on agb, agbgrass and agbforb; 3) agb was measured during the peak growing season, and these data were compiled into a database; data not obtained during the peak growing season were excluded; 4) if experimental data from a particular site was published in different journal articles, the most recent paper or the paper with the longest record was chosen; 5) the means, sample sizes, standard deviations (sds) and/or standard errors (ses) of the treatments and controls were collected or calculated for each case study.
data_analysis: the authors conducted a sensitivity analysis to determine how robust the results were based on the decisions and assumptions made in the meta-analysis (the data structure can take a variety of forms), and a mixed model was used to calculate the weighted response ratio. the relationships between the response ratio of agb and the experimental design parameters and soil and climatic conditions were examined. specifically, regression analysis was used to analyse the relationships between the response ratio of agb and the n addition rates, study durations, climatic factors, soil available n, soil available p, soil water content and soil ph. spss software was used for regression and correlation analyses, and graphs were drawn using origin.
background: Nitrogen (N) deposition has increased globally and has profoundly influenced the structure and function of grasslands. Previous studies have discussed how N addition affects aboveground biomass (AGB), but the effects of N addition on the AGB of different functional groups in grasslands remain unclear.
objective: in this study, the authors conducted a meta-analysis to quantitatively synthesize available studies on the changes in agb, the agb of grasses (agbgrass) and the agb of forbs (agbforb) in grasslands from around the world following n addition. the authors asked the following questions: 1) what are the response patterns of agb to n addition in grasslands around the world? do all plant functional groups respond in a similar way? 2) do different n addition rates, study durations or climatic conditions influence the effects of n addition on agb, agbgrass and agbforb?
result1: across all of the studies at the global scale, n addition significantly increased agb and agbgrass, with average increases of 31% and 79%, respectively, but did not significantly affect agbforb.
result2: NA
general_conclusion: n addition has a positive effect on aboveground biomass of grass while it has no effect on aboveground biomass of forbs. overall, n fertilisation has a positive effect on aboveground biomass.

search_strategy: the authors searched the isi web of science database for published peer-reviewed papers with the topic matching the query ‘phosphorus and grass* and (fertili*er or fertili*ation) and (uptake or yield)’, for all years, to a cut-off date of 31 december 2016.
selection_criteria: 1) field studies with an experimental duration of at least one growing season; 2) studies reporting yield of grass and/or grass/legume mixtures as response variable; 3) studies with experimental treatments for which a suitable control treatment could be identified. control treatments were deemed suitable if experimental factors (i.e. site, sampling time, soil characteristics, and n application rate) were identical to those in the experimental treatment, and the control treatment did not receive any p fertilisation.
data_analysis: the authors performed a mixed‐effects meta‐analysis in r, using the rma.uni function in the “metafor” package18, and weighting ln(r) and pae by the inverse of their variance. they estimated missing variances using the average coefficient of variation across the dataset. the results from all analyses on ln(r) were back‐transformed and reported as the percentage change under p fertilisation ((r − 1) × 100%). both effect sizes were analysed using a mixed-effects model to calculate 95% confidence intervals19. for all analyses, the authors inferred an effect of p fertilisation if the 95% ci of the mean effect size did not overlap with 0. they used a wald test to determine whether treatment effects were statistically different between study categories. to test for possible interactions among controlling factors, spearman’s rank correlation coefficient was calculated for the relationships between factors. rosenthal’s fail-safe n technique at p = 0.05 was used to test the potential impact of publication bias.
background: Because phosphorus (P) is one of the most limiting nutrients in agricultural systems, P fertilisation is essential to feed the world. However, declining P reserves demand far more effective use of this crucial resource.
objective: the authors use a meta-analysis on a global database of 67 studies and 1227 observations with a wide range of soil properties and climatic conditions to assess the general effect of p fertilisation on grassland production across the world. furthermore, they identify soil-related driving factors that determine the success of fertiliser applications.
result1: p fertilisation increased grassland yield by 37% (95% confidence interval: 33 to 40%) averaged over all grasslands, soil types, and fertility levels, resulting in a p agronomic efficiency of 32 kg kg−1.
result2: the phosphorus agronomic efficiency decreased with p application rates: yields increased by 53 kg per kg p applied at rates lower than 25 kg p ha−1, but only by 12 kg kg−1 p at rates higher than 100 kg p ha−1. this indicates that finding a balance between p input and yield response is crucial for optimising fertiliser effectivity, as the agronomic efficiency decreases with higher application rates.
general_conclusion: p fertilisation has a positive effect on crop yield in grassland.

search_strategy: a literature survey of peer-reviewed publications was performed using web of science and google scholar, with the keywords of ‘n2o’, ‘no3−leaching’, ‘n uptake’ or ‘plant yield’and ‘urine’or ‘dung’and ‘soil’or ‘grassland’in combination with ‘ni’, ‘ui’, or ‘biochar’, before february 2016.
selection_criteria: the inhibitor types considered for the analysis were dcd (a ni), pyrazole derivatives (pd, a ni), and n-(n-butyl) thiophosphoric triamide (nbpt, a ui). only direct measurements were included and no data were obtained from modeling studies. studies performed under laboratory, greenhouse, and field conditions were all included. only studies with a measurement period that lasted longer than 30 days were considered.
data_analysis: the effect sizes were calculated for each grouping using a categorical random effects model. the mean effect size for each category and the bias-corrected 95% confidential intervals (cis) were generated by a bootstrapping procedure (9999 iterations). the meta-analysis was conducted using meta-win version 2.0. publication bias was analyzed by rank correlation test using meta-win version 2.0.
background: Excreta (urine and dung) patches on grazed grasslands are significant sources of nitrogen (N) trace gas emissions and leaching. Nitrification inhibitors (NIs), urease inhibitors (UIs) and biochar have been tested to reduce N losses and increase N utilization in various agro-ecosystems. Although the effectiveness of NIs, UIs or biochar on N losses or N utilization for chemical N fertilizers and manures have been evaluated in previous studies, there has been no comprehensive assessment on their effectiveness for excreta patches of grazing animals on grassland.
objective: the authors conducted a comprehensive meta-analysis of their effects on n2o emissions, no3−leaching, plant n uptake, and plant yields  to better understand the effects of inhibitors and biochar on the major n dynamics in excreta patches. the following two main objectives were addressed: 1) evaluating the effects of inhibitors and biochar on n losses or uptake; 2) investigating the main factors that affect the efficacy of inhibitors and biochar in grazed grassland ecosystems.
result1: plant yields were increased significantly after the application of dcd(l) (6%, 4–9%), dcd(z) (14%, 6–25%), pd (3%, 1–5%), nbpt (7%, 6–9%), and nbpt+dcd(l) (12%, 10–14%), whereas biochar addition caused a significant decline in plant yield (−3%, −5% to −2%).
result2: the plant yield increase following nbpt + dcd(l) application was signifi- cantly higher than those with dcd(l), pd, and nbpt.
general_conclusion: dcd inhibitors have a positive effect on yield. biochar has a negative effect on yield.

search_strategy: all peer-reviewed publications that investigated the effects of plant diversity on carbon pools and fluxes in grasslands using the isi web of science, google scholar, and the china national knowledge infrastructure through december 31, 2019. authors used different keyword combinations for the search, including grassland, biomass, production/productivity, aboveground, below-ground, root, soc, rs, rh, carbon pool, carbon flux, diversity, mixtures, pure, monoculture, and richness.
selection_criteria: 1) experiments had at least one pair of data at the same temporal and spatial scales (under monoculture and mixtures), including carbon pools and fluxes; 2) the effect of diversity was clearly described, including diversity level (species richness) and experimental duration; 3) the means, standard deviations/errors and samples size of variables in the monoculture and mixtures groups could be extracted directly from the context, tables, or digitized graphs.
data_analysis: random effects models were used to analyze the weighted average response ratio and meta-regression in the study and the between-sampling variability was estimated by the rma function based on restricted maximum likelihood estimation (reml) with the lme4 package in r 3.5.1. the weights for studies was estimated by sampling standard deviations and the between-sampling variability. to prevent overfitting, the most parsimonious model was selected among all alternatives as long as plant diversity and experimental duration were retained, because they were part of the core hypotheses to be tested. random-effects meta-regression were used to evaluate the relationships among the response ratio of carbon attributes, plant diversity, and experimental duration.
background: Positive relationships between plant species diversity and carbon attributes have been observed in grasslands, but synthesis studies of how plant diversity affects the carbon balance of grasslands and how the response ratio changes over time both remain limited.
objective: to examine the effects of plant diversity loss on natural and manipulated grasslands, measured as the ratio of the main carbon inputs (aboveground biomass, belowground biomass, and total biomass), outputs (soil respiration and heterotrophic respiration), and balance (soil organic carbon) in plant mixtures to the average of those in monocultures. specifically authors tested whether: 1) plant mixtures showed a greater carbon sink than monocultures in grasslands; 2) the positive effects of plant diversity on six carbon attributes increased with experimental duration; and 3) the reduction in carbon sequestration of grassland ecosystems following plant diversity loss would be exacerbated over time.
result1: aboveground biomass increased significantly by an average of 63.6% in plant mixtures compared with the average of those in monocultures.
result2: total biomass increased significantly by an average of 119.5% in plant mixtures compared with the average of those in monocultures.
general_conclusion: across all studies, the average effects of plant mixtures on carbon input attributes were larger than carbon outputs. aboveground biomass increased significantly by an average of 63.6% (95% confidence interval 58.9%–68.6%), total biomass by 119.5% (95% confidence interval, 97.1%–144.3%).

search_strategy: from february to june in 2020, authors conducted a comprehensive search of relevant peer-reviewed articles and dissertations published from the year of 1990 to 2020 in the web of science and proquest databases using combinations of the following search string: (plant ‘diversity’ or ‘biodiversity’ or ‘tree diversity’ or ‘species diversity’ or ‘plant species richness’ or ‘species mixture’ or ‘plant community composition’) and (‘plant growth’ or ‘plant productivity’ or ‘plant biomass’ or ‘basal area’) and (‘soil microbial*’ or ‘soil biota’ or ‘soil bac- terial and fungal*’) and (‘soil carbon’ or ‘soil organic carbon’). authors then cross-checked the references of the relevant articles to identify other relevant book chapters and peer-reviewed reports.
selection_criteria: papers were excluded if were 1) natural diversity gradient studies, 2) controlled global change experiments, in which plant diversity has been altered by global change factors, but not having a direct diversity treatment, 3) meta-analysis studies or review studies, 4) papers not including c storage and other variables that were in the focus of this study. authors kept the papers from biodiversity-ecosystem functioning experiments and experiments that had one-species and mixed-species plantations.
data_analysis: effect sizes and variances were calculated using random-effects models (with restricted maximum-likelihood estimators). to control for the existing non-independence, the factors ‘study’ and ‘site’ were used as random factors in the analyses to account for the non-independence of data coming from the same study. the total heterogeneity of effect sizes was tested within each model. the publication bias was estimated by the dnorm function. all statistical analyses were conducted with the ‘metafor’ package in r.
background: Plant diversity has a strong impact on a plethora of ecosystem functions and services, especially ecosystem carbon (C) storage. However, the potential context-dependency of biodiversity effects across ecosystem types, environmental conditions and carbon pools remains largely unknown.
objective: to explore the effects of plant diversity on different c pools, including aboveground and below- ground plant biomass, soil microbial biomass c and soil c content across different ecosystem types. here, results for grasslands are reported.
result1: aboveground biomass significantly increased in grasslands with higher plant diversity.
result2: NA
general_conclusion: this meta-analysis provides strong empirical evidence that plant species richness significantly enhances ecosystem c storage, with stronger effects on aboveground biomass than on soil c content.

search_strategy: authors used a combination of terms in web of science and examined the title, keywords and abstract to assess the potential eligibility of the study. references from these studies were also used to locate relevant articles.
selection_criteria: only field studies were included in this analysis.
data_analysis: meta-analyses were conducted in r. random effects models generated with the “rma.mv” function of themetaphor package. metaregressions were run on all response variables. to account for non-independence of observations made on the same experimental plots, all models included observation number and publication as random variables. to select models that best explain the heterogeneity in effect sizes, the glmulti package was used. authors used a candidate set of models with only first-level variable combinations (no interactions) for model averaging. relevant variables were narrowed using automated model selection and selected variables for further analyses when the variable importance was 0.8 and above. using the selected variables from this model, authors fitted metaregression models with interactions with the metaphor package using all possible combinations of a single continuous and a single categorical variable. authors used variance inflation factors using the function “vif” in the metaphor package to determine multicollinearity and fit only combinations of variables that were determined to be non-collinear. model fit was compared to the no-interaction model using akaike’s information criterion corrected for small sample size (aicc). marginal and conditional coefficients of determination (r2) and pseudo-r2 were also calculated as metrics of model explanatory power.
background: Biosolids are a source of nutrient-rich organic material that can be used to improve degraded or disturbed soils. Research on vegetation responses to the land application of biosolids has increased in the past 20 years, but there is no consensus on how plant communities respond to biosolids applications.
objective: to explore how the application of biosolids impacts ecosystem processes, including above-ground productivity, total vegetative cover, and plant community responses (species richness, shannon diversity and exotic species success) on reclaimed land. specifically, this study explores how application rates of biosolids or biosolids mixtures (e.g., biosolids mixed with ash, wood chips, lime, etc.) may affect productivity and plant community responses and if these factors impact how long the effect of biosolids persists following its application. here, results for the effects on above-ground net primary productivity and total vegetative cover are reported.
result1: the use of biosolids on degraded lands led to a significant overall increase in above-ground net productivity (p < 0.0001, log response ratio [lrr] = 1.27 [95% confidence interval {ci}: 0.83, 1.71], number of observations [k] = 269) and total vegetative cover (p < 0.0001, lrr = 1.17 [0.81, 1.53], k = 214).
result2: NA
general_conclusion: the land application of biosolids significantly increased productivity and cover on degraded lands restored into grasslands.

search_strategy: the following web databases were searched for documents: isi web of science, science direct, jstor, google (100 first hits) and google scholar (100 first hits). a high-sensitivity and low-specificity approach was used to ensure that all important relevant information was found. the databases searches were carried out between september 2012 and january 2013. any apparently relevant citations or links were followed one step away from the original hit. in addition, national and international experts on the subject were asked for any related literature and unpublished data
selection_criteria: 1) relevant subjects: natural or seminatural grasslands in temperate mountain zones. mediterranean, subtropical and arid climates that occur within the temperate latitudes were excluded; 2) types of intervention: addition of nitrogen (alone or in combination with other nutrients); 3) types of comparator: non fertilized control plots (experimental studies) or suitable reference areas that have not been fertilized (observational studies). control plots had to be managed in the same way as treatment plots with the exception; types of outcome: species richness or shannon index of diversity (h0) of at least one taxonomic group. changes in biomass production or absolute abundance of functional groups were also recorded if provided. the authors limit this review to vascular plants.
data_analysis: random- and mixed-effects meta-analytical models were used. here, the q test and i2 statistic were used to assess heterogeneity among studies.in addition to the weighted mas that utilized variances among replicates, unweighted meta-analyses were applied to a larger data set that included effect sizes without associated variances. publication bias was assessed using funnel plots, by applying a regression test for funnel plot asymmetry. all statistics were performed using r version 3.1.2.
background: Although the influence of nitrogen (N) addition on grassland plant communities has been widely studied, it is still unclear whether observed patterns and underlying mechanisms are constant across biomes.
objective: this systematic review thus focuses on temperate mountain ecosystems including montane, subalpine and alpine grasslands. it aims at assessing the available evidence regarding the effects of n addition upon biodiversity and productivity of temperate zone mountain grasslands. in particular, it investigates how abiotic factors that potentially interact with n addition drive the variable plant community responses that are commonly observed in nature. the term n addition refers here to n from anthropogenic origin, either in the form of agricultural fertilization (sometimes in combination with other nutrients) or atmospheric deposition.
result1: vascular plant and grass biomass were higher in fertilized compared to unfertilized plots.
result2: sedge and legume biomass did not change following n addition, while forb biomass exhibited a significant increase with weighted ma.
general_conclusion: overall vascular plant biomass was higher in fertilized compared to unfertilized plots.

search_strategy: peer-reviewed publications were searched using web of science to build a compiled database, which included the responses to p addition of different variables related to plant biomass production, plant n and p concentrations, and soil available n and p concentrations.
selection_criteria: 1) measurements and data were only collected from field manipulative experiments of p addition that conducted in natural terrestrial ecosystems; 2) the examined variables were plant biomass production at the community level, plant n and p concentration, and soil n and p concentration; 3) when data from the same site were presented in multiple publications, a single measurement from the latest sample date was used to meet the statistical assumption of independence among observations.
data_analysis: the authors used the metawin software 2.1 to calculate to calculate the rr, the variance, the weighting factor, the weighted response ratio (rr++), and the 95% confidence interval of rr++ for the purpose of statistic tests. to examine whether n addition will stimulate p limitation, the authors compare the effect size of p addition between the groups of with or without n addition. t-test was used to test the statistic differences. the statistic differences between the effect sizes of p addition and that of n addition were also analyzed by t-test. the authors used the linear regression methods to analyze the relationships of biomass response ratios with the response ratios of soil p availability, leaf p concentration, soil and plant n : p ratios. the regression analysis was conducted with the spss software.
background: Nitrogen (N) and phosphorus (P), either individually or in combination, have been demonstrated to limit biomass production in terrestrial ecosystems. Field studies have been extensively synthesized to assess global patterns of N impacts on terrestrial ecosystem processes. However, to our knowledge, no synthesis has been done so far to reveal global patterns of P impacts on terrestrial ecosystems, especially under different nitrogen (N) levels.
objective: the objective of this study was to assess effects of p addition on biomass production, plant and soil n and p concentrations, and n : p ratio under different ecosystem types, fertilizer forms and rates, and experimental durations. the authors conducted a meta-analysis of results from field experiments on responses of aboveground (agb) and belowground biomass production (bgb) to manipulative p addition under ambient and enriched n conditions. the specific questions this synthesis addressed were as follows: 1) what are the global patterns of the responses of terrestrial biomass production, plant and soil n and p concentrations, and n : p ratios to p addition? 2) whether p limitation is enhanced under increased n loading? 3) whether the p- induced increase in ecosystem biomass production is correlated with changes in soil p availability, leaf p concentration, or n : p ratio?
result1: in grassland, p addition increased agb by 30% with n addition, but did not significantly change agb without n addition.
result2: NA
general_conclusion: p fertilisation compatred to no fertilisation showed no effect on aboveground biomass of grassland with ambient n conditions while it showed positive effect in grassland with elevated nitrogen conditions.

search_strategy: the authors systematically searched for published field studies that reported effects of organic amendments on one or more ecosystem properties. they first performed a web of science search and then identified additional studies by screening cited references in papers obtained. gray literature cited by a peer-reviewed paper was considered eligible if it met all other criteria.
selection_criteria: 1) field experiment with control (no amendment) and treatment (amendment) plots; 2) non forested ecosystem with sufficient plant biomass to support livestock grazing; 3) carbon-based amendment to which synthetic nutrients had not been added; 4) soil not subjected to “severe disturbance” within the 20-year period prior to experiment initiation (as reported by the paper's authors). the authors considered severe disturbance to include activities such as mining, roadcuts, and agricultural tillage; 5) arid, semiarid, or mediterranean köppen–geiger climate zone; 6) reported effect of amendment addition on at least one of 20 prospective response variables.
data_analysis: all analyses were conducted in r. the authors chose five predictors—climate zone, days between amendment application and measurement, amount of amendment applied, amendment total n concentration, and (for soil outcomes) soil sample depth—that were reported for 91%–100% of observations.
background: Interest in land application of organic amendments—such as biosolids, composts, and manures—is growing due to their potential to increase soil carbon and help mitigate climate change, as well as to support soil health and regenerative agriculture. While organic amendments are predominantly applied to croplands, their application is increasingly proposed on relatively arid rangelands that do not typically receive fertilizers or other inputs, creating unique concerns for outcomes such as native plant diversity and water quality.
objective: the authors present a meta‐analysis of organic amendment additions to rangelands in arid, semiarid, and mediterranean climates, synthesizing amendment effects on a suite of ecosystem outcomes. specifically, they analyzed 11 ecosystem outcomes that had sufficient published data: soil organic carbon concentration, soil water holding capacity, aboveground net primary productivity (anpp), plant species diversity, plant tissue nitrogen (n) concentration, soil co2 emissions, soil lead (pb) concentration, plant tissue pb concentration, runoff quantity, runoff phosphorus, and runoff nitrate. here, results for aboveground net primary productivity are provided.
result1: amendment addition increased aboveground net primary production - anpp (mean = 1.43×).
result2: NA
general_conclusion: amendment addition to rangeland increased aboveground net primary production.

search_strategy: the authors searched for peer-reviewed journal articles published up to 7 february 2020 and catalogued in the isi web of science using the search terms “fertilization” or “fertilisation” or “nutrients” or “nutrient addition” or “micronutrient” or “nitrogen” or “phosphorus” or “potassium” or “npk” and “arthropods” or “insects” and “prairie” or “grassland” or “pasture” or “savannah” or “savanna” or “steppe” or “old field”. to provide a more adequate representation of fertilization effects and help reduce publication bias, the authors additionally searched the lter (long term ecological research) database for raw experimental data.
selection_criteria: the authors included only those studies that were non-cage field experiments in non-agricultural grassland ecosystems (although the experimental area could be mowed, grazed, or have been previously used for agriculture). additionally, the authors selected only studies that included both a fertilization treatment and a control (no fertilization) treatment, and from which they were able to obtain either raw arthropod abundances or both means and standard deviations of arthropod abundances in treatment and control plots.
data_analysis: to identify which fertilizer predictor variables best estimated arthropod responses to fertilization (effect sizes), the authors used an akaike information criterion (aic) framework. to test how both the underlying gradients and responses of plant biomass and plant nutrient content to fertilization mediated arthropod response to fertilization the authors used linear models within an aic framework. the authors used egger’s regression test in the r package metafor  and a funnel plot to test for publication bias effects and found none.
background: Ongoing alterations to Earth’s biogeochemical cycles are expected to impact plants, plant consumers and all subsequent trophic levels. While fertilization experiments often reveal arthropod nutrient limitation by nitrogen and phosphorus via effects on plant nutrient density and biomass, these macronutrients are only two of many nutrients important to arthropod fitness. Micronutrients are key to osmoregulation and enzyme function and can interact synergistically with macronutrients to shape the geography of arthropod abundance.
objective: the primary goal was to test for the ubiquity of n, p, k and micronutrient limitation – or some combination of the above – on total arthropod abundance and the abundance of six common feeding guilds: chewing herbivores, sucking herbivores, omnivores, predators, pollinators and detritivores.
result1: aboveground plant biomass response to fertilization varied from no response in the case of k + micronutrients and pk + micronutrients fertilization to a positive response, with np fertiliser addition resulting in the greatest increase in plant biomass (effect size: +1.3).
result2: NA
general_conclusion: aboveground plant biomass response to fertilization showed a positive response for n, p, np, npk, npk + micronutrients, nk + micronutrients, while it showed no effect for pk + micronutrients and k + micronutrients.

search_strategy: the search for data concerning n addition experiments focused on peer-reviewed articles that studied the impact of n addition on biomass, the number of species per unit area (species richness) or both variables at the community level. relevant studies were identiﬁed through searches of the bibliographic database of the isi web of knowledge and the references therein (1955 to 2009). the search terms nitrogen, addition, vegetation and experiment* were used, singly and in various combinations.
selection_criteria: 1) only data from in situ n addition experiments were incorporated into the database. ex situ n addition experiments or papers considering vegetation change as a consequence of atmospheric depositions were not considered; 2) the authors included studies performed in terrestrial ecosystems and classiﬁed them into forest understoreys, heathlands, grasslands and three types of wetland. grassland studies were only included if the area had been continuously grassland for the last 20 years. 3) only experiments in which inorganic n was added (to be comparable with n additions through atmospheric depositions) were included. simultaneous additions of phosphorus or potassium were omitted, as the impact of these nutrients may interfere with the effect of n. 4) to unravel the relative impact of n addition from all other environmental variables being randomly assigned to treatments, only studies reporting results for both n-treated and control plots were selected. 5) the authors focused on articles reporting data on the impact of n addition on biomass or species richness or on both variables.
data_analysis: the authors calculated the effect size and a 95% bootstrapping conﬁdence interval (ci) with n = 1000 iterations using resampling stats v.4.0. due to a lack of standard deviation or error estimates in some studies, the bootstrapping approach used was more appropriate than the standard meta-analytical procedures.
background: Elevated inputs of biologically reactive nitrogen (N) are considered to be one of the most substantial threats to biodiversity in terrestrial ecosystems. Several attempts have been made to scrutinize the factors driving species loss following excess N input, but generalizations across sites or vegetation types cannot yet be made.
objective: the authors conducted a large-scale meta-analysis of in situ n addition experiments, focusing on the effects on the vegetation’s biomass and species richness. here, results for biomass are reported.
result1: signiﬁcant positive effects of n addition on biomass were found for grassland.
result2: NA
general_conclusion: nitrogen addition showed positive effect on biomass in grassland.

search_strategy: a literature survey of peer-reviewed publications was performed using web of science and google scholar, with the keywords of ‘n2o’, ‘no3−leaching’, ‘n uptake’ or ‘plant yield’and ‘urine’or ‘dung’and ‘soil’or ‘grassland’in combination with ‘ni’, ‘ui’, or ‘biochar’, before february 2016.
selection_criteria: the inhibitor types considered for the analysis were dcd (a ni), pyrazole derivatives (pd, a ni), and n-(n-butyl) thiophosphoric triamide (nbpt, a ui). only direct measurements were included and no data were obtained from modeling studies. studies performed under laboratory, greenhouse, and field conditions were all included. only studies with a measurement period that lasted longer than 30 days were considered.
data_analysis: the effect sizes were calculated for each grouping using a categorical random effects model. the mean effect size for each category and the bias-corrected 95% confidential intervals (cis) were generated by a bootstrapping procedure (9999 iterations). the meta-analysis was conducted using meta-win version 2.0. publication bias was analyzed by rank correlation test using meta-win version 2.0.
background: Excreta (urine and dung) patches on grazed grasslands are significant sources of nitrogen (N) trace gas emissions and leaching. Nitrification inhibitors (NIs), urease inhibitors (UIs) and biochar have been tested to reduce N losses and increase N utilization in various agro-ecosystems. Although the effectiveness of NIs, UIs or biochar on N losses or N utilization for chemical N fertilizers and manures have been evaluated in previous studies, there has been no comprehensive assessment on their effectiveness for excreta patches of grazing animals on grassland.
objective: the authors conducted a comprehensive meta-analysis of their effects on n2o emissions, no3−leaching, plant n uptake, and plant yields  to better understand the effects of inhibitors and biochar on the major n dynamics in excreta patches. the following two main objectives were addressed: 1) evaluating the effects of inhibitors and biochar on n losses or uptake; 2) investigating the main factors that affect the efficacy of inhibitors and biochar in grazed grassland ecosystems.
result1: there were significant reductions in no3− leaching following the application of dcd(l) (−46%, −52% to −40%), dcd(z) (−34%, −58% to −13%), and nbpt+dcd(l) (−42%, −50% to −35%).
result2: NA
general_conclusion: dcd inhibitors have a positive effect in reducing no3 leaching.
