search_strategy: the authors searched literature on the response of aboveground net primary production (anpp) to n addition that was published in journals included on the web of science from 1900 to 2015.
selection_criteria: 1) the studies must be implemented in terrestrial ecosystems, not including agricultural systems; 2) the experiments include at least two levels of n addition plus a control treatment under the same condition; 3) the means and sample sizes for the response variables are explicitly shown.
data_analysis: data were analyzed with the spss 21.0 software. the authors used a non parametric analysis of bootstrap resampling (repeated n = 5000 times) to determine the means of nitrogen response efficiency (nre) and the difference in nre between n levels (δnre) and their 95% confidence internal (ci) at the global scale, across different ecosystem types (forest, grassland and wetland) and different ranges of n addition rates.
background: The continually increasing nitrogen (N) deposition is expected to increase ecosystem aboveground net primary production (ANPP) until it exceeds plant N demand, causing a nonlinear response and N saturation for ANPP. However, the nonlinear response of ANPP to N addition gradient and the N saturation threshold have not been comprehensively quantified yet for terrestrial ecosystems.
objective: the authors test the n saturation for anpp by analyzing nitrogen response efficiency (nre) and the difference in nre between n levels (δnre) in each study. in order to identify which ecosystems or areas are more likely to be saturated with n, the authors analyzed the variations of plant nre with ecosystem types and environmental factors. specifically, they address the following questions: 1) how terrestrial anpp responds to n addition gradient at the global scale and in different ecosystems, linearly or non-linearly? 2) if it shows a nonlinear response, what are the n saturation thresholds for anpp non linearity in different ecosystems? 3) how ecosystem type, n addition rate and environmental factors influence the n saturation thresholds?
result1: n addition has a positive effect on nitrogen response efficiency.
result2: NA
general_conclusion: n addition has a positive effect on nitrogen response efficiency.

search_strategy: the search was conducted in the database web of science for papers using the title words ‘input’, ‘deposition’, or ‘fertili*’ and the keywords ‘soil’ ‘nitrogen’ ‘microbial’ and ‘biomass’. articles cited in review papers or meta-analyses that analyzed data from n fertilization trials were also included in the search. the literature search was concluded in may 2015.
selection_criteria: 1) the data were from field trials with annual crops (except lowland rice cropping systems in paddy soils) or permanent grassland; 2) the study reported microbial biomass both from an unfertilized control and a treatment with mineral n addition; 3) trials in which fertilization treatments were discontinued more than a year before soil sampling were not included in the analysis.
data_analysis: the meta-analysis was performed using the program metawin. the same software was used for meta-regression analyses to investigate the effects of trial duration. the missing standard deviations were calculated using the average coefficient of variation (cv) of the datasets where the standard deviation was reported. separate cvs were calculated for the control and fertilized treatment of each ecosystem. all statistics were performed using r version 2.13.0.
background: Anthropogenic inputs of reactive nitrogen (N) to terrestrial ecosystems have increased considerably over the past several decades.
objective: to quantify the long- and short-term effects of mineral n input (ammonium, nitrate or urea) on soil microorganisms in permanent grassland and annual cropping systems. specifically, to test the hypotheses that 1) the response of the microbial biomass to n addition differs between annual cropping systems and permanent grassland, that 2) the effects of n addition become more pronounced over time, and that 3) the differences can be explained by shifts in the microbial community composition. here, the results for natural grasslands are reported.
result1: for soil microbial biomass, the negative effect of n input was significant only in long-term trials, but not in shorter-term studies.
result2: NA
general_conclusion: in the short term, n inputs may increase primary production in natural grassland. however, n inputs gradually reduce grassland plant species richness which likely leads to the observed decrease in soil microbial biomass. over time, the effect of plant species richness on soil microbial biomass becomes more pronounced.

search_strategy: a search of peer-reviewed journal articles was conducted using the web of science, google scholar and china national knowledge infrastructure from 1995 to december 2017 using the following search term combinations: (n addition/simulated n deposition/n enrichment/ n fertilizer) and (soil microbial biomass/microbial communities/microbial respiration/microbial activity/microbe/enzyme).
selection_criteria: 1) experiments included at least two treatments (control and n treatment) at the same site; 2) only field-based experiments were included; 3) the means, standard deviations (sds) or standard errors (ses) and sample sizes could be directly extracted from content, tables or digitized graphs of the publication; 4) the biomass of fungi, bacteria, actinomycetes and amf was determined by measuring the level of phospholipid fatty acids (plfas), and microbial biomass carbon (mbc) and microbial biomass nitrogen (mbn) were measured by chloroform fumigation extraction.
data_analysis: the r software package was used to conduct this meta-analysis. natural logs of the rrs for individual and combined treatments were determined by specifying studies as random factors in the model with the “metafor“ package. if the 95% confidence intervals (cis) of the rr did not overlap with zero, the rr was considered indicative of a significant n-induced response.
background: Soil microbes play an important role in ecosystem processes, including carbon (C) and nutrient cycling. Nitrogen (N) enrichment is known to affect soil microbes, but whether other factors affect the impact of N enrichment on soil microbial biomass and composition and extracellular enzyme activities (EEAs) remains unclear.
objective: the primary goal was to understand the reason for the conflicting results presented to date and to expand our knowledge regarding the response of soil microbes to n enrichment. they address the following issues: 1) how soil microbial biomass, microbial community composition and enzyme activities respond to n enrichment; 2) whether there are other factors that are correlated with the inconsistent effects of n enrichment on soil microbes; and 3) whether there are threshold effects associated with microbial responses to n enrichment and do they differ among the microbial characteristics.
result1: n enrichment had no effect on total microbial biomass, and showed negative effects on mbc and mbn in grassland.
result2: NA
general_conclusion: n enrichment has no effect on microbial biomass and negative effect on microbial biomass c and n.

search_strategy: the authors searched the relevant journal articles published before september 2020 in the datasets of the web of science and the china knowledge resource integrated database, with the keywords “ch4” or “methane” or “ghg” or “greenhouse gas” and “n” or “nitrogen” or “nh4” or “nh3” or “ammonium” or “nitrate” and “addition” or “deposition” or “input” or “application” or “fertilization” or “amendment” or “enrichment”.
selection_criteria: 1) both control and treatment experiments are included; (2) n addition experiments are conducted in the field, rather than in laboratory incubation; 3) the means, standard errors (se) or standard deviations (sd), and sample sizes are clearly reported or can be determined arbitrarily; 4) n addition duration is longer than a growing season or a full year; 5) the data obtained under different n addition levels, durations, forms, and experimental locations are independent.
data_analysis: the percentage change (%) transformed from the weighted response ratio (rr++) is used to quantify the magnitude of the impacts of n addition. if the 95% ci of rr++ for a selected variable does not overlap zero, the impact of n addition on this variable is considered to be significant at p < 0.05. furthermore, between-group heterogeneity tests (qb tests) are conducted to analyze whether there is a statistical difference among the impacts ofn addition in different groups.
background: Elevated nitrogen (N) addition from anthropogenic activities has great impacts on soil methane (CH4) uptake, which could interrupt the existing global CH4 balance and cause feedbacks to climate and biogeochemical processes. Previous studies have come to inconsistent conclusions on both the quantification of the response of CH4 uptake to N addition and understanding of its underlying mechanisms, probably due to the lack of experimental data.
objective: the aims of the meta-analysis was to quantify the response of ch4 uptake to n addition, and further reveal its underlying mechanisms, based on the most recent papers published before september 2020. specifically, the following questions are addressed: what are the differences in the responses of ch4 uptake to n addition in different ecosystems? how do experimental conditions (n addition level, duration, and forms) affect the ch4 uptake response? based on previous experimental and synthesis studies, the authors hypothesize that: 1) the upland soil ch4 uptake could be reduced on average under n addition; and 2) there exists a threshold of n addition (level and/or duration) which indicates a shift of the effects of n addition on soil ch4 uptake to an opposite trend.
result1: n fertilisation showed no effect on microbial biomass carbon and microbial biomass nitrogen.
result2: NA
general_conclusion: n fertilisation showed no effect on microbial biomass carbon and microbial biomass nitrogen.

search_strategy: the peer-reviewed articles reporting effects of n addition on soil microbes in terrestrial ecosystems were collected globally by searching the web of science, google scholar, and china national knowledge infrastructure till november 2016. the keywords and terms used for the literature online-searching were “(nitrogen deposition or nitrogen addition or nitrogen enrichment or nitrogen fertilizer or nitrogen amendment or nitrogen elevated) and (microbial biomass or microbial communities or fungi or bacteria) and (soil)”.
selection_criteria: 1) only field experiments were included; 2) experimental and control plots must be established within the same experimental site (same microclimate, vegetation and soil types between the treatments); 3) the n addition rates were clearly reported.
data_analysis: if the number of data points used for assessing rr++ of a concerned variable was greater than 20, the 95% ci was calculated. if the number of data points was less than 20, the bootstrapping method was used to obtain the lowest and highest 2.5% values as the bootstrap confidence based on 5000 iterations. principal component analyses (pca) were conducted in order to identify the multivariate effects of soil acidification, increased n availability, climate factors (latitude, mat, and map), and n addition regimes (n addition rate and study duration) on the rrs of microbial biomass (pooled mbc and total plfa) and community composition (f:b and gp:gn) and their interactions.
background: Anthropogenic nitrogen (N) deposition is expected to increase substantially and continuously in the future. Soil N availability regulates microbial communities and the decomposition and formation of soil organic matter, which have great impacts on global carbon (C) cycling.
objective: the objectives were to explore general responses of soil microbial communities to n addition and the underlying mechanisms.
result1: n addition decreased the microbial carbon biomass but increased the total microbial biomass in grassland.
result2: nitrogen addition decreased microbial nitrogen in grassland.
result3: n addition increased bacteria biomass, but decreased fungi and arbuscolar mycorrhizal biomass. no effect was reported for actinomycetes.
general_conclusion: n fertilization has a positive effect on bacteria, gram +, gram - biomass, negative effect on microbial carbon biomass, fungi biomass and arbuscolar mycorrhizal fungi biomass and no effect on phospholipid fatty acid (plfa), microbial nitrogen and actinomycetes biomass.

search_strategy: authors systematically searched all peer-reviewed journal articles and theses that investigated the effects of plant diversity on microbial biomass, fungi: bacteria ratio, g+:g− bacteria ratio, microbial c:n ratio and respiration, using the web of science and google scholar, up to 1st november, 2018. various keyword combinations were used for the search, such as (species diversity or tree diversity or richness or mix species or mix tree or mixture or intercrop) and (microbial abundance or microbial biomass or microbe or microbial or soil biota or microbial community or fungi or bacteria or microbial biomass nitrogen or microbial respiration or basal respiration or microbial activity).
selection_criteria: 1) studies isolated the effects of plant diversity from other factors, such as stand age and topography; 2) the microbial attributes could be extracted directly from the text, tables, and figures.
data_analysis: the number of replications was used for weighting effect sizes. for each microbial attribute, authors tested whether its response to plant mixtures differed from zero and whether the effect size was affected by plant species richness, stand age, and ecosystem type. the analysis were conducted using restricted maximum likelihood estimation with the lme4 package with wr as the weight for each corresponding observation. to prevent overfitting, authors selected the most parsimonious model among all alternatives with the condition to keep plant species richness ans stand age, as they were part of the core hypotheses to be tested. the model selection was accomplished by using the ‘dredge’ function of the mumin package. all analyses were performed in r 3.5.2.
background: Soil microorganisms make up a significant portion of biodiversity and play a critical role in many ecological processes, such as the cycling of carbon and nutrients. Despite the critical influence of plant diversity on plant resources available for soil microorganisms and alterations to the micro-environment, the global effect of reduced plant diversity on soil microorganisms remains uncertain.
objective: to investigate the effects of plant diversity on total microbial, bacterial, and fungal biomass, fungi:bacteria ratio, g+:g− bacteria ratio, microbial c:n ratio, respiration, and metabolic quotient across global terrestrial biomes. here, results for grasslands are reported.
result1: soil microbial biomass in grassland increased in species mixtures.
result2: soil bacterial biomass in grassland did not significantly differ in species mixtures compared to monocultures.
result3: soil fungal biomass in grassland did not significantly differ in species mixtures compared to monocultures.
general_conclusion: this study underlines strong relationships between plant diversity and soil microorganisms across global terrestrial ecosystems and suggests the importance of plant diversity in maintaining belowground ecosystem functioning.

search_strategy: from february to june in 2020, authors conducted a comprehensive search of relevant peer-reviewed articles and dissertations published from the year of 1990 to 2020 in the web of science and proquest databases using combinations of the following search string: (plant ‘diversity’ or ‘biodiversity’ or ‘tree diversity’ or ‘species diversity’ or ‘plant species richness’ or ‘species mixture’ or ‘plant community composition’) and (‘plant growth’ or ‘plant productivity’ or ‘plant biomass’ or ‘basal area’) and (‘soil microbial*’ or ‘soil biota’ or ‘soil bac- terial and fungal*’) and (‘soil carbon’ or ‘soil organic carbon’). authors then cross-checked the references of the relevant articles to identify other relevant book chapters and peer-reviewed reports.
selection_criteria: papers were excluded if were 1) natural diversity gradient studies, 2) controlled global change experiments, in which plant diversity has been altered by global change factors, but not having a direct diversity treatment, 3) meta-analysis studies or review studies, 4) papers not including c storage and other variables that were in the focus of this study. authors kept the papers from biodiversity-ecosystem functioning experiments and experiments that had one-species and mixed-species plantations.
data_analysis: effect sizes and variances were calculated using random-effects models (with restricted maximum-likelihood estimators). to control for the existing non-independence, the factors ‘study’ and ‘site’ were used as random factors in the analyses to account for the non-independence of data coming from the same study. the total heterogeneity of effect sizes was tested within each model. the publication bias was estimated by the dnorm function. all statistical analyses were conducted with the ‘metafor’ package in r.
background: Plant diversity has a strong impact on a plethora of ecosystem functions and services, especially ecosystem carbon (C) storage. However, the potential context-dependency of biodiversity effects across ecosystem types, environmental conditions and carbon pools remains largely unknown.
objective: to explore the effects of plant diversity on different c pools, including aboveground and below- ground plant biomass, soil microbial biomass c and soil c content across different ecosystem types. here, results for grasslands are reported.
result1: responses of soil biota were not significant when analysed for grasslands.
result2: microbial biomass c in grassland significantly increased in grasslands with higher plant diversity.
general_conclusion: responses of soil biotic environment to plant diversity were not significant when analysed for grasslands.

search_strategy: peer-reviewed publications published prior to june 2019 which investigated the effects of plant diversity on soil organi carbon (soc) and soil microbial biomass carbon (smbc) using the isi web of science and google scholar with the search term: ’soil organic carbon or microbial biomass carbon or soil microbial quotient and diversity or richness or mixture or pure or polyculture or monoculture or overyielding’, and also authors searched references within these papers.
selection_criteria: 1) papers were purposely designed to test the effects of plant diversity on soc content, soc stock, and smbc in mineral soils; 2) they had at least one species mixture treatment and corresponding monocultures; 3) they had the same initial climatic and soil properties in the monoculture and mixture treatment plots.
data_analysis: the number of replications was used for weighting effect sizes. models were tested using the restricted maximum likelihood estimation with the lme4 package. to prevent overfitting, authors selected the most parsimonious model among all alternatives with the condition to retain species richness, as it was intrinsic to the purpose of the study to assess the effect of the species richness in mixtures. the model selection was accomplished by using the ’dredge’ function of the mumin package. in order to assess whether results were biased by the relatively few data points with higher species richness (e.g. a species richness of 60 in some experiments), authors conducted the same analysis for the data set after removing observations with 60 species. they compared the estimates and species-richness trends for the data sets with and without a species richness of 60, and found that both data sets yielded qualitatively similar estimates and trends. all statistical analyses were performed in r 3.5.2.
background: Soil organic carbon (SOC) is a valuable resource for mediating global climate change and securing food production. Despite an alarming rate of global plant diversity loss, uncertainties concerning the effects of plant diversity on SOC remain, because plant diversity not only stimulates litter inputs via increased productivity, thus enhancing SOC, but also stimulates microbial respiration, thus reducing SOC.
objective: to examine the overall effects of species mixture on soil organic carbon (soc) content and stock, soil microbial biomass carbon (smbc), and smbc/soc in mineral soils. furthermore, to test whether these effects increase with species richness (or functional group richness) in mixtures and with stand age, and whether these effects differ across a wide range of ecosystem types, mean annual temperatures, and annual aridity indices at the study sites, and across soil depths. here, results on grassland ecosystems are reported.
result1: plant species mixtures increased smbc in grasslands.
result2: NA
general_conclusion: plant species mixtures increased smbc in grasslands.

search_strategy: authors compiled published and unpublished data from experiments that orthogonally manipulated grassland plant diversity and at least one global environmental change factor.
selection_criteria: 1) each study had at least three levels of plant species richness and two levels of global environmental change factor treatment.
data_analysis: the mean log-response ratios from different studies were calculated using random effect models [restricted maximum- likelihood estimator (reml)] with 10 000 bootstrapped 95% confidence intervals (bias-corrected estimates) based on the sample variances of log-response ratio using the metafor package for r statistical software version 3.1.0. bootstrapping was carried out in the boot package. effect size estimates were weighted for each study based on the sum of the study variance and the estimate of random-effects variance.
background: Soil microbial biomass is a key determinant of carbon dynamics in the soil. Several studies have shown that soil microbial biomass significantly increases with plant species diversity, but it remains unclear whether plant species diversity can also stabilize soil microbial biomass in a changing environment.
objective: to examine the consistency of main and interactive effects of plant diversity and global environmental change factors on soil microbial biomass in experimental grasslands.
result1: significant positive effects of plant diversity (high vs. low plant diversity and intermediate vs. low plant diversity) on soil microbial biomass were found.
result2: plant diversity effects were greater in high vs. low and inter vs. low contrasts as compared to high vs. intermediate plant diversity contrasts.
general_conclusion: results show that higher plant diversity significantly enhances soil microbial biomass with the strongest effects in long-term field experiments.

search_strategy: the authors searched journal articles published before october 2015 using the web of science. the keywords and phrases used for the literature search were ‘nitrogen deposition’ or ‘nitrogen addition’ or ‘nitrogen enrichment’ or ‘nitrogen fertilizer’ or ‘nitrogen amendment’ or ‘nitrogen elevated’ and ‘soil extracellular enzymes’ and ‘terrestrial’ or ‘soil’ or ‘land’.
selection_criteria: 1) only field experiments were included, and only studies with durations longer than 1 year. control and n-addition treatments had to be at the same experimental site; that is, the microclimate and vegetation and soil types had to be similar between treatments; 2) standard deviations (sds) and numbers of replicates were reported.
data_analysis: to determine whether n addition had a significant effect, the authors applied a random model using metawin, in which bootstrap 95% confidence intervals were calculated for each categorical group. pearson correlation analyses were used to evaluate the relationships between the rrs for the soil eeas and 1) environmental variables, 2) n-addition methods and 3) substrate n concentrations. the total heterogeneity (qt) for each categorical group was divided into heterogeneities among groups (qm) and between groups (qb). due to the preferential publication of larger over smaller effects, the authors used a series of statistical measures to evaluate publication bias within each group.
background: Unprecedented levels of nitrogen (N) have been deposited in ecosystems over the past century, which is expected to have cascading effects on microbially mediated soil respiration (SR). Extracellular enzymes play critical roles on the degradation of soil organic matter, and measurements of their activities are potentially useful indicators of SR. The links between soil extracellular enzymatic activities (EEAs) and SR under N addition, however, have not been established.
objective: the objectives of this study were: 1) to test whether the response of sr to n addition could be linked to the responses of soil eeas; 2) and, if so, to investigate the responses of these eeas to the additional n in various types of ecosystems and the different methods of n addition; 3) to further explore the factors affecting the possible links between soil eeas and sr, such as substrate n availability and ph.
result1: nitrogen addition significantly increased glycosidase activity by 5.5% in grassland.
result2: glycosidase activity effect sizes were positively correlated with soil respiration effect sizes for grassland.
general_conclusion: n addition has a positive effect on soil glycosidase activity.

search_strategy: the authors systematically searched for published field studies that reported effects of organic amendments on one or more ecosystem properties. they first performed a web of science search and then identified additional studies by screening cited references in papers obtained. gray literature cited by a peer-reviewed paper was considered eligible if it met all other criteria.
selection_criteria: 1) field experiment with control (no amendment) and treatment (amendment) plots; 2) non forested ecosystem with sufficient plant biomass to support livestock grazing; 3) carbon-based amendment to which synthetic nutrients had not been added; 4) soil not subjected to “severe disturbance” within the 20-year period prior to experiment initiation (as reported by the paper's authors). the authors considered severe disturbance to include activities such as mining, roadcuts, and agricultural tillage; 5) arid, semiarid, or mediterranean köppen–geiger climate zone; 6) reported effect of amendment addition on at least one of 20 prospective response variables.
data_analysis: all analyses were conducted in r. the authors chose five predictors—climate zone, days between amendment application and measurement, amount of amendment applied, amendment total n concentration, and (for soil outcomes) soil sample depth—that were reported for 91%–100% of observations.
background: Interest in land application of organic amendments—such as biosolids, composts, and manures—is growing due to their potential to increase soil carbon and help mitigate climate change, as well as to support soil health and regenerative agriculture. While organic amendments are predominantly applied to croplands, their application is increasingly proposed on relatively arid rangelands that do not typically receive fertilizers or other inputs, creating unique concerns for outcomes such as native plant diversity and water quality.
objective: the authors present a meta‐analysis of organic amendment additions to rangelands in arid, semiarid, and mediterranean climates, synthesizing amendment effects on a suite of ecosystem outcomes. specifically, they analyzed 11 ecosystem outcomes that had sufficient published data: soil organic carbon concentration, soil water holding capacity, aboveground net primary productivity (anpp), plant species diversity, plant tissue nitrogen (n) concentration, soil co2 emissions, soil lead (pb) concentration, plant tissue pb concentration, runoff quantity, runoff phosphorus, and runoff nitrate. here, results for runoff quantity are provided.
result1: amendment addition decreased runoff quantity (mean = 0.18×).
result2: NA
general_conclusion: amendment addition to rangeland decreased runoff quantity.

search_strategy: peer-reviewed journal articles were searched using web of science and china national knowledge to compile a database, which included the responses of agb, agbgrass, agbforb, soil available n and p, soil water content, and soil ph to n addition. the following key words were used to identify studies: n addition/deposition/enrichment, n + p addition, n + water (w) addition, biomass production, agb, aboveground net primary production, soil available n and p, and grasslands.
selection_criteria: 1) the experimental data must be collected from field experiments involving n addition and conducted in natural grasslands; 2) experiments must include n-addition treatments and a control treatment; if the field experiment only had n addition as a treatment, the original experimental control was used to estimate the response ratio of only n addition for agb, agbgrass and agbforb; if the n-addition treatments were combined with p or w, the treatments with only p or w addition were regarded as the control treatments to eliminate the effects of other factors on agb, agbgrass and agbforb; 3) agb was measured during the peak growing season, and these data were compiled into a database; data not obtained during the peak growing season were excluded; 4) if experimental data from a particular site was published in different journal articles, the most recent paper or the paper with the longest record was chosen; 5) the means, sample sizes, standard deviations (sds) and/or standard errors (ses) of the treatments and controls were collected or calculated for each case study.
data_analysis: the authors conducted a sensitivity analysis to determine how robust the results were based on the decisions and assumptions made in the meta-analysis (the data structure can take a variety of forms), and a mixed model was used to calculate the weighted response ratio. the relationships between the response ratio of agb and the experimental design parameters and soil and climatic conditions were examined. specifically, regression analysis was used to analyse the relationships between the response ratio of agb and the n addition rates, study durations, climatic factors, soil available n, soil available p, soil water content and soil ph. spss software was used for regression and correlation analyses, and graphs were drawn using origin.
background: Nitrogen (N) deposition has increased globally and has profoundly influenced the structure and function of grasslands. Previous studies have discussed how N addition affects aboveground biomass (AGB), but the effects of N addition on the AGB of different functional groups in grasslands remain unclear.
objective: in this study, the authors conducted a meta-analysis to quantitatively synthesize available studies on the changes in agb, the agb of grasses (agbgrass) and the agb of forbs (agbforb) in grasslands from around the world following n addition. the authors asked the following questions: 1) what are the response patterns of agb to n addition in grasslands around the world? do all plant functional groups respond in a similar way? 2) do different n addition rates, study durations or climatic conditions influence the effects of n addition on agb, agbgrass and agbforb?
result1: n addition significantly increased the soil available n concentrations by 115% but did not significantly affect the available p concentrations.
result2: NA
general_conclusion: n addition had positive effect on soil nitrogen while it has no effect on soil phosphorus.

search_strategy: authors systematically searched all peer-reviewed publications that were published before june 2020 that investigated the effects of plant diversity on soil total n, inorganic n and net n mineralization rate using the web of science core collection, google scholar and the china national knowledge infrastructure with the search term ‘soil nitrogen or soil n or nitrate or ammonia or no3 or nh4 or nitrogen mineralization and plant diversity or richness or mixture or pure or polyculture or monoculture or overyielding’. authors also searched for references within these papers. the survey also included studies summarized in previously published diversity–ecosystem functioning meta-analyses.
selection_criteria: 1) papers that purposely designed to test the effects of plant diversity on soil total n (both total n content and stock), total inorganic n, no3–, nh4+ and net n mineralization rate in mineral soils; 2) had at least one species mixture treatment and constituent monocultures; 3) had the same initial climatic and soil properties in the monoculture and mixture treatment plots. to better represent responses of soil n under natural conditions,  greenhouse and mesocosms studies were not included.
data_analysis: authors employed the number of replications for weighting. analyses of mixed effect models were conducted using the restricted maximum likelihood estimation with the lme4 package. to prevent overfitting, authors selected the most parsimonious models among all alternatives. species richness in mixures, stand age and their interaction effect were kept in the models as they were intrinsic to the purpose of the study. model selection was accomplished by using the ‘dredge’ function of the mumin package. for soil total n and net n mineralization rate, there was more than one best model and models with the lowest aic and highest weight for interpretation were selected. finally, fitted coefficients were bootstrapped by 1,000 iterations. the potential for publication was tested using egger’s regressions test for funnel plot asymmetry on mixed-effects models.
background: Plant diversity continues to decline globally due to habitat conversion and degradation, but its influence on soil N remains uncertain. Nitrogen is an essential element for all living organisms and is often the main limiting nutrient for plant carbon assimilation in terrestrial ecosystems worldwide. Consequently, changes in soil total N can alter the global carbon cycle, thereby impacting both global climate change and human food security.
objective: to quantify the effects of species mixtures on soil n variables, including total n, net n mineralization rate, total inorganic n, nh4+, no3- and the ratio of no3−/nh4+. here, results for grasslands are reported.
result1: soil total n increased in grasslands with increased species mixtures.
result2: NA
general_conclusion: soil total n increased in grasslands with increased species mixtures.

search_strategy: peer‐reviewed journal articles were searched using google scholar and web of science with the following keywords/phrases: (“nutrient addition” or “nitrogen addition” or “n addition” or “phosphorus addition” or “p addition” or “micronutrient addition” or “fertilization” or “deposition” or “enrichment” or “limitation”) and (“nitrogen fixation” or “n fixation” or “n2 fixation” or “dinitrogen fixation” or “nitrogenase”) and were further searched from the reference lists of relevant articles.
selection_criteria: 1) control and fertilization plots had to be established within the same study sites, that is, same microclimate, vegetation, and soil types; 2) field studies with at least one of the three treatments, including n addition (e.g., urea, hh4no3, nh4cl), p addition (e.g., nah2po4, kh2po4, ca(h2po4)2), and micro addition (either single or combined additions of mo, fe, copper [cu], manganese [mn], boron [b], and zinc [zn]; note that studies with a combination of multiple treatments [e.g., n + p fertilization and elevated co2 + n fertilization] were excluded); 3) variables of bnf rates in soil, litter, moss, lichen, leaf, and plant nodule samples; 4) bnf rates measured using acetylene reduction assay (ara) or 15n tracing methods; 5) measurements in different sites and compartments (soil, litter, moss, lichen, leaf, and nodule) or under different treatments that were considered to be independent experiments; and 6) the last time point selected if multiple time points of measurements were available (because the bnf responses may be unstable right after nutrient addition).
data_analysis: for comparison and analysis, the nutrient‐addition rates per unit area (for both continuous and single addition experiments) were transformed to the unified unit of “kg ha−1 year−1,” and the duration of nutrient addition (i.e., length of time between the start of treatment and sampling) was transformed to the unified unit of “year.” the authors used metawin 2.1 software to calculate the weighted response ratio (rr++) and 95% ci. linear or logarithmic regression models, which have a higher degree of fitting, were used to examine the relationships between response ratios or nutrient concentrations and fertilization regimes, environmental factors (including the full range of each environmental factor and the two categories of each environmental factor), or latitude.
background: Biological nitrogen (N) fixation (BNF), an important source of N in terrestrial ecosystems, plays a critical role in terrestrial nutrient cycling and net primary productivity. Currently, large uncertainty exists regarding how nutrient availability regulates terrestrial BNF and the drivers responsible for this process.
objective: to examine whether fertilization regimes (nutrient‐addition rates, duration, and total load) and environmental factors (mean annual temperature [mat], mean annual precipitation [map], and background n deposition) affect the extent of bnf in response to nutrient addition. the authors hypothesized that n addition would inhibit terrestrial bnf but that p and micro addition would stimulate terrestrial bnf.
result1: nitrogen addition inhibited bnf in grassland (37.8% [31.6%‒43.4%]).
result2: phosphorus addition stimulated bnf in grassland (176.0% [104.3%‒251.4%]).
general_conclusion: biological nitrogen fixation in grassland was inhibited by nitrogen addition but stimulated by phosphorus addition.

background: Nitrogen (N) deposition has increased globally and has profoundly influenced the structure and function of grasslands. Previous studies have discussed how N addition affects aboveground biomass (AGB), but the effects of N addition on the AGB of different functional groups in grasslands remain unclear.
objective: in this study, the authors conducted a meta-analysis to quantitatively synthesize available studies on the changes in agb, the agb of grasses (agbgrass) and the agb of forbs (agbforb) in grasslands from around the world following n addition. the authors asked the following questions: 1) what are the response patterns of agb to n addition in grasslands around the world? do all plant functional groups respond in a similar way? 2) do different n addition rates, study durations or climatic conditions influence the effects of n addition on agb, agbgrass and agbforb?
result1: n addition did not significantly affect the soil water content.
result2: NA
general_conclusion: n addition had no significant effect on soil water content across all studies.

search_strategy: the authors systematically searched for published field studies that reported effects of organic amendments on one or more ecosystem properties. they first performed a web of science search and then identified additional studies by screening cited references in papers obtained. gray literature cited by a peer-reviewed paper was considered eligible if it met all other criteria.
selection_criteria: 1) field experiment with control (no amendment) and treatment (amendment) plots; 2) non forested ecosystem with sufficient plant biomass to support livestock grazing; 3) carbon-based amendment to which synthetic nutrients had not been added; 4) soil not subjected to “severe disturbance” within the 20-year period prior to experiment initiation (as reported by the paper's authors). the authors considered severe disturbance to include activities such as mining, roadcuts, and agricultural tillage; 5) arid, semiarid, or mediterranean köppen–geiger climate zone; 6) reported effect of amendment addition on at least one of 20 prospective response variables.
data_analysis: all analyses were conducted in r. the authors chose five predictors—climate zone, days between amendment application and measurement, amount of amendment applied, amendment total n concentration, and (for soil outcomes) soil sample depth—that were reported for 91%–100% of observations.
background: Interest in land application of organic amendments—such as biosolids, composts, and manures—is growing due to their potential to increase soil carbon and help mitigate climate change, as well as to support soil health and regenerative agriculture. While organic amendments are predominantly applied to croplands, their application is increasingly proposed on relatively arid rangelands that do not typically receive fertilizers or other inputs, creating unique concerns for outcomes such as native plant diversity and water quality.
objective: the authors present a meta‐analysis of organic amendment additions to rangelands in arid, semiarid, and mediterranean climates, synthesizing amendment effects on a suite of ecosystem outcomes. specifically, they analyzed 11 ecosystem outcomes that had sufficient published data: soil organic carbon concentration, soil water holding capacity, aboveground net primary productivity (anpp), plant species diversity, plant tissue nitrogen (n) concentration, soil co2 emissions, soil lead (pb) concentration, plant tissue pb concentration, runoff quantity, runoff phosphorus, and runoff nitrate. here, results for soil water holding capacity are provided.
result1: amendment addition increased soil water holding capacity (mean = 1.11×).
result2: NA
general_conclusion: amendment addition to rangeland increased soil water holding capacity.

search_strategy: a systematic review of worldwide literature was conducted using scopus, returning articles from 1950 until november 2017. title, keywords and abstracts were searched for the following terms: (graz*) and (*divers* or biomass or “carrying capacity” or “weight gain” or conserv* or richness or product* or “ground cover” or “groundcover” or “bare ground”) and (rotation* or cell or tactical or holistic or adaptive or “short duration” or planned or continuous or “set stocked” or “set stocking” or shepherd* or “high intensity” or “low frequency” or “time controlled” or “time control” or “multi paddock” or multipaddock or “restorative” or “grazing management” or rest or regenerat* or “grazing system” or “grazing regime” or “grazing strategy” or nomadic or herding or herder or seasonal or “active grazing”).
selection_criteria: 1) studies where grazing animals were domesticated ruminants (e.g. cattle, sheep, goats, deer), 2) were published in english, and 3) reported above‐ground biotic or animal production variables; 4) studies based on models or simulations were not included.
data_analysis: authors undertook meta‐analyses using the metafor (v.1.9‐6) and metagear (v.0.4) packages within the r open‐source software environment (version 3.4.0). a weighted analysis was conducted to account for the heterogeneity in sample size and variance among studies. analyses that included studies with multiple contrasts and common treatments were weighted with a variance–covariance matrix that accounted for this dependency. multi‐level random‐effect (mlre) models were fitted for the effect sizes of each response variable for strategic-rest grazing (srg)–continuous grazing (cg) and srg–ungrazed (ug) comparisons separately. a nested random term region/study/livestock type was included in all models. in the models of plant species richness, diversity and ground cover, the random effect was further nested to account for calculation method of how species richness and diversity were estimated in each study. in models of the effect size of plant diversity, the random term was further nested to include the diversity index. in the animal production per hectare models, an additional nested level for the type of unit was added. effect‐size heterogeneity in each model was assessed using the least squares extension of cochran's q‐test. mlre models were fitted using maximum likelihood. the significance of the fixed effects was assessed using two tests: an omnibus test (qm) and likelihood‐ratio tests (χ2). model selection was guided by assessment of the akaike information criterion (aic) and its small sample size correction (aicc). publication bias was assessed using egger's regression test.
background: Grazing management practices that incorporate periods of planned rest (i.e. strategic‐rest grazing) may be an alternative to grazing exclusion or continuous grazing that could achieve ecological and animal production outcomes simultaneously.
objective: to investigate how strategic‐rest grazing (srg) mediates ecological (i.e., plant richness), biophysical (plant biomass and ground cover) and production response variables (animal weight gain and animal production per hectare) compared to continuously grazed (cg) or ungrazed (ug) areas. specifically, the research questions are: 1) how do differences in grazing management systems affect ecological outcomes (plant richness)?; 2) how do differences in grazing management systems affect bio-physical outcomes (biomass and ground cover)?; 3) how do differences in grazing management systems affect animal production outcomes (weight gain and animal production per hectare)?; 4) to what extent do climate, differences in stocking rate and the length of the graze and rest periods mediate ecological, biophysical and livestock production responses? here, results for animal production are reported.
result1: overall, there was no difference in weight gain between srg and cg systems (z = 0.30, p = 0.765) but animal production per hectare was significantly greater under srg than cg (z = −2.09, p = 0.036).
result2: NA
general_conclusion: incorporating periods of rest into grazing regimes improves animal production per hectare and  these benefits are more pronounced with increases in the length of time land is rested for. this extended rest also improves weight gain compared to continuous grazing systems.

search_strategy: a literature search was conducted in may 2017 using the isi web of science and scopus databases. searches were limited to peer-reviewed journals or edited book series. keyword combinations were developed to identify papers that included livestock, grazing, and grouse. all terms were used for both title and topic searches to ensure returning the greatest number of papers possible. common names of grouse species were included to capture studies that examined other grouse species absent from searches using the generic term “grouse.” the literature cited from the papers used in our analysis was also included. no temporal or language restrictions were applied to searches.
selection_criteria: only papers that compared grouse population metrics within ≥2 grazing intensities (e.g., heavy grazing, reduced grazing, or no grazing) were retained for the meta-analysis.
data_analysis: all meta-analytic models were calculated using metawin 2.1.5. because these meta-analysis relied on small sample sizes, bootstrapping replications with replacement were run to improve approximations of the confidence intervals. data were analysed using a categorical random-effects model in meta-win 2.1.5. weighted averages were used in the models to estimate the cumulative effect size by calculating the reciprocal of each studies’ sampling variance. the percentage of total variation across studies that is due to heterogeneity was calculated using the i2 statistic. publication bias was tested for the “file drawer problem” (i.e., when only studies reporting significant results are published) using the approaches developed by egger, smith, schneider, and minder (1997).
background: Livestock grazing affects over 60% of the world’s agricultural lands and can influence rangeland ecosystem services and the quantity and quality of wildlife habitat, resulting in changes in biodiversity. Concomitantly, livestock grazing has the potential to be detrimental to some wildlife species while benefiting other rangeland organisms. Many imperiled grouse species require rangeland landscapes that exhibit diverse vegetation structure and composition to complete their life cycle. Grouse, as a suite of upland gamebirds, are often considered an umbrella species for other wildlife and thus used as indicators of rangeland health.
objective: to determine the current knowledge of the effects of livestock grazing on grouse populations (i.e., chick production and population indices) worldwide.
result1: livestock grazing had a negative effect on lagopus lagopus scotica and lyrurus tetrix adult counts and chick production.
result2: NA
general_conclusion: an overall negative effect on both adult counts and chick production was found for two populations of european grouse species that are in decline.
knowledge_gaps: this meta-analysis highlighted the general lack of knowledge of the direct effects of livestock grazing needed to develop best management practices (bmps) for grouse in general and individual species specifically.

search_strategy: the web of science database was used to search for titles, abstracts and author keywords of articles published between 1960 and 2017 that included the following search strings: grazing and (richness or diversity) and plant. studies that concerned aquatic environments or invertebrate grazers, were then eliminated by searching the collection for the following keywords: seagrass, aquatic, marine, lake, algae, phytoplankton, insect, nematode, termite, grasshopper, beetle.
selection_criteria: 1) studies that reported species richness and its standard error or standard deviation, and sample size under both grazing exclusion and grazing. grazing treatments may include several grazing intensities. 2) studies whose grazing animals are livestock, e.g. cattle, goats, sheep, horse, etc. 3) studies that were conducted in terrestrial ecosystems, excluding aquatic ecosystems. salt marshes were included. 4) studies that reported geographic location, in order to document their aridity.
data_analysis: a random-effects model was conducted and the residual maximum likelihood (reml) estimation was used to estimate the variance between studies. then, each single effect size was weighted by the inverse of its total variance. regression deletion diagnostics were conducted to evaluate the influence of each data point and detect possible outliers. to detect possible skewness in effect sizes from publication bias, authors checked the funnel plot of standard errors on effect sizes and found the funnel plot was symmetric, indicating no publication bias. in addition, correlations were found between effect sizes and sampling unit sizes. in order to estimate heterogeneity in effect size of grazing on species richness, and stratify the source of heterogeneity, sub-group and meta-regression analyses were conducted. all statistical analyses and plots were performed in r packages “metafor”, "multcomp" and “ggplot2”.
background: A major challenge in rangeland ecology is understanding diverse responses of diversity to grazing, what factors determine these responses and what their relative importance is.
objective: to estimate the mean effect of grazing on plant richness and to assess the relative importance of different regional and local (or site-specific) variables, including evolutionary history of grazing, aridity, vegetation type, stocking rate, duration of grazing exclusion, soil carbon and nitrogen, aboveground biomass, vegetation cover, and species evenness. here, results for grasslands are reported.
result1: in grasslands, effect size was significantly positive when comparing grazing exclusion with grazed grasslands.
result2: NA
general_conclusion: globally, grazing significantly increased plant richness compared to grazing exclusion.

search_strategy: the authors comprehensively searched published literature to obtain a set of studies that analyzed the effect of domestic livestock grazing on birds, doing keyword searches in the scopus database and the first 600 results of google scholar. online search was conducted from 11 march 2019 to 8 april 2021, based on the following search terms: “(bird* or avian) and graz* and (livestock or cattle or cow* or goat* or sheep * or horse* or yak* or llama* or reindeer*)”. the keyword search was supplemented by reviewing references cited in studies already selected.
selection_criteria: the authors select only those studies that report bird species richness or abundance for ungrazed (i.e. control) and grazed (i.e. treatment) areas by domestic livestock in natural habitats.
data_analysis: the authors conducted a random-effects multilevel linear model to estimate differences across studies, for each response variable (bird abundance and species richness). the model uses fixed (moderators) and random effects, assuming that studies do not share a common mean effect but that there is a random variation among them, in addition to within-study sampling variation. heterogeneity of effect sizes was examined by estimating the q statistic, whose significance was tested using a x2 test with a minimum level of significance of 0.05. publication bias in our set of studies was visually examined using funnel plots, which represent the relationship between effect size and standard error of each study.
background: Livestock grazing is one of the main activities triggering habitat degradation and land-use change around the world. Its effects on biodiversity have been widely explored, with birds being the most studied vertebrates. However, its impact seems to be contradictory given the disparity of the results.
objective: the authors conduct a meta-analysis to review and synthesize the published literature on how bird richness and abundance are affected by livestock grazing. particularly, the authors address the following questions: 1) does the livestock grazing affect bird richness and abundance similarly? 2) does the effect of livestock grazing depend on habitat type (i.e. grassland, wooded areas, riparian, and salt marsh) and bio-geographic realm (i.e. nearctic, neotropic, palearctic, afro-tropic, and australasia)? 3) does livestock grazing effect depend on management decisions, such as livestock type (i.e. cattle, sheep, goat, horse, yak, llama, reindeer, or a mix of them), and grazing intensity?
result1: bird abundance in grassland did not show substantial differences .
result2: grazing in grassland has no effect on bird species richness
general_conclusion: grazing has no effect on bird abundance and bird species richness.

search_strategy: authors conducted a literature search of articles published since 1980 using the following keywords in the isi web of knowledge database: ‘‘spider’’ and ‘‘management’’, ‘‘spider’’ and ‘‘fragmentat⁄’’, ‘‘spider’’ and ‘‘insecticid⁄’’, ‘‘spider’’ and ‘‘organic farm⁄’’, ‘‘spider’’ and ‘‘fire’’, ‘‘spider’’ and ‘‘logging’’, ‘‘spider’’ and ‘‘graz⁄’’, ‘‘araneae’’ and ‘‘fragmentat⁄’’, ‘‘araneae’’ and ‘‘insectid⁄’’, ‘‘araneae’’ and ‘‘organic farm⁄’’, ‘‘araneae and ‘‘logging’’, ‘‘araneae’’ and ‘‘graz⁄’’, ‘‘araneae’’ and ‘‘fire’’. they also reviewed the literature cited by the references found.
selection_criteria: not provided
data_analysis: a weighted mixed model of meta-analysis was chosen using the program metawin. the bootstrap ci (confidence interval) was utilized to test the significance of the effect size. the heterogeneity in the size effect between units of analysis, q, was tested by means of a chi-square test. the heterogeneity for the global meta-analysis and for subsets of the data set categorized by managements or systems was also tested. the rosenthal fail-safe method and the visual exploration of funnel plotswere utilized to explore the potential publication bias.
background: Spiders are important predators in terrestrial ecosystems, biological control agents against pests in agroecosystems and forests, and useful indicators due to their sensibility to changes in habitat structure and microclimate. Effects of land use on spiders have been reviewed several times but existing reviews are narrative and usually focused on one single kind of management.
objective: the main objective is to summarize the impacts of land use on spider abundance and species richness in a quantitative way, by using meta-analysis. the specific objectives were the following: 1) to identify the kinds of management and land use potentially influencing spider species richness and abundance; 2) do those kinds of land management increase or decrease richness and abundance of spiders?; 3) do land uses in different systems (forests, agroecosystems and rangelands) affect spiders differently?; and 4) do different kinds of management within a system (forest or agroecosystems) affect spiders in different ways? here, results for the effect of grazing on spider richness and abundnace in rangelands are reported.
result1: a negative but non significant effect of grazing was found for spider species richness.
result2: grazing significantly decreased spider abundance.
general_conclusion: reduction of mechanical disturbances such as grazing will increase spider diversity in rangelands.

search_strategy: authors searched isi web of knowledge, sciverse scopus and google scholar covering the time period from 1966 to june 2018. the keywords used were: ["population loss" or "population decline" or "extinction" or "loss of biodiversity" or "biodiversity loss" or "loss of species" or "species loss" or "species persistence" or "population increase” or "population persistence" or "population abundance"] and [mammal*or marsupialia or insectivora or afrosoricida or artiodactyla or carnivora or chiroptera or cingulata or dasyuromorphia or dermoptera or didelphimorphia or hyracoidea or lagomorpha or macroscelidea or monotremata or perissodactyla or pholidota or pilosa or primates or proboscidea or rodentia or scandentia or soricomorpha or tubulidentata] and [grassland or savanna or shrubland or steppe or prairie]. they searched for these words in article titles, abstracts or keywords. additional studies were found based on the references of these first papers.
selection_criteria: exclusion criteria: 1) field analyses on a forest-like ecosystem; 2) analyzing the effect of an anthropogenic disturbance on other taxonomic groups other than mammals; 3) not analyzing the effect of an anthropogenic disturbance; 4) presenting analyses that could not be used for meta-analysis, 5) their vegetation is not dominated by grasses (poaceae) or other graminoids (e.g. cyperaceae, juncaceae), that is, plant communities mostly composed of woody species are excluded; 6) papers analyzing alien species; 7) articles that had the word pleistocene in their title.
data_analysis: besides using the r values from the regression analyses, data from anova and t-test were also used, obtaining the r values through arithmetical transformations from f statistics and student’s t values using meta-win calculator.  the variance of each study is calculated  based on the study sample size. additionally, effect sizes are weighted by the variance of the estimate. for each anthropogenic activity, the mean effect size among all the species that were studied under this anthropogenic activity was calculated and its confidence interval (95%) through bootstrap. data were analyzed using random- effect models. q statistics was used to analyze whether the variance among effect sizes is greater than expected by chance. three methods were used to explore potential publication bias. first of all, authors used the frequency histogram to verify if there is a depression on effect size distribution close to zero. they also analyzed the funnel plot of effect sizes vs. sample sizes. at last, they calculated the fail-safe number. all analyses were performed with the statistical software metawin 2.0. visual exploration of the data sets using funnel plots was conducted. for each response variable, authors tested the relationship between the standardized effect size and sample size using a spearman rank correlation, but these relationships were non-significant, consistent with lack of publication bias.
background: Grasslands and savannas are among the most degraded biomes in the world, and are often taken as secondary successional stages, with a less important biodiversity and an opportunity for agriculture activities. These biomes face a diverse number of anthropogenic threats, and despite this scenario, little attention is given to their conservation and sustainable use.
objective: the general goal is investigating whether and how grassland and savanna biodiversity is threatened using mammals as an indicator of ecosystem conditions. specific objectives were 1) to analyze the mean effect of anthropogenic activities on abundance of mammals’ species on grasslands and savannas and 2) to compare the effect of five different anthropogenic activities previously known to threaten mammals: cropland activities; cattle ranching; fire; shrub/woody encroachment; and urbanization. here, the results for cropland activities and cattle ranching are reported.
result1: cattle ranching had a negative non-significant effect on mammal abundance in comparison to lower grazing intensities or places where the cattle were removed in the past (−0.22 / −0.40 to 0.04, mean effect size / 95% confidence interval by bootstrap).
result2: the q statistics showed that variance among effect sizes is not greater than expected by chance.
result3: two of the three publication bias analyses supported the robustness of this meta-analysis even when considering a possible lack of studies with no significant effects.
general_conclusion: anthropogenic activities are reducing mammalian abundance in the analyzed ecosystems.

search_strategy: the final collection of studies occurred on 9th december 2016. the authors used the database of isi web of science searching articles from 1985 to 2016 under the following topics: a) 1° search - “grazing and biodiversity”, “grazing and *indicator*”, “pastoral activit* and biodiversity”, “pastoral activit* and *indicator*”, “pastoral and biodiversity” and “pastoral and *indicator*”; b) 2° search - “abandonment”; 3° search - “pasture and biodiversity” and “pasture and *indicator*”. the total search was refined selecting europe as the study area and including the following categories: ecology, environmental sciences, biodiversity conservation, entomology, and zoology. furthermore, the authors added studies related to the common agricultural policy (cap) by using other categories: agricultural multidisciplinary, agriculture dairy animal science, multidisciplinary science, environmental studies, and biology.
selection_criteria: articles not directly linked to pastoral activities on biodiversity were excluded, for example: grazing made by invertebrates (animal phyla other than chordata); studies performed on other continents; studies wrongly identified by isi web of science (e.g. studies focused on gas production by cattle). even though the authors did not search explicitly for the topic “plants”, a high number of studies were actually found (many articles analysed both animals and plants, despite several only being about plants), so the authors decided to include them.
data_analysis:
the authors extracted mean or median values, variances, and associated sample sizes for each variable, grazing regime, and taxonomic group. the authors converted the different variance measures (e.g. confidence intervals 95 % , standard error, interquartile range) into standard
deviations.
background: Land-use changes, both in terms of land abandonment and intensification, have led to fragmentation and loss of traditional agricultural habitats. Extensive grazing is among the forms of land use that have undergone the greatest changes. This represents one of the main threats to biodiversity; consequently, a comprehensive overview about the impacts on the biodiversity of changes that are happening in pastoral activities is needed.
objective: to collect and review all the publications related to the impact of pastoral activities on animal biodiversity in europe in a systematic manner. the main questions were: 1) when and where were the studies performed?; 2) which kind of grazing regime was the most considered, and which were the most widespread grazers? 3) which were the main target groups used to evaluate impacts on biodiversity? 4) are there different impacts of grazing pressure on various orders of arthropods? 3) what was the best practice for biodiversity conservation?
result1: abandonment had significantly higher richness values than both traditional and overgrazing.
result2: traditional pastoral systems had an average higher number of species than overgrazing.
result3: overall, tests for heterogeneity were almost always significant, meaning that there is extra-variation not accounted for only by differences among grazing regimes.
general_conclusion: traditional extensive grazing was the best practice, since it leads to the highest biodiversity values, creating a mosaic of habitats suitable for many species, mainly in southern europe and mountainous ecosystems. conversely, short term abandonment had positive effects in central europe and lowlands, when following overgrazing, but not in southern european mountains. on the contrary, in lowlands mostly characterized by over-simplified and homogeneous habitats, abandonment of some grazing patches augments habitat diversification and creates new habitats for more species. by contrast, overgrazing caused a significant decrease in biodiversity, homogenising the landscape and destroying habitat that is essential for many species.
knowledge_gaps: there was a bias towards lowlands in comparison to uplands, as well as a lack of long-term studies.

search_strategy: studies were collected in two batches. the first batch contained literature entirely based on a former review for the globio3 model, yielding 15 papers on grazing intensity. the second batch was compiled from a search using the keyword sequence species and [grassland or rangeland] and graz* and [intact or natural or primary or virgin or mature or pristine] and [*diversity or richness or abundance*] of the scopus database. this search yielded 300 papers.
selection_criteria: the authors selected papers from 10 journals with >10 papers that met the search criteria and rejected those that were obviously not of interest according to title and abstract. from the 49 remaining papers only those were selected that met the following criteria: 1) does the paper contain data on species abundance? 2) could one of the land-use categories studied be considered natural or close to natural? 3) does the paper describe the effect of grazing?
data_analysis: ratios of the abundance of single species found in disturbed and undisturbed ecosystems are the basis on which to calculate mean species abundance (msa). a random-effects metaanalysis was done, using the r 2.12.0 software, to derive a pooled effect size for the different grazing intensities. linear mixed- effect models were estimated for msa to check for differences between regions and taxa.
background: Biodiversity in rangelands is decreasing, due to intense utilization for livestock production and conversion of rangeland into cropland; yet the outlook of rangeland biodiversity has not been considered in view of future global demand for food.
objective: using the globio3 approach, this paper presents a first attempt to quantify biodiversity impacts of livestock production in rangeland ecosystems.
result1: all categories showed a value statistically significant below 1 (p < 0.05).
result2: ungrazed, abandoned rangelands presented an average mean species abundance of 0.7.
result3: no significant regional differences were found for mean species abundance values and no differences between taxa were found.
result4: the globio model suggests that biodiversity, in terms of global average of mean species abundance, will continue to decline, between 2000 and 2050, in rangeland ecosystems in both the baseline scenario and, to a lesser extent, in the high-akst variant.
general_conclusion: all rangeland and man-made grasslands uses have a negative effect on biodiversity compared to natural rangelands.

search_strategy: using google scholar, isi webofscience, and china national knowledge infrastructure the authors searched for journal articles that reported plant, arthropod, and microbial diversity in response to grazing intensity during 1900–2018, the following search term combinations: (graz or grazing or grazed or fence* or enclosed or enclosure or enclos) and (plant or arthropod* or microbe* or diversity* or richness* or insects* or microbial* or biodiversity) and (effect* or respon* or affect* or impact* or increas* or decreas* or alter*) not (medic* or chemist*).
selection_criteria: 1) experiments were conducted in the field using both enclosed and grazing treatments at the same temporal and spatial scales; experiments also included an analyses of species richness and shannon wiener index; 2) grazing intensity was clearly described in the paper, such as light, moderate, and heavy; 3) the means, standard deviations/errors, and samples sizes of variables in the enclosed and grazing treatments could be extracted directly from the text, tables or digitized graphs.
data_analysis: all data were analyzed using metawin 2.4 and r 3.5.1; the statistical results were considered to be statistically significant at p < 0.05. the authors further evaluated to see if rr++ was affected by grazing intensity, the total heterogeneity among group (qt) was partitioned into within-group (qw) and between-group (qb) heterogeneity.
background: Livestock grazing is an important component and driver of biodiversity in grassland ecosystems. While numerous studies and a few meta-analyses had been conducted on the response of single taxon diversity to grazing in grasslands, a synthesis of how multi-taxa diversity is affected has been largely missing, especially reflecting its changes along a grazing intensity gradient.
objective: the objective of this study was to quantitatively evaluate grazing-induced changes in biodiversity and elucidate the potential mechanisms involved. the objectives of this study were to 1) quantify the effect of grazing on species richness (sr) and the shannon– wiener index (h′) of different taxa in grasslands; 2) assess the effects of grazing intensity on the sr and h′ of plants, arthropods, and microbes; 3) and identify the underlying mechanisms for the effects of grazing intensity on the diversity of plants, arthropods, and microbes. here, results for plants and arthropods are provided.
result1: across all studied taxa, grazing resulted in enhanced species richness.
result2: among different taxa, species richness of plant significantly increased.
result3: species richness of arthropods significantly decreased.
general_conclusion: grazing significantly affected the biodiversity in grasslands, but the effects varied with different taxa and grazing intensities. plant species richness markedly increased with light and moderate grazing and decreased with heavy grazing.

search_strategy: keyword searches in scopus and web of science were used to identify peer-reviewed literature quantifying the effects of livestock grazing on the ecosystem properties of salt marshes. authors retrieved papers published from 1950 to november 2015 containing the terms (saltmarsh* or “salt marsh*” or salt-marsh or “salt meadow” or “coastal marsh”) and (graz* or herbivor* or livestock or cow* or cattle or sheep or horse* or deer) in their title, abstract or keywords. additionally, the doctoral thesis repository ethos was searched in november 2015 for phd theses containing these terms.
selection_criteria: 1) studies must have measured an ecosystem property on a grazed and ungrazed area of salt marsh. 2) only ungulate grazers were considered. 3) both observational and experimental studies were included, as were those that replicated the effects of livestock by clipping or trampling.
data_analysis: a weighted meta-analysis, by inverse of variance, was used to calculate an overall average effect of grazing for every ecosystem property (ep) that had mean and variance values from ≥3 separate publications. for each ep, a random effects, multilevel linear model was used to combine individual effect sizes to estimate an overall mean effect with 95% ci. models were fitted with a restricted maximum likelihood (reml) structure using the rma.mv function within the metafor package in r. study (i.e. publication) nested within site was included as a random factor to account for non-independence of multiple entries extracted from the same study, and multiple studies conducted at the same site. in addition, funnel plots were examinated to assess publication bias.
scale: global: 89 single studies (75 in eu; 12 in america, 2 in asia)
background: How livestock affect the structure and functions of sensitive coastal ecosystems has hitherto lacked synthesis. Grazing-induced changes in salt marshes have the potential to alter the provision of valuable ecosystem services, such as coastal protection, blue carbon and biodiversity conservation.
objective: to investigate how livestock alter soil, vegetation and faunal properties in salt marshes. stocking density, grazing duration, grazer identity, continent and vegetation type were also analysed as potential modifiers of the grazing effect. here, the results for biodiversity are reported.
result1: biodiversity responses depended on focal group, with positive effects of grazing on vegetation species richness, but negative effects on invertebrate richness. grazing reduced the abundance of herbivorous invertebrates, which may affect fish and crustaceans that feed in the marsh. overall vertebrate abundance was not affected.
result2: the majority of the vertebrate data were extracted from studies on bird abundance (85% of entries) and goose abundance in particular (62%).
result3: for most properties, no bias was evident from visual assessment of funnel plots. the exceptions was plant richness, that showed bias towards reporting of negative effects in smaller, less precise studies (those with a larger standard error). this indicates that the true effects on plant richness may be more positive than the values calculated here.
general_conclusion: authors found that livestock grazing affected 11 of the 21 ecosystem properties tested, spanning soil, vegetation and faunal response variables.

search_strategy: a systematic review of worldwide literature was conducted using scopus, returning articles from 1950 until november 2017. title, keywords and abstracts were searched for the following terms: (graz*) and (*divers* or biomass or “carrying capacity” or “weight gain” or conserv* or richness or product* or “ground cover” or “groundcover” or “bare ground”) and (rotation* or cell or tactical or holistic or adaptive or “short duration” or planned or continuous or “set stocked” or “set stocking” or shepherd* or “high intensity” or “low frequency” or “time controlled” or “time control” or “multi paddock” or multipaddock or “restorative” or “grazing management” or rest or regenerat* or “grazing system” or “grazing regime” or “grazing strategy” or nomadic or herding or herder or seasonal or “active grazing”).
selection_criteria: 1) studies where grazing animals were domesticated ruminants (e.g. cattle, sheep, goats, deer), 2) were published in english, and 3) reported above‐ground biotic or animal production variables; 4) studies based on models or simulations were not included.
data_analysis: authors undertook meta‐analyses using the metafor (v.1.9‐6) and metagear (v.0.4) packages within the r open‐source software environment (version 3.4.0). a weighted analysis was conducted to account for the heterogeneity in sample size and variance among studies. analyses that included studies with multiple contrasts and common treatments were weighted with a variance–covariance matrix that accounted for this dependency. multi‐level random‐effect (mlre) models were fitted for the effect sizes of each response variable for strategic-rest grazing (srg)–continuous grazing (cg) and srg–ungrazed (ug) comparisons separately. a nested random term region/study/livestock type was included in all models. in the models of plant species richness, diversity and ground cover, the random effect was further nested to account for calculation method of how species richness and diversity were estimated in each study. in models of the effect size of plant diversity, the random term was further nested to include the diversity index. in the animal production per hectare models, an additional nested level for the type of unit was added. effect‐size heterogeneity in each model was assessed using the least squares extension of cochran's q‐test. mlre models were fitted using maximum likelihood. the significance of the fixed effects was assessed using two tests: an omnibus test (qm) and likelihood‐ratio tests (χ2). model selection was guided by assessment of the akaike information criterion (aic) and its small sample size correction (aicc). publication bias was assessed using egger's regression test.
background: Grazing management practices that incorporate periods of planned rest (i.e. strategic‐rest grazing) may be an alternative to grazing exclusion or continuous grazing that could achieve ecological and animal production outcomes simultaneously.
objective: to investigate how strategic‐rest grazing (srg) mediates ecological (i.e., plant richness), biophysical (plant biomass and ground cover) and production response variables (animal weight gain and animal production per hectare) compared to continuously grazed (cg) or ungrazed (ug) areas. specifically, the research questions are: 1) how do differences in grazing management systems affect ecological outcomes (plant richness)?; 2) how do differences in grazing management systems affect bio-physical outcomes (biomass and ground cover)?; 3) how do differences in grazing management systems affect animal production outcomes (weight gain and animal production per hectare)?; 4) to what extent do climate, differences in stocking rate and the length of the graze and rest periods mediate ecological, biophysical and livestock production responses? here, results for plant richness are reported.
result1: there was no significant difference overall between the grazing treatments for plant species richness (srg–cg: z = −0.64, p = 0.524; srg–ug: z = 0.77, p = 0.443).
result2: NA
general_conclusion: overall, plant richness did not differ between grazing treatments.
