search_strategy: the authors performed a systematic search in three different databases, scopus, portal periódicos capes (a website provided by the brazilian government that includes web of science, pubmed, sciencedirect and scielo, besides scientific journals), and google scholar. the peco was designated as: population – spiders, exposure – managed grasslands, comparison – different types of grazing management and, outcome – species abundance and species richness. the authors tested different combinations of the words ‘araneae’, ‘spider’, ‘livestock’, ‘grazing’, ‘cattle’, ‘sheep’, ‘goat’, ‘horse’ to make the best boolean terms and access our target studies. at last, the authors choose the combination of the boolean terms ‘araneae’ and (‘grazing’ or ‘cattle’ or ‘sheep’ or ‘goat’ or ‘horse’) since these were those that returned more studies. due to the great number of papers produced on our topic, the search strategy was delimited to the last decade, from january 2009 until may 2019, avoiding grey literature and without writing language restriction.
selection_criteria: the authors excluded papers by incompatible topic and outcome. they excluded grey literature.
data_analysis: the authors used generalised linear mixed models (glmm) with negative binomial error to assess the effects of random and fixed terms in the following response variables: 1) species abundance, 2) species richness, 3) guild abundance, and 4) guild richness. the random effect was applied to the glmm intercepts.
background: Grassland ecosystems have been used worldwide for food production through pastoral and cropping activities. In these ecosystems, spiders constitute important mesopredators, which are affected by grassland management in opposite ways. Historically, the spider taxonomic diversity has been the main focus in studies of grazing impacts in grassland ecosystems, while the intrinsic variability of traits within spiders have been neglected, which may have led to mistaken conclusions.
objective: here the authors performed a systematic review on the effects of grazing on global patterns of spiders from grassland ecosystems. the approach is achieved in two steps, where first the authors treat spiders as a single group, in a taxonomic perspective, looking at effects on species' abundance and richness. secondly, the authors reinterpret the literature data, accommodating species in guilds, and explore the effects of grazing from a functional guild perspective to contrast with the taxonomic perspective.
result1: neither the number of livestock types nor grazing pressure precluded species abundance and species richness.
result2: NA
general_conclusion: grazing has no effetc on spider species abundance and richness.

search_strategy: search was conducted in the web of science and scopus databases in december 2017 using the search string: (reptile* or lizard* or snake* or squamat* or gecko* or skink* or lacertid* or agamid* or varanid* or iguan* or python* or elapid* or colubrid* or viper* or amphisbaen*) and (“land use” or logging or silvicultur* or forestry or agricultur* or farm* or crop* or grazing or pasture or pastoral or plantation or “habitat disturbance” or “habitat alteration” or “habitat degradation” or “habitat destruction” or “habitat modification” or “habitat loss” or “habitat fragmentation” or matrix or urban* or mining or mined or weed* or “exotic plant” or “invasive plant”).
selection_criteria: 1) be a peer-reviewed journal article containing data on squamate abundance at the species level. 2) data needed to be collected using standardized sampling methods from at least one modified habitat treatment and an unmodified reference treatment and standardized for sampling effort. habitat modification treatments were classified as livestock grazing, agriculture, logging, plantations, mining, patch size reduction or “other”.  3) “unmodified” reference areas needed to be situated in the same vegetation and landform types as disturbed areas in order to provide a suitable representation of the original fauna. reference areas in many studies were not completely unmodified because no such areas exist in many ecosystems. thus, reference treatments often represent areas that were less disturbed or modified than the modified treatments. 4) studies where data were presented only for species that exhibited a statistically significant response to disturbance were excluded because this represents a reporting bias. 5) unreplicated studies (only one survey site in each treatment) and studies where it was not possible to calculate sample sizes or standard deviations were excluded.
data_analysis: standardized mean differences (hedges’ g) and sampling variances with the “escalc” function in the metafor package in r were calculated. to assess the sensitivity of results to the use of hedges’ g, the logarithmic response ratio was also calculated. bayesian mixed effects models were used to analyse variation in effect sizes, implemented in the brms package in r. fitted models assumed a normal distribution and included random effects for species and study identity to account for non-independence between effect sizes from the same study or species. to account for sampling variance, effect sizes were weighted using their standard errors. to identify an appropriate random effects structure, authors fitted and ranked six models containing different combinations of study identity, species and taxonomic family as random effects, in addition to a phylogenetic covariance matrix. a univariate model was fitted for each predictor variable that excluded the intercept. a funnel plot and egger’s test were used to  assess potential publication bias. visual inspection of the funnel plot suggested no systematic asymmetry in effect sizes, although egger’s test was significant for asymmetry (z = −2.20, p = .028).
background: There have been no large-scale analyses assessing how reptile populations respond to anthropogenic habitat modification across a range of species, ecosystems and disturbance types. Such knowledge is crucial because the extinction process begins with extirpations of populations.
objective: to determine how reptile populations respond to anthropogenic habitat modification and determine whether species traits and environmental factors influence such responses. here, results on the effect of grazing as anthropogenic disturbance are reported.
result1: grazing had a negative effect on reptile abundance. though several species were more abundant in grazed compared with ungrazed areas.
result2: NA
general_conclusion: habitat modification is a key cause of reptile population declines, although there is variability in responses both within and between species, families and vegetation types.

search_strategy: the authors searched published articles, reports and congress proceedings tabulated in scopus and google scholar until july 2016. the authors used ‘grazing intensity’, ‘grazing gradient’ or ‘stocking rate’ as keywords, together with variables describing plant community structure such as ‘species richness’ or ‘species diversity’. the authors also reviewed all volumes of grassland science in europe (proceedings of the european grassland federation), journal of range management (currently rangeland ecology and management) and references cited by the selected papers.
selection_criteria: 1) at least two stocking rates other than grazing exclusion had been experimentally manipulated; 2) plant species richness or a species diversity index was used as response variable; 3) vegetation physiognomy was either grassland or shrubland that had not been sown in the past; 4) grazers had to be domestic herbivores, thus excluding small rodents and other non-comparable grazers.
data_analysis: mean response ratio for each treatment was calculated using fixed effects models with bias-corrected 95% confidence intervals (ci) generated by a bootstrapping procedure (5000 iterations) using meta-win software. the authors regressed the response ratio of the two most extreme stocking rates (high versus low) against the log ratio of the corresponding stocking rates. the authors regressed the response ratios of the first analysis against continuous variables (precipitation, evapotranspiration, aridity and length of the experiment), by means of simple regressions and quantile regressions.
background: Most of our knowledge of the effect of grazing on grassland structure is based on grazed–ungrazed contrasts. The effects of grazing in the most common scenario, where grazing intensity varies from low to high grazing intensity, are less known.
objective: to assess how variation across low, moderate, and high stocking rates of domestic herbivores affects species richness and diversity of grasslands worldwide. the predictions were: 1) species diversity will peak at intermediate stocking rates; 2) grazing-induced changes of species diversity will be larger in more productive than in less productive ecosystems.
result1: overall, stocking rate had little effect on species richness: most studies that compared high versus moderate or low versus moderate stocking rates reported small positive and negative effects around zero.
result2: the response ratio for species richness was between –0.25 and +0.25 in 72% of the high versus moderate contrasts and in 77% of the low versus moderate contrasts.
general_conclusion: high compared to moderate stocking rate has a negative effect on plant richness. low compared to moderate stocking rate has no effect on plant richness.

search_strategy: searches for relevant literature have been made using online publication databases, search engines, specialist websites and bibliographies of literature reviews (17 online publication databases). searches were also made for swedish, norwegian, finnish and russian.  websites of the specialist organisations were searched for links or references to relevant publications and data, including grey literature.
selection_criteria: articles sorted under the categories listed below were considered to have high susceptibility to bias and were therefore excluded from the review: 1) methodology inadequately described; 2) inappropriate comparator (comparison between different seasons, use of small-mesh exclosures that prevented grazing by small mammals as well as reindeer, or comparator difficult to interpret for the purposes of this review). studies that compare grazing in different seasons have usually been made in areas where summer and winter ranges are separated by a fence. since the effects of grazing on bare and snow-covered ground are entirely different, such a study design makes it difficult to judge which of the two ranges that is more heavily grazed, even if reindeer densities are known in both of them; 3) no replication at lowest level (no replication of exclosures or site comparators). studies based on comparison of so-called reindeer-herding districts or regions have not been excluded, however, even though study units representing such a district may be seen as pseudoreplicates in a strict statistical sense. since the study units represent different geographical contexts within the district and thus also differ in terms of biology and reindeer impact, the interpretation of them as pseudoreplicates is not justified in an ecological sense; 4) no data on variability; 5) vegetation data difficult to interpret (such as when methods used to assess vegetation have differed between sites or sampling seasons); 6) reindeer data difficult to interpret (such as when conclusions on the presence of reindeer have been based on weak and circumstantial evidence).
data_analysis: meta-analyses were carried out using the metafor package within the r environment v. 3.0.2. standardised mean difference (smd) effect sizes were derived for all responses using hedges’ g statistic. the authors calculated summary effect sizes by using random effects models. heterogeneity was estimated by the hedges’ method, and data are presented in forest plots showing mean effect sizes and 95% confidence intervals. models were weighted by the inverse of the variance. the authors used univariate mixed effects models in order to test whether the impact of reindeer exposure on vegetation varied with reindeer density, vegetation cover or mean annual temperature. funnel plots were created to visually check for systematic heterogeneity and publication bias in the data set. no publication bias was detected.
background: The reindeer (or caribou, Rangifer tarandus L.) has a natural range extending over much of Eurasia’s and North America’s arctic, alpine and boreal zones, yet its impact on vegetation is still unclear. This lack of a common understanding hampers both the management of wild and semi-domesticated reindeer populations and the preservation of biodiversity.
objective: the ultimate aim of this review is to facilitate evidence-based management of reindeer grazing systems, with a particular focus on fennoscandian conditions.
result1: vascular plant species richness showed a significant negative overall response to reindeer exposure.
result2: non-vascular cryptogam species richness also showed a negative overall response, but this was not significant.
general_conclusion: reindeer grazing has a negative effect on species richness of vascular plants and no effect on non vascular plants.
knowledge_gaps: while this review has gathered a large body of research into vegetation responses to reindeer grazing, the authors still have to conclude that the evidence base is too weak and scattered to inform policy or management in a detailed way.

search_strategy: a literature search was conducted using online search engines (google scholar, isi web of knowledge) and electronic bibliographic databases (science direct, springerlink) and was focused on in-situ studies under grasslands. the key words that were used to search the literature were soc; c sequestration; soil c storage; c depletion; grazing and grasslands.
selection_criteria: 1) studies that reported the concentration of soc for a grazed grassland compared to a non-grazed grassland and the soc was expressed as proportion of the total soil mass and the soil bulk density (rb); 2) reported soc stock; which is the quantity of carbon per unit area expressed in kg c m-2 or kg c ha-1; 3) determined soc by dry combustion using the c and n elemental analyzer.
data_analysis: the data was analyzed using metawin 2.1 software. a resampling based on 4999 bootstrap samples was used to generate the mean effect size of each categorical variable and 95% confidence intervals. meta-analysis was performed using a non-parametric weighting function and 95% confidence intervals (cis) were generated using bootstrapping. effect sizes were weighted by replication.
background: Grasslands occupy about 40% of the world’s land surface and store approximately 10% of the global soil organic carbon (SOC) stock. This SOC pool, in which a larger proportion is held in the topsoil (0–0.3 m), is strongly influenced by grassland management. Despite this, it is not yet fully understood how grassland SOC stocks respond to degradation.
objective: to elucidate the impact of grassland degradation on changes in soc stocks and the main environmental controls, worldwide.
result1: overall, grassland degradation (grazing) induced an average 9% decline in soc with a 95% confidence interval of -14% to -4%.
result2: NA
general_conclusion: grassland degradation reduced soc stocks in grassland soils, although the effect size varied with degradation intensity, classes for climatic factors (mean annual precipitation and temperature), soil texture, soil ph, and grass type.

search_strategy: to collect published studies that have investigated the impacts of grazing intensity (gi) on soil organic carbon (soc) and other selected soil properties (tn, ph and bd) under grassland, the authors performed a comprehensive search on the web of science database (accessed between january 2015 and july 2017) using the following keywords: grazing; soil organic carbon; grassland; gi; total nitrogen and carbon sequestration. in an attempt to have the best possible coverage; the authors also checked all references in the papers found in the web of science search.
selection_criteria: only studies which were longer than one year and measured soc or tn were selected. the authors also accounted for the differences in grass growing seasons at each experimental site.
data_analysis: the authors used minitab 17 to conduct the data exploration, conditioning and analyses. the descriptive statistics of the annual change in soc, tn, bd and ph due to grazing including mean, median, standard deviation, and 95% confidence intervals for each were calculated. one way anovas were performed to investigate the impact of factors: climate, grazing intensity, grass and animal types on soc, tn and other selected soil properties, and the rates of change. principle component analysis was used to determine significant explanatory variables and response variables and determine the differences between climatic zones. in addition, regressions or mixed models such as glm's, were used to determine significant explanatory variables.
background: Livestock grazing intensity (GI) is thought to have a major impact on soil organic carbon (SOC) storage and soil quality indicators in grassland agroecosystems. Understanding the impacts of GI on SOC accumulation and storage in grasslands is crucial to provide the most effective soil C management options. However, although all of these previous reviews are valuable, scientific understanding would be improved by normalizing the sampling depth and GI.
objective: the major objective of this meta-analysis was to investigate the impacts of gi on soc in extensively grazed grassland soils at a global scale. additionally, and because of its importance for c biogeochemistry, the authors considered the impacts of gi on total nitrogen (tn) and other soil properties (mainly ph and bulk density) in grasslands.
result1: grazing intensity was associated with a decrease of overall soc stocks by a response ratio of −0.0774 (−8%; stdev = 0.358).
result2: NA
general_conclusion: grazing intensity was associated with a decrease in soil organic carbon, although its impact on soc is climate-dependent.

search_strategy: research literature and data were predominantly sourced from web of science, google scholar, and cnki under the following search conditions: (1) “grassland” or “steppe” or “rangeland” or “pasture” or “meadow” or “prairie” (2) “restoration succession” or “grazing exclusion” (3) “soil microbial biomass” or “soil “microbial activity” or “microbial community structure” or “total plfa” or “fungi” or “bacteria” or “actinomycetes” or “16srna” were the keywords, and relevant documents published before july 2019 were identified and collected.
selection_criteria: 1) the research object was a grassland ecosystem; 2) the article clearly mentioned the number of restoration years; 3) in the study method, the control group and the treatment group were in the same location with no less than three replicates; 4) each parameter in the selected article displayed information of average values, standard deviations or standard errors, and repetitions; and 5) restoration succession studies were conducted under natural conditions without other treatment or interference.
data_analysis: regression analysis was calculated based on the lnr between different indicators. analyses and calculations were carried out using metawin software.
background: Microorganisms play an important role in the restoration of grassland ecosystems; however, there is no systematic research summary on how microbial communities respond to natural restoration succession in degraded grasslands.
objective: to comprehensively analyze the current understanding on microbial responses to natural restoration succession and to answer the following questions: 1) what mechanisms drive microbial change under natural restoration succession? 2) what factors affect changes in microorganisms? here, results for soil organic carbon are reported.
result1: soil organic carbon significantly decreased by 4.88%.
result2: NA
general_conclusion: changes in soil organic carbon indicated that c sequestration decreased with grazing.

search_strategy: the authors searched peer-reviewed publications using the web of science from 1900 to 2016 and the china knowledge resource integrated database before 2016. the searching terms were: (grazing) and (soil) and (carbon dioxide/co2, methane/ch4 or nitrous oxide/n2o).
selection_criteria: 1) only field experiments were included with the same condition between control and grazing plots, such as microclimate, vegetation and soil types. the authors also excluded other confounding treatments (i.e. fertilization and land conversion), focusing on grazing impacts alone; 2) simulated grazing experiments were eliminated, such as mowing and trampling studies; 3) soil ghg fluxes were explicitly indicated by their means, variances and number of replicates; 4) grazing intensity, duration, animals and ecosystem type need to be clearly described.
data_analysis: the 95% confidence interval (ci) was estimated as ln(rr++) ± 1.96se(lnrr++). if the 95% ci does not cover zero, it implies a significant impact by grazing. these grazing impacts at global level were analyzed by metawin 2.1 software. grazing impacts on soil ghg fluxes were further evaluated at subgroup levels, such as grazing intensity (light, moderate and heavy grazing), grazing duration (<5, 5–10 and >10 years) and precipitation (<400 and ≥400 mm). furthermore, a linear function was used to examine the relationships of soil ghg fluxes with aboveground biomass, soil organic carbon or total nitrogen, soil bulk density, and that of soil moisture with aboveground biomass.
background: Grazing degrades worldwide grasslands and possibly suppresses soil greenhouse gas (GHG: CO2, CH4 and N2O) fluxes. However, the global patterns of these three gas fluxes in response to grazing and the general mechanisms remain poorly understood.
objective: the authors conducted a global synthesis of 63 grazing experiments in grasslands to reveal the general response patterns of soil co2 and n2o emissions and ch4 uptake to grazing, and uncover the underlying mechanisms at the global scale. specifically, the authors addressed the following questions: 1) how grazing differently influences three soil ghg fluxes across global grasslands? 2) how grazing intensity, grazing duration and precipitation regulate these response patterns? 3) what are the general mechanisms underlying grazing-induced changes in these three ghg? here we report only the results on the effect of grazing on soil organic carbon.
result1: soil organic carbon was decreased by heavy grazing, while no effect was reported for light and moderate grazing.
result2: NA
general_conclusion: light and moderate grazing have no effect on soil organic carbon while heavy grazing has a negative effect.

search_strategy: keyword searches in scopus and web of science were used to identify peer-reviewed literature quantifying the effects of livestock grazing on the ecosystem properties of salt marshes. authors retrieved papers published from 1950 to november 2015 containing the terms (saltmarsh* or “salt marsh*” or salt-marsh or “salt meadow” or “coastal marsh”) and (graz* or herbivor* or livestock or cow* or cattle or sheep or horse* or deer) in their title, abstract or keywords. additionally, the doctoral thesis repository ethos was searched in november 2015 for phd theses containing these terms.
selection_criteria: 1) studies must have measured an ecosystem property on a grazed and ungrazed area of salt marsh. 2) only ungulate grazers were considered. 3) both observational and experimental studies were included, as were those that replicated the effects of livestock by clipping or trampling.
data_analysis: a weighted meta-analysis, by inverse of variance, was used to calculate an overall average effect of grazing for every ecosystem property (ep) that had mean and variance values from ≥3 separate publications. for each ep, a random effects, multilevel linear model was used to combine individual effect sizes to estimate an overall mean effect with 95% ci. models were fitted with a restricted maximum likelihood (reml) structure using the rma.mv function within the metafor package in r. study (i.e. publication) nested within site was included as a random factor to account for non-independence of multiple entries extracted from the same study, and multiple studies conducted at the same site. in addition, funnel plots were examinated to assess publication bias.
scale: global: 89 single studies (75 in eu; 12 in america, 2 in asia)
background: How livestock affect the structure and functions of sensitive coastal ecosystems has hitherto lacked synthesis. Grazing-induced changes in salt marshes have the potential to alter the provision of valuable ecosystem services, such as coastal protection, blue carbon and biodiversity conservation.
objective: to investigate how livestock alter soil, vegetation and faunal properties in salt marshes. stocking density, grazing duration, grazer identity, continent and vegetation type were also analysed as potential modifiers of the grazing effect. here, the results for soil carbon are reported.
result1: soil carbon content was unaffected.
result2: no bias was evident from visual assessment of funnel plots.
general_conclusion: authors found that livestock grazing affected 11 of the 21 ecosystem properties tested, spanning soil, vegetation and faunal response variables.

search_strategy: the authors conducted a comprehensive search of the isi web of knowledge database with the keywords: soil carbon and grazing; soil organic carbon and grazing; soil carbon storage and grazing; carbon sequestration and grazing; grazing intensity and carbon; livestock grazing and soil carbon.
selection_criteria: the authors were including only those studies that compared a grazed sample plot to an ungrazed plot and reported grazer effects on soil carbon density (mass per unit area), or % c together with bulk density, from which the authors could calculate carbon density, and by including only the most recent results from any ongoing long-term experiments.
data_analysis: effect size was used as the dependent variable in the univariate ancova analysis. with ibm spss statistical software the authors tested univariate relationships between effect size and each of the six variables using linear regression.
background: Soils of grasslands represent a large potential reservoir for storing CO2, but this potential likely depends on how grasslands are managed for large mammal grazing. Previous studies found both strong positive and negative grazing effects on soil organic carbon (SOC) but explanations for this variation are poorly developed
objective: the authors performed a multifactorial meta-analysis of grazer effects on soc density on 47 independent experimental contrasts from 17 studies. the authors explicitly tested hypotheses that grazer effects would shift from negative to positive with decreasing precipitation, increasing fineness of soil texture, transition from dominant grass species with c3 to c4 photosynthesis, and decreasing grazing intensity, after controlling for study duration and sampling depth.
result1: the authors found that grazing has significantly large, but highly variable, effects on soc density that depend on the context of climate, soils, grass type, and grazing intensity.
result2: grazer effects on soc, whether positive or negative, are potentially large, with cumulative changes of up to 1.6 kg m-2 (16 tons ha-1) over 10–30 years and annual changes as large as +/-150 g m-2 (1.5 tons ha-1 yr-1).
result3: soil type and precipitation exhibited a strong interaction in their influence on grazer effects. the authors also found a significant interaction between grazing intensity and grass type. specifically, higher grazing intensity was associated with increased soc in grasslands dominated by c4 grasses, but with lower soc in grasslands dominated by c3 grasses
result4: the authors discovered a significant interaction between study duration and sampling depth. this interaction showed that in short-term studies, sampling to deeper depths (>40 cm) tended to result in positive effects of grazing, while sampling to intermediate (15–40 cm) depths produced more negative effects. over the longer term, there was little to no effect of sampling depth, as mean effect sizes approached zero for all depth classes.
general_conclusion: overall grazing has no effect on soil organic carbon. grazing has significantly large, but highly variable, effects on soc density that depend on the context of climate, soils, grass type, and grazing intensity.

search_strategy: peer-reviewed journal articles published before october 2015 were searched using web of science and china knowledge resource integrated database with the following search term combinations: (grazing or herbivory or defoliation) and (carbon or nitrogen) and (grassland or pasture or meadow).
selection_criteria: 1) experiments were conducted in the field and had at least one pair of data (under control and treatment); 2) grazing regimes were clearly defined with both quantitative and/or qualitative descriptions for grazing intensity, experimental duration and livestock type (i.e., cattle, sheep or others); 3) to avoid short-term noise, experiments with durations less than one growing season were excluded; 4) initial environmental and climate conditions, soil parameters and species compositions in the control and treatments were the same; 5) the mean, standard error (se) or standard deviation (sd) and sample size (n) of selected variables in control and treatment groups could be extracted directly from tables, digitized graphs or contexts.
data_analysis: the means of response ratio (rr++) are calculated from individual rr of each paired comparison between the control and grazing treatments with the weight of each rr. the 95% confidence interval (95% ci) is rr++ +/- 1.96 s (rr++). the authors applied a t-test to examine the significance of variation in each variable between the control and treatment, and the difference in rr++ between grazing intensity, climate type, grazing type and soil depth. the effect of livestock grazing was considered to be significant if the 95% ci of a response variable did not overlap zero. pearson correlation analyses were performed to examine the relationships between the response ratio of scp and snp with environmental conditions (i.e., grazing duration, latitude, mean annual temperature and mean annual precipitation).
background: Livestock grazing activities potentially alter ecosystem carbon (C) and nitrogen (N) cycles in grassland ecosystems. Despite the fact that numerous individual studies and a few meta-analyses had been conducted, how grazing, especially its intensity, affects belowground C and N cycling in grasslands remains unclear.
objective: in this study, a meta-analysis was conducted on 622 paired comparisons from 115 experimental studies to evaluate the responses of belowground c and n cycles to grazing intensities. specifically, the objectives were to 1) examine global patterns of belowground c and n responses to livestock grazing; 2) assess effects of grazing intensities on the belowground c and n dynamics; 3) investigate regulation of the environmental factors on soil c pools (scp) and soil n pools (snp) alteration in response to grazing.
result1: on average, grazing signiﬁcantly decreased carbon pools in bulk soils, root, soil and litter by 10.28%, 13.72%, and 8.93%, respectively.
result2: NA
general_conclusion: grazing has a negative effect on soil carbon, root carbon and litter carbon pools.

search_strategy: the authors searched for peer-reviewed papers published before june 2018 in web of science and china knowledge resource integrated database (cnki), using the following search terms: (grazing or herbivory or defoliation) and (c:n or c:p or n:p or c:n:p) and (grassland or pasture or meadow).
selection_criteria: 1) the experiment was conducted in the field and included non-grazed plots and at least one grazing treatment, 2) experimental duration was longer than one growing season; 3) the initial climatic conditions, soil properties, and species compositions in the non-grazed and grazing treatments were the same; 4) all plots were free of grazing for at least 10 years prior to the start of the experiment; 5) the dominant species were clearly described and the grazing intensity was quantitatively and/or qualitatively reported; 6) the mean, standard error (se) or standard deviation (sd), and sample size (n) of the relevant variables could be extracted from the tables, digitized graphs or the text.
data_analysis: the 95% confidence interval (ci) for rr++ was rr++ ± 1.96 × s(rr++). the influence of livestock grazing was considered significant if the 95% ci did not overlap zero. the percentage change of a variable was calculated as [exp (rr++) – 1] × 100%. a t test was applied to examine the difference in rr++ between differential grazing intensities in groups with different climate (mean annual temperature, mean annual precipitation), elevation, dominant species (c3 and c4), and soil depth.
background: Livestock grazing can alter carbon (C), nitrogen (N) and phosphorus (P) cycles, thereby affecting the C : N : P stoichiometry in grasslands.
objective: the authors investigate the general response pattern of above- and belowground c : n : p stoichiometry to different grazing intensities. specifically, the objectives were: 1) to examine global patterns of above- and belowground c : n : p stoichiometry in response to livestock grazing; 2) to explore links between grazing effects on above- and belowground c : n : p stoichiometry;  3) to evaluate whether grazing effects on soil c : n : p stoichiometry depend on grazing intensity, climate, soil depth, and vegetation type.
result1: grazing decreased soil c.
result2: NA
general_conclusion: grazing decreased soil c.

search_strategy: 287 publications were selected from 1,260 referred english papers published from 2007 to 2019. the publications were discovered by searching google scholar using the keywords “grazing” and “soil” in the titles of papers to collect data and compile dataset.
selection_criteria: 1) soil property data under various grazing intensities (>3) and the un-grazing from different field sites at 0–30 cm depth were collected. because grazing data cannot be compared to un-grazing at the same time, this study excluded temporal comparisons data (before and after grazing) of the same site; 2) data at sites grazed by domestic animals such as cattle (bos taurus l.), sheep (ovis aries l.) (including goat and deer), or their mixture were selected; 3) this study defined non-adjacent sites to have a distance greater than 46 km (an approximate distance of 25’ in lat- itude range). non-adjacent site data were considered independent and included in the database. adjacent site data were only limited to one site to avoid dependent data with different sites; 4) data collected within a year for each site were averaged. data collected over multiple years could be time-dependent. as a result, only the data from the most recent year were included; 5) site information including grazing intensity, overgrazing, grazing animals, grazing period, land-use, sampling year, soil depth, latitude, longitude, altitude, country, soil texture, mean annual precipitation, and mean daily temperature were all collected.
data_analysis: this study used the mixed model method in proc mixed in sas9.4 to conduct this meta- analysis.
background: Grazing effects on soil properties under different soil and environmental conditions across the globe are often controversial. Therefore, it is essential to evaluate the overall magnitude and direction of the grazing effects on soils.
objective: utilizing comprehensive meta-analytical approach based on publications from 2007 to 2019, the objective ofthis study was to address the overall effects of global grazing intensities on 15 soil properties: soil bulk density (bd), penetration resistance (pr), soc, total nitrogen (tn), c: n ratio, ammonium (nh4+), nitrate (no3 -), microbial biomass carbon (mbc), microbial biomass nitrogen (mbn), available phosphorus (p) and potassium (k), cation exchange capacity (cec), ph, electrical conductivity (ec), and water content (wc). here, results for soc are reported.
result1: heavy grazing intensity significantly decreased the soc [-10.8% (-17.7- -3.8%)] at the 0–10 cm depth and soc [-22.5% (-33.9- -10.2%)] at the 10–30 cm depth.
result2: moderate grazing significantly decreased the soc [-16.4% (-28.7- -3.0%)] at the 10-30 cm depth.
result3: light grazing significantly increased the soc [10.8% (1.1–20.8%)] and nh4 + [28.7% (3.6–60.0%)] at the 0–10 cm depth.
general_conclusion: heavy grazing has a negative effetc on soc (0-10 cm depht) and moderate grazing has a negative effect on soc (10-30 cm depht) and no effetc on soc (0-10 cm depht). light grazing has a positive effetc on soc (0-10 cm depht) but no effect on soc (10-30 cm depht).

search_strategy: the authors conducted a scopus database query to identify peer-reviewed articles matching predetermined title–abstract–keyword search criteria to match grazing strategies and intensities to desired response variables.
selection_criteria: 1) at least one field season of treatment and control monitoring; 2) experimentally manipulated ruminant livestock grazing only; 3) grazing strategy (continuous and/or rotational) and intensity (heavy, moderate, and/or light) that were clearly identified either quantitatively or qualitatively; 4) at least one paired response of treatment (grazing strategy or intensity) and control (no grazing or continuous grazing) mean and variance for either soil organic carbon (soc), bulk density (bd), c/n ratio (cn), or total n (tn) that was extractable from text, tables, charts, or appendices.
data_analysis: for each effect size, 95% confidence intervals (cis) were calculated to describe the range, and effect sizes were considered significant if their lower or upper cis reached zero but did not overlap zero. the authors did not include results with less than two paired observations. for just the continuous grazing vs. no grazing controls data subset, the authors performed multiple linear regression with model averaging to examine whether grazing treatment effects (effect sizes) on soc, bd, cn, and tn were moderated by environmental (aridity, latitude, elevation, plant community, percentage sand, percentage clay) and study (study duration and grazing intensity) variables. the authors only included complete observations for this analysis and selected the best models using a cutoff of two akaike information criteria (small sample size corrected). all analyses were conducted in rstudio using the metafor and glmulti packages, and standard diagnostics were used to confirm that analysis assumptions were met.
background: Grazing lands support the livelihoods of millions of people across nearly one-half of the globe. Soils are the backbone of stability and resilience in these systems.
objective: the authors conducted a global meta-analysis to examine the effects of grazing strategy (i.e., no grazing, continuous grazing, and rotational grazing), grazing intensity (heavy, moderate, and light grazing), and site-specific environmental factors on three important contributors to soil function and health—soil c and n cycling and bulk density (bd). here we report only results on soil organic carbon.
result1: averaged across all studies and grazing intensities, continuous grazing significantly reduced soc (−0.08, ci [−0.11, −0.05]) relative to no grazing controls.
result2: the magnitude of soc reduction significantly increased with continuous grazing intensity.
result3: rotational grazing had significantly higher soc (0.25, ci [0.10, 0.41]) than continuous grazing.
result4: the grazing strategy comparisons were minimally conditioned by aridity class (i.e., arid, subhumid, and humid).
result5: elevation, aridity, absolute latitude, percentage sand and clay, and study duration all had significant moderating effects on soc (n = 73) responses to grazing treatment effects (continuous grazing vs. no grazing effect size).
general_conclusion: continuous grazing has a negative effect compared to no grazing on soc, and no effect for light grazing. rotational grazing has a positive effect on soc compared to continuous grazing.
knowledge_gaps: the authors strongly suggest that future research focus on advancing understanding of interactions among important environmental factors and grazing management and resulting soil health outcomes.

search_strategy: the authors searched peer-reviewed publications using the web of science from 1900 to 2016 and the china knowledge resource integrated database before 2016. the searching terms were: (grazing) and (soil) and (carbon dioxide/co2, methane/ch4 or nitrous oxide/n2o).
selection_criteria: 1) only field experiments were included with the same condition between control and grazing plots, such as microclimate, vegetation and soil types. the authors also excluded other confounding treatments (i.e. fertilization and land conversion), focusing on grazing impacts alone; 2) simulated grazing experiments were eliminated, such as mowing and trampling studies; 3) soil ghg fluxes were explicitly indicated by their means, variances and number of replicates; 4) grazing intensity, duration, animals and ecosystem type need to be clearly described.
data_analysis: the 95% confidence interval (ci) was estimated as ln(rr++) ± 1.96se(lnrr++). if the 95% ci does not cover zero, it implies a significant impact by grazing. these grazing impacts at global level were analyzed by metawin 2.1 software. grazing impacts on soil ghg fluxes were further evaluated at subgroup levels, such as grazing intensity (light, moderate and heavy grazing), grazing duration (<5, 5–10 and >10 years) and precipitation (<400 and ≥400 mm). furthermore, a linear function was used to examine the relationships of soil ghg fluxes with aboveground biomass, soil organic carbon or total nitrogen, soil bulk density, and that of soil moisture with aboveground biomass.
background: Grazing degrades worldwide grasslands and possibly suppresses soil greenhouse gas (GHG: CO2, CH4 and N2O) fluxes. However, the global patterns of these three gas fluxes in response to grazing and the general mechanisms remain poorly understood.
objective: the authors conducted a global synthesis of 63 grazing experiments in grasslands to reveal the general response patterns of soil co2 and n2o emissions and ch4 uptake to grazing, and uncover the underlying mechanisms at the global scale. specifically, the authors addressed the following questions: 1) how grazing differently influences three soil ghg fluxes across global grasslands? 2) how grazing intensity, grazing duration and precipitation regulate these response patterns? 3) what are the general mechanisms underlying grazing-induced changes in these three ghg?
result1: light and moderate grazing had no significant effect on soil ch4 uptake, n2o and co2 emission, whereas heavy grazing reduced them significantly.
result2: the magnitudes of ch4 (30.23%) and n2o responses (38.97%) were larger than co2 (27.84%).
general_conclusion: light and moderated grazing has generally no effect on co2 and n2o emissions and ch4 uptake, while heavy grazing increased co2 and n2o emissions and reduced ch4 uptake.

search_strategy: research literature and data were predominantly sourced from web of science, google scholar, and cnki under the following search conditions: (1) “grassland” or “steppe” or “rangeland” or “pasture” or “meadow” or “prairie” (2) “restoration succession” or “grazing exclusion” (3) “soil microbial biomass” or “soil “microbial activity” or “microbial community structure” or “total plfa” or “fungi” or “bacteria” or “actinomycetes” or “16srna” were the keywords, and relevant documents published before july 2019 were identified and collected.
selection_criteria: 1) the research object was a grassland ecosystem; 2) the article clearly mentioned the number of restoration years; 3) in the study method, the control group and the treatment group were in the same location with no less than three replicates; 4) each parameter in the selected article displayed information of average values, standard deviations or standard errors, and repetitions; and 5) restoration succession studies were conducted under natural conditions without other treatment or interference.
data_analysis: regression analysis was calculated based on the lnr between different indicators. analyses and calculations were carried out using metawin software.
background: Microorganisms play an important role in the restoration of grassland ecosystems; however, there is no systematic research summary on how microbial communities respond to natural restoration succession in degraded grasslands.
objective: to comprehensively analyze the current understanding on microbial responses to natural restoration succession and to answer the following questions: 1) what mechanisms drive microbial change under natural restoration succession? 2) what factors affect changes in microorganisms? here, results for aboveground biomass are reported.
result1: aboveground biomass significantly decreased by 76.58% with grazing.
result2: NA
general_conclusion: aboveground biomass in degraded grasslands significantly increased under restoration succession by grazing exclusion.

search_strategy: the authors searched peer-reviewed publications using the web of science from 1900 to 2016 and the china knowledge resource integrated database before 2016. the searching terms were: (grazing) and (soil) and (carbon dioxide/co2, methane/ch4 or nitrous oxide/n2o).
selection_criteria: 1) only field experiments were included with the same condition between control and grazing plots, such as microclimate, vegetation and soil types. the authors also excluded other confounding treatments (i.e. fertilization and land conversion), focusing on grazing impacts alone; 2) simulated grazing experiments were eliminated, such as mowing and trampling studies; 3) soil ghg fluxes were explicitly indicated by their means, variances and number of replicates; 4) grazing intensity, duration, animals and ecosystem type need to be clearly described.
data_analysis: the 95% confidence interval (ci) was estimated as ln(rr++) ± 1.96se(lnrr++). if the 95% ci does not cover zero, it implies a significant impact by grazing. these grazing impacts at global level were analyzed by metawin 2.1 software. grazing impacts on soil ghg fluxes were further evaluated at subgroup levels, such as grazing intensity (light, moderate and heavy grazing), grazing duration (<5, 5–10 and >10 years) and precipitation (<400 and ≥400 mm). furthermore, a linear function was used to examine the relationships of soil ghg fluxes with aboveground biomass, soil organic carbon or total nitrogen, soil bulk density, and that of soil moisture with aboveground biomass.
background: Grazing degrades worldwide grasslands and possibly suppresses soil greenhouse gas (GHG: CO2, CH4 and N2O) fluxes. However, the global patterns of these three gas fluxes in response to grazing and the general mechanisms remain poorly understood.
objective: the authors conducted a global synthesis of 63 grazing experiments in grasslands to reveal the general response patterns of soil co2 and n2o emissions and ch4 uptake to grazing, and uncover the underlying mechanisms at the global scale. specifically, the authors addressed the following questions: 1) how grazing differently influences three soil ghg fluxes across global grasslands? 2) how grazing intensity, grazing duration and precipitation regulate these response patterns? 3) what are the general mechanisms underlying grazing-induced changes in these three ghg? here we report only the results on the effect of grazing on aboveground biomass.
result1: moderate and heavy grazing significantly reduced aboveground biomass.
result2: light grazing has no effect on aboveground biomass.
general_conclusion: moderate and heavy grazing have a negative effect on aboveground biomass while no effect was reported for light grazing.

search_strategy: keyword searches in scopus and web of science were used to identify peer-reviewed literature quantifying the effects of livestock grazing on the ecosystem properties of salt marshes. authors retrieved papers published from 1950 to november 2015 containing the terms (saltmarsh* or “salt marsh*” or salt-marsh or “salt meadow” or “coastal marsh”) and (graz* or herbivor* or livestock or cow* or cattle or sheep or horse* or deer) in their title, abstract or keywords. additionally, the doctoral thesis repository ethos was searched in november 2015 for phd theses containing these terms.
selection_criteria: 1) studies must have measured an ecosystem property on a grazed and ungrazed area of salt marsh. 2) only ungulate grazers were considered. 3) both observational and experimental studies were included, as were those that replicated the effects of livestock by clipping or trampling.
data_analysis: a weighted meta-analysis, by inverse of variance, was used to calculate an overall average effect of grazing for every ecosystem property (ep) that had mean and variance values from ≥3 separate publications. for each ep, a random effects, multilevel linear model was used to combine individual effect sizes to estimate an overall mean effect with 95% ci. models were fitted with a restricted maximum likelihood (reml) structure using the rma.mv function within the metafor package in r. study (i.e. publication) nested within site was included as a random factor to account for non-independence of multiple entries extracted from the same study, and multiple studies conducted at the same site. in addition, funnel plots were examinated to assess publication bias.
scale: global: 89 single studies (75 in eu; 12 in america, 2 in asia)
background: How livestock affect the structure and functions of sensitive coastal ecosystems has hitherto lacked synthesis. Grazing-induced changes in salt marshes have the potential to alter the provision of valuable ecosystem services, such as coastal protection, blue carbon and biodiversity conservation.
objective: to investigate how livestock alter soil, vegetation and faunal properties in salt marshes. stocking density, grazing duration, grazer identity, continent and vegetation type were also analysed as potential modifiers of the grazing effect. here, the results for different productivity metrics are reported.
result1: all measures of above-ground plant material (canopy height, cover, above-ground biomass) were decreased by grazing.
result2: for most properties, no bias was evident from visual assessment of funnel plots. the exceptions was plant cover, that showed bias towards reporting of negative effects in smaller, less precise studies (those with a larger standard error). this indicates that the true effects on plant cover may be more positive than the values calculated here.
general_conclusion: authors found that livestock grazing affected 11 of the 21 ecosystem properties tested, spanning soil, vegetation and faunal response variables.

search_strategy: a systematic review of worldwide literature was conducted using scopus, returning articles from 1950 until november 2017. title, keywords and abstracts were searched for the following terms: (graz*) and (*divers* or biomass or “carrying capacity” or “weight gain” or conserv* or richness or product* or “ground cover” or “groundcover” or “bare ground”) and (rotation* or cell or tactical or holistic or adaptive or “short duration” or planned or continuous or “set stocked” or “set stocking” or shepherd* or “high intensity” or “low frequency” or “time controlled” or “time control” or “multi paddock” or multipaddock or “restorative” or “grazing management” or rest or regenerat* or “grazing system” or “grazing regime” or “grazing strategy” or nomadic or herding or herder or seasonal or “active grazing”).
selection_criteria: 1) studies where grazing animals were domesticated ruminants (e.g. cattle, sheep, goats, deer), 2) were published in english, and 3) reported above‐ground biotic or animal production variables; 4) studies based on models or simulations were not included.
data_analysis: authors undertook meta‐analyses using the metafor (v.1.9‐6) and metagear (v.0.4) packages within the r open‐source software environment (version 3.4.0). a weighted analysis was conducted to account for the heterogeneity in sample size and variance among studies. analyses that included studies with multiple contrasts and common treatments were weighted with a variance–covariance matrix that accounted for this dependency. multi‐level random‐effect (mlre) models were fitted for the effect sizes of each response variable for strategic-rest grazing (srg)–continuous grazing (cg) and srg–ungrazed (ug) comparisons separately. a nested random term region/study/livestock type was included in all models. in the models of plant species richness, diversity and ground cover, the random effect was further nested to account for calculation method of how species richness and diversity were estimated in each study. in models of the effect size of plant diversity, the random term was further nested to include the diversity index. in the animal production per hectare models, an additional nested level for the type of unit was added. effect‐size heterogeneity in each model was assessed using the least squares extension of cochran's q‐test. mlre models were fitted using maximum likelihood. the significance of the fixed effects was assessed using two tests: an omnibus test (qm) and likelihood‐ratio tests (χ2). model selection was guided by assessment of the akaike information criterion (aic) and its small sample size correction (aicc). publication bias was assessed using egger's regression test.
background: Grazing management practices that incorporate periods of planned rest (i.e. strategic‐rest grazing) may be an alternative to grazing exclusion or continuous grazing that could achieve ecological and animal production outcomes simultaneously.
objective: to investigate how strategic‐rest grazing (srg) mediates ecological (i.e., plant richness), biophysical (plant biomass and ground cover) and production response variables (animal weight gain and animal production per hectare) compared to continuously grazed (cg) or ungrazed (ug) areas. specifically, the research questions are: 1) how do differences in grazing management systems affect ecological outcomes (plant richness)?; 2) how do differences in grazing management systems affect bio-physical outcomes (biomass and ground cover)?; 3) how do differences in grazing management systems affect animal production outcomes (weight gain and animal production per hectare)?; 4) to what extent do climate, differences in stocking rate and the length of the graze and rest periods mediate ecological, biophysical and livestock production responses? here, results for biomass and ground cover are reported.
result1: overall, biomass and ground cover were significantly higher under srg compared to cg management (biomass: z = −4.17, p < 0.001; ground cover: z = −2.67, p = 0.008). when the srg stocking rate was equal to cg, ground cover was always greater under srg.
result2: biomass and ground cover were significantly lower under srg than ug (biomass: z = 2.39, p = 0.017; ground cover: z = 3.04, p = 0.002).
general_conclusion: incorporating periods of rest into grazing regimes improves ground cover and these benefits are more pronounced with increases in the length of time land is rested for. this extended rest also improves biomass production compared to continuous grazing systems.

search_strategy: searches for relevant literature have been made using online publication databases, search engines, specialist websites and bibliographies of literature reviews (17 online publication databases). searches were also made for swedish, norwegian, finnish and russian.  websites of the specialist organisations were searched for links or references to relevant publications and data, including grey literature.
selection_criteria: articles sorted under the categories listed below were considered to have high susceptibility to bias and were therefore excluded from the review: 1) methodology inadequately described; 2) inappropriate comparator (comparison between different seasons, use of small-mesh exclosures that prevented grazing by small mammals as well as reindeer, or comparator difficult to interpret for the purposes of this review). studies that compare grazing in different seasons have usually been made in areas where summer and winter ranges are separated by a fence. since the effects of grazing on bare and snow-covered ground are entirely different, such a study design makes it difficult to judge which of the two ranges that is more heavily grazed, even if reindeer densities are known in both of them; 3) no replication at lowest level (no replication of exclosures or site comparators). studies based on comparison of so-called reindeer-herding districts or regions have not been excluded, however, even though study units representing such a district may be seen as pseudoreplicates in a strict statistical sense. since the study units represent different geographical contexts within the district and thus also differ in terms of biology and reindeer impact, the interpretation of them as pseudoreplicates is not justified in an ecological sense; 4) no data on variability; 5) vegetation data difficult to interpret (such as when methods used to assess vegetation have differed between sites or sampling seasons); 6) reindeer data difficult to interpret (such as when conclusions on the presence of reindeer have been based on weak and circumstantial evidence).
data_analysis: meta-analyses were carried out using the metafor package within the r environment v. 3.0.2. standardised mean difference (smd) effect sizes were derived for all responses using hedges’ g statistic. the authors calculated summary effect sizes by using random effects models. heterogeneity was estimated by the hedges’ method, and data are presented in forest plots showing mean effect sizes and 95% confidence intervals. models were weighted by the inverse of the variance. the authors used univariate mixed effects models in order to test whether the impact of reindeer exposure on vegetation varied with reindeer density, vegetation cover or mean annual temperature. funnel plots were created to visually check for systematic heterogeneity and publication bias in the data set. no publication bias was detected.
background: The reindeer (or caribou, Rangifer tarandus L.) has a natural range extending over much of Eurasia’s and North America’s arctic, alpine and boreal zones, yet its impact on vegetation is still unclear. This lack of a common understanding hampers both the management of wild and semi-domesticated reindeer populations and the preservation of biodiversity.
objective: the ultimate aim of this review is to facilitate evidence-based management of reindeer grazing systems, with a particular focus on fennoscandian conditions.
result1: for herbs/forbs, the overall response to reindeer exposure, including all vegetation categories and aspects (cover, biomass and abundance), was significantly negative with a standardised mean difference (smd) of −0.28 (ci: −0.48, −0.09).
result2: for graminoids, the overall response was close to zero, although grass abundance showed a significant negative overall effect with a standardised mean difference of −0.25 (ci: −0.46, –0.03).
result3: woody plants showed a non-significant overall response to reindeer exposure.
result4: lichens showed a significant negative overall response (smd: −1.14, ci: −2.03, −0.25)).
result5: bryophytes showed no overall response to reindeer herbivory, while the cover of bare ground showed an overall (non-significant) tendency to increase (smd: 0.27, ci: −0.06, 0.59).
general_conclusion: reindeer grazing has a negative effect on herbs/forbs and lichens overall productivity while it has no effect on graminoids, woody plants, bryophytes and bare ground.
knowledge_gaps: while this review has gathered a large body of research into vegetation responses to reindeer grazing, the authors still have to conclude that the evidence base is too weak and scattered to inform policy or management in a detailed way.

search_strategy: authors conducted a search in isi web of science on 11 january 2013 with no restriction on publication year, using the search term combinations (disturb*) and (plant inva* or exotic plant* or alien plant* or invas* or non-native*) and species richness or diversity or cover* or abundance or density or biomass). the reference lists of the retrieved articles for other relevant publications were also retrieved.
selection_criteria: 1) studies had to include a quantitative comparison of the diversity and/or abundance of non-native plant species in both disturbed and undisturbed plots in natural or semi-natural ecosystems; 2) importantly, they usually contained at least some non-native plant species and therefore represented invaded rather than pristine plant communities; 3) the studies, which could be either observational or experimental, had to report the response of non-native plant communities to one or more of the following six biotic or abiotic disturbance types: fire, plant removal, grazing, soil disturbance, nutrient addition, and anthropogenic disturbance.
data_analysis: categorical random effects models were used to assess the effect of different explanatory variables (disturbance type, disturbance frequency, habitat type, spatial and temporal scale) on the diversity and abundance of non-native species, and on the diversity of native species. for each grouping category, the mean effect size with 95% cis was obtained. for groups of ten or more entries, cis were calculated using bias-corrected bootstrapping with 9999 iterations, while for groups with fewer data points, more conservative parametric 95% cis were used. the software metawing was used. visual exploration of the data sets using funnel plots and normal quantile plots revealed no evidence of publication. for each response variable, the relationship between the standardized effect size and sample size was tested using a spearman rank correlation, but these relationships were non-significant, consistent with lack of publication bias.
background: Disturbances, such as fire and grazing, are often claimed to facilitate plant species richness and plant invasions in particular, although empirical evidence is contradictory.
objective: to synthesise the published literature on how disturbances influence the diversity and abundance of plant species, focusing in particular on non-native species. in addition to testing for an overall effect of disturbance on non-native plant communities, the aim is to investigate how habitat and disturbance types, and methodological factors modify the disturbance – diversity and disturbance – abundance relationships. here, results on the effct of grazing in grasslands are reported.
result1: grazing in grasslands leads to higher abundance of non-native plant species.
result2: NA
general_conclusion: grazing in grasslands leads to higher abundance of non-native plant species.

search_strategy: the authors searched the isi web of science, scopus, cab abstracts, biological abstracts, agricola and agris bibliographical databases. records included were published up until october 2011. to minimise potential publication bias associated with the ‘file drawer problem’, the authors also searched for grey literature using the google web search engine and by approaching contacts (nature conservation organisations, scientists) in 26 european countries with a request for relevant reports and unpublished studies available in languages accessible to the authors.
selection_criteria: 1) studies that compared the species richness and/or abundance of the focal taxa (apiformes, lepidoptera, syrphidae) between sites with agrienvironmental measures (not necessarily need to be part of a formal agri-environmental scheme as long as they included environmentally friendly practices that could potentially benefit pollinators) and conventionally managed control sites; 2) reported means, sd, sem or ci and sample sizes for both treatment and control (in the text, tables, graphs or after requesting the authors) to allow calculation of effect sizes; 3) included at least four spatial replicates; 4) were geographically restricted to europe.
data_analysis: random effect models were used to estimate the effect of agri-environmental measures on species richness and abundance of pollinators. effectiveness of agri-environmental measures was examined across farmland type (croplands vs. grasslands) and type of measures (flower strips, extensive grasslands or grass-sown or naturally regenerated field margin or set-aside). when sample size allowed it, the factors affecting agri-environmental measures' effectiveness were investigated separately for croplands and grasslands. results heterogeneity was tested. 95% ci around mean effect sizes were computed. publication bias in all data sets (except the data sets used in the meta-regressions) was assessed.
background: As biodiversity continues to decline, it is pivotal to know what ecological factors explain success or failure of agri-environmental measures. Effectiveness, i.e. enhancement of biodiversity in sites under agri-environmental management compared to control sites, has been hypothesised to be influenced by a number of factors.
objective: using a meta-analytic approach, this study examines the factors affecting the effectiveness of agri-environmental measures by addressing the following questions: 1) are agri-environmental measures more effective in simple than in complex or cleared landscapes? 2) does the effectiveness of agri-environmental measures decline with increasing land-use intensity? 3) is measure-induced contrast in resource availability positively related to effectiveness of agri-environmental measures? here, results for grasslands under extensive grazing schemes are reported.
result1: overall, agri-environmental measures had significant positive effects on species richness and abundance of pollinators in agroecosystems.
result2: in grasslands, different types of measures varied in their effectiveness for both species richness and abundance. for both species richness and abundance, effect sizes were largest for sown flower strips, smaller for extensive grasslands.
result3: regarding the flower strips, meta-regressions showed that the number of flower species that were sown was positively related with effect size for pollinator abundance but not species richness. however, when only the obligate pollen feeding bees were considered, the number of sown flower species in strips was significantly related with the effectiveness of flower strips in increasing both species richness and abundance.
general_conclusion: this study shows that agri-environmental measures generally enhance local pollinator species richness and abundance in agroecosystems compared to traditional intensive grasslands.

search_strategy: to identify published studies of how pollinators respond to anthropogenic disturbance, the authors conducted an isi web of science search covering the time period from 1945 to march 2007 using the following search terms: (pollinator* or bee or bees or apoidea or pollinat*) and (fragmentation or disturbance or perturbation or grazing or fire or deforestation or pesticide* or landscape). the authors also used the bibliographies of 24 recent papers, including a 2007 u.s. national academy of sciences report on the status of pollinators (nrc 2007), to search for additional studies.
selection_criteria: 1) presents data on how pollinator abundance or species richness changes with anthropogenic disturbance; 2) includes replication; 3) reports the sample size; and 4) reports either the mean and standard deviation of each treatment (for categorical independent variables), or statistics such as correlation or regression coefficients (for continuous independent variables), as these are necessary to calculate effect sizes.
data_analysis: the analyses were conducted using metawin version 2.0. confidence intervals of effect sizes were calculated using bias-corrected boot-strap resampling procedures as described in adams et al. (1997), except for groups with small sample sizes (≤10 effect sizes), in which case bootstrap procedures were not used because they are biased due to resampling from the same small set of values. an effect of anthropogenic disturbance was considered significant if the 95% confidence intervals (ci) of the effect size (d) did not overlap zero. data were analyzed using random-effect models. the heterogeneity of effect sizes was examined with q statistics, which can be used to determine whether the variance among effect sizes is greater than expected by chance.the authors explored the possibility of publication bias using funnel plots.
background: Pollinators may be declining globally, a matter of concern because animal pollination is required by most of the world's plant species, including many crop plants. Human land use and the loss of native habitats is thought to be an important driver of decline for wild, native pollinators, yet the findings of published studies on this topic have never been quantitatively synthesized.
objective: the authors address the following questions: 1) do different forms of anthropogenic disturbance affect bees similarly? 2) do results differ between more- and less-disturbed study systems? 3) is there variation among bee taxa in their response to disturbance? 4) do social and solitary bees exhibit different responses to disturbance? 5) are the bee fauna of different biomes differently affected by disturbance? the authors performed separate analyses for unmanaged wild species, and for honey bees.
result1: grazing has no effect on unmanaged bee abundance and richness.
result2: NA
general_conclusion: grazing has no effect on unmanaged bee abundance and richness.

search_strategy: the authors searched journal articles published between 1991 and 2016 using the web of science in both english and chinese and china knowledge resource integrated database. the following keywords and combinations were used for the searching: (1) “grazing” or “microbe” or “microbial” or “fungi” or “bacterial” and (2) “grazing” or “soil microbial carbon”.
selection_criteria: 1) all results were from field experiments; 2) grazing and grazing exclusion treatments had to be made at the same experimental sites; 3) data collection was limited to results in which means, standard deviations (sds), and replicate numbers were reported; 4) grazing protocols (grazing intensity, grazing exclusion year) had to be clearly described or accessible from the cited articles; 5) if more than one grazing experiment was reported in the same article but with different environmental variables, each was regarded as an independent study.
data_analysis: the authors used the metawin software to calculate overall weighted response ration (rr++) and 95% bootstrap confidence intervals (cis) for the whole dataset and the grouped dataset. significant responses (p < 0.05) were determined if cis of rr++ did not overlap with 0. the authors sequentially compared rr++ among measurements, grazing intensity, grazing and exclusion year. a linear regression analysis was used to examine the relationships between the rrs of microbial, fungal, and bacterial community size and mean annual temperature, mean annual precipitation, latitude, elevation, and rrs of soil respiration. due to the preference for publishing larger effects than smaller ones, the authors used kendall’s tau rank and spearman’s rank correlation to infer publication biasness.
background: Soil microorganisms regulate carbon (C) transfer from terrestrial sources to the atmosphere, therefore playing a pivotal role in soil C dynamics. Worldwide, grazing is one of the most prevalent grassland management stra- tegies, yet the effects of grazing on soil microbial community size and soil respiration (SR) are still active areas of debate.
objective: the authors conducted a meta-analysis on the responses of soil microbial community size and soil respiration to grazing. specifically, the objectives were to: 1) examine global patterns of soil microbial community size responses to grazing; 2) assess effects of grazing intensities on the soil microbial community size; 3) illustrate the responses of soil microbial community size would be tightly coupled with the changes in soil respiration.
result1: across all studies, soil microbial community size significantly decreased following grazing by an average of 11.74%.
result2: light and moderate grazing intensity increased soil microbial community size by 5.05 and 1.87%, respectively, whereas, heavy grazing intensity significantly decreased microbial community size by 18.12%.
result3: light and moderate grazing intensity increased soil microbes by 2.09 and 3.14% respectively, while heavily grazing intensity decreased by the same by 14.79%. furthermore, while light and moderate grazing intensity increased fungal community size by 17.01 and 0.80%, respectively, heavy grazing intensity decreased fungal community size by 16.48%. however, bacterial community size under moderate and heavy grazing intensity decreased by 0.28 and 28.12%, respectively.
result4: the authors found significant linear relationship between total soil microbial community size and soil respiration. however, total microbial community size was positively related with soil respiration under light grazing intensity (n = 58, r = 0.51), whereas, under heavy grazing intensity, they observed a negative association with total total soil microbial community size and soil respiration (n = 32, r = 0.37).
general_conclusion: grazing, as overall and heavy grazing, has a negative effect on microbial community size, while moderate grazing and light grazing have no effect.

search_strategy: research literature and data were predominantly sourced from web of science, google scholar, and cnki under the following search conditions: (1) “grassland” or “steppe” or “rangeland” or “pasture” or “meadow” or “prairie” (2) “restoration succession” or “grazing exclusion” (3) “soil microbial biomass” or “soil “microbial activity” or “microbial community structure” or “total plfa” or “fungi” or “bacteria” or “actinomycetes” or “16srna” were the keywords, and relevant documents published before july 2019 were identified and collected.
selection_criteria: 1) the research object was a grassland ecosystem; 2) the article clearly mentioned the number of restoration years; 3) in the study method, the control group and the treatment group were in the same location with no less than three replicates; 4) each parameter in the selected article displayed information of average values, standard deviations or standard errors, and repetitions; and 5) restoration succession studies were conducted under natural conditions without other treatment or interference.
data_analysis: regression analysis was calculated based on the lnr between different indicators. analyses and calculations were carried out using metawin software.
background: Microorganisms play an important role in the restoration of grassland ecosystems; however, there is no systematic research summary on how microbial communities respond to natural restoration succession in degraded grasslands.
objective: to comprehensively analyze the current understanding on microbial responses to natural restoration succession and to answer the following questions: 1) what mechanisms drive microbial change under natural restoration succession? 2) what factors affect changes in microorganisms? here, results for soil biological quality are reported.
result1: results showed that soil microbes displayed no significant changes at the early stage (≤5 years) of natural restoration succession (grazing exclusion), but significantly increased 6–10 years after grazing exclusion, before decreasing with the continuation of succession.
result2: changes in microbial activity mainly occurred in the 0–20 cm soil depth layer. soil microbial biomass carbon significantly decreased with grazing by 8.65%.
result3: numbers of bacteria, fungi, and actinomycetes significantly decreased at the six to 10 year stagegrazing exclusion.
result4: after 10 years of grazing exclusion, most microorganisms began to decrease.
result5: chao 1 index for bacteria and fungi did not signifcantly change with grazing exclusion.
general_conclusion: these results indicated that the optimal period for the natural restoration succession after grazing exclusion in degraded grassland was approximately 10 years to ensure that the microbes of the grassland system returned to relatively high levels.

search_strategy: the authors searched publications by using web of science in english and china national knowledge infrastructure database in chinese before 2019. the searching terms were: (arbuscular mycorrhiza*) and (grazing or stocking rate or livestock).
selection_criteria: 1) field experiments were selected in which conditions, such as microclimate, soil parameters and species composition, were the same in control and grazing plots; 2) the studies must have control and grazing treatments. the authors eliminated other confounding experimental treatments, such as fertilisation, to focus on grazing effects alone; 3) features of the grazing regimes were clearly described, including grazing intensity, duration of the experiment, identity of the livestock and ecosystem type; 4) to avoid short-term noise, the authors excluded experiments in which grazing duration was less than one growing season; 5) simulated grazing experiments, such as defoliation and trampling experiments, were excluded; 6) the mean, standard error (se) and sample size (n) in the control and grazing treatments could be collected from tables or digitised figures.
data_analysis: when the 95% ci does not cover 0, it indicates that grazing have a significant effect on response variables. these grazing effects were analysed by metawin 2.1 software. the authors further tested grazing effects on am fungal abundance based on grazing intensity, grazing duration and annual precipitation. furthermore, they examined the linear relationship between the response ratios (rrs) of am fungal abundance and the rr of above-ground biomass.
background: Livestock grazing activities substantially contribute to worldwide grassland degradation and potentially alter the growth of arbuscular mycorrhizal fungi. The global patterns of arbuscular mycorrhizal fungi in response to grazing, especially grazing intensity, are still unclear.
objective: the authors performed a global meta-analysis to assess the response of arbuscular mycorrhizal fungal abundance to grazing intensity. the objectives were to examine global patterns of arbuscular mycorrhizal fungal abundance in relation to livestock grazing. they also examined whether am fungal responses to grazing would change with grazing duration and annual precipitation.
