result1: the results showed that moderate and heavy grazing greatly reduced am fungal abundance by 9.14% and 34.38%, respectively (p < 0.05), whereas light grazing had little effect (1.64%).
result2: precipation, duration of grazing and plant type were factors affecting the results.
result3: the results also showed that the response ratio of am fungal abundance was significantly positively correlated with the response ratio of aboveground biomass.
general_conclusion: the overall effect of grazing on arbuscolar mycorrhizas fungal abundance in grassland is negative. heavy grazing and moderate grazing have a negative effect on arbuscolar mycorrhizas fungal abundance in grassland while light grazing has no effect.

search_strategy: using google scholar, isi webofscience, and china national knowledge infrastructure the authors searched for journal articles that reported plant, arthropod, and microbial diversity in response to grazing intensity during 1900–2018, the following search term combinations: (graz or grazing or grazed or fence* or enclosed or enclosure or enclos) and (plant or arthropod* or microbe* or diversity* or richness* or insects* or microbial* or biodiversity) and (effect* or respon* or affect* or impact* or increas* or decreas* or alter*) not (medic* or chemist*).
selection_criteria: 1) experiments were conducted in the field using both enclosed and grazing treatments at the same temporal and spatial scales; experiments also included an analyses of species richness and shannon wiener index; 2) grazing intensity was clearly described in the paper, such as light, moderate, and heavy; 3) the means, standard deviations/errors, and samples sizes of variables in the enclosed and grazing treatments could be extracted directly from the text, tables or digitized graphs.
data_analysis: all data were analyzed using metawin 2.4 and r 3.5.1; the statistical results were considered to be statistically significant at p < 0.05. the authors further evaluated to see if rr++ was affected by grazing intensity, the total heterogeneity among group (qt) was partitioned into within-group (qw) and between-group (qb) heterogeneity.
background: Livestock grazing is an important component and driver of biodiversity in grassland ecosystems. While numerous studies and a few meta-analyses had been conducted on the response of single taxon diversity to grazing in grasslands, a synthesis of how multi-taxa diversity is affected has been largely missing, especially reflecting its changes along a grazing intensity gradient.
objective: the objective of this study was to quantitatively evaluate grazing-induced changes in biodiversity and elucidate the potential mechanisms involved. the objectives of this study were to 1) quantify the effect of grazing on species richness (sr) and the shannon– wiener index (h′) of different taxa in grasslands; 2) assess the effects of grazing intensity on the sr and h′ of plants, arthropods, and microbes; 3) and identify the underlying mechanisms for the effects of grazing intensity on the diversity of plants, arthropods, and microbes. here, results for soil microbes are provided.
result1: across all studied taxa, grazing resulted in enhanced species richness.
result2: species richness for microbe increased after grazing.
result3: bacterial species richness increased with light and moderate intensity and decreased with heavy intensity grazing, while fungal species richness increased with light intensity and declined with moderate and heavy intensity grazing.
general_conclusion: grazing resulted in a significant enhancement of biodiversity, with increases in microbial diversity.

search_strategy: peer-reviewed journal articles published before october 2015 were searched using web of science and china knowledge resource integrated database (cnki) with the following search term combinations: (grazing or herbivory or defoliation) and (carbon or nitrogen) and (grassland or pasture or meadow).
selection_criteria: 1) experiments were conducted in the field and had at least one pair of data (under control and treatment); 2) grazing regimes were clearly defined with both quantitative and/or qualitative descriptions for grazing intensity, experimental duration and livestock type (i.e., cattle, sheep or others); 3) to avoid short-term noise, experiments with durations less than one growing season were excluded; 4) initial environmental and climate conditions, soil parameters and species compositions in the control and treatments were the same; 5) the mean, standard error (se) or standard deviation (sd) and sample size (n) of selected variables in control and treatment groups could be extracted directly from tables, digitized graphs or contexts.
data_analysis: the means of response ratio (rr++) are calculated from individual rr of each paired comparison between the control and grazing treatments with the weight of each rr. the 95% confidence interval (95% ci) is rr++ +/- 1.96 s (rr++). the authors applied a t-test to examine the significance of variation in each variable between the control and treatment, and the difference in rr++ between grazing intensity, climate type, grazing type and soil depth. the effect of livestock grazing was considered to be significant if the 95% ci of a response variable did not overlap zero. pearson correlation analyses were performed to examine the relationships between the response ratio of scp and snp with environmental conditions (i.e., grazing duration, latitude, mean annual temperature and mean annual precipitation).
background: Livestock grazing activities potentially alter ecosystem carbon (C) and nitrogen (N) cycles in grassland ecosystems. Despite the fact that numerous individual studies and a few meta-analyses had been conducted, how grazing, especially its intensity, affects belowground C and N cycling in grasslands remains unclear.
objective: in this study, a meta-analysis was conducted on 622 paired comparisons from 115 experimental studies to evaluate the responses of belowground c and n cycles to grazing intensities. specifically, the objectives were to 1) examine global patterns of belowground c and n responses to livestock grazing; 2) assess effects of grazing intensities on the belowground c and n dynamics; 3) investigate regulation of the environmental factors on soil c pools (scp) and soil n pools (snp) alteration in response to grazing.
result1: among the variables, microbial biomass c (-21.62%) and n (-24.40%) showed the largest decrease in response to grazing compared to other variables.
result2: NA
general_conclusion: grazing has a negative effect on both microbial biomass carbon and nitrogen.

search_strategy: the authors searched for peer-reviewed papers published before june 2018 in web of science and china knowledge resource integrated database (cnki), using the following search terms: (grazing or herbivory or defoliation) and (c:n or c:p or n:p or c:n:p) and (grassland or pasture or meadow).
selection_criteria: 1) the experiment was conducted in the field and included non-grazed plots and at least one grazing treatment, 2) experimental duration was longer than one growing season; 3) the initial climatic conditions, soil properties, and species compositions in the non-grazed and grazing treatments were the same; 4) all plots were free of grazing for at least 10 years prior to the start of the experiment; 5) the dominant species were clearly described and the grazing intensity was quantitatively and/or qualitatively reported; 6) the mean, standard error (se) or standard deviation (sd), and sample size (n) of the relevant variables could be extracted from the tables, digitized graphs or the text.
data_analysis: the 95% confidence interval (ci) for rr++ was rr++ ± 1.96 × s(rr++). the influence of livestock grazing was considered significant if the 95% ci did not overlap zero. the percentage change of a variable was calculated as [exp (rr++) – 1] × 100%. a t test was applied to examine the difference in rr++ between differential grazing intensities in groups with different climate (mean annual temperature, mean annual precipitation), elevation, dominant species (c3 and c4), and soil depth.
background: Livestock grazing can alter carbon (C), nitrogen (N) and phosphorus (P) cycles, thereby affecting the C : N : P stoichiometry in grasslands.
objective: the authors investigate the general response pattern of above- and belowground c : n : p stoichiometry to different grazing intensities. specifically, the objectives were: 1) to examine global patterns of above- and belowground c : n : p stoichiometry in response to livestock grazing; 2) to explore links between grazing effects on above- and belowground c : n : p stoichiometry;  3) to evaluate whether grazing effects on soil c : n : p stoichiometry depend on grazing intensity, climate, soil depth, and vegetation type.
result1: grazing decreased soil microbial c.
result2: grazing increased soil microbial n.
result3: grazing has no effect on soil microbial p.
general_conclusion: grazing has a negative effect on soil microbial c, positive effect on soil microbial n and no effect on soil microbial p.

search_strategy: the authors started a literature search for studies measuring effects of real or simulated herbivory, removing leaves and ⁄or shoots, on mycorrhizas (amf and ecm), with the following search string, [mycorrh* and (mow* or clip* or defoliat* or cut* or insect* or graz* or feed* or brows* or pastur* or herbivor* or cattle or cow* or sheep or horse* or rabbi*)]. the search was conducted on 24 march 2009, using the web of science citation index expanded data base and including all articles published since 1965.
selection_criteria: in order to be considered a separate system, experiments had to differ in at least one of the following factors: study site, plant species, amf species, fertilization treatment (yes or no) and method or degree of defoliation. where multiple experiments differed only in treatment duration, only the longest time period was considered.
data_analysis: all analyses were conducted in r, with the ‘meta’ package and the ‘mima’ function. the authors performed a continuous meta-analysis using a mixed-effects model where the overall analysis was performed with a random-effects model using the dersimonian–laird method, and comparisons across subgroups during tests of moderators were performed using a fixed-effects model.
background: In managed and natural ecosystems, herbivory can have a major impact on plant growth. Defoliation and shoot removal reduce the photosynthetic capacity of plants and are also thought to reduce allocation of carbon to roots and mycorrhizal fungi. However, evidence supporting this assumption remains equivocal.
objective: the authors conducted a meta-analysis in order to summarize quantitatively published reports on the sensitivity of mycorrhizal fungi to herbivory or clipping of their plant hosts, and to determine how that sensitivity is moderated by the type of mycorrhiza, fertilization, treatment, experimental setting, host plant type, duration of the experiment, year of publication, and frequency and degree of defoliation.
result1: overall, herbivory or clipping reduced root colonization by mycorrhizal fungi by about 3 percentage points [wmd = -2.96 (-5.48; -0.49); z = -2.3683, p = 0.0179].
result2: there was significant heterogeneity among experiments (q = 1 122 352.36, d.f. = 98, p < 0.0001), indicating that other experimental treatments, or moderators, may have influenced results. the type of mycorrhiza, fertilization, setting and duration of the experiment did not affect effect sizes. in mowed or clipped sites, the number of cuts per year had no effect on effect sizes (n=60, qe = 10 026.56, qme = 1.5945, d.f. = 1, p = 0.2067).
general_conclusion: the results suggest that herbivory, real or simulated, reduces mycorrhizal colonization by biologically meaningful amounts only in a limited subset of systems.
knowledge_gaps: the authors did not find strong negative effects in any plants, but they found strong positive effects of herbivory in mixtures of perennial grasses and forbs. however, only five experiments from three publications used mixtures of plants, so additional work must be carried out before concluding that this trend persists.

search_strategy: 287 publications were selected from 1,260 referred english papers published from 2007 to 2019. the publications were discovered by searching google scholar using the keywords “grazing” and “soil” in the titles of papers to collect data and compile dataset.
selection_criteria: 1) soil property data under various grazing intensities (>3) and the un-grazing from different field sites at 0–30 cm depth were collected. because grazing data cannot be compared to un-grazing at the same time, this study excluded temporal comparisons data (before and after grazing) of the same site; 2) data at sites grazed by domestic animals such as cattle (bos taurus l.), sheep (ovis aries l.) (including goat and deer), or their mixture were selected; 3) this study defined non-adjacent sites to have a distance greater than 46 km (an approximate distance of 25’ in lat- itude range). non-adjacent site data were considered independent and included in the database. adjacent site data were only limited to one site to avoid dependent data with different sites; 4) data collected within a year for each site were averaged. data collected over multiple years could be time-dependent. as a result, only the data from the most recent year were included; 5) site information including grazing intensity, overgrazing, grazing animals, grazing period, land-use, sampling year, soil depth, latitude, longitude, altitude, country, soil texture, mean annual precipitation, and mean daily temperature were all collected.
data_analysis: this study used the mixed model method in proc mixed in sas9.4 to conduct this meta- analysis.
background: Grazing effects on soil properties under different soil and environmental conditions across the globe are often controversial. Therefore, it is essential to evaluate the overall magnitude and direction of the grazing effects on soils.
objective: utilizing comprehensive meta-analytical approach based on publications from 2007 to 2019, the objective ofthis study was to address the overall effects of global grazing intensities on 15 soil properties: soil bulk density (bd), penetration resistance (pr), soc, total nitrogen (tn), c: n ratio, ammonium (nh4+), nitrate (no3 -), microbial biomass carbon (mbc), microbial biomass nitrogen (mbn), available phosphorus (p) and potassium (k), cation exchange capacity (cec), ph, electrical conductivity (ec), and water content (wc). here, results for mbc and mbn are reported.
result1: heavy grazing intensity significantly decreased mbc [-27.9% (-45.5- -4.6%)] at at the 0–10 cm depth.
result2: NA
general_conclusion: heavy grazing has negative effect on mbc, and no effect on mbn. moderate grazing showed no effect on mbc and mbn, light grazing has no effect on mbc.

search_strategy: to collect published studies that have investigated the impacts of grazing intensity (gi) on soil organic carbon (soc) and other selected soil properties (tn, ph and bd) under grassland, the authors performed a comprehensive search on the web of science database (accessed between january 2015 and july 2017) using the following keywords: grazing; soil organic carbon; grassland; gi; total nitrogen and carbon sequestration. in an attempt to have the best possible coverage; the authors also checked all references in the papers found in the web of science search.
selection_criteria: only studies which were longer than one year and measured soc or tn were selected. the authors also accounted for the differences in grass growing seasons at each experimental site.
data_analysis: the authors used minitab 17 to conduct the data exploration, conditioning and analyses. the descriptive statistics of the annual change in soc, tn, bd and ph due to grazing including mean, median, standard deviation, and 95% confidence intervals for each were calculated. one way anovas were performed to investigate the impact of factors: climate, grazing intensity, grass and animal types on soc, tn and other selected soil properties, and the rates of change. principle component analysis was used to determine significant explanatory variables and response variables and determine the differences between climatic zones. in addition, regressions or mixed models such as glm's, were used to determine significant explanatory variables.
background: Livestock grazing intensity (GI) is thought to have a major impact on soil organic carbon (SOC) storage and soil quality indicators in grassland agroecosystems. Understanding the impacts of GI on SOC accumulation and storage in grasslands is crucial to provide the most effective soil C management options. However, although all of these previous reviews are valuable, scientific understanding would be improved by normalizing the sampling depth and GI.
objective: the major objective of this meta-analysis was to investigate the impacts of gi on soc in extensively grazed grassland soils at a global scale. additionally, and because of its importance for c biogeochemistry, the authors considered the impacts of gi on total nitrogen (tn) and other soil properties (mainly ph and bulk density) in grasslands.
result1: grazing intensity was associated with an increase in soil total nitrogen of 0.06 (+6%; stdev = 0.772).
result2: NA
general_conclusion: grazing intensity was associated with an increase in soil total nitrogen.

search_strategy: the authors searched peer-reviewed publications using the web of science from 1900 to 2016 and the china knowledge resource integrated database before 2016. the searching terms were: (grazing) and (soil) and (carbon dioxide/co2, methane/ch4 or nitrous oxide/n2o).
selection_criteria: 1) only field experiments were included with the same condition between control and grazing plots, such as microclimate, vegetation and soil types. the authors also excluded other confounding treatments (i.e. fertilization and land conversion), focusing on grazing impacts alone; 2) simulated grazing experiments were eliminated, such as mowing and trampling studies; 3) soil ghg fluxes were explicitly indicated by their means, variances and number of replicates; 4) grazing intensity, duration, animals and ecosystem type need to be clearly described.
data_analysis: the 95% confidence interval (ci) was estimated as ln(rr++) ± 1.96se(lnrr++). if the 95% ci does not cover zero, it implies a significant impact by grazing. these grazing impacts at global level were analyzed by metawin 2.1 software. grazing impacts on soil ghg fluxes were further evaluated at subgroup levels, such as grazing intensity (light, moderate and heavy grazing), grazing duration (<5, 5–10 and >10 years) and precipitation (<400 and ≥400 mm). furthermore, a linear function was used to examine the relationships of soil ghg fluxes with aboveground biomass, soil organic carbon or total nitrogen, soil bulk density, and that of soil moisture with aboveground biomass.
background: Grazing degrades worldwide grasslands and possibly suppresses soil greenhouse gas (GHG: CO2, CH4 and N2O) fluxes. However, the global patterns of these three gas fluxes in response to grazing and the general mechanisms remain poorly understood.
objective: the authors conducted a global synthesis of 63 grazing experiments in grasslands to reveal the general response patterns of soil co2 and n2o emissions and ch4 uptake to grazing, and uncover the underlying mechanisms at the global scale. specifically, the authors addressed the following questions: 1) how grazing differently influences three soil ghg fluxes across global grasslands? 2) how grazing intensity, grazing duration and precipitation regulate these response patterns? 3) what are the general mechanisms underlying grazing-induced changes in these three ghg? here we report only the results on the effect of grazing on soil total nitrogen.
result1: soil total nitrogen was decreased by heavy grazing, while no effect was reported for light and moderate grazing.
result2: NA
general_conclusion: light and moderate grazing have no effect on soil total nitrogen while heavy grazing has a negative effect.

search_strategy: the authors searched web of science, google scholar and china national knowledge infrastructure using the following keywords: ‘grazing or grazer or grazed or ungulate or herbivore or degraded or degradation’ and ‘nitrogen or phosphorus’. the authors supplemented this database by searching more general keywords, for example, ‘stocking rate’, ‘defoliation’, ‘grassland’ and ‘plant and soil nutrient’.
selection_criteria: 1) plant species must be vascular plants; 2) ungulate herbivore species must belong to artiodactyla and perissodactyla taxa; 3) studies were carried out in rangeland ecosystems (including grasslands and pastures) that directly compared plant and/or soil nutrient in response to grazing and grazing exclusion without other experimental treatments (e.g. warming, sowing, fertilizer, mowing or fire); 4) mean value, standard error (se) or standard deviation (sd) and the sample size were given in the original studies; 5) plant and soil were sampled at the peak period of grass biomass production, as sampling time can affect plant and soil nutrient status.
data_analysis: if the 95% ci of the rr++ of a variable overlapped with zero, the effect of grazing on the variable was not considered significant between two treatments. otherwise, grazing was considered causing a significant difference in the value of that specific variable. z- tests were performed to examine potential differences among levels of a given explanatory variable (e.g. grazing intensity) in bsda package. the authors estimated the potential publication bias using funnel plots and kendall rank correlation coefficient.
background: The overall responses of plant and soil N:P stoichiometry to animal grazing addressed in previous individual studies are associated with a great deal of uncertainty. There is thus the need to study potential general patterns of N:P stoichiometry across different grazing systems and environmental conditions through a meta-analysis approach.
objective: a meta-analysis was conducted on 3,482 paired comparisons (i.e. grazing vs. grazing exclusion) from 173 experimental studies globally to evaluate the response of plant and soil n:p stoichiometry to animal grazing. specifically, the key objectives of this study were to: 1) examine the response of twelve variables associated with changes in plant and soil n:p stoichiometry to grazing; 2) explore the correlation among the response ratios of plant and soil n:p stoichiometry as affected by different environmental factors; 3) investigate whether and how grazing intensity, duration, regime, herbivore assemblage, grassland type and other environmental factors might affect the responses of plant and soil n:p stoichiometry to grazing.
result1: mean effect sizes of soil total n, total p, available n, available p were significantly lower than zero and decreased by 7%, 5%, 2% and 5%, respectively.
result2: NA
general_conclusion: grazing has a negative effect on soil nutrients (soil total n, soil total p).

search_strategy: the authors conducted a scopus database query to identify peer-reviewed articles matching predetermined title–abstract–keyword search criteria to match grazing strategies and intensities to desired response variables.
selection_criteria: 1) at least one field season of treatment and control monitoring; 2) experimentally manipulated ruminant livestock grazing only; 3) grazing strategy (continuous and/or rotational) and intensity (heavy, moderate, and/or light) that were clearly identified either quantitatively or qualitatively; 4) at least one paired response of treatment (grazing strategy or intensity) and control (no grazing or continuous grazing) mean and variance for either soil organic carbon (soc), bulk density (bd), c/n ratio (cn), or total n (tn) that was extractable from text, tables, charts, or appendices.
data_analysis: for each effect size, 95% confidence intervals (cis) were calculated to describe the range, and effect sizes were considered significant if their lower or upper cis reached zero but did not overlap zero. the authors did not include results with less than two paired observations. for just the continuous grazing vs. no grazing controls data subset, the authors performed multiple linear regression with model averaging to examine whether grazing treatment effects (effect sizes) on soc, bd, cn, and tn were moderated by environmental (aridity, latitude, elevation, plant community, percentage sand, percentage clay) and study (study duration and grazing intensity) variables. the authors only included complete observations for this analysis and selected the best models using a cutoff of two akaike information criteria (small sample size corrected). all analyses were conducted in rstudio using the metafor and glmulti packages, and standard diagnostics were used to confirm that analysis assumptions were met.
background: Grazing lands support the livelihoods of millions of people across nearly one-half of the globe. Soils are the backbone of stability and resilience in these systems.
objective: the authors conducted a global meta-analysis to examine the effects of grazing strategy (i.e., no grazing, continuous grazing, and rotational grazing), grazing intensity (heavy, moderate, and light grazing), and site-specific environmental factors on three important contributors to soil function and health—soil c and n cycling and bulk density (bd). here we report only results on soil total nitrogen.
result1: averaged across all studies and grazing intensities, continuous grazing significantly reduced soil total nitrogen (−0.05, ci [−0.10, 0.00]) relative to no grazing controls.
result2: the grazing strategy comparisons were minimally conditioned by aridity class (i.e., arid, subhumid, and humid).
result3: elevation, aridity, absolute latitude, percentage sand and clay, and study duration all had significant moderating effects on soil total nitrogen (n = 25) responses to grazing treatment effects (continuous grazing vs. no grazing effect size).
general_conclusion: overall, continuous grazing has a negative effect compared to no grazing on soil total nitrogen, and no effect for heavy and light grazing. rotational grazing has no effect on soil total nitrogen compared to continuous grazing.
knowledge_gaps: the authors strongly suggest that future research focus on advancing understanding of interactions among important environmental factors and grazing management and resulting soil health outcomes.

search_strategy: authors systematically searched in scopus and scholar google for peer‐reviewed studies using the following combination of terms: (evapotranspiration or transpiration or infiltration or “hydraulic conductivity” or permeability) and (replace* or transform or afforest or deforest or forest or reforest or wood or “land use” or degrade or grazing or crop or cultivated or pasture or livestock or cattle or trampling) and (grass or graz* or rangeland* or pasture or savannah* or forage* or herbage* or meadow or praire or steppe), including papers until 2016.
selection_criteria: excluded papers were those that 1) clearly did not focus on comparisons of infiltration or evapotranspiration in grasslands and other types of vegetation; 2) did not perform pairwise contrast, between grasslands replaced by crop or forest and grasslands with grazing effects; or 3) had not reported statistic design, statistical measures (mean values, sample size, and variance estimation), evidence of reasonable comparing conditions of soil type, climatic conditions, and methodology.
data_analysis: a categorical random‐effect meta‐analysis model was used to calculate the mean effect sizes assuming a random variation among observations, and 95% confidence intervals were calculated around the mean effect sizes using bootstrapping with 999 iterations. to explore if the response ratios were affected by environmental variables, linear and nonlinear (polynomial and logarithmic) regression model equations were fitted for each type of lulc (crops, forest, or grazing). to check for publication bias, rosenthal's fail‐safe number was calculated. authors also checked publication bias using funnel plots. response ratio calculations and statistical analyses were performed using metawin 2.0.
background: In order to support public policies attending to the consequences of different grassland modifications and replacements, general patterns and models about their consequences on water regulation are needed.
objective: two specific questions were addressed: 1) how are the evapotranspiration and infiltration processes affected by different land cover changes (from grasslands to crops or to forests) and/or land uses (grazing) and 2) how land use/land cover changes impact evapotranspiration and infiltration in different climates and soils. here, results for the effect of grazing are reported.
result1: in grasslands, soil water infiltration is significantly reduced by grazing on average by 51%.
result2: grazing caused a mean decrease of 11% on the evapotranspiration, but the effect was not significant.
result3: the reduction of infiltration with grazing decreases with soil sand content and increases with the mean annual precipitation (ppt) and the ratio ppt/mean annual potential evapotranspiration.
general_conclusion: this meta‐analysis confirms the hypothesis that grazing affects negatively the infiltration process, reducing it by 51%.

search_strategy: the authors searched peer-reviewed publications using the web of science from 1900 to 2016 and the china knowledge resource integrated database before 2016. the searching terms were: (grazing) and (soil) and (carbon dioxide/co2, methane/ch4 or nitrous oxide/n2o).
selection_criteria: 1) only field experiments were included with the same condition between control and grazing plots, such as microclimate, vegetation and soil types. the authors also excluded other confounding treatments (i.e. fertilization and land conversion), focusing on grazing impacts alone; 2) simulated grazing experiments were eliminated, such as mowing and trampling studies; 3) soil ghg fluxes were explicitly indicated by their means, variances and number of replicates; 4) grazing intensity, duration, animals and ecosystem type need to be clearly described.
data_analysis: the 95% confidence interval (ci) was estimated as ln(rr++) ± 1.96se(lnrr++). if the 95% ci does not cover zero, it implies a significant impact by grazing. these grazing impacts at global level were analyzed by metawin 2.1 software. grazing impacts on soil ghg fluxes were further evaluated at subgroup levels, such as grazing intensity (light, moderate and heavy grazing), grazing duration (<5, 5–10 and >10 years) and precipitation (<400 and ≥400 mm). furthermore, a linear function was used to examine the relationships of soil ghg fluxes with aboveground biomass, soil organic carbon or total nitrogen, soil bulk density, and that of soil moisture with aboveground biomass.
background: Grazing degrades worldwide grasslands and possibly suppresses soil greenhouse gas (GHG: CO2, CH4 and N2O) fluxes. However, the global patterns of these three gas fluxes in response to grazing and the general mechanisms remain poorly understood.
objective: the authors conducted a global synthesis of 63 grazing experiments in grasslands to reveal the general response patterns of soil co2 and n2o emissions and ch4 uptake to grazing, and uncover the underlying mechanisms at the global scale. specifically, the authors addressed the following questions: 1) how grazing differently influences three soil ghg fluxes across global grasslands? 2) how grazing intensity, grazing duration and precipitation regulate these response patterns? 3) what are the general mechanisms underlying grazing-induced changes in these three ghg? here we report only the results on the effect of grazing on soil moisture.
result1: soil moisture was decreased by heavy grazing, while no effect was reported for light and moderate grazing.
result2: NA
general_conclusion: light and moderate grazing have no effect on soil moisture while heavy grazing has a negative effect.

search_strategy: peer-reviewed journal articles published before october 2015 were searched using web of science and china knowledge resource integrated database (cnki) with the following search term combinations: (grazing or herbivory or defoliation) and (carbon or nitrogen) and (grassland or pasture or meadow).
selection_criteria: 1) experiments were conducted in the field and had at least one pair of data (under control and treatment); 2) grazing regimes were clearly defined with both quantitative and/or qualitative descriptions for grazing intensity, experimental duration and livestock type (i.e., cattle, sheep or others); 3) to avoid short-term noise, experiments with durations less than one growing season were excluded; 4) initial environmental and climate conditions, soil parameters and species compositions in the control and treatments were the same; 5) the mean, standard error (se) or standard deviation (sd) and sample size (n) of selected variables in control and treatment groups could be extracted directly from tables, digitized graphs or contexts.
data_analysis: the means of response ratio (rr++) are calculated from individual rr of each paired comparison between the control and grazing treatments with the weight of each rr. the 95% confidence interval (95% ci) is rr++ +/- 1.96 s (rr++). the authors applied a t-test to examine the significance of variation in each variable between the control and treatment, and the difference in rr++ between grazing intensity, climate type, grazing type and soil depth. the effect of livestock grazing was considered to be significant if the 95% ci of a response variable did not overlap zero. pearson correlation analyses were performed to examine the relationships between the response ratio of scp and snp with environmental conditions (i.e., grazing duration, latitude, mean annual temperature and mean annual precipitation).
background: Livestock grazing activities potentially alter ecosystem carbon (C) and nitrogen (N) cycles in grassland ecosystems.
