general_conclusion: reduced tillage intensity increases soil organic carbon stock compared to deep inversion (with the exception of non-inversion in the top soil where no difference was found) but not compared to shallow inversion.

search_strategy: the authors collected data from 69 paired ct and nt experiments in peer-reviewed research papers that reported the change in soil organic c (soc) contents of different soil depth.
selection_criteria: the following criteria to select paired experiments: (1) in some studies, there were several types of tillage treatments, in which cases the tillage treatment that disturbed soil the most (e.g., moldboard plowing) was selected as ct. (2) the authors specifically focused on studies involving soil sampling deeper than 40 cm. in addition, only the studies that provide data to estimate soil c content on area basis were selected for comparison purpose. (3) further, only the studies that had the similar soil type, aspect, and managements (e.g., cropping system, fertilization, and irrigation) in both the ct and nt treatments were included. in each individual study the ct and nt treatments must be conducted at the same site with same experimental duration.
data_analysis: meta-analysis was used to determine changes in soil c content after adoption of nt at different soil layers. the 95% confidence interval (ci) for the effect size were computed. the same calculation process was applied to compare the differences in soil c content between cultivated soils and adjacent natural soils. the random effects model of meta-analysis was conducted using mix software. regression analysis was applied to examine the relationship between the relative changes of cumulative soil c content and soil depth. the authors analyzed the effects of cropping systems (single or double cropping systems; the experiments with single cropping systems were grouped into three sub-groups based on the number of crop types involved in the experiment) on soil c dynamics after the conversion from ct to nt. the authors also applied regression analysis to examine the relationship of the relative change of cumulative soil c down to 60 cm with mean annual rainfall, mean annual temperature, n application rate, and the duration of experiments.
background: Adopting no-tillage in agro-ecosystems has been widely recommended as a means of enhancing carbon (C) sequestration in soils. However, study results are inconsistent and varying from significant increase to significant decrease. It is unclear whether this variability is caused by environmental, or management factors or by sampling errors and analysis methodology.
objective: the objective of this study is to assess the response of soil organic carbon (soc) to conversion of management practice from conventional tillage (ct) to no-tillage (nt).
result1: compared to ct, nt led to an increase of 3.15 +/- 2.42 t/ha in soil c in the surface 10 cm of soil, but a decline of 2.40 +/- 1.05 t/ha and 0.90 +/- 0.60 t/ha in the 20-30 and 30-40 cm soil layers, respectively. below 40 cm, there was no significant difference in soil c content between the ct and nt treatments. considering the change of total soil c content down to a specific soil depth, an exponential decay function well fitted the changes of cumulative soil c content with increasing soil depth. when all data were pooled together, on average, adoption of nt increased soil c accumulation in the surface 30 cm of soil. when deeper soil layers (>40 cm depth) were included, the total soil c content kept almost stable, with an insignificant increase of around 2.8% (p = 0.094 for the constant value 0.028 when fitting the exponential decay function).
result2: conversion from ct to nt did not increase the overall soc stock in most cases, except for those with double cropping systems (two crops per year).
general_conclusion: conversion from ct to nt significantly altered the vertical distribution of soil c in the soil profile, resulting in increased soil c in the 0-10 cm soil and similar or decline in soil c in the >10 cm soil.

search_strategy: the authors collected the available peer-reviewed literature reporting comparisons between rmp and conventional management under mediterranean climatic conditions. studies were selected after searching simultaneously the keywords “mediterranean”, “conventional” and “soil” in the isi web of knowledge electronic database.
selection_criteria: selected studies were performed in field conditions, in the mediterranean areas, laboratory and experimental greenhouse studies were excluded. the selected studies included pair-wise comparisons of the performance of rmps and conventional management, performed under similar pedo-climatic conditions, and after at least 3 or more years of management. the analysis was restricted to croplands, including arable crops, orchards and horticulture, but excluding permanent grassland and forests.
data_analysis: response ratio (rr) was used as the effect size unit for soc content comparisons. raw difference in means was chosen as the effect size for sequestration rate comparisons. studies were weighted using the product of 2 weighting measures to provide more weight to larger studies and studies with multiple observations. weighted mean effect sizes of each category were calculated, with bias-corrected 95% confidence intervals (cis) generated by a bootstrapping procedure (10,000 iterations).
background: Mediterranean croplands are seasonally dry agroecosystems with low soil organic carbon (SOC) content and high risk of land degradation and desertification. The increase in SOC is of special interest in these systems, as it can help to build resilience for climate change adaptation while contributing to mitigate global warming through the sequestration of atmospheric carbon (C).
objective: the present work aims to compare a wide range of recommended management practices (rmps, e.g. solid organic amendments, land treatment, cover crops, slurry applications, conservation tillage, combined practices and organic management) with conventional management. the authors conducted a meta-analysis to: (i) estimate the mean change in soc content and soc sequestration rate associated to the adoption of rmps and to the application of different c input rates; (ii) analyze the effect of different cropping systems and practices on c sequestration, and to (iii) identify the main sources of uncertainty in the available information. the results regarding conservation tillage (i.e. no tillage or reduced tillage) are reported here.
result1: both of the studied conservation tillage categories enhanced c sequestration. nt showed an average increase of 11.4% in soc resulting in a c sequestration rate of 0.44 mg c ha/yr, whereas under rt, soc content increased by 15% and c sequestration rate by 0.32 mg c ha/yr.
result2: the relatively lower effect of nt on soc is influenced by the inclusion of 5 woody crops treatments. soc increased by 18.2% (n = 28) under nt in herbaceous crops, but decreased by 22.9% (n = 5) in woody crops.
general_conclusion: this study shows that soc content and c sequestration rate are significantly higher than in conventional soils for both conservation tillage categories.
knowledge_gaps: bulk density (bd) is not provided in many cases; soc stock calculation is biased by changes in bd; coarse soil fraction (>2 mm) is usually neglected; experiment length is usually short or medium-term (average 8.7 years); sampling depth is commonly insufficient (average 23 cm); information on c input was only provided in 42.2% of the data sets studied, and in most cases this information was incomplete.

search_strategy: literature searches were conducted in scopus, targeting peer reviewed articles published online through july 2019. the results included 187 experimental treatments from 46 peer-reviewed articles, including the countries of spain, italy, france, portugal, greece,turkey, slovenia, tunisia, chile and the united states of america. to obtain the papers listed, we used the keywords “almond or olive or citrus or vineyard or grapevine or orchard”,“and”combinations of the following items:“mediterranean climate”,“cover crop”,“inter-cropping”,“alley crop”,“multicrop”,“agroforestry”,“crop yield”and“soil”.
selection_criteria: laboratory or greenhouse studies were excluded, and only studies performed in field conditions and carried out in a mediterranean climate were chosen. when several papers included data from the same experiment, the longest study with the most soil and crop variables was chosen.
data_analysis: the response ratio (rr) was calculated as aproportionate change in the indicator value of the treatment group (sustainable management: intercropping, organic fertilization and no-tillage/minimum tillage) compared to the pairwise control group (conventional management: mono-cropping, inorganic fertilization and conventional tillage). the natural logarithm of the response ratio was used for the analysis (log (rr)). we decided to weight observations using thesample sizes to ensure statistical significance by keeping a sufficient sample size: studies with larger sample sizes were weighted higher during aggregation. for the uncertainty analysis, we reported the means and 95% confidence intervals (cis). the cis were constructed by non-parametric bootstrapping (nboot = 10 000).the bootstrapping was only carried out for treatments with n>=8, as the bootstrap is unreliable when the sample size is too small.
background: There is now a growing emphasis on crop diversification and optimized use of resources, including with the production of food, feed or industrial products that contribute to long-term sustainability of the agroecosystems and climate change mitigation and adaptation.
objective: assess the benefits of crop diversification, conservation tillage (minimum tillage/no-tillage) and organic fertilization as alternatives to intensive conventional mono-cropping in field studies. we focus here on conservation tillage.
result1: both mt and nt were associated with a significant increase in soc compared to conventional tillage.
result2: on average, c sequestration rate also increased by 1.54 mg ha-1yr-1 in mt and 1.40 mg ha-1yr-1 in nt, with 75% and 78% of studies showing a positive rate, respectively.
general_conclusion: conservation tillage has a positive effect on soil c..

search_strategy: the data used in this study derive from the systematic review of haddaway et al. (2017) which reviews a total of 351 studies within boreo-temperate regions (cfa, cfb, cfc, csa, csb, csc, dfa, dfb, dfc, according to the köppen-geiger classification) dealing with tillage effects on changes in soc concentrations and stocks to fixed depth.  a more detailed description of the search process (e.g. websites and resources) and criteria that led to exclusion of a study is given in the systematic review protocol of haddaway et al. (2016).
selection_criteria: only long-term experiments (ltes) with a study duration of at least 10 years were included. in order to calculate soc stocks considering esm principles, only studies that reported soil c (stocks or concentrations) in combination with ρb for the same sampling depth were included. to overcome the bias of an over-representation of single experimental sites, only the most recently published study per trial was included. a more detailed description of the search process (e.g. websites and resources) and criteria that led to exclusion of a study is given in the systematic review protocol of haddaway et al. (2016).
data_analysis: meta-analysis was used to evaluate the mean difference between absolute soc stocks after conversion from high intensity to reduced tillage management using raw mean differences as effect sizes and standard deviations (sd) as measures of variability. where sd could not be extracted or calculated, it was imputed for each study in two ways: 1) it was reassigned as 1/10 of the mean; 2) the maximum sd reported across the evidence base was substituted. both approaches were considered in separate analyses and an additional analysis was made including only studies which reported sd for both soc and bulk density. separate analyses were undertaken for each of the three tillage comparisons and available soil layers. the linear relationship between stock changes and selected environmental, soil, and management-related parameters was determined for single soil depths and treatment comparisons using the pearson correlation coefficient. these analyses were done using the relative stock changes.
background: Shifting from high intensity (HT) to intermediate intensity (IT) or no tillage (NT) practices has been credited as being a promising agricultural management option towards climate change mitigation due to carbon (C) sequestration in the soil.
objective: in this study, the authors used the equivalent soil mass (esm) approach to evaluate soc stock changes following the conversion from ht to it and nt considering studies compiled within a systematic review.
result1: with the two approaches concerning missing variances applied in this study (i.e. assigning the standard deviation a tenth of the mean and the maximum value, respectively), higher stock increases were found in the upper 30 cm after conversion of ht and were 3.22 +/- 1.48 and 3.50 +/- 1.66, and 4.19 +/- 1.82 and 4.23 +/- 1.92 mg/ha (md +/- se) when the conservational treatment was it and nt, respectively.
result2: due to shallow sampling depth, ht vs. it and it vs. nt comparisons were limited to 0-30 cm depth, but the effect of ht to nt conversion could also be determined for 0-60 cm. the results indicate that the nt sequestration potential is overvalued when neglecting deeper depths, since the soc storage capacity was reduced to< 0.10 mg ha/yr
result3: relative stock changes showed a decreasing trend with depth for all tillage conversions.
result4: a closer investigation on the treatment effects for each depth generally showed that none of the investigated covariates had a consistent impact, although high correlations were occasionally found for individual depths.
general_conclusion: the meta-analysis highlighted that both intermediate (it) and no tillage (nt) practices increase soil c stocks in the first 30 cm compared to high-intensity tillage (ht) in boreo-temperate climate.
knowledge_gaps: stoniness, which may be a considerable source of error when estimating soc stocks, was not considered due to the lack of information. due to shallow sampling depth, ht vs. it and it vs. nt comparisons were limited to 0-30 cm depth. the authors did not investigate shortterm effects, as the database used in this study did not include experiments with less than ten years.

search_strategy: the search (october 2019) covered the electronic databases of isi web of knowledge and scopus, using the keywords “soil organic carbon”, “soil organic matter” or “soil carbon sequestration” and “vineyard” or “vitis vinifera”. seeking complete coverage, a second search of the same databases used the keywords “cover crop”, “no-tillage”, “amendment”, “biochar”, “hedge”, “agroforestry”, “pruning”, “soil erosion” or “ph” in com- bination with “vineyard” or “vitis vinifera”.
selection_criteria: (i) they included experiments measuring soc or som levels within existing vineyards or through experimental manipulation of vineyard management practices; (ii) they were performed under field conditions (laboratory studies and pot experiments were excluded) for a minimum period of three years; and (iii) they were published in or after 2000. when several studies contained data from the same field experiment, only the longest study was selected to avoid redundancy in the data.
data_analysis: the collected data harmonised to a depth of 0.3 m was used to calculate three effect sizes for soc stock comparisons: (i) the soc stock response ratio (rr), to estimate the change in soc stocks under soil carbon sequestration (scs) practices relative to conventional management, (ii) the soc stock rate of change (r), as a measure of the annual growth rate in soc stocks under scs management relative to conventional management, and (iii) the raw difference in means of soc stocks for soc sequestration rate comparisons. effect sizes were weighted according to their sample sizes. bias-corrected 95% confidence intervals were generated for each weighted mean effect size by bootstrapping procedure with 10,000 iterations
background: Vineyards are usually cultivated in soils characterised by low soil organic carbon (SOC) content and have high risks of soil erosion and degradation. Increasing SOC stocks in these cropping systems has the potential to contribute to climate change mitigation through SOC sequestration and to enhance soil quality.
objective: this paper presents a meta-analysis of the response of soc stocks in 0-30 cm depth in vineyards to different soil carbon sequestration management practices from a global sample of individual field studies. it also compares the changes in soc stocks depending on climate and study length.
result1: no tillage has a significant positive effect on soc stock and sequestration rate.
result2: the positive effect of nt is stronger when associated with organic amendment and cover crop.
general_conclusion: no tillage has a significant positive effect on soc stock and sequestration rate.

search_strategy: the search was restricted to terrestrial mineral soils of the tem- perate zone such as retisols, luvisols, cambisols, phaeozems, chernozems and kastanozems. we compiled data from publications in english, russian and german language via key words, including: soc, sequestration, carbon stocks, humus, land-use change, abandonment, organic matter recovery, ex-arable land, old field succession, no-till and agro-ecosystems. key word searching allowed us to widen our database to the “grey” literature as well, to ensure maximum retrieval of edaphic and climatic data necessary for the present soc study.
selection_criteria: not clearly defined.
data_analysis: because most soc studies did not provide error estimates, an unweighted meta-analysis was conducted. mean effect sizes were calculated with bootstrapped 95% confidence intervals based on 1000 bootstrap replications using the package ‘boot’ (canty and ripley, 2013) in r3.0.2 software (r core team, 2013). the mean effect sizes was considered to be significantly different from zero if the 95% confidence intervals did not overlap with zero and were significantly different from each other at a level of α = 0.05 (gurevitch and hedges, 2001).
background: In agroecosystems conservational tillage practices and the abandonment of formerly plowed fields (ex-arable land) are shown to have the highest potential to sequester SOC. Nevertheless reported sequestration rates vary and the effects of environmental site conditions remain poorly understood.
objective: how do soc stocks develop after conversion to conservational tillage
result1: soc stocks in arable fields under no-till increased significantly by 14.4% ± 7.9%, effect size: 0.12 ± 0.05 (mean ± 95% confidence inter- val) in comparison to conventional tillage methods.
result2: compared to con- ventional till, reduced till led to an increase of soc stocks of only 2.9% ± 2.2% (effect size: 0.03 ± 0.02).
general_conclusion: no-till and reduced till increase soil organic carbon stock compared to conventional till

search_strategy: in this study, more than 500 published, peer-reviewed articles were collected from the web of science (r) and google scholar (1900–2016) databases. the searches were performed with the keywords “dissolvable organic carbon, soil, extractable, doc, water extractable organic carbon”, and 120 articles were selected for the meta-analysis. the references cited by the chosen articles were also reviewed to complement the keyword-based search.
selection_criteria: the chosen articles were selected according to the following five criteria: i) the measurements were conducted under field conditions; ii) the experiment was implemented with a pair-wise design, including control and treatment groups; iii) there were spatial replicates randomly assigned for either the control or the treatment(s) in a field study; iv) the extractant for eoc was distilled water or a salt solution at room temperature instead of an oxidant, and the extraction was carried out at room temperature (approximately 25 °c) instead of at high temperature. as hot water extracts different organic carbon constituents compared to cold or room-temperature water and hot water extraction are different from the natural conditions, the authors excluded the data of eoc when extracted by hot water. in addition, the salts cacl2, k2so4 and kcl as extractants were categorized into separate sub-groups regardless of their concentrations due to the lack of field data; v) to investigate the influence of land use and management practices, the studies with samples collected below 30 cm soil depth were excluded. this condition was set because the effects from any factors on eoc or doc occurred mainly within the topsoil.
data_analysis: all the collected data were divided into different categories or subcategories that considered the factors that could influence the concentrations of eoc and/or doc. the agronomic practices of cultivated lands included amendments of synthetic nitrogen fertilizers for both eoc and doc and applications of lime, crop straw, organic manure and tillage methods for eoc alone. a categorical random effects model was used when the estimated pooled variance was > 0; otherwise, a fixed effects model was used. the overall mean effect size and the 95% confidence interval (ci) for each group of control-treatment pairs were generated by bootstrapping (9999 iterations).
background: Quantifications of soil dissolvable organic carbon concentrations, together with other relevant variables, are needed to understand the carbon biogeochemistry of terrestrial ecosystems. Soil dissolvable organic carbon can generally be grouped into two incomparable categories. One is soil extractable organic carbon (EOC), which is measured by extracting with an aqueous extractant (distilled water or a salt solution). The other is soil dissolved organic carbon (DOC), which is measured by sampling soil water using tension-free lysimeters or tension samplers. The authors hypothesized that the measured concentrations of either EOC or DOC were significantly influenced by observation methods and that the responses to land use, management practice, soil depth and season were different between EOC and DOC.
objective: the objectives of this study were to (i) investigate the effects of different but widely adopted observation methods on measured concentrations of eoc and/or doc; (ii) quantify the responses of eoc and/or doc concentrations to variations of some natural and/or anthropogenic factors; and (iii) identify future research needs for eoc or doc concentrations in terrestrial ecosystems.
result1: significant reductions of 17% on average were induced by tillage practices compared to no-tillage practices. the results suggest that soil dissolvable organic carbon availability may be enhanced in soil conservation by means of reduced tillage or no-tillage practices.
result2: NA
general_conclusion: eoc was on average higher in no-tillage, suggesting that soil dissolvable organic carbon availability may enhanced by no-tillage.
knowledge_gaps: no data for other measures of soil carbon (e.g., dissolvable organic carbon, used for other impacts in the same study).

search_strategy: published journal articles from january 1987 to january 2020 were searched using the isi web of science (http://apps.webofknowledge.com/) and china knowledge resource integrated database (http://www.cnki.net/) using the keywords: “soil organic carbon” or “soil organic matter” or “carbon stock” or “carbon sequestration” or “soil quality” or “chemical properties” and “conservation practice” or “tillage” or “till”.
selection_criteria: (1) paired observations involving a ct–ct with (ctr) or without residue retention (ct), and only field–based experiments were included. specific conservation tillage practices chosen for comparison were rt or rt plus residue retention (rtr), and nt or nt plus residue retention (ntr). if a study used more than one conservation tillage practice at the same site, different conservation tillage practices were separately paired with the ct control; (2) the mean and standard deviation (sd) or standard error (se) of the results obtained from replicated field plots (>two replications) were used in the meta–analysis; (3) the residue retention and tillage practices were treated as main treatments while keeping other agronomic practices and factors such as cropping intensity, study duration, fertilizer management, and irrigation the same among the main treatments.
data_analysis: to derive the overall response effect of the treatment group relative to the control group, the weighted response ratio between treatment and control groups was calculated according to hedges et al. (1999); luo et al. (2006). the meta–analysis was performed using the ‘metafor’ package  in the r statistical software (version 3.4.2). study id was set as a random effect because several papers contributed more than one effect size. for each group (soil texture, study duration, cropping intensity, ai, soil sampling depth), the mean effect size (lnrr) and its 95% ci were calculated with bias–correction generated via bootstrapping (4999 iterations). a chi–square test was used to determine whether the heterogeneity among the lnrr of changes in soc stocks under conservation tillage treatments significantly exceeded the expected sampling error. a randomization test was used to determine the significance of the between−group heterogeneity. chi–square tests were also used to determine whether the remaining within−group heterogeneity was significant. publication bias was determined by using rosenthal's fail-safe number.
background: Crop residue retention and minimum tillage (including no–tillage, NT, and reduced tillage, RT) are common conservation tillage practices that have been extensively applied for improving soil health and reducing the negative environmental impact caused by intensive farming. However, the effects of minimum tillage, coupled with crop residue retention (including no–tillage plus residue retention, NTR, and reduced tillage plus residue retention, RTR), on soil organic carbon (SOC) stock have not been systematically analyzed.
objective: 1) determine the direction and magnitude of change in soc stock of 0–30 cm soil in response to a combination of residue retention and tillage practices; and 2) evaluate the effect of external abiotic (e.g., soil texture, climate factors) and management practices (cropping intensity, duration of conservation tillage practices) on soc stock in the 0–30 cm of the soil.
result1: relative to conventional tillage (ct), minimum tillage (including no tillage nt and reduced tillage rt) increased soc stock ( p < 0.01), and nt increased soc stock 9% more than rt.
result2: nt with residue retention resulted in 13% greater soc stock than nt, while no difference was observed between nt with residue retention and reduced tillage with residue retention.
result3: when the study duration was <6 years, nt but not rt increased soc stock relative to ct (p < 0.001), and nt significantly increased soc stock in comparison to rt.
result4: mat, soil ph, and experimental duration were critical for increasing soc stock with minimum tillage alone, while response ratio of soc stock under coupled residue retention and minimum tillage were insensitive to changes in those factors.
general_conclusion: the meta–analysis showed that conservation tillage practices could generally increase soc stock. specifically, a combination of minimum tillage and residue addition is more effective than minimum tillage alone in increasing overall mean soc stock in the 0–30 cm soil, though these effects were more evident in the topsoil.
knowledge_gaps: due to restrictions caused by limited data, the comparison of rtr vs. rt was excluded in subgroup meta–analysis; only semi–humid, humid, and perhumid climates were studied due to insufficient data from arid or semiarid regions

search_strategy: to assess changes in soc mineralization and concentration between nt (including nt and reduced tillage) and pt, 21 peer-reviewed papers with 57 comparisons were collected. these peer-reviewed papers were published in chinese (china national knowledge infrastructure) or english (web of science) until june 2020.
selection_criteria: i) the field experiment was conducted under residue retention; ii) tillage and duration were clearly stated and the other management practices were the same; and iii) information on mean, replications, and magnitude of soc concentration and mineralization was both available or could be calculated.
data_analysis: the effects of nt on soc mineralization by calculating the natural logarithm of the response ratio of nt vs. pt. the ratios were weighted based on the number of replicates.
background: There is no consensus regarding the effect of no tillage (NT) and plow tillage (PT) practices on soil organic carbon (SOC) mineralization.
objective: the objectives of this study are to (i) assess the effects of the tillage, experiment duration, and their interaction on soc mineralization and accumulation, (ii) identify the relationship between soc mineralization and accumulation, and (iii) determine its potential mechanism using soc fractions and physical protection.
result1: nt significantly increased soc mineralization by 21 % when the experiment duration was >16 years (p < 0.05).
result2: the meta-analysis showed that nt significantly increased soc concentration by 28 % compared with pt (p < 0.05). no significant difference in soc concentration was observed between nt and pt when the experiment duration was < 8 years. however, nt significantly increased soc concentration by 34 % and 39 % when the experiment duration was 8–16 years and >16 years, respectively (p < 0.05).
general_conclusion: no-tillage significantly increased soil organic carbon concentration and decreased soil organic carbon mineralization compared with plow tillage. the difference in soc concentration and mineralization between the two systems increased over time.

search_strategy: a total of 49 datasets were collected from peer reviewed research papers using the search term 'zero (or no) tillage and carbon' in web of science.
selection_criteria: only those papers with paired conventional tillage (ct) and zero-tillage (zt) treatments were selected.
data_analysis: regression equations were developed to explore the potential for c sequestration with zero and conventional tillage separately and under tropical and temperate conditions. the aim was to derive conclusions regarding the effect of duration of zero tillage on sequestration of c and soil depth on net sequestration c rate.
background: There is general agreement that reduced and zero-tillage practice can conserve and enhance soil organic carbon (C) levels to some extent. However, their applicability in mitigating climate change has been debated extensively, especially when the whole profile of C in the soil is considered, along with a reported risk of enhanced nitrous oxide (N2O) emissions.
objective: the objective of the current paper were  to evaluate zero tillage for: (i) mitigation of climate change by sequestration of c and by reducing or balancing emissions of major ghgs from the soil and (ii) its effect on crop yield. the results related to the impact of zero tillage on climate change mitigation by sequestration of c are reported here.
result1: the c sequestration capabilities increased considerably with an increase in duration of zero tillage, with the increment more evident under tropical conditions (non-significant (ns) for overall dataset and in case of temperate, but p < 0.05 for tropical). in the current analysis, c under zero tillage in tropical regions was significantly correlated with the time since conversion (r2 = 0.22, p <= 0.001), but this was not significant for temperate regions.
result2: the present analysis suggests the c sequestration rate under zero tillage of the top 25 cm soil (ploughing depth) was 864 kg/ha/year in tropical regions against 173 kg/ha/year in temperate soils (p < 0.001 for overall dataset, p < 0.05 for tropical, and p < 0.001 for temperate).
result3: significantly higher c was sequestered under zero tillage compared to conventional tillage, under both tropical (r2 = 0.30, p < 0.05) and temperate conditions (r2 = 0.38, p < 0.001) up to a depth of 160 cm. multiple linear regression of c sequestration with depth and duration of tillage also indicated significant c increases under tropical (p < 0.01) and temperate conditions (p < 0.001).
general_conclusion: research suggests zero tillage is effective in sequestering c in both soil surface and sub-soil layers in tropical and temperate conditions.

search_strategy: an extensive dataset was obtained from the peer-reviewed literature by searching isi web of 113 science and google scholar, with the final date of searching being june 2016.
selection_criteria: (i) the studies had to report on the 115 impacts of long-term changes in land-use (≥ 15 years in all instances other than for organic 116 agriculture for which a cut-off of ≥ 5 years was used due to the low numbers of long-term 117 studies available), (ii) concentrations of soc were reported in addition to at least one of the 118 three nutrients of interest (total n, total p, or total s) (concentrations of p were recorded even 119 if soc concentrations were not, as discussed later), and (iii) the depth(s) within the profile 120 from which the soil was collected was stated. it was also desirable, but not essential, for 121 studies to list other variables, such as average annual rainfall, clay content, and the rates at 122 which inorganic and organic fertilizers and amendments were applied.
data_analysis: NA
background: Quantifying changes in stocks of C, N, P, and S in agricultural soils is important not only for managing these soils sustainably as required to feed a growing human population, but for C and N, they are also important for understanding fluxes of greenhouse gases from the soil environment.
objective: investigate changes in soil stocks of organic c, total n, total p, and total s associated with long-term land-use changes.
result1: the conversion of conventional cropping systems to no-till systems increased stocks.
result2: NA
general_conclusion: c stocks were higher in no-tillage systems. (reviewers’ note: results labelled as uncertain due to the lack of statistical testing).

search_strategy: all articles were identified from the web of science. the search keywords were “soil organic carbon” and “tillage” for conservation tillage treatments
selection_criteria: (a) soc was measured in field experiments (to estimate the potential of biochar to increase soil carbon, we also included soil incubation and pot experiments with regard to biochar use); (b) observations were conducted on croplands exclud‐ ing orchards and pastures; (c) ancillary information was provided, such as experiment duration, replication, and sampling depth; and (d) other agronomic management practices were included besides the three target management practices in this study. we considered conventional tillage as the control for nt and rt.
data_analysis: a random‐effect model of meta‐analysis was used to explore en‐ vironmental and management variables that might explain the re‐ sponse of soc to csa management practices. the data analysis was performed in r (r development core team, 2009). the response ratio (rr) was defined as the ratio between the outcome of csa management practices and that of the control group. the logarithm of rr (lnrr) was calculated as the effect size of each observation and was weigthed. publication bias was analyzed by the method of fail‐ safe number, which suggests that the meta‐analysis can be considered robust if the fail‐safe number is larger than 5 × k + 10 (where k is the number of observed studies; rothstein, sutton, & borenstein, 2005).
background: Effects of climate smart agriculture practices on SOC sequestration are variable and highly dependent on experiment designs and site‐specific condi‐ tions such as climate and soil properties
objective: (a) evaluate and compare the effects of conservation tillage, cover crops, and biochar use on soc; (b) examine how environmental fac‐ tors (e.g., soil properties and climate) and other agronomic practices (e.g., nitrogen fertilization, residue management, irrigation, and crop rotation) influence soc in these csa management environments. here, we focus on conservation tillage (no tillage nt, or reduced tillage rt).
result1: when investigating different types of conservation tillage, nt and rt had similar effects on soc (approximately 8% increase). all results were statistically significant.
result2: no‐till increased soc by 16% in silty clay and silty clay loam soils, compared to 12% in sandy loam soils and 7% in loamy sand soils. reduced tillage increased soc by 21%, 7%, and 15% in silty clay and silty clay loam soils, loam soils, and loamy sand soils, respectively.
result3: the nt‐induced soc uptake was slightly higher in arid areas than that in humid areas (9% and 8%, respectively). however, the rt‐induced soc increment in arid areas was two times greater than that in humid areas.
result4: nt and rt could significantly increase soc most at 0–10 cm depth (22% and 17%, respectively). although reduced soc was observed in the 10–20 cm and 20–50 cm soil layers (−4% and −10%, respectively), nt could still enhance soc sequestration in the entire soil profile up to 120 cm. in comparison, rt could increase soc in the 0–70 cm soil profile although decreased soil carbon (not statistically significant) was observed in the 10–50 cm soil layer.
result5: no‐till increased soc by 6% in acid soils and 13% in alkaline soils. the soc increased by rt was greater in alkaline soils (9%) than in acid soils (6%), but rt had no significant influence on soc in neutral soils. no‐till significantly increased soc by 13% in the long‐term experiments, followed by medium‐term (7%) and short‐ term experiments (6%). reduced tillage increased soc by 12% in long‐term studies, followed by medium‐term (9%) and short‐term experiments (3%).
general_conclusion: no tillage and reduced tillage have positive effect on soil organic carbon.

search_strategy: the studies included in the analysis were those cited in isi web of science database until february 2019 with the keywords ‘soil organic carbon’ or ‘soil organic matter’ and ‘no-till’, ‘no tillage’ or ‘zero tillage’ or ‘direct seeding’.
selection_criteria: (a) experiments of no-till lasting more than 5 years, which were used to reduce the instabilities at the beginning of the experiment; (b) the duration of conventional tillage and no-till were the same; (c) measured thick- ness of soil layers was not less than 30 cm; and (d) reduced tillage and minimum tillage practices were excluded and only continuous no-till (i.e. complete absence of tillage) was selected.
data_analysis: to include as many studies as possible, studies were weighted by sample size: w=ncnt∕(nc+nt), where w refers to the specific weight of a given pair of data, and nc and nt are sample sizes for the control and no-till respectively. given that studies differed in sample sizes, more weights are given to large sample sizes. resampling methods (e.g. bootstrapping) were used to cal- culate bias-corrected 95% confidence intervals (cis) around the mean effect size. if the 95% ci of the effect size for a variable did not overlap with zero, the effect of restoration on the variable was considered significant.
background: Conservation agriculture has been shown to have multiple benefits for soils, crop yield and the environment, and consequently, no-till, the central practice of conservation agriculture, has rapidly expanded. However, studies show that the potential for carbon (C) sequestration in no-till farming sometimes is not realized, let alone the ability to maintain or improve crop yield.
objective: global analysis of no-till-induced changes of soil c and crop yield
result1: relative to local conventional tillage, arid regions can benefit more from no tillage. the increase of soc resulting from no tillage decrease with the humidity index.
result2: NA
general_conclusion: no-tillage has a positive effect on soc compared to conventional tillage in arid regions and the effect decreases with the increased humidity. no effect of no-tillage in very humid region.

search_strategy: several databases were used, such as web of science, google scholar and scopus to search peer-reviewed publications (before april 2020). the keywords used in the search were “cropland or crop or wheat or maize or barley or rice,” “soc or soil organic matter,” and/ or “ch4, n2o and yield (grain).”
selection_criteria: each study selected contains measurements of ghg emissions for both control and treatment management practices. studies with the following measurements were excluded: (i) measurements made in pot, laboratories or greenhouses and (ii) measurements conducted in organic (peaty) soils where n2o are much higher than those in mineral soils and where soil carbon fluxes are different.
data_analysis: we performed our analysis on mean difference (md) weighted by study replication, on unweighted effect sizes. then, a random-effects model, which is more adaptable to ecological synthesis compared to a fixed-effects model, was selected to estimate the md of the variable x for a certain cropland management practice. the effect of the management practice was considered not significant if 95% confidence interval (ci) of the md overlapped with zero. the estimations of the md and associated 95% ci of were conducted in r version 4.0.1 with “meta” and “metaphor” packages
background: Smart cropland management practices can mitigate greenhouse gas (GHG) emissions while safeguarding food security.
objective: the objective of this study was to evaluate the integrated effects of alternative management practices on cropland net greenhouse gaz budget and grain yield. here, the results obtained on the effect of no-tillage on soil organic carbon sequestration rate are reported.
result1: no-tillage significantly improved soil organic carbon sequestration rate for upland crops (maize, wheat etc.), especially in warm climates (mat > 12°c) and under high n fertilizer application rates (>200 kg n ha-1 yr-1). no significant effect on rice.
result2: although temperature and n fertilizer application rate hardly explained the variance of the effect of no- tillage on soc sequestration, the effect was significantly greater in warm regions with high n fertilization areas (socsr: −6.7 mg co2 eq ha−1 year−1) than in cool areas with lower fertilization rates (socsr: 0.2 mg co2 eq ha−1 year−1).
general_conclusion: compared to conventional tillage, no-tillage increases soil organic sequestration rate in upland crops, while no significant difference was found in rice systems.

search_strategy: searches of 17 academic databases were undertaken as part of the published systematic map between the 16th and 19th september 2013. a search update was undertaken in september 2015 to capture research published since the original search in september 2013. the update was restricted to four academic databases, academic search premier, pub med, scopus, web of science (web of science core collection, biosis citation index, chinese science citation database, data citation index, scielo citation index), and one academic search engine, google scholar, which has been shown to be effective at identifying both academic and grey literature.
selection_criteria: a total of 311 studies were already identified as part of the recent systematic map. these studies were originally assessed according to predefined inclusion criteria as part of the systematic map. these original inclusion criteria were modified for the purposes of this systematic review by the inclusion of a requirement for studies to have investigated tillage interventions.
data_analysis: meta-analyses were conducted in r using the rma.mv function the metafor package, which allows moderators to be declared as nested random factors. for all models, study id (a unique code for each independent study) was nested within study site and declared as a random factor. all models used maximum likelihood (ml) to estimate random effects. heterogeneity was tested for amongst the evidence base by calculating τ2 and performing q/qe tests for heterogeneity/residual heterogeneity [50], integrated into the rma functions within metafor. significant heterogeneity indicates the presence of a moderator that has not been accounted for in the model. heterogeneity was tested for in simple univariate meta-analysis models (declaring study code and site as nested random factors) and again following the addition of moderators to examine the influence of including moderators on residual heterogeneity. the presence of publication bias was investigated by performing an egger’s regression test, and by plotting funnel plots (effect sizes against standard errors) and looking for asymmetry, which is indicative of publication bias.
background: The promotion of less intensive tillage practices and no tillage (NT) (the absence of mechanical soil disturbance) aims to mitigate negative impacts on soil quality and to preserve soil organic carbon (SOC).
objective: what is the impact of reduced tillage intensity on soc?
result1: soc concentration was significantly higher in nt relative to both it [1.18 g/kg +/- 0.34 (se)] and ht [2.09 g/kg +/- 0.34 (se)] in the upper soil layer (0-15 cm). it was also found to be significant higher [1.30 g/kg +/- 0.22 (se)] in soc concentration than ht for the upper soil layer (0-15 cm).
result2: at lower depths, only it soc compared with ht at 15-30 cm showed a significant difference; being 0.89 g/kg [+/- 0.20 (se)] lower in intermediate intensity tillage.
result3: for stock data nt had significantly higher soc stocks down to 30 cm than either ht [4.61 mg/ha +/- 1.95 (se)] or it [3.85 mg/ha +/- 1.64 (se)].
general_conclusion: positive effect of nt and it on soc at the upper soil-layer (0-15 cm) relative to ht. at lower depths (15–30 cm), soc was lower in it compared with ht. down to 30 cm, nt had significantly higher soc stocks than ht. no other comparisons were significant.
knowledge_gaps: key knowledge gaps exist around the combined effects of tillage and amendments (such as farmyard manure application and stubble management) on soc. similarly, the combined effects of tillage and fertiliser were poorly studied.

search_strategy: a data set of long-term tillage studies was compiled from a survey of the scientifi c literature and included studies from previous tillage literature reviews (west and post, 2002; alvarez, 2005).
selection_criteria: studies were included in the data set if the following criteria were met: (i) studies compared nt and fit systems; (ii) studies were replicated experimental designs with the same soil type, crop, fertilizer, and residue management for both tillage treatments; (iii) soc was sampled to depths of 30 cm and deeper, with at least three depth increments; and (iv) tillage treatments were applied for at least 5 yr. tillage methods referred to as conventional or conservation tillage such as sub-till, chisel, disk, or ridge tillage were not included in the data set because they do not fully invert the soil during tillage operations
data_analysis: at each depth, the student’s t value was used to test the hypothesis that the mean ratio was zero. analyses were performed on log-transformed data when not normally distributed. outlier data  points  were  tested  with  dixon’s  q-test. regression coefficients between the soc (nt − fit)/fit ratio and c stocks, and precipitation, temperature, clay content, and duration of study were evaluated using linear regression.
background: While the adoption of no-till (NT) usually leads to the accumulation of soil organic C (SOC) in the surface soil layers, a number of studies have shown that this effect is sometimes partly or completely offset by greater SOC content near the bottom of the plow layer under full-inversion tillage (FIT).
objective: the specific purpose of this study was to review published data on the infl uence of fit on soc content in the soil profile and, from this meta-analysis, to determine the factors controlling the occurrence and extent of sequestration below the soil surface under fit.
result1: as expected, in almost all studies where the relevant statistics were reported, soc content was significantly greater under nt than fit in the soil layers close to the soil surface (0 to 5-10 cm). conversely, there were also several cases (around 20) for which soc content was greater under fit than nt. most of these involved soil layers near or at the bottom of the plow layer. these results further highlight the importance of taking the whole soil profile into consideration when comparing nt vs. fit situations.
result2: values were in general > 0 for the 0- to 10-cm soil depth, further emphasizing the lower soc content under fit than nt at that position in the soil profile. the mean ratio was significantly greater than 0 at the 1- to  5- and 6- to 10-cm depth intervals (p <= 0.001 and 0.02, respectively). at the depth intervals of 11 to 15 and 16 to 20 cm, the (nt - fit)/fit ratio was not significantly different from 0 (p > 0.05).
result3: at the depth interval of 21 to 25 cm, the mean (nt - fit)/fit ratio was significantly smaller than 0 (p < 0.001), suggesting that the average soc content was greater under fit than nt at that depth. at the depth interval of 26 to 35 cm, the mean ratio was also significantly smaller than 0 (p = 0.01). the average soc content was therefore slightly greater under fit than nt just below the average depth of plowing (23 cm).
general_conclusion: in the soil layers close to the soil surface (0 to 5-10 cm), soc content was significantly greater under nt than fit. in the 11-20 cm soil, it was similar in nt and fit. below 21 cm soil, soc content was greater under fit than nt. this highlights the importance of taking into account the whole soil profile when comparing soil c stocks.
knowledge_gaps: the majority of the studies originated from north america.

search_strategy: google, google scholar, science direct, springerlink, and scifinder were used. in order to make the search process as efficient as possible, a list of topic-related keywords was used such as “soil carbon losses under tillage compared to no-tillage”, “soil co2 emissions under tillage and no-tillage”, “land management practices and greenhouse gases emissions”, “land management effects on co2 emissions”, “effects of tillage vs. no-tillage on soil co2 emissions” and “soc”.
selection_criteria: only studies that reported co2 emissions measured in the field for both tillage and no-tillage from the same crop and during the same period were used. in addition, we selected only studies that consistently reported total soil respiration (heterotrophic + belowground autotrophic respiration). the crops considered in this study were maize, wheat, barley, oats, soybean, paddy rice and fallow. the practices considered as tillage in this review are those that involve physical disturbance of the topsoil layers for seedbed preparation, weed control, or fertilizer application.
data_analysis: the metawin 2.1 software was used for analyzing the data and generating a bootstrapped (4999 iterations) to calculate 95 % confidence intervals. the means of effect size were considered to be significantly different from each other if their 95 % confidence intervals were not overlapping and were significantly different from zero if the 95 % level did not overlap zero.
background: The management of agroecosystems plays a crucial role in the global carbon cycle with soil tillage leading to known organic carbon redistributions within soils and changes in soil CO2 emissions.
objective: quantify tillage impact on co2 emissions and assessing the main controls.
result1: when compared across all studies, mean soil organic carbon content under tillage was 10 % lower than under no-tillage.
result2: in arid climates, soc content in tillage was 11 % lower than no-tillage, whereas in humid climates soc content under tillage was only 8 % less than for no-tillage. however, the differences in soc content between the two climatic zones were found to be non-significant.
general_conclusion: higher soil organic carbon content in ni-till systems
knowledge_gaps: long-term process studies of the entire soil profile are needed to better quantify the changes in soc following tillage abandonment and to clarify the changes in the dynamics of carbon inputs and outputs in relation to changes in microbial activity, soil structure and microclimate.

search_strategy: an exhaustive literature search of studies investigating n2o emissions from grain cropping systems was conducted with isi-web of science for articles published before june 2014. because the first search produced a limited numbers of papers for enhanced efficiency fertilizers, cover crops and diversified rotations, we conducted a second search focusing on these practices in december 2015 to increase the size of the database.
selection_criteria: only studies conducted in field conditions that were at least one growing season in duration were included.
data_analysis: we performed an unweighted meta-analysis because roughly more than half of the studies did not report a measure of variance. bias-corrected 95% confidence intervals (95% cis) were generated through a boot- strapping procedure in metawin 2.0 (5000 iterations). bootstrapping cis can be biased due to re-sampling from a small dataset (bancroft et al. 2007; montero- castano and vila 2012) so for groups with <10 observation pairs, we used the more conservative 95% cis instead of bias-corrected 95% ci. the 95% cis were converted to the percent change of n2o emissions from treatment groups compared to the controls for easier interpretation. a ci not overlapping with zero suggests a significant treatment effect and non-overlapping cis indicate significant difference between groups.
background: Understanding how agricultural management practices impact nitrous oxide (N2O) emissions is prerequisite for developing mitigation protocols.
objective: assess how management (including reduced tillage) affects n2o emissions.
result1: using reduced tillage compared to conventional tillage resulted in moderate decrease in yields for 71% of the pairs, among which nearly half had increased n2o emissions in conjunction with reduced yields.
result2: NA
general_conclusion: using reduced tillage compared to conventional tillage resulted in moderate decrease in yields. (reviewers’ note: results labelled as uncertain due to the lack of statistical testing.)

search_strategy: a literature survey of peer-reviewed published literature in the isi-web of science and cab abstracts (ovid) between 1910 and 2013 was conducted to identify papers reporting results from studies using reduced tillage in organic farming. the following search terms and their variations were used in various combinations: reduced/minimum/shallow/chisel, tillage/ploughing/plowing, intensity, no-till/direct seeding, organic/ecological, farming/systems/agriculture/management.
selection_criteria: (i) experiment under organic management for at least 3 years prior to the date of response measurement; (ii) at least two levels of tillage intensity included as a treatment; (iii) no “mixing” of treatments, i.e., only tillage varied between experimental treatments; and (iv) included climatic zones found in europe
data_analysis: data were analyzed using unweighted meta-analysis techniques. the significance of effect sizes was tested using linear mixed effects models in the “lme4” package in r with random effects specified as experiment/year. the fixed effects of tillage class or climate were tested using this model. the effect of tillage class within a given soil type or crop class was tested after first subsetting the data by soil type or crop class and then using a mixed effects model as described above. for all analyses, least-square means and confidence intervals were generated using the “lsmeans” package in r. means were considered significantly different from zero if the 95 % ci did not overlap zero, and different from one another if their 95 % cis were non-overlapping (hedges et al. 1999). the results of each mean ratio (r) were expressed as % effect size (e), where e = (r − 1) × 100.
background: NA
objective: NA
result1: on average across all environments and management practices yields were 7.6 % lower when tillage intensity was reduced in organic systems compared to deep inversion tillage
result2: reductions in yield for both double-layer ploughing (7 %) and shallow inversion tillage (5.5 %) were relatively small and for shallow non-inversion tillage the reduction of 3 % was non-significant.
result3: shallow non-inversion (less than 10 cm) which did not significantly reduce yield
result4: there was no yield difference between no tillage and deep inversion.
general_conclusion: among the different classes of reduced tillage practice, shallow non-inversion tillage resulted in non-significant reductions in yield relative to deep inversion; whereas deep non-inversion tillage resulted in the largest yield reduction. no tillage resulted in non-signification reductions in yield compared to deep inversion.

search_strategy: a literature survey was performed using the web of science and google scholar (1900–2017). key words used for the initial search included tillage, greenhouse gases, co2, ch4,, and n2o.
selection_criteria: 1) ghg emissions were measured in situ for the entire cropping season. 2) the conventional tillage versus no tillage comparison was done under otherwise similar agronomic management practices. 3) information regarding means, standard deviations (or standard errors), replications, and the magnitude of seasonal cumulative ghg emissions was either available or could be calculated.
data_analysis:
response ratios (r) comparing nt and ct, for ghg emissions and crop yield, were calculated as follows: r = (xnt/xct) where x is the variate (co2, ch4, n2o, gwp, or crop yield) mean, for either the nt or the ct treatment. the variance (υ) of lnr (the effect size) was
computed and the weight of each effect size w = 1/variance. sas software was used to analyze the data by applying the macros for meta-analysis procedure.
background: The net effect of No Tillage (NT) greatly depends on the trade-offs between NT-induced changes in crop yield and GHG emissions. These trade-offs are regulated by a suite of climatic and soil factors, which have not been well addressed in past studies.
objective: NA
result1: crop yields were similar between nt and ct.
result2: NA
general_conclusion:
crop yields were similar between nt and ct, suggesting that yield loss should not be a deterrent to nt adoption as a climate smart agriculture practice. however, the net effect of nt (relative to ct) was influenced by several environmental and agronomic factors (climatic conditions, tillage duration, soil texture, ph, crop species).
ch4 emission was the major contribution of nt management to ghg mitigation.
knowledge_gaps: to identify other climate smart agriculture (csa) management practices that are suitable at local, regional and/or global scales, future csa research programs that systematically investigate agroecosystem responses (e.g., crop yield, ghg emissions) using diverse methods (e.g., observation, meta-analysis, and agroecosystem modeling) are needed.

search_strategy: literature searches were conducted in scopus, targeting peer reviewed articles published online through july 2019. the results included 187 experimental treatments from 46 peer-reviewed articles, including the countries of spain, italy, france, portugal, greece,turkey, slovenia, tunisia, chile and the united states of america. to obtain the papers listed, we used the keywords “almond or olive or citrus or vineyard or grapevine or orchard”,“and”combinations of the following items:“mediterranean climate”,“cover crop”,“inter-cropping”,“alley crop”,“multicrop”,“agroforestry”,“crop yield”and“soil”.
selection_criteria: laboratory or greenhouse studies were excluded, and only studies performed in field conditions and carried out in a mediterranean climate were chosen. when several papers included data from the same experiment, the longest study with the most soil and crop variables was chosen.
data_analysis: the response ratio (rr) was calculated as aproportionate change in the indicator value of the treatment group (sustainable management: intercropping, organic fertilization and no-tillage/minimum tillage) compared to the pairwise control group (conventional management: mono-cropping, inorganic fertilization and conventional tillage). the natural logarithm of the response ratio was used for the analysis (log (rr)). we decided to weight observations using thesample sizes to ensure statistical significance by keeping a sufficient sample size: studies with larger sample sizes were weighted higher during aggregation. for the uncertainty analysis, we reported the means and 95% confidence intervals (cis). the cis were constructed by non-parametric bootstrapping (nboot = 10 000).the bootstrapping was only carried out for treatments with n>=8, as the bootstrap is unreliable when the sample size is too small.
background: There is now a growing emphasis on crop diversification and optimized use of resources, including with the production of food, feed or industrial products that contribute to long-term sustainability of the agroecosystems and climate change mitigation and adaptation.
objective: assess the benefits of crop diversification, conservation tillage (minimum tillage/no-tillage) and organic fertilization as alternatives to intensive conventional mono-cropping in field studies. we focus here on conservation tillage.
result1: tillage systems had no significant effect
result2: NA
general_conclusion: conservation tillage had no significant effects oncrop yield compared to conventional systems.

search_strategy: aiming at a near-exhaustive review, literature databases (scopus, web of knowledge) were searched for the terms “legume”, “protein crop” and the english and scientific names of different grain legume crops in combination with the terms “previous crop”, “preceding crop”, “pre-crop”, “break crop”, “rotation”, “economic”, and “profitability”. the search was further broadened by checking relevant references of the literature obtained. similarly, grey literature was searched to increase coverage and reduce publication bias with respect to reported pre-crop benefits. the same keywords and their respective translations in german or french language were searched for in google scholar, conference proceedings (e.g. esa, lca food) and websites of relevant organisations (ufop, unip, regional agricultural research institutes).
selection_criteria: references were required to report replicated field trials on the effect of grain legumes and a reference pre-crop on the yield of subsequent cereals or rapeseed. they had to allow for a pair-wise comparison of legume to non-legume pre-crops, and report level of nitrogen (n) fertilisation to the pre-crops and subsequent crops. references were excluded when they (a) did not report field experiments but model results, pot experiments or statistical data from practice, (b) reported pre-crop effects of legumes grown for forage, (c) did not allow for pairwise comparison of legume to non-legume pre-crops, (d) reported yield benefits to crops other than cereals or rapeseed, or (f) did not specify important experimental data, especially replications, n level, or absolute yield values. for economic profitability, included literature was required to (a) report gross margin (gm) of grain legumes in europe in comparison to another reference crop, (b) clearly present the method of gm calculation, yield, price, subsidies and variable costs included, and (c) where applicable, present the nature and size of pre-crop benefits considered.
data_analysis: different crop comparisons, n levels, and sites within experiments were included as individual observations, whereas they were averaged over years and other treatments, where applicable (e.g. tillage system, crop varieties, type and timing of fertilisation) in order to avoid a bias towards longer or larger experiments. inner quartile range of included experiments was chosen to provide a range of effect sizes that are probable estimates in a typical situation. gms were distinguished at the scale of single crops (gm) or at the scale of crop sequence (gmexp), crop rotation (gmrot), and cropping system (gmdal). by crop sequence we describe a temporal sequence of two to three crops grown consecutively.
background: Information on the magnitude of grain legume pre-crop effects is diverse and specific to sites and farming systems and has not been synthesised for European agriculture.
objective: this review has two objectives: (1) analyse and quantify benefits of grain legumes to the cropping system shown in european experiments; and (2) review economic assessments of grain legumes based on crop gross margins (gm) and alternative methods for gross margin calculation that include cropping system benefits. here the results regarding the objective (1) under conservation tillage are reported.
result1: in mediterranean, water-limited sites of spain, cereals following grain legumes reacted with slightly increased or maintained yields to reduced or zero tillage, which resulted in increased gms. also reduced yields of a vetch-barley rotation have been reported with reduced tillage in central spain, but this may not negatively affect gm considering potential cost reductions. applying reduced tillage to all crops in the rotation is also feasible, as the grain legume crops themselves were found to react with maintained or even increased yields to reduced or zero tillage, and their gm increased relative to other crops.
result2: NA
general_conclusion: this narrative review reports positive effect of reduced tillage on yield of subsequent crop after legume cultivation in several experiments. grain legume rotations were more competitive under conservation tillage systems (zero or reduced tillage) if gross margin calculations accounted for cost savings arising from adjusted machinery requirements. in absence of statistical analysis of the data, the results are reported as uncertain.

search_strategy: similar search strategy as pittelkow et al. (2015): the authors searched the peer-reviewed literature for publications investigating the effects of no-till in relation to the other two conservation agriculture principles on crop yields from jan 1980 to may 2013 using scopus (elsevier). search terms included ‘tillage’, ‘no till’, ‘zero till’, ‘direct drill*’, or ‘conservation ag*’ in the article title and ‘yield’ in the article title, abstract, or keywords.
selection_criteria: similar selection critera as pittelkow et al. (2015) but individual studies were not required to report residue management or crop rotation practices to be included in the database. here are reported the selection criteria from pittelkow et al. (2015): studies had to represent field experiments containing side-by-side comparisons of no-till and conventional tillage practices; (2) no-till treatments consisted of zero tillage immediately before crop establishment for a given growing season (that is, reduced tillage treatments such as strip-tillage were rejected); (3) crop yields were reported; (4) location of the experiment was stated; (5) confounding effects between treatments were absent (that is, differences in residue management, seeding rates, fertilizer rates, etc. were determined to be negligible). conference proceedings and non-english language publications were excluded. studies were rejected if it was unclear from reading the experimental methods whether factors other than tillage differed between treatments with the exception of herbicides (the absence of tillage as a weed control strategy generally requires changes in herbicide management under no-till). owing to the large size of the database, particular attention was given to avoiding data duplication (for example, when different studies reported the same data). thus, if it was unclear whether a publication contained duplicate data, it was rejected.
data_analysis: a meta-analysis was performed following the procedures reported in pittelkow et al. (2015). to quantify impacts of each input variable in relation to each other, we applied non parametric recursive partitioning techniques to the dataset. unbiased variable importance rankings were determined using random forest. to maintain consistency with the meta-analysis subcategories, the dataset was restricted to observations with duration and n fertilizer addition (zero or inorganic n fertilizer addition) information available. the potential for publication bias was investigated and sensitivity analyses were conducted to examine how individual observations influenced weighted mean effect sizes. because sampling variances were not available for individual observations, funnel plots were created for each crop category using approximated standard errors (regression tests for data asymmetries in funnel plots revealed no significant evidence of publication bias). sensitivity analyses were conducted using the jackknife procedure: centered bootstrap values for the 0.05, 0.5, and 0.95 quantiles are depicted as hatched horizontal lines and the effects of omitting individual observations from bootstrap calculations are displayed as changes in the distribution of the quantiles (there was little influence of individual observations on the weighted mean effect size within each crop category, suggesting the bootstrapped estimates are relatively insensitive to the inclusion of specific data points).
background: In terms of how no-till influences crop productivity, there is little consensus as to whether yields are maintained or yield increases or decreases can be expected despite these practices being widely investigated
objective: at a global scale, the objectives of this study were to (i) evaluate the influence of crop and environmental variables on no-till productivity and (ii) identify factors contributing to no-till yield gaps to provide the scientific support for evidence-based crop management and international development strategies.
result1: across all observations (all crop categories and locations), no-till reduced yields by 5.1%.
result2: yield response to no-till varied across crops, latitude, aridity, treatment duration, nitrogen fertilization.
result3: the negative impacts of no-till decreased when crop rotation and residue retention practices were implemented for the overall category. yet, this relationship varied for individual crop categories.
result4: regardless of crop category, positive responses to residue retention and crop rotation (i.e. a reduction in yield decline with no-till) were observed only in dry climates. in contrast, yield declines remained similar regardless of these practices in humid climates. as residue management and crop rotation were considered as factor, these results are reported as factor.
general_conclusion: this meta-analysis shows that, when averaged across all observations, the implementation of no-till leads to a significant decrease in yield. conservation agriculture has positive effect only in dry regions, showing that residue retention along with crop rotation are particularly important practices when implementing no-till in these regions.
knowledge_gaps: the average yield decrease reported here refers to the effects of no-till in the absence of other crop management modifications relative to conventional tillage, which limits the interpretation of the results. this analysis did not account for the fact that no-till may represent a more profitable management system due to the potential for reduced costs such as fuel savings. the majority of studies did not contain soil texture data. similarly, cumulative precipitation values for each growing season, and particularly the distribution of precipitation within a growing season, were not reported in the majority of individual studies. for several critical factors that were considered sufficient experimental details were not provided in many studies which prevented extraction of this information. there was a strong geographical bias in the dataset that likely has implications for the results of this analysis. north america, asia, africa, and europe were overrepresented in the database, accounting for 47, 9, 23, and 13% of studies.

search_strategy: the authors searched the peer-reviewed literature for publications investigating the effects of nt on crop yields from january 1980 to may 2013 using scopus (elsevier, amsterdam, netherlands). search terms included ���tillage���, ���no till���, ���zero till���, ���direct drill*���, or ���conservation ag*��� in the article title and ���yield��� in the article title, abstract, or keywords.
selection_criteria: studies reporting differences in management between nt and ct treatments such as variations in residue management, crop rotation, n fertilization, or irrigation were not included. n fertilizer management observations from studies that reported a range of n rates across sites, crops, or years, were only included in the database if exact rates were provided or if the range of values was smaller than 15 kg n/ha (for these studies, the midpoint was chosen). in addition, the database was further confined to: (1) observations for which crop rotation information was available (observations with a preceding cover crop were categorized as having a crop rotation); (2) observations for which the duration of the nt/ct yield comparison was reported; (3) observations from plots where residues were not reported to have been burned (4) observations on non-legume crops.
data_analysis: bootstrapping procedures were used to generate 95% confidence intervals (ci) for weighted mean effect sizes with 4999 iterations. the relative importance of the independent variables (n fertilizer rate; duration of the nt/ct yield comparison; residue retention (yes/no/not stated); crop rotation (yes/no); irrigation (yes/no/not stated); aridity index (mean annual precipitation divided by potential annual evapotranspiration); crop type) was determined via conditional random forest classification and regression approaches. interactive effects between tillage, the rate of n fertilization, and the other independent variables, exploratory linear mixed-effects models were developed. to determine the n rate at which nt yield declines were no longer observed when moving from low to high n rates, yield response ratios were fit to a plateau model.
background: The objective of this study was to determine whether and how the rate of N fertilization interacts with other management variables and affects the relationship between NT and CT yields in both tropical/subtropical and temperate regions.
objective: no-till (nt), a fundamental component of conservation agriculture (ca), has been shown to reduce yields in many cases. in order to maintain yields following adoption of ca, it has been recently suggested that fertilizer application should be an integral component of ca.
result1: the implementation of nt led to a significant decline in yield that was more extreme in tropical/subtropical regions (mean = -10.7%; 95% ci: -14.8% to -6.5%) than in temperate regions (mean = -3.7%; ci: -5.3% to -2.2%).
result2: in tropical/subtropical regions the rate of n fertilization was the most important variable for explaining yield changes due to nt. in contrast, site aridity, the least important variable for explaining yield declines in the tropical/subtropical regions, was the most important explanatory variable in temperate regions. additionally, although in temperate regions n rate accounted for similar proportions of the variance as crop rotation, it was approximately half as important as residue management and two-thirds as important as nt duration in explaining the yield changes.
result3: based on both the linear and nonlinear mixed modeling approaches, the most unambiguous interactive effects of tillage and n rate on crop yields apply to nt durations of at least 2 years and n rates lower or equal than 85+/-12 standard error (se) kg n/ha/yr in tropical/subtropical regions.
result4: for observations where rates of n fertilization were lower or equal to 100 kg n/ha/yr, nt yields were -27% (ci: -34% to -17%) lower than ct yields for nt durations lower or equal to 2 years, -34% (ci: -45% to -19%) lower for observations where residues had been removed, and -31% (ci: -37% to -23%) lower for observations where no crop rotation had been practiced. in contrast, for observations where rates of n fertilization were >100 kg n/ha/yr, nt yields were equal to ct yields in 2 of the 3 subsets. in these subsets nt yield changes were -0.3% (ci: -3% to 4%) for nt durations lower or equal to 2 years, -8% (ci: -13% to -3%) for observations with residues removed, and 5% (ci: -3% to 13%) for observations where crop rotation was not practiced.
general_conclusion: overall, this study shows that nt yields decreased relative to ct in tropical/subtropical and temperate regions.

search_strategy: the data used in this meta-analysis were collected from peer- reviewed publications, which measured the ghgs emissions under nt compared to ct from the search engines of web of science, scopus and google scholar to a cut-off date of april 2020. the search keywords ‘soil tillage’ or ‘no-tillage’ or ‘zero-tillage’ and ‘ghgs’ ‘carbon dioxide’ or ‘co2’ and ‘methane’ or ‘ch4’ and ‘nitrous oxide’ or ‘n2o’ were used to search the peer-reviewed articles.
selection_criteria: a) research studies conducted in the field; b) studies measuring cumulative emissions (kg ha-1) of ghgs either co2, ch4, and/or n2o under both nt and ct treatments at the same study site; c) means, standard deviations (or standard errors), and the number of replications that was either reported and/or could be calculated; d) experimental duration, n application rate, and water management practices that were clearly reported.
data_analysis: the response ratio (rr) was used to compare the ghgs emissions, crop yield and overall gwp under nt and ct. we used a natural log-transformed response ratio (lnrr) as the effect size to calculate the effects of nt and ct on ghgs emissions from agricultural soils. metawin 2.1 software was used to calculate the mean effect sizes of the dataset and 95% bootstrapped confidence intervals (cis) were generated using 4999 iterations. the results were considered significant if the 95% ci of cumulative co2, n2o and ch4 emissions did not overlap with zero and the randomization tests resulted p < 0.05.
background: The effects of no tillage (NT) on greenhouse gas emissions have been intensively debated and ominously vary among individual research studies
