objective: the main objectives of this meta-analysis study were to: a) examine the responses of ghgs emissions, global warming potential (gwp), and crop yield to nt, b) check the impact of soil physicochemical properties (i.e. soil ph, c:n ratio, and soil texture), climatic zones and crop man- agement (n application rate, crop types and growth duration and water management) on ghgs emission and crop yield under nt as compared to ct practices.
result1: crop yields were not significantly different (lnrr = 2.1%, 95% ci = −0.8%, 5.2%) between nt and ct because 95% ci overlapped with zero.
result2: NA
general_conclusion: absence of difference in crop yield was observed both under nt and ct practices.

search_strategy: a review of the existing literature was made to compile a dataset for comparing crop yield under zero tillage and conventional tillage. sixty one datasets were used, from peer-reviewed research papers that made one-to-one comparisons with zero tillage and conventional tillage found using the search terms ‘crop yield and zero (or no) tillage’ in web of science.
selection_criteria: only those papers with paired conventional tillage (ct) and zero-tillage (zt) treatments were selected.
data_analysis: linear regressions were carried out on the yield differences against duration of zero tillage.
background: The potential for any mitigation by zero tillage needs to be considered together with its impact on crop yields, as climate change and global food security are intrinsically linked.
objective: the objective of the current paper were  to evaluate zero tillage for: (i) mitigation of climate change by sequestration of c and by reducing or balancing emissions of major ghgs from the soil and (ii) its effect on crop yield. the results related to the impact of zero tillage on crop yield are reported here.
result1: current analysis suggests there is a lack of consistently reported effects of zero tillage on yield: 0.53 of publications examined in the present study reported an increase in crop yield with zero tillage, whereas 0.47 reported higher yield under conventional management (n = 61).
result2: the most negative effects have been recorded in maize with an average of 0.36 reduction in maize yield by following zero tillage over 10 years reported in 15 publications (yield advantage under zero tillage in maize = -0.5081 * years under zero tillage - 8.5045, r2 = 0.01).
result3: the data on winter wheat (n = 20, yield advantage under zero tillage in winter wheat = -0.7799 * years under zero tillage + 8.7384, r2 = 0.06) generally suggested little effect on yield following the adoption of zero tillage over conventional tillage (1% reduction), though an 8% reduction in barley yield was observed over 10 years. however, the research in this area is conflicting.
result4: one study found increased yield under soybean of 7.7% with zero tillage over 10 years compared to conventional tillage.
general_conclusion: current analysis suggests there is a lack of consistently reported effects of zero tillage on yield, with negative impact reported for maize, positive impact on soybean, and uncertain effect in cereals.

search_strategy: the authors comprehensively searched the peer-reviewed literature for publications investigating the effects of no-till in relation to the other two conservation agriculture principles on cropyields fromjan 1980 to may 2013 using scopus (elsevier). search terms included ‘tillage’, ‘no till’, ‘zero till’, ‘direct drill*’, or ‘conservation ag*’ in the article title and ‘yield’ in the article title, abstract, or keywords.
selection_criteria: this search produced a total of 2,471 publications, which were screened on the basis of the following criteria: (1) studies had to represent field experiments containing side-by-side comparisons of no-till and conventional tillage practices; (2) no-till treatments consisted of zero tillage immediately before crop establishment for a given growing season (that is, reduced tillage treatments such as strip-tillage were rejected); (3) crop yields were reported; (4) location of the experiment was stated; (5) management information regarding at least one other conservation agriculture principle was available (that is, residue management or crop rotation); and (6) confounding effects between treatments were absent (that is, differences in residue management, seeding rates, fertilizer rates, etc. were determined to be negligible). conference proceedings and non-english language publications were excluded. studies were rejected if it was unclear from reading the experimental methods whether factors other than tillage differed between treatments with the exception of herbicides (the absence of tillage as a weed control strategy generally requires changes in herbicide management under no-till). owing to the large size of the database, particular attention was given to avoiding data duplication (for example, when different studies reported the same data). thus, if it was unclear whether a publication contained duplicate data, it was rejected.
data_analysis:
the authors calculated the natural log of the response ratio (the ratio of no-till to conventional tillage yields) as the effect size in the meta-analysis. because within-study variance measures for mean yields were
available for less than a few percent of studies, individual observations were weighted by replication. bootstrapping procedures were used to generate 95% confidence intervals for weighted mean effect sizes using 4,999 iterations. between-group heterogeneity was assessed using randomization procedures based on 4,999 replications.
background: Conservation agriculture represents a set of three crop management principles that has received strong international support to help address this challenge, with recent conservation agriculture efforts focusing on smallholder farming systems in sub-Saharan Africa and South Asia.However, conservation agriculture is highly debated, with respect to both its effects on crop yields and its applicability in different farming contexts.
objective: here, the authors synthesized current scientific evidence at a global scale to assess crop yields under no-till in relation to implementation of the other two conservation agriculture principles, residue retention and crop rotation.
result1: overall, the authors found that no-till negatively impacts crop yields by 5.7%. importantly, the negative impacts of no-till are minimized when both of the other conservation agriculture principles are also applied (-2.5%) (no till + residues retention + crop rotation vs conventional till + residues retention + crop rotation). the largest yield declines occur when no-till is implemented alone (-9.9%) or with only one other conservation agriculture principle (-5.2 and -6.2% for residue retention and crop rotation, respectively).
result2: the analysis shows that no till significantly enhances yields (7.3%) under rainfed agriculture in dry climates when the other two conservation agriculture principles are also implemented. yet, the reverse is true when no-till is applied alone (-11.9%). furthermore, yields decrease with no-till regardless of whether the other principles are applied in humid climates.
result3: regardless of whether the other two conservation agriculture principles are implemented, no till reduces yields in the first few years following adoption. however, the yield decline in initial years is minimized when all three principles are applied compared with one principle (-3.0% versus -11.4%, respectively). moreover, despite no-till yields in all categories becoming comparable with conventional tillage in the medium term, after 10+ years yields begin to decline when only no-till is implemented.
result4: when considering the relative importance of crop rotation versus residue management practices in enhancing yield of no-till systems, this meta-analysis does not provide evidence that one principle regulates productivity more than the other. across all observations, the individual effects of residue retention and crop rotation reduce the negative impacts of no-till by 4.8 and 3.8%, respectively, although differences between categories are insignificant. however, in dry climates these principles each have a much stronger effect on rainfed crop yields, reducing yield losses by 10.1 and 11.0%, respectively.
general_conclusion: to help close the yield gap with conventional tillage, these findings suggest that instead of implementing no-till as the first step towards conservation agriculture in cropping systems where residue retention and crop rotation are absent (and anticipating that these two principles will follow in time), the primary focus should be on implementing no-till systems that already employ the other two principles.

search_strategy: the authors used a dataset on no-tillage by pittelkow et al (2015), which was based on a peer-reviewed literature search from jan 1980 to may 2013 using scopus. search terms included ‘tillage’, ‘no till’, ‘zero till’, ‘direct drill*’, or ‘conservation ag*’ in the article title and ‘yield’ in the article title, abstract, or keywords.
selection_criteria: only field experiments containing side-by-side yield comparisons were included in the database to ensure comparability of the cropping system treatments. because the focus of this study was on temporal yield stability, i.e., annual variability across years, single year comparisons from the original datasets were combined in order to create observations that were based on several years for each crop investigated (i.e., multiple year observations (myo)). the authors focused on studies with a minimum of 4 years of observation for the same crop, thus excluding short term studies.
data_analysis: two measures to asses temporal stability: (1) the ‘absolute stability ratio’, which is based on the standard deviation of both treatments as an indicator for variability, and (2) the ‘relative stability ratio’, which is based on the coefficient of variation (cv: standard deviation across years divided by the mean across those years) of both treatments as indicator for variability. therefore, in the latter measure the variability is standardized per unit yield (i.e., the variability relative to the yield level). in order to account for the sampling uncertainty in each observation the sampling variances were used.
background: Plant yield analyses neglect temporal yield stability, or the variability and reliability of production across years.
objective: to assess temporal yield stability of three major cropping systems: organic agriculture and conservation agriculture (no-tillage) vs. conventional agriculture. this analysis focuses on tillage systems.
result1: the temporal stability (-3%) of no-tillage does not differ significantly from those of conventional tillage.
result2: NA
general_conclusion: the temporal stability (−3%) of no-tillage does not differ significantly from those of conventional tillage indicating that a transition to no-tillage does not affect yield stability.
knowledge_gaps: 1) it is important to investigate under which conditions no-tillage has the most beneficial effects on yield and yield stability; 2) assess yield stability at the farm scale (with a range of crops planted in different fields) or at a regional, national or global scale; 3) further modelling and work at different scales (e.g., farm, regional, national and global) is necessary to understand how farmers and policy makers can enhance the stability of the food supply.

search_strategy: the data used in this study were obtained from on-station trials conducted by the researchers (a total of 3482 paired data points from 323 on-station studies) and from those conducted on-farm by the farmers in participation with the researchers (a total of 396 paired data from 9 on-farm studies) throughout the rice-growing world. the on-station data were archived from 205 original peer-reviewed publications and 118 proceedings/book chapters/reports/bulletins/newsletters through the web of science and google scholar search, libraries, and personal communications.
selection_criteria: studies that met the following criteria were included only: 1) tillage/ce practices that fall within the broad categories of five key options; 2) ct-tpr(wet) was included as a control; 3) the same location and soil type in ct-tpr(wet) and other tillage/ce options; 4) the same crop management, including fertilizer management in ct-tpr(wet) and other tillage/ce options within a study excepting treatment-specific changes such as weed and water management involved; 5) the same performance parameters and their methods of measurements in ct-tpr(wet) and other tillage/ce options within a study.
data_analysis: the meta-analysis was performed in two stages. at first, the effect size was calculated for each study. since most studies did not report the variance of the means of response variables, the effect sizes were weighted based on the number of replicates. effect sizes from individual studies were then combined using a mixed-effect model to calculate the cumulative effect size and the 95% confidence intervals (cis) through bootstrapping with 4999 iterations. the data were subjected to mixed model analysis to estimate the effects of the tillage and ce options over ct-tpr(wet) as the control, and to test the differences among them for yield (mg/ha), cost of cultivation, and net economic returns (us$/ha) across all studies included in the analysis. mixed model analysis was also performed for yield estimates to quantify differences among (i) wet and dry seasons, (ii) transplanted and direct-seeded conditions, and (iii) different soil textures. the analysis was carried out taking the different tillage/ce options, including the control (ct-tpr), as fixed effects and the studies as random effects. to investigate the effect of tillage (ct vs zt), the data points of options 1 and 2 (those including conventional tillage) were combined to form the ct group and options 4 (rt-dsr(dry)) and 5 (zt-dsr(dry)) were combined to form the rt/zt group [no data were available for rt/zt combination in sandy (coarse) group]. least squares means were compared using the algorithm for a compact letter display of comparisons for unbalanced data.
background: Hundreds of individual on-station and on-farm trials have compared yields and other performance parameters of various tillage/rice establishment options, but an attempt to synthesize information on a global scale is critically lacking. Such a synthesis is essential to (a) prioritize research and development issues, including precise technology targeting, and (b) articulate policy and institutional measures to facilitate large-scale adoption.
objective: the authors performed a comprehensive meta-analysis and mixed model analysis on data from on-station (1980–2016) and on-farm studies (2009–2016) carried out globally to compare the performances of five major options of rice tillage and crop establishment (ce) options with that of conventional tillage (puddling) and transplanting. performance parameters considered in the meta-analysis and the mixed model analysis included (a) grain yield, (b) water input, (c) ghg emissions, and (d) cost of cultivation and net economic returns.
result1: rice yield declined when both ct and tpr were substituted by reduced tillage (rt) or zero tillage (zt) and dsr. the yields of rt-uptpr(wet), rt-dsr(dry), and zt-dsr(dry) did not differ from each other but, compared with the yield of ct-tpr(wet), three options incurred yield losses ranging from 7.0% to 7.4% according to the meta-analysis, and 4.6-6.3% of ct-tpr(wet) by mixed model analysis of both on-station and on-farm data.
result2: the seasonal comparison of different tillage/ce options showed that the overall yield performance was superior in the dry season (increases of 2.8%) compared with the wet season (decreases of 0.8%). all the tillage/ce options had yield response ranging from negative to positive in varying soil texture-groups except rt-uptpr(wet), which had negative yield responses (-7.3% to -15.3%) in all the soil texture-groups. the tillage (ct vs zt) comparisons showed that grain yield responded (a) positively to zt in the clayey group, with an average increase of 3.5%, (b) remained unchanged in moderately fine loamy soil, and (c) responded negatively in medium loamy (2.9%) and moderately coarse loamy (8.2%) groups.
general_conclusion: when the intensity of tillage was reduced (rt) or tillage was eliminated (zt), a significant yield loss was observed, irrespective of whether the rice was direct-seeded or transplanted.
knowledge_gaps: this analysis was based on published and unpublished (through personal communication) data, which do not necessarily come from experiments in which soil texture was included as a testable variable. soil texture is a major factor affecting yield, primarily due to variations in water and nutrient dynamics, the latter being strongly connected to irrigation management. in flooded soil, the effect of texture becomes minimized compared with unsaturated conditions in which the texture primarily controls water-nutrient dynamics. additionally, the irrigation management in direct-seeded rice could be sufficiently different from that of puddled-transplanted rice. we could not include studies from the north american and latin american regions where ct-tpr(wet) as a control is not reported.

search_strategy: the studies included in the analysis were those cited in isi web of science database until february 2019 with the keywords ‘soil organic carbon’ or ‘soil organic matter’ and ‘no-till’, ‘no tillage’ or ‘zero tillage’ or ‘direct seeding’.
selection_criteria: (a) experiments of no-till lasting more than 5 years, which were used to reduce the instabilities at the beginning of the experiment; (b) the duration of conventional tillage and no-till were the same; (c) measured thick- ness of soil layers was not less than 30 cm; and (d) reduced tillage and minimum tillage practices were excluded and only continuous no-till (i.e. complete absence of tillage) was selected.
data_analysis: to include as many studies as possible, studies were weighted by sample size: w=ncnt∕(nc+nt), where w refers to the specific weight of a given pair of data, and nc and nt are sample sizes for the control and no-till respectively. given that studies differed in sample sizes, more weights are given to large sample sizes. resampling methods (e.g. bootstrapping) were used to cal- culate bias-corrected 95% confidence intervals (cis) around the mean effect size. if the 95% ci of the effect size for a variable did not overlap with zero, the effect of restoration on the variable was considered significant.
background: Conservation agriculture has been shown to have multiple benefits for soils, crop yield and the environment, and consequently, no-till, the central practice of conservation agriculture, has rapidly expanded. However, studies show that the potential for carbon (C) sequestration in no-till farming sometimes is not realized, let alone the ability to maintain or improve crop yield.
objective: global analysis of no-till-induced changes of soil c and crop yield
result1: relative to local conventional tillage, arid regions can benefit from no tillage.
result2: relative to local conventional tillage, arid regions can benefit the most from conservation agriculture.
general_conclusion: there was a positive effect of no-tillage or conservation agriculture on crop yied in arid region but negative effect in humid regions.

search_strategy: several databases were used, such as web of science, google scholar and scopus to search peer-reviewed publications (before april 2020). the keywords used in the search were “cropland or crop or wheat or maize or barley or rice,” “soc or soil organic matter,” and/ or “ch4, n2o and yield (grain).”
selection_criteria: each study selected contains measurements of ghg emissions for both control and treatment management practices. studies with the following measurements were excluded: (i) measurements made in pot, laboratories or greenhouses and (ii) measurements conducted in organic (peaty) soils where n2o are much higher than those in mineral soils and where soil carbon fluxes are different.
data_analysis: we performed our analysis on mean difference (md) weighted by study replication, on unweighted effect sizes. then, a random-effects model, which is more adaptable to ecological synthesis compared to a fixed-effects model, was selected to estimate the md of the variable x for a certain cropland management practice. the effect of the management practice was considered not significant if 95% confidence interval (ci) of the md overlapped with zero. the estimations of the md and associated 95% ci of were conducted in r version 4.0.1 with “meta” and “metaphor” packages
background: Smart cropland management practices can mitigate greenhouse gas (GHG) emissions while safeguarding food security.
objective: the objective of this study was to evaluate the integrated effects of alternative management practices on cropland net greenhouse gaz budget and grain yield. here, the results obtained on the effect of no-tillage on soil organic carbon sequestration rate are reported.
result1: grain yield was found generally unaffected by no-tillage (p > .05).
result2: NA
general_conclusion: no-tillage has no significant effect on crop yield.

search_strategy: an exhaustive literature survey of peer-reviewed publications was carried out using isi-web of science and google scholar (google inc., mountain view, ca, usa) for articles published before august 2011.
selection_criteria: the literature survey focused on n2o emissions from cropping systems but excluded flooded systems such as rice paddies. studies had to meet specific criteria to be included in the data set. first, n2o fluxes must have been measured under field conditions for an entire season (i.e., period from planting to harvest). second, crop yield data needed to be available, in some cases from other publications or via personal communication. third, means and the number of field replicates (i.e., plots per treatment combination) had to be reported for both ct and nt/rt systems. because of the importance of n fertilizer application rate in regulating both crop yields and n2o emissions, only comparisons where the n fertilizer application rate between tillage treatments differed by less than 15 kg n/ha/yr were included (only 5 of the 239 comparisons in the data set did not use identical n rates).
data_analysis: the authors performed meta-analyses using a nonparametric weighting function and generated confidence intervals (cis) using bootstrapping. effect sizes were weighted by replication. to avoid bias toward studies reporting results for multiple years, the weight of each effect size was divided by the number of years for which data were included from the corresponding study. they used metawin 2.1 to calculate mean effect sizes and to generate 95% bootstrapped cis (4999 iterations).
background: No-tillage and reduced tillage (NT/RT) management practices are being promoted in agroecosystems to reduce erosion, sequester additional soil C and reduce production costs. The impact of NT/RT on N2O emissions, however, has been variable with both increases and decreases in emissions reported.
objective: the objective of this study is to conduct a meta-analysis of peer-reviewed studies to evaluate the effects of nt/rt on n2o emissions and crop yield relative to conventional tillage (ct), with emissions expressed on both an area- and yield-scaled basis and to examine how these effects vary with respect to (i) duration of the tillage practice (more or less than 10 years), (ii) climate regime (humid or dry), and (iii) placement of n fertilizer (shallow or deep). here the effect on crop yield is reported.
result1: averaged across all comparisons, nt/rt led to a significant decline in yield of 5% compared to ct.
result2: there was no significant difference in yield decline relative to ct between nt and rt operations, did not depend on experimental duration.
result3: the yield decline with nt/rt was significantly greater in dry climates (11%) than that in humid climates (3%). however, in humid climates, the decline in yield was only significant for long-term nt/rt implementation (6%), whereas in dry climates the decline was only significant for short-term implementation (12%). for studies with deep fertilizer-n placement, nt/rt resulted in a yield decline of 10% compared to ct, while tillage had no significant effect on yield for studies with shallow n placement. in humid climates, the yield decline with nt/rt was limited to studies with deep n placement, whereas in dry climates, a significant yield decline with nt/rt was observed for both fertilizer placement categories.
general_conclusion: this study found a highly significant reduction in yield for nt and rt.

search_strategy: an exhaustive literature search of studies investigating n2o emissions from grain cropping systems was conducted with isi-web of science for articles published before june 2014. because the first search produced a limited numbers of papers for enhanced efficiency fertilizers, cover crops and diversified rotations, we conducted a second search focusing on these practices in december 2015 to increase the size of the database.
selection_criteria: only studies conducted in field conditions that were at least one growing season in duration were included.
data_analysis: we performed an unweighted meta-analysis because roughly more than half of the studies did not report a measure of variance. bias-corrected 95% confidence intervals (95% cis) were generated through a boot- strapping procedure in metawin 2.0 (5000 iterations). bootstrapping cis can be biased due to re-sampling from a small dataset (bancroft et al. 2007; montero- castano and vila 2012) so for groups with <10 observation pairs, we used the more conservative 95% cis instead of bias-corrected 95% ci. the 95% cis were converted to the percent change of n2o emissions from treatment groups compared to the controls for easier interpretation. a ci not overlapping with zero suggests a significant treatment effect and non-overlapping cis indicate significant difference between groups.
background: Understanding how agricultural management practices impact nitrous oxide (N2O) emissions is prerequisite for developing mitigation protocols.
objective: assess how management (including reduced tillage) affects n2o emissions.
result1: no significant differences in n2o emissions compared to the controls.
result2: NA
general_conclusion: no significant differences in n2o emissions between reduced tillage and conventional tillage.

search_strategy: a literature survey was performed using the web of science and google scholar (1900–2017). key words used for the initial search included tillage, greenhouse gases, co2, ch4,, and n2o.
selection_criteria: 1) ghg emissions were measured in situ for the entire cropping season. 2) the conventional tillage versus no tillage comparison was done under otherwise similar agronomic management practices. 3) information regarding means, standard deviations (or standard errors), replications, and the magnitude of seasonal cumulative ghg emissions was either available or could be calculated.
data_analysis:
response ratios (r) comparing nt and ct, for ghg emissions and crop yield, were calculated as follows: r = (xnt/xct) where x is the variate (co2, ch4, n2o, gwp, or crop yield) mean, for either the nt or the ct treatment. the variance (υ) of lnr (the effect size) was
computed and the weight of each effect size w = 1/variance. sas software was used to analyze the data by applying the macros for meta-analysis procedure.
background: The net effect of No Tillage (NT) greatly depends on the trade-offs between NT-induced changes in crop yield and GHG emissions. These trade-offs are regulated by a suite of climatic and soil factors, which have not been well addressed in past studies.
objective: 1) examine soil ghg emissions and crop yield with nt soil management in various environmental and management conditions; 2) identify factors contributing to food security and climate change mitigation in support of nt as an effective csa management practice.
result1: on average, co2 emission rate was not significantly different between nt and ct.
result2: for sites with net ch4 emission, nt reduced ch4 emission by 15.5% these effects seem to diminish with long-term duration of nt.
result3: for locations exhibiting net ch4 uptake, we found no difference between nt and ct.
result4: nt significantly increased n2o emission by 10.4% these effects seem to diminish with long-term duration of nt.
result5: for those studies that measured fluxes of all three ghgs, nt exhibited no difference in gwp compared to ct.
general_conclusion: on average, co2 emission rate was not significantly different between nt and ct. nt significantly increased n2o emission by 10.4%. nt decreased soil ch4 emission by 15.5% and had no effect on soil ch4 uptake. nt exhibited no difference in global warming potential compared to ct. the net effect of nt (relative to ct) was influenced by several environmental and agronomic factors (climatic conditions, tillage duration, soil texture, ph, crop species).
knowledge_gaps: to identify other climate smart agriculture (csa) management practices that are suitable at local, regional and/or global scales, future csa research programs that systematically investigate agroecosystem responses (e.g., crop yield, ghg emissions) using diverse methods (e.g., observation, meta-analysis, and agroecosystem modeling) are needed. there is some evidence of a reduction in overall gwp in nt given specific conditions, which needs to be verified with further observations.

search_strategy: the data used in this meta-analysis were collected from peer- reviewed publications, which measured the ghgs emissions under nt compared to ct from the search engines of web of science, scopus and google scholar to a cut-off date of april 2020. the search keywords ‘soil tillage’ or ‘no-tillage’ or ‘zero-tillage’ and ‘ghgs’ ‘carbon dioxide’ or ‘co2’ and ‘methane’ or ‘ch4’ and ‘nitrous oxide’ or ‘n2o’ were used to search the peer-reviewed articles.
selection_criteria: a) research studies conducted in the field; b) studies measuring cumulative emissions (kg ha-1) of ghgs either co2, ch4, and/or n2o under both nt and ct treatments at the same study site; c) means, standard deviations (or standard errors), and the number of replications that was either reported and/or could be calculated; d) experimental duration, n application rate, and water management practices that were clearly reported.
data_analysis: the response ratio (rr) was used to compare the ghgs emissions, crop yield and overall gwp under nt and ct. we used a natural log-transformed response ratio (lnrr) as the effect size to calculate the effects of nt and ct on ghgs emissions from agricultural soils. metawin 2.1 software was used to calculate the mean effect sizes of the dataset and 95% bootstrapped confidence intervals (cis) were generated using 4999 iterations. the results were considered significant if the 95% ci of cumulative co2, n2o and ch4 emissions did not overlap with zero and the randomization tests resulted p < 0.05.
background: The effects of no tillage (NT) on greenhouse gas emissions have been intensively debated and ominously vary among individual research studies
objective: the main objectives of this meta-analysis study were to: a) examine the responses of ghgs emissions, gwp, and crop yield to nt, b) check the impact of soil physicochemical properties (i.e. soil ph, c:n ratio, and soil texture), climatic zones and crop man- agement (n application rate, crop types and growth duration and water management) on ghgs emission and crop yield under nt as compared to ct practices.
result1: on average, nt significantly increased co2, n2o, and ch4 emissions by 7.1% (95% ci = 4.3%, 9.8%), 11.9% (95% ci = 8.3%, 15.7%), and 20.8% (95% ci = 18.0%, 10.8%), respectively.
result2: for gwp analysis, only those research studies were included who simultaneously reported co2, n2o and ch4 emissions. overall, nt significantly reduced gwp by 7.5% (95% ci = -14.3%, -0.3%) as compared to ct. only 11 publications were used to measure the gwp and it might be the reason in the reduction of overall gwp.
general_conclusion: nt management practice as compared to ct significantly increased co2, n2o and ch4 emissions by 7.1%, 11.9% and 20.8%. on the other hand, nt decreased overall gwp of ghgs emissions by 7.5% as compared to ct. only 11 publications were used to measure the gwp and it might be the reason in the reduction of overall gwp.

search_strategy: a comprehensive literature review was carried out in web of science to identify peer-reviewed articles with n2o emissions comparisons for conservation tillage with conventional tillage in side-by-side paired field trials. conservation tillage in this meta-analysis included no-tillage and reduced tillage practices, such as chisel tillage and shallow/lower depth tillage. the keywords ‘tillage’, ‘nitrous oxide’, ‘n2o’, and ‘greenhouse gas’ were used as search terms.
selection_criteria: specific criteria considered in selecting paired trials were: i) studies conducted in the field; ii) studies reported cumulative soil n2o emissions (kg n2o-n/ha) for at least one entire crop season duration for both conservation and conventional tillage treatments; iii) studies reported the mean and number of field replicates; and iv) studies for which n input rate was reported or could be accurately calculated.
data_analysis: a random-effects meta-analysis was conducted to assess n2o emission under conservation tillage versus conventional tillage. this meta-analysis was specifically designed to explore the influence of soil properties, climate regimes and agricultural practices on n2o emission in conservation tillage systems.  a categorical randomized-effects meta-analysis model was developed to compare the categorical mean effect size and determine any significant differences among categorical groups. total heterogeneity (qt) for each variable was partitioned into two parts, within-group heterogeneity (qw) and between-group heterogeneity (qb) using chi-square distributions. overall mean effect size and generated 95% bootstrapped confidence intervals (cis, 4999 interactions) were calculated.
background: A detailed assessment of the influence of conservation tillage practices on soil N2O emission is critical to determine the potential for conservation tillage practices to mitigate climate change.
objective: this study aimed to assess the effects of conservation tillage on soil n2o emission relative to conventional tillage by conducting a meta-analysis of peer-reviewed field studies. specifically, we attempt to address the following questions: i) how do climate regime and experimental duration affect soil n2o emissions following application of conservation tillage practices? ii) do initial soil properties affect the response of n2o emission to conservation tillage practices? and iii) can agricultural practices mitigate n2o emission associated with conservation tillage?
result1: overall, the mean effect size of soil n2o emission for conservation tillage versus conventional tillage was 17.8% (95% ci: 9.6-27.3%).
result2: no-tillage showed a significant increase in soil n2o emission as compared to conventional tillage (average: 19.2%, 95% ci: 9.3to29.8%), while no significant effect was observed in the reduced tillage systems (average: 12.3%, 95% ci: -0.5-31.7%). however, the categorical randomized-effects model showed no significant differences in soil n2o emissions for the two conservation tillage systems compared to conventional tillage (p = 0.552). residue management  (p<0.001) and crop rotation  (p=0.049) significantly affected soil n2o emissions in conservation tillage. compared to conventional tillage, conservation tillage increased n2o emissions when residues were not removed. the effect of conservation tillage was significant in both systems with or without crop rotation.
result3: the categorical randomized-effects model showed a significant difference between climate regimes (p<0.001). the effect size of conservation tillage on n2o emission was also dependent on the duration of the field trial as indicated by the significant differences among various levels of experimental duration. additionally, the n2o emission effect size showed a significant increase with increasing n application rates (p = 0.008). soil ph and clay content significantly affected soil n2o emissions after adoption of conservation tillage compared to conventional tillage (p<0,05). there was a significant but highly variable response of n2o emissions between different water management practices (p = 0.003). conservation tillage induced soil n2o emission varied significantly among various cropping systems when compared to conventional tillage (p = 0.048).
general_conclusion: application of conservation tillage significantly increased soil n2o emission compared to conventional tillage in this analysis. no-tillage showed a significant increase in soil n2o emission as compared to conventional tillage, while no significant effect was observed in the reduced tillage systems.

search_strategy: isi web of knowledge was searched on may 2020 to collect papers dealing with methane emissions in agricultural soils under both ct and nt. the operators “soil and till* and (methane or ch4)” were used. in addition to the broad search and careful  screening, the references of the included publications were inspected to include any studies that might have been missed.
selection_criteria: (i) the study reported simultaneous measurements (same sampling date) of ch4 fluxes from soils with at least two tillage types and (ii) one of the tillage types had to be no-till.
data_analysis: (i) a random-effects model was adopted and (ii) regulating factors were investigated to explain the effect size (es). the random-effects model was assumed since some random variability be- tween different studies was expected. after the estimation of the ess, a summary analysis was performed assuming a random-effects model. between- studies variance was calculated using the dersimonian and laird (1986) method and i statistic  was calculated to express the ratio of true heterogeneity to total variance. the summary effect (grand mean) was calculated assigning to each study a specific weight that accounted for both within- and between-studies variance.
background: Due to the overwhelming impact of tillage on soils and the sensitivity of methanotrophs to management, we should expect tillage to have a major influence over soil CH4 emissions. However, not unique results have been reported so far with higher, lower, or no difference in soil CH4 emissions comparing no tillage (NT) with conventional tillage (CT).
objective: this paper aimed to use a meta-analytical approach to summarize and synthesize peer-reviewed literature comparing the differences in soil ch4 emissions between conventional tillage (ct) and no tillage (nt).
result1: the raw ch4 fluxes measured in the 90 case studies ranged from -2.883 to 41.400 mg m-2 h-1 for ct and from -0.128 and 32.550 mg m-2 h-1 for nt. the median was 0.005 and 0.002 mg m-2 h-1 for ct and nt, respectively, indicating that in both treatments at least half of the values were close to 0 or slightly negative.
result2: the grand mean (i.e. the weighted mean of all the es) did not show a significant departure from the 0 line (hedges g: -0.097, ci: -0.292, 0.098)
result3: with rice production, nt significantly reduces ch4 emissions compared to ct (hedges g: -0.457, ci: -0.790, -0.125). the reduction is about 23 %, from an average of 12.39 mg m-2 h-1 of ct to 9.55 of nt.
general_conclusion: the analysis shows there was little-to-no effect of no tillage when used in arable soils. on the other hand, in rice production (and likely other paddy soil agriculture) no tillage shows promise to reduce ch4 emissions by 23 % on average.

search_strategy: peer-reviewed publications were collected by searching web of science (http://apps.webofknowledge.com) and china national knowledge infrastructure database (https://www.cnki.net) with various combinations of keywords “nitrous oxide” or “n2o,” “nitric oxide” or “no,” and “agricultural soils.”
selection_criteria: (i) the n2o and no emissions were simultaneously measured during at least a whole growing season; (ii) only the field measurements were included, without considering incubation, pot and lysimeter experiments or modelling results; (iii) the experiments on upland soils and paddy soils during the non-waterlogging period were included, without considering those on the flooded paddy soils; and (iv) the spatial replicates and standard deviation of each treatment were clearly recorded.
data_analysis: mean effect size and the 95 % confidence intervals were generated by a bootstrapping procedure with 999 iterations using metawin 2.1. individual effect sizes were weighted. the management effects were back-transformed and reported as percentage changes ([rr-1] × 100). the effects were considered significant if the 95 % confidence intervals did not overlap with zero.
background: Evidence from individual field measurements indicates that N2O and NO emissions respond to a certain management practice in a similar or divergent manner, mostly depending on the prevailing processes, such as denitrification or nitrification, contributing to each gas.
objective: the objective of this study is to quantify the effects of various management practices on n2o and no emissions by performing a pairwise meta-analysis. results on n2o are reported here.
result1: no-tillage increased n2o emissions (by 6.1 %).
result2: NA
general_conclusion: no-tillage increased n2o emissions.

search_strategy: a total of 49 datasets were collected from peer reviewed research papers using the search term 'zero (or no) tillage and carbon' in web of science.
selection_criteria: not reported
data_analysis: not reported.
background: There is general agreement that reduced and zero-tillage practice can conserve and enhance soil organic carbon (C) levels to some extent. However, their applicability in mitigating climate change has been debated extensively, especially when the whole profile of C in the soil is considered, along with a reported risk of enhanced nitrous oxide (N2O) emissions.
objective: the objective of the current paper were  to evaluate zero tillage for: (i) mitigation of climate change by sequestration of c and by reducing or balancing emissions of major ghgs from the soil and (ii) its effect on crop yield. the results related to the impact of zero tillage on climate change mitigation by reducing or balancing emissions of major ghgs from the soil are reported here.
result1: in contrast to co2 emissions, most research reports increased n2o emissions under zero tillage compared to conventional tillage.
result2: most previous studies indicate increased absorption of ch4 in soils under zero tillage due to reduced surface disruption, greater pore continuity (developed over time) and the presence of more micro-sites for methanotrophic bacteria. however, both increased and decreased ch4 consumption has been reported in zero-till soils.
result3: the most consistent trend in the literature suggests that overall, zero tillage reduces ghg emissions in the long term (c. 20 years), but crucially some uncertainty still exists as to when the positive effects are first recorded and how long these effects can be observed.
general_conclusion: most research included in this study reports decreased co2 emissions and increased n2o emissions under zero tillage compared to conventional tillage. however, both increased and decreased ch4 consumption has been reported in zero-till soils. the most consistent trend in the literature suggests that overall, zero tillage reduces ghg emissions in the long term, but crucially some uncertainty still exists as to when the positive effects are first recorded and how long these effects can be observed. in absence of formal statistical analyses, the results are considered as "uncertain".
knowledge_gaps: large uncertainties still remain and further work is needed both to define the underlying mechanisms and understand the variation between agricultural systems.

search_strategy: the data used in this study were obtained from on-station trials conducted by the researchers (a total of 3482 paired data points from 323 on-station studies) and from those conducted on-farm by the farmers in participation with the researchers (a total of 396 paired data from 9 on-farm studies) throughout the rice-growing world. the on-station data were archived from 205 original peer-reviewed publications and 118 proceedings/book chapters/reports/bulletins/newsletters through the web of science and google scholar search, libraries, and personal communications.
selection_criteria: studies that met the following criteria were included only: 1) tillage/ce practices that fall within the broad categories of five key options; 2) ct-tpr(wet) was included as a control; 3) the same location and soil type in ct-tpr(wet) and other tillage/ce options; 4) the same crop management, including fertilizer management in ct-tpr(wet) and other tillage/ce options within a study excepting treatment-specific changes such as weed and water management involved; 5) the same performance parameters and their methods of measurements in ct-tpr(wet) and other tillage/ce options within a study.
data_analysis: the meta-analysis was performed in two stages. at first, the effect size was calculated for each study. since most studies did not report the variance of the means of response variables, the effect sizes were weighted based on the number of replicates. effect sizes from individual studies were then combined using a mixed-effect model to calculate the cumulative effect size and the 95% confidence intervals (cis) through bootstrapping with 4999 iterations. the data were subjected to mixed model analysis to estimate the effects of the tillage and ce options over ct-tpr(wet) as the control, and to test the differences among them in ch4 and n2o emissions (ch4-c kg/ha and n2o-n kg/ha, respectively) across all studies included in the analysis.
background: Hundreds of individual on-station and on-farm trials have compared yields and other performance parameters of various tillage/rice establishment options, but an attempt to synthesize information on a global scale is critically lacking. Such a synthesis is essential to (a) prioritize research and development issues, including precise technology targeting, and (b) articulate policy and institutional measures to facilitate large-scale adoption.
objective: the authors performed a comprehensive meta-analysis and mixed model analysis on data from on-station (1980–2016) and on-farm studies (2009–2016) carried out globally to compare the performances of five major options of rice tillage and crop establishment (ce) options with that of conventional tillage (puddling) and transplanting. performance parameters considered in the meta-analysis and the mixed model analysis included (a) grain yield, (b) water input, (c) ghg emissions, and (d) cost of cultivation and net economic returns.
result1: ch4 emissions were also significantly lower in the alternative tillage/ce options for which data were available than those of ct-tpr(wet), with the largest (63.4%) reduction in zt-dsr(dry). the reduction in ch4 emissions by rt-uptpr(wet) was comparatively less (20.1%).
result2: n2o emissions in meta-analysis remained unchanged in rt-uptpr(wet) and zt-dsr(dry).
general_conclusion: ch4 emissions were significantly lower in the alternative tillage options than those of ct-tpr(wet), while n2o emissions in meta-analysis remained unchanged in rt-uptpr(wet) and zt-dsr(dry).
knowledge_gaps: the authors could not include studies from the north american and latin american regions where ct-tpr(wet) as a control is not reported.

search_strategy: several databases were used, such as web of science, google scholar and scopus to search peer-reviewed publications (before april 2020). the keywords used in the search were “cropland or crop or wheat or maize or barley or rice,” “soc or soil organic matter,” and/ or “ch4, n2o and yield (grain).”
selection_criteria: each study selected contains measurements of ghg emissions for both control and treatment management practices. studies with the following measurements were excluded: (i) measurements made in pot, laboratories or greenhouses and (ii) measurements conducted in organic (peaty) soils where n2o are much higher than those in mineral soils and where soil carbon fluxes are different.
data_analysis: we performed our analysis on mean difference (md) weighted by study replication, on unweighted effect sizes. then, a random-effects model, which is more adaptable to ecological synthesis compared to a fixed-effects model, was selected to estimate the md of the variable x for a certain cropland management practice. the effect of the management practice was considered not significant if 95% confidence interval (ci) of the md overlapped with zero. the estimations of the md and associated 95% ci of were conducted in r version 4.0.1 with “meta” and “metaphor” packages
background: Smart cropland management practices can mitigate greenhouse gas (GHG) emissions while safeguarding food security.
objective: the objective of this study was to evaluate the integrated effects of alternative management practices on cropland net greenhouse gaz budget and grain yield. here, the results obtained on the effect of no-tillage on soil organic carbon sequestration rate are reported.
result1: changes in ch4 and n2o emissions were insignificant and small for upland crops. for rice, they were significantly lower with no tillage. taking into account soil carbon, the net greenhouse gas budget is decreased in upland crops and does not change with no tillage in rice.
result2: NA
general_conclusion: no-tillage does not significantly decrease n2o and ch4 emissions in upland crops, but the effect is significant in rice. however, when considering soil carbon sequestration, the net ghg budget is decreased with no-tillage in upland crops while it does not change with no-tillage in rice.

search_strategy: literature survey of peer-reviewed papers published before december 2016 that reported the effects of nt/rt on both ch4 and n2o emissions using google scholar and isi-web of science. the keywords used in literature search were soil tillage, no-tillage, reduced tillage, ch4, n2o, and greenhouse gas emission.
selection_criteria: 1) the nt/rt and ct plots must be conducted at the same site with the same crop, agronomic management options (e.g., fertilizer, irrigation,), and experiment duration; 2) ch4 and n2o fluxes were both measured by using statistic chamber methods in field conditions for an entire crop growing season; and 3) the n application rate, crop straw returning methods, experimental duration, and water management practices were clearly recorded.
data_analysis: considering that upland and paddy fields showed a great difference in ch4 and n2o emissions, the authors examined the effect of nt/rt on ghg emissions for these two land use types separately. this meta-analysis was performed by using a nonparametric weighting function and the confidence intervals (cis) were generated by using bootstrapping because only 22.4% of selected studies reported the standard deviation or error of ch4, n2o and global warming potential. effect size was weighted by the number of experiment replicates and the number of ch4 and n2o flux measurements per month. this weighting approach assigned more weight to field experiments that were well replicated. the mean effect size, 95% confidence intervals (cis), group heterogeneity and publication bias were calculated by metawin 2.1.
background: The effect of no- and reduced tillage (NT/RT) on greenhouse gas (GHG) emission was highly variable and may depend on other agronomy practices. However, how the other practices affect the effect of NT/RT on GHG emission remains elusive.
objective: 1) to quantitatively summarize the effects of nt/rt on the total global warming potential of ch4 and n2o emissions and 2) to investigate the effects of cropping system, crop residue management, fertilizer split application, irrigation and tillage duration on the effectiveness of nt/rt.
result1: overall, reduced tillage system (nt/rt) did not exhibit significant effects on ch4 and n2o emissions as compared with ct. however, their effects on the overall gwp of ch4 and n2o emissions was marginally significant. the overall gwp was mitigated by 6.6% by nt/rt as compared with ct.
result2: the performance of nt/rt depended on land use type and tillage methods. in uplands, the effect of nt/rt on ch4 uptake did not show an obvious relationship with its impact on n2o emission. the overall gwp was reduced 11.6% by nt as compared with ct. whereas the effects of rt on ch4 uptake, n2o emission and overall gwp were not significant. in rice paddies, nt tended to mitigate the ch4 emission, whereas it increased the n2o emission, resulting in no significant impact on the overall gwp in rice paddies. however, rt significantly increased the ch4 emission and overall gwp compared with ct.
result3: in uplands, nt significantly reduced ch4 uptake, n2o emission, and overall gwp by 18.4%, 21.0% and 20.8% under the double crops rotation system. rt's effect on the overall gwp was not significant under the double crops rotation system. as in the paddy fields, nt significantly reduced the overall gwp by its cumulative abatement on ch4 and n2o emissions under the rice-upland crops rotation system.
result4: in uplands, when the crop straw was returned, the effect sizes of ntand rt  on ch4 uptake, n2o emission, and overall gwp were not significant. as in paddy fields, nt did not affect the overall gwp when crop straw was returned. rt significantly increased the ch4 emission and overall gwp when crop straw was returned.
result5: the effectiveness of nt/rt on ch4 and n2o emissions was influenced by the percentage of basal n fertilizer (pbn), irrigation, and tillage duration.
general_conclusion: overall, no and reduced tillage systems did not exhibit significant effects on ch4 and n2o emissions as compared with conventional tillage. however, their effects on the overall gwp of ch4 and n2o emissions was marginally positive. the effectiveness of no and reduced tillage depended on tillage methods, land use type, and agricultural practices.
knowledge_gaps: more field studies are needed to investigate the temporal effect of no tillage on ghg emission in paddy fields under different agricultural practices.

search_strategy: peer-reviewed journal articles published in english from 1985 to 2016, and referenced in the web of science and scopus systems, were collected to build the database used for this meta-analysis. the literature search was conducted using the following sets of topic keywords: (i) direct drilling or direct sowing or tillage or plow or plow, (ii) phosphorus or water quality, and (iii) soybean [gylcine max (l.) merr.] or corn (zea mays l.) or wheat (triticum aestivum l.). the authors selected those three crops on the basis of fao crop production statistics showing that these crops are likely to be cultivated using both nt and ct practices.
selection_criteria: a total of 1772 and 914 articles were identified from web of science and scopus, respectively. out of this total, only articles that reported the concentration and/or load of p in paired nt versus ct practices, including lysimeter studies under field conditions, were included in the database. since the authors focused on understanding the effect of nt (including its long-term impact) on p loss, they did not include articles stemming from studies involving “one-time tillage” experiments at sites previously under long-term nt.
data_analysis: to quantify the difference in p export due to nt, meta-analysis was used to construct the confidence intervals (cis) for each categorical variable. since standard deviation was reported in only four (out of 27) articles, the authors performed an unweighted analysis using the log response ratio (lnr) to calculate bootstrapped confidence limits to include studies that did not report sample size or standard deviation. to improve the reliability of lnr in estimating the effect size of the response ratio, a diagnostic test was performed. bootstrapping was also iterated 9999 times to improve the probability that the ci was calculated around the cumulative mean effect size for each categorical variable.
scale: mainly north america, one study in finland
background: Agriculture is a significant contributor to phosphorus (P) enrichment in aquatic ecosystems. No-till (NT) farming has been proposed as an alternative approach to conventional tillage (CT) in reducing soil P export, but published data have shown contrasting impacts, likely due to the interacting effects of different physical (climate region, rainfall variability, transport pathway, slope gradient) and management variables (NT duration, crop species).
objective: the authors conducted a meta-analysis to understand the extent to which each of these variables controls the concentration and load of different p fractions (dissolved p, particulate p) in agricultural runoff and leaching.
result1: in general, nt management resulted in increased concentration and load of dissolved p but significantly reduced the load and concentration of particulate and total p transferred to aquatic ecosystems.
result2: there has been, however, a large variability on the effect of nt on p loss, and this variability is associated with several physical and management factors, including climate (dryland vs. non-dryland), rainfall (wet vs. dry year), transport pathway (leaching vs. runoff), landscape topography (slope gradient), crop species (soybean, corn. and wheat), and tillage duration (short vs. medium).
general_conclusion: the results of this meta-analysis showed that nt can effectively reduce the amount and concentration of particulate p in agricultural catchment waters, but increases dissolved p.
knowledge_gaps: data availability constraints led to non-representation of some categories in the analysis or some categorical variables being investigated in only a few studies, which could limit the explanatory power of these variables.

search_strategy: a literature survey of peer-reviewed published literature in the isi-web of science and cab abstracts (ovid) between 1910 and 2013 was conducted to identify papers reporting results from studies using reduced tillage in organic farming. the following search terms and their variations were used in various combinations: reduced/minimum/shallow/chisel, tillage/ploughing/plowing, intensity, no-till/direct seeding, organic/ecological, farming/systems/agriculture/management.
selection_criteria: (i) experiment under organic management for at least 3 years prior to the date of response measurement; (ii) at least two levels of tillage intensity included as a treatment; (iii) no “mixing” of treatments, i.e., only tillage varied between experimental treatments; and (iv) included climatic zones found in europe
data_analysis: data were analyzed using unweighted meta-analysis techniques. the significance of effect sizes was tested using linear mixed effects models in the “lme4” package in r with random effects specified as experiment/year. the fixed effects of tillage class or climate were tested using this model. the effect of tillage class within a given soil type or crop class was tested after first subsetting the data by soil type or crop class and then using a mixed effects model as described above. for all analyses, least-square means and confidence intervals were generated using the “lsmeans” package in r. means were considered significantly different from zero if the 95 % ci did not overlap zero, and different from one another if their 95 % cis were non-overlapping (hedges et al. 1999). the results of each mean ratio (r) were expressed as % effect size (e), where e = (r − 1) × 100.
background: NA
objective: NA
result1: relative to both deep and shallow inversion tillage, reducing tillage intensity in organic systems increases weed incidence.
result2: for this set of data, the overall average increase in weed incidence was 54 % with only shallow inversion and no-tillage showing no increase in weed incidence relative to the control; however, the number of observation pairs for no-till is very low leading to a high degree of uncertainty in the estimate of effect size.
general_conclusion: the overall average increase in weed incidence in reduced intensity tillage relative to control was 54 %, with only shallow inversion and no-tillage showing no increase in weed incidence (with few observation pairs for no-till, leading to a high degree of uncertainty in the estimate of effect size).

search_strategy: papers were searched for the insect- and slug- herbivore analyses using the following search terms in web of science (© 2019, clarivate analytics): “tillage and insect*”, “till* insect* pest*”, “tillage herbiv*”, and combinations of “till*”, “plow*”, “plough*”, “arthropod*”, “insect*”, and “predat*”. we also found papers by searching previous reviews on the topic: all (1980); lawani (1982), and stinner and house (1990). papers published before 1 feb 2019 were included in this analysis.
selection_criteria: to be considered in the analysis of invertebrate abundance, studies need to have (1) compared invertebrate abundances in a reduced-disturbance to a high-disturbance tillage operation, (2) reported means and variance from both reduced and high-disturbance tillage fields to be included in effect size calculations, and (3) focused on annual grain, fiber, and vegetable crops, as we encountered too few studies investigating arthropod and slug response to tillage practices in orchard crops to include them in our analyses. to analyze effects of tillage on arthropod diversity, studies needed to have (1) compared arthropod or slug abundances in a reduced-disturbance to a high-disturbance tillage operation, (2) identified and quantified all arthropods and slugs from one sampling method to allow us to calculate diversity metrics, and (3) focused on annual grain, fiber, and vegetable crops. however, studies in our diversity analysis did not need to report variance, because variances were not used for this analysis.
data_analysis: to calculate a mean effect size, a mixed effects model was fitted with study as a random factor to account for the non-independence of measurements from the same experiment, using rma.mv in metafor. additionally, the taxonomic order of insect and slug herbivores or arthropod predators was used as a random factor to account for possible non-independence within phylogenetic groups. 95 % confidence intervals around each mean were computed. potential publication bias was assessed using funnel plots and fail-safe n values were computed using the rosenthal approach, which indicates the number of studies necessary to render any significant effect sizes non-significant, and plot asymmetry was assessed using egger’s regression tests. “leave 1 out” analysis was used to examine undue influence of any particular study on the overall result of our analyses
background: Farmers who have adopted reduced-tillage systems can struggle with a suite of insect and mollusc pests; however, reducing the frequency and intensity of tillage may increase predator populations and improve biological control.
objective: determine how tillage intensity influences populations of arthropod pests and natural enemies
result1: overall, the authors did not find that pest abundances were significantly higher in reduced-tillage treatments compared to higher-disturbance treatments.
result2: pests were not more abundant in no-till treatments compared to high-disturbance treatments, nor in medium-disturbance compared to high-disturbance.
result3: the abundance of soil-associated pests was not significantly different between high-disturbance tillage environments and reduced-tillage environments. foliar pest abundance was significantly greater in high-disturbance tillage systems than in reduced-tillage systems, although the size effect on foliar pests was small.
result4: compared to high-disturbance systems, we found that soil-collected predators were more abundant in reduced-tillage systems (fig. 2e). similarly, predators in no-till treatments were more abundant than in high-disturbance treatments (fig. 2e). predators in medium-disturbance systems, however, had similar abundances as those in high-disturbance systems
result5: foliar predator abundances did not differ between high-disturbance tillage systems and reduced-tillage systems. abundances of foliar predators were not greater in either medium- nor no-disturbance tillage practices compared to high-disturbance tillage treatments
general_conclusion: overall, total pest and soil-associated abundances, as well as total predators and foliar predators abundances were similar in reduced-tillage compared to higher-disturbance treatments, and in no-tillage compared to higher-disturbance treatments. however, foliar pest abundance was significantly greater in high-disturbance tillage systems compared to reduced-tillage systems, but was similar in no- compared to high-disturbance tillage systems. compared to high-disturbance systems, soil predators were more abundant in reduced-tillage systems and in no-till treatments.

search_strategy: journal articles published from 1990 to 2017 were searched using the isi web of science database (http://apps.webofknowledge.com/) and the china knowledge resource integrated database (http://www.cnki.net/).
selection_criteria: the following criteria were used when selecting paired experiments: (1) each experiment had similar topography and soil type, in addition to having a control (ct); (2) the mean and standard deviation (or standard error) of cmic and nmic and qmic were provided, with the number of replicates described either in the experimental design or in figure captions, and at least two replications were used in the experiment; and (3) tillage and residue management were included as treatments and other agronomic practices such as cropping intensity and irrigation were similar.
data_analysis: for each group (map, mat, experimental duration, soil texture and soil ph), the mean effect size (rr) and its 95% confidence interval (ci) were calculated with bias-correction generated by a bootstrapping procedure. a chi-square test was used to determine whether the heterogeneity among the rr of changes to cmic and nmic under nt and rt treatments (qtotal) was significantly larger than the expected sampling error. then, a randomization test was used to determine the significance of the between group heterogeneity (qb) and to test whether the rr of the categories differed between the levels of the factor. chi-square tests were also used to determine whether the remaining within group heterogeneity (qw) was significant. multiple linear regression analyses were conducted to determine the relationship among rr of cmic, nmic, and qmic and mat, map, soil ph, soil sampling depth, experimental duration, initial soc concentration, and soil c to n ratio (c:n) under nt and rt practices.
background: Conservation agriculture through the use of crop residue retention and no-tillage (NT) has been widely practiced to improve agricultural soil quality, such as to increase soil organic carbon (C) content and the microbial population size. However, there has been no quantitative analysis on the effect of conservation agriculture, particularly in relation to crop residue retention, on soil microbial biomass C (Cmic) and nitrogen (Nmic), and the microbial quotient (qMIC, Cmic-to-organic C ratio), which are frequently used as indicators of soil health under different agricultural practices.
objective: the objectives of the conducted a meta-analysis are to: 1) determine the direction and magnitude of change of cmic, nmic and qmic in response to different ca practices; and 2) evaluate the effect of environmental conditions and management practices on the source of variability in cmic, nmic and qmic.
result1: the rt, ntr, ntr0 and nt practices significantly increased cmic by 22.2, 25.1, 33.3 and 27.6%, respectively, as compared to ct. relative to ct, ntr and nt increased nmic by 64.1 and 43.4%, respectively. the rt, ntr, and nt practices significantly increased qmic by 47.8, 57.3 and 47.9%, respectively, as compared with ct.
result2: rt, nt, ntr, and nt0 effects on the different metrics varied according to soil ph, soil texture, experiment duration, map, and mat.
general_conclusion: this meta-analysis based on a global dataset demonstrates that rt, nt, ntr, and ntr0 generally significantly increase microbial activity, with the exception of ntr0 (no effect on nmic and qmic) and rt (no effect on nmic).
knowledge_gaps: due to insufficient data, straw retention rate, straw type, and the initial soc concentration were not considered in our subgroup meta-analysis.

search_strategy: the authors collected data from studies investigating the effect of agricultural practices on soil nematodes. studies should include nematode data and evaluate the effects of at least one of the four main agricultural practices (manipulation of plant diversity, pesticide use, tillage, fertilization) or those of different types of agricultural systems (“system”) on the nematode community. to reach this goal, a literature search was conducted, last updated in october 2019, using the web of science (thomson reuters) search engine. studies of interest were identified based on the following search string: “nemat* and (legum* or “cover crop” or cover-crop or agro or legum* or fallow or arable or crop or perennial or agroecosystem or rotation or association or agrofor* or “plant diversity” or diversity or weeds or cultiv* or intensi* or manag* or unmanag* or intercropping or “agricultural practices” or agri* or “agro-chemicals” or “biological control” or interculture or leguminous or pesticide* or nematicide or solariz* or biofumigation or “chemical control” or “catch crop” or disinfect*or carbofuran or input* or nutrient* or ferti* or amend* or compost* or residue* or litter or addition manur* or addition* or nitrogen or phosphorus or conservati* or compaction or tilla* or working or plough* or plow*)”. the authors used this search string to find articles based on the title or abstract of the article.
selection_criteria: all the sampled articles (3925) were screened based on their titles and abstracts and discarded articles considering only one plant-parasitic nematode species, review articles, studies conducted in greenhouses, in unmanaged ecosystems (forests or savannah) and articles not on the soil system (e.g., fresh water). after this first step of the selection, 465 articles were screened according to inclusion criteria: (1) data should be available in the articles either in table or in graphical forms; (2) nematode data should be a measurement of the abundance of nematode trophic groups (bacterial feeding (bf), fungal feeding (ff), omnivores and predators (op) and plant feeding nematodes (pf), and/or nematode diversity) and/or nematode indices (taxonomic richness (s) and shannon diversity (h′). nematode indices were the maturity index (mi), plant-parasitic index (ppi), structure index (si), enrichment index (ei), and nematode channel ratio (ncr)); (3) studies needed to evaluate the effects of at least one of the four main agricultural practices: managing plant diversity (rotation, cover crop and association), pesticide input (herbicide, biocides and nematicide), tillage, organic and mineral fertilization. any experimental data reporting multiple treatments combined into one, e.g., treatment (fertilization + tillage) versus control (no fertilization and no tillage) was discarded to avoid confounding effects. the effect of pesticide application, fertilization, tillage and plant diversity management had to be clearly distinct and identifiable with a control and an associated treatment. the effect of agricultural systems, that is the conversion of conventional agriculture to conservation or organic agriculture, include several distinct practices and had to be defined as such by the authors. conservation agriculture is based on no-tillage and cover crop; pesticides are use only when necessary. conventional systems use pesticide, mineral fertilizers and tillage. organic agriculture does not use synthetic pesticide and mineral fertilizers. tillage is used for weed management; (4) the samples should be collected from the topsoil layer (soil depth between 0 and 30 cm maximum). (5) studies needed to report means (x_), standard deviations (sd) or standard errors (se) and sample size (n, number of true replications) of nematode variables in control and treatment groups. when sd, se or sample size were missing, articles were discarded as these data are required to compute the effect size.
data_analysis: to calculate the combined effect size and its corresponding variance, we used a multilevel meta-analysis model (mixed model). the “study identification” (study id) was included in the model as a random factor to take into account the dependencies among estimates from the same study. to estimate the overall effect of agricultural practices on nematode variables under investigation, a random-effects model without any moderator variables was first ran for i) every type of agricultural practice and its respective subgroups and ii) each type of agricultural system. the average response ratios were tested for heterogeneity using the qe statistic. when the qe was significant (p-value < 0.05), moderators have been added in the models to explain this heterogeneity. when the qe was not significant, we did not perform further models with moderators. to further determine whether the moderators explained the heterogeneity of effect sizes, a mixed model with moderator variables as a fixed factor and ‘study id’ as a random factor was used. this second mixed-model was run separately for each moderator variable under study. levels of significance for meta-regressions were adjusted and corrected with the truncated product method for combining p-values. publication bias was first evaluated by conducting a visual inspection of the funnel plot to identify asymmetrical distributions and heterogeneity. asymmetry of effect sizes was tested using the variance of effect size “vi” as a moderator in the meta-analysis model. overall, 65% of the effect sizes were not significant, indicating that publication bias was unlikely in the meta-analysis. this approach was completed using rosenberg's fail-safe number, which yielded the number of studies with an effect size of zero that would need to be included to overturn the result. the rosenberg's fail-safe number for each model was on average 6256 (657 times the number of observations), indicating that the results are robust. however, 3 models (1.7% of the total number of models) presented effect size distribution asymmetry and a rosenberg's fail-safe number corresponding to less than 3 times the number of observations collected in this meta-analysis (pesticide biocide-mi model, rosenberg's number = 20; pesticide nematicide-si model, rosenberg's number = 14; agricultural system conventional-mi model, rosenberg's number = 161). the effect sizes of these models were not interpreted.
background: Agricultural practices significantly affect soil biodiversity and functions, altering biogeochemical cycles and potentially compromising food production. Increased employment of sustainable agricultural practices is of growing policy concern and requires a better understanding and quantification of how agriculture affects soil functioning.
objective: the study aimed to quantify the impact of a set of agricultural practices (tillage, pesticides use, fertilization, manipulation of above-ground plant including cover crop, rotation and agricultural system shift i.e. the conversion from the conventional to conservation or organic agriculture systems) on soil nematode communities using meta-analysis modeling. the results related to the effects of tillage are reported here.
result1: the absolute abundance of omnivore-predators was significantly reduced by conventional tillage (-14.4%), especially when the initial nematode abundance was high.
result2: the maturity and structure of the nematode community were reduced by tillage (-15.1% and -26.2%, respectively) while bf and fungal-feeder nematodes (ff) were not significantly impacted by tillage.
result3: the effects of conventional and conservation tillage (any tillage) on soil nematode were similar except for the abundance of omnivore-predators and si.
result4: conservation or organic agricultural systems improved nematode abundance, irrespective of trophic groups. conservation agriculture significantly improved the total abundance of nematodes (+96%) and the absolute abundance of fungal feeders (+54.9%), omnivore-predators (+237.2%) and plant feeders. bacterial feeders were also more abundant under conservation agriculture than under conventional agriculture (+126%). beyond this increase in abundance, conservation agriculture also improved taxonomic richness (+16.3%), shannon diversity (+10.2%) and the enrichment index (+28.4%).
result5: the positive effect of conservation agriculture on the abundance of omnivore-predators was more pronounced in regions with high mean annual precipitation.
general_conclusion: the absolute abundance of omnivore-predators was significantly higher when no-tillage was performed. taxonomic richness, maturity index, and plant-parasite indices of nematode communities were reduced by tillage. other metrics were not significantly impacted by tillage.
knowledge_gaps: these findings are dependent on the current limits of soil nematology, in particular (i) the possible lack of consideration of rare taxa due to the low number of individuals identified per soil sample, (ii) the low resolution of the taxonomic assignment (genus or family) which can lead to underestimating taxonomic richness, or (iii) the low consideration of the functional traits that may better capture the ecological strategies of nematodes. the global pattern was mainly influenced by the three geological areas (asia, europe and america) and thus may not represent fully the worldwide pattern, corroborating limitations for global soil nematode samples distribution. consequently, the number of studies for certain practices and types of agricultural systems may appear to be relatively low compared to the total studies published on these issues.

search_strategy: web of science, the china national knowledge infrastructure (http://www.cnki.net/) and google scholar (https://scholar.google.com/) were used to search for articles. the search terms were ‘no-till*’ or ‘zero-till*’ and ‘microbial community’ or ‘bacterial community’ or ‘fungal community’.
