result1: substitution of mineral fertilizers with organic fertilizer significantly increased soil organic carbon sequestration rate by 925 kg c ha−1 yr−1.
result2: soil organic carbon sequestration rate showed an increasing trend due to the substitution of mineral fertilization with organic fertilizers as the fertilization rate increased.
general_conclusion: organic fertiliser substitution significantly promoted soil organic carbon sequestration.

search_strategy: we collected data from relevant peer-reviewed publications. the publications were identified using the online database isi web of science, within the period 1997–2017. publications were searched using the keywords “organic amendment” and the results were refined using additional words—“long-term”, “yield”, “manure”, “compost”, “olsen p”, and “microbial biomass”. additionally, articles cited in review papers which had analysed data from long-term agricultural studies (≥ 10 years)  were also included in the dataset.
selection_criteria: 1) studies that reported crop yield, soil organic carbon, microbial biomass (mb) and/or plant-available p data for at least two types of treatments: (a) those that did not receive any fertiliser (‘nil control’); or (b) those where only inorganic npk fertiliser (if, ‘standard control’) was applied, and (c) where organic amendments (oa) with or without supplemental if was used. we defined oa as raw or composted materials derived from animals (e.g., manure), plant (e.g., straw) and municipal waste (e.g., sludge). the standard control did not always receive equivalent nutrient rates to those in oa and oa + if treatments; 2) crop yield data were included only for wheat, barley, corn, and rice grain in order to minimise differences in nutrient needs and rooting systems.
data_analysis: the meta-analysis was performed according to hedges et al. (1999) and cayuela et al. (2014) using metawin 2.0 software. the effect sizes (responses) of soil oc, mb, and olsen p were calculated  using a categorical random effects model, where the effect size is weighted by the inverse of the variance.
background: In recent years there has been a renewed interest in using organic amendments (OA) to agricultural soils as partial or full substitutes for inorganic fertilisers (IF) in order to manage nutrients more cost effectively, decrease our dependence on non-renewable resources (for example, P from phosphate rock), reduce and recycle waste that would otherwise be disposed to landfill, and increase soil organic matter.
objective: the present work aims to investigate the effect of oa and oa + if additions on soil nutrient fertility by carrying out a meta-analysis based on results from 132 long-lasting fertility trials (≥ 10 years) worldwide. in this study, the responses of crop yield—along with those of soil organic carbon (oc), size of mb, and plant-available p (i.e., olsen p)—to oa and oa + if relative to if alone (standard control) and no fertilisation (nil control) are determined. here results of the effect of oa and oa + if additions on crop yield are reported.
result1: the change in yield relative to the standard control was only significant (p < 0.05) for yield at the end of experiment (yieldf), with a mean increase of 5.3 ± 5.1% (bootstrap ci 95%); the yield during the experiment (yiledm) during the experiment was 0.4 ± 2.4% (bootstrap ci 95%).
result2: despite the lack of mean yieldm response of oa and oa + mf when compared with the standard control, some categorical variables had a significant influence on yieldm. precisely, the addition of oa and oa + if caused > 10% decrease in mean yieldm when biosolids was used as oa; likewise, when the oa was added to a soil in which barley was grown.
result3: results showed that the addition of oa without mf had a significant negative effect on yieldm, with a mean effect size of − 7.7 ± 4.6% (bootstrap ci 95%).
result4: the tenuous mean yieldf response to the addition of oa and oa + mf compared to the standard control was mostly associated with specific categorical variables.
result5: at low initial soil concentrations for these three categorical variables relative yieldf increases were between 24 and 28%, whereas the rest of groups within these variables had little influence, with increases < 6%, if  existent. other categorical variables for which there was a mean yieldf  increase > 10% were tropical climate, sandy texture, an initial soil ph between 6.6 and 7.3, the use of straw as oa, and a n application rate at 100–200 kg ha−1 year−1 along with that of oa.
general_conclusion: the overall effect of oa alone on yield was significant when compared with the nil control (no fertilisation), but not when compared with the standard control (inorganic fertilisation). only when oa and mineral fertilisers were added to soils that met specific conditions (low initial fertility, sandy texture, near-neutral ph values, under tropical climate) they rendered a significantly greater yieldf than the corresponding standard controls.

search_strategy: publications were searched for in the isi web of science database over the 1997–2016 period using the following key words: “vermicompost” and “primary production” or “plant growth” or “plant production” or “grain yield” or “plant biomass” or “aboveground biomass” or “belowground biomass” or “plant yield” or “role of vermicompost” or “influence ofvermicompost” or “poten- tial effect of vermicompost.” the same search was also performed for the 1997–2010 period, using the scopus database.
selection_criteria: 1) the presence of a mean value for both a vermicompost (vc) treatment and a control soil without vermicompost (c) for root, shoot, or total biomass values, shoot–root ratio, or commercial yield; 2) the number of replicates for each treatment; 3) a parameter describing the deviation around the average value (variance, standard deviation, or standard error)
data_analysis: meta-analysis using metawin 2.0 software. the effect size on plant commercial yield, aboveground biomass, belowground biomass, and total biomass were calculated. to compute the mean effect size, each individual effect size was weighted with the reciprocal of the sum of the within-study variance and the estimate of the between-study variance. mean effect sizes of the subgroups defined by different modalities of co-variables (e.g., plant type, variation in the soil fertility, use ofa fertilizer, climatic conditions) were compared using a random effects model. the pooled variance estimate for all subgroup analyses was used. subgroups were compared using a q test of heterogeneity, where the measure of heterogeneity was cochran’s q, calculated as the weighted sum of the squared differences between individual study effects and the pooled effect across studies. only variables with a sufficient number of observations in each subgroup (n >10) were considered.
background: Vermicomposting is an interesting solution for both recycling the increasing amount of organic waste and reducing the use of fertilizers. Moreover, the large-scale use of composts is a good way to increase the soil content in organic matter. Many studies have evaluated the effect of vermicompost on plant growth, but a quantitative summary of these studies is still missing.
objective: to assess the mean impact of vermicompost on plant aboveground and belowground biomass production; i.e. 1) root, 2) shoot, or 3) total biomass and 4) commercial yield. and to determine the influence of different factors on the size ofthe vermicompost effect, such as the proportion of vermicompost in the growth medium, the type of experiment (field, greenhouse, climatic chamber), the addition of a mineral fertilizer, the use of a standard culture medium (metro-mix 360), the type oforganic matter from which vermicompost was obtained (green waste, urban waste, cattle manure…) and plant functional type (herb, grass, tree, legume). here, only results for commercial yield production are reported.
result1: plant yield increased by 26% with the addition of vermicompost to the soil.
result2: the original material that provided the highest effect size of vermicompost was cattle manure, with an increase of 27% in yield.
result3: mineral fertilization decreased the positive effect of vermicompost addition from 38 to 14% for the commercial yield.
result4: the addition of vermicompost had a positive effect on the commercial yield of all plant families present in our database with the strongest effect on lamiaceae (n = 21, + 31%), solanaceae (n = 34, + 28%), and poaceae (n =50, + 15%).
result5: there was a general positive effect of the addition of vermicompost on commercial yield whatever the functional group.
general_conclusion: overall, this study provides synthetic information on the beneficial effects of vermicompost for increasing crop yield, which could help bring waste management and agriculture together towards a society with a more circular economy.

search_strategy: literature searches were conducted in scopus, targeting peer reviewed articles published online through july 2019. to obtain the papers listed, the authors used the keywords “almond or olive or citrus or vineyard or grapevine or orchard”, “and” combinations of the following items: “mediterranean climate”, “cover crop”, “intercropping”, “alley crop”, “multicrop”, “agroforestry”, “crop yield” and “soil”.
selection_criteria: 1) laboratory or greenhouse studies were excluded, and only studies performed in field conditions and carried out in a mediterranean climate were chosen; 2) when several papers included data from the same experiment, the longest study with the most soil and crop variables was chosen.
data_analysis: the authors decided to weight observations using the sample sizes to ensure statistical significance by keeping a sufficient sample size: studies with larger sample sizes were weighted higher during aggregation. for the uncertainty analysis, we reported the means and 95% confidence intervals (cis). the cis were constructed by non-parametric bootstrapping (nboot = 10 000). the bootstrapping was only carried out for treatments with n ≥ 8, as the bootstrap is unreliable when the sample size is too small. the effect of treatment was considered as significant if the 95% bootstrap ci did not overlap with zero.
background: Perennial crops, such as almond, olive, citrus or grapevines, represent ∼16% of the agroecosystems in the Mediterranean area, with great economic importance. Intensive tree cultivation in Mediterranean soils frequently causes land degradation by depletion of soil organic matter (SOM), erosion, and also, under irrigation farming, soil and water pollution.
objective: to assess the implication of fertilization in mediterranean orchards on soil nutrients, soil organic carbon and crop yield. here, results on crop yields are reported.
result1: the use of organic fertilizers did not significantly affect yield, however with 67% of studies showing a positive effect, compared to inorganic fertilizers. these results indicate that most studies showed positive effects of organic fertilization compared to inorganic fertilization.
result2: NA
general_conclusion: organic fertilisers had no significant effects on crop yields, compared to conventional systems.

search_strategy: papers were derived from the web of science.
selection_criteria: 1) field experiments were conducted for more than than 10 years. thus, those field experiments conducted less than 10 years and laboratory incubation studies were excluded; 2) chemical fertilizer treatment was n, p, k balanced application. thus the treatments of n or p or k application alone were not included in the data compilation; 3) gross rates of soil n transformations were measured using 15n pool dilution technique and 15 n tracing model; 4) no fertilizer application treatment was used as the control.
data_analysis: effect size for the response of variables gross rates of n transformations, soil properties, and crop yield were weighted and the variance of the natural log of the response ratio was calculated from the sample sizes and the standard deviations for the control and fertilization treatments. a fixed-effect model was used in our meta-analysis to determine whether long-term fertilization had a significant effect on the studied variables using metawin 2.1 software. 95% confidence intervals (ci) of the weighted effect size were generated using bootstrap resampling procedure with 9999 iterations.
background: Appropriate fertilizer managements are required to enhance crop yield, improve soil fertility, while minimize negative environmental impacts. It is important to take into account the effects of long-term organic or chemical fertilizer applications on gross rates of soil N transformations, which can provide an understanding of N dynamics in the different N fertilizer managements and help to optimize N fertilizer management.
objective: to explore if there is a general pattern of fertilizer application effects on gross rates of soil n transformations, to identify the mechanisms of fertilizer applications affecting soil n transformations, and to propose the appropriate fertilizer management for agricultural production. here the results for the effect of organic fertilization application on crop yield are reported.
result1: the response of crop yield to long-term fertilizer application was the highest in organic fertilizer only treatments, which was significantly higher than combination of organic and chemical fertilizers treatments.
result2: NA
general_conclusion: organic fertiliser alone or combination of organic and chemical fertiliser could not only improve crop yield, but also increase soil fertility and reduce the n losses potential.
knowledge_gaps: other factors, such as soil type, cropping system, and climate, also probably affected the response of soil gross n transformation rates to long-term fertilization. however, the authors did not discuss these aspects due to the limited number of data in the present study. in further studies, above-mentioned aspects should be investigated to comprehensively clarify the mechanisms of the effects of fertilization on soil n transformations.

search_strategy: a literature search was conducted using isi web of science and google scholar databases. keywords ‘salix’ or ‘willow’ in combination with ‘fertilization’, ‘biomass’, or ‘nitrogen’.
selection_criteria: 1) only field-based studies were considered, excluding greenhouse or pot studies; 2) a fertilized treatment was directly compared to a control (unfertilized); 3) the amount of n in fertilizer (organic or synthetic) was explicitly stated; 4) species of shrub willow or bred cultivars with pedigree was clearly stated; 5) studies involving contaminated soils or phytoremediation studies were avoided; 6) studies conducted in the context of soil remediation were avoided; 7) studies investigating the effects of sewage sludge or municipal wastewater treatments on growth were included, however, treatments involving contaminated or toxic waste streams were not used; 8) only studies published in english were considered.
data_analysis: as only 41% of the collected observations had some measure of error reported, alternative weights were applied based on within-study replication, giving more weight to studies with larger sample sizes. the use of these alternative weights coupled with a resampling procedure to bootstrap confidence intervals for the effect size estimates resulted in a nonparametric approach to estimating differences between group mean effect sizes. the mean effect size of fertilization is calculated as the sum of the weighted, transformed response ratios divided by the sum of the weights. observations were also grouped by categorical variables such as source of n fertilizer and effect sizes for each group were calculated as above. bootstrapping was performed to obtain 95% ci using 4000 iterations for the mean effect for groups of observations based on classification variables using the proc surveyselect procedure in sas software version 9.4.
background: Second-generation lignocellulosic bioenergy crops such as short rotation coppice willow are often presented as a lower input, less intensive alternative for providing the feedstocks needed for biofuel production compared to first-generation crops. Assumptions about low nutrient demand in lignocellulosic crops have led to the expectation that very little or no fertilizer N will be needed which can greatly impact GHG emissions. When nutrient demand of shrub willow for biomass production is addressed in the literature, conflicting or contradictory statements can be found.
objective: this literature review has three main objectives: (1) compile and compare specific n fertilizer recommendations in the peer-reviewed literature and from published growers’ guidelines; (2) summarize data from the peer- reviewed literature to quantify variability in above- ground biomass n pools and n export rates; and (3) use meta-analytic techniques to explore potential differences in yield response to n fertilization across various categorical factors among studies. here we focus on objective 3), specifically on the effect of organic fertilization on yields.
result1: the different organic fertilization categories showed a yield increase over the unfertilized control treatment, with all categories (animal manures, municipal sludge, composted sludge, and irrigation with municipal wastewater) having a significant effect.
result2: organic fertilizer sources from treated municipal wastes, sludges, or wastewater had a strong positive response on yields.
general_conclusion: overall, this quantitative review has shown that fertilisation of willow can substantially improve yields. important factors have been identified that can influence yield response, including willow species or species hybrids, fertiliser source, the age of above- ground biomass at harvest, growing climate, and the unfertilised yield potential of a particular location.

search_strategy: a literature search was conducted using web of science to find studies reporting a direct comparison between swine manure and synthetic n fertiliser in crop yield and/or n2o emissions. search terms included: “swine,” “pig,” “hog,” “manure,” “slurry,” “effluent,” “commercial,” “synthetic,” “mineral,” “urea,” “fertilizer,” “crop yield,” “fertilization,” and “production.” the search included only peer reviewed articles published before 1 june 2018.
selection_criteria: 1) replicated experimental design in field conditions; 2) comparisons made within the same cropping and management system; 3) no extreme conditions, such as flooding or major pest damage, occurred during the experiment; 4) only studies with approximately the same amount of plant-available n supplied from the fertiliser.
data_analysis: a random-effect meta-analysis model was applied assuming the effect sizes in the dataset are not intrinsically associated with each study. the random-effects model was applied separately for crop yield and n2o emissions, as well as each moderator variable.
background: Swine manure has potential for reuse as fertilizer on cropland and pastureland. Currently, producers may be hesitant to land apply swine manure because information regarding the impacts to crop production and environmental quality has been inconsistent.
objective: compare the effects of swine manure and synthetic fertilizer on both a measure of production, crop yield and a measure of environmental quality, nitrous oxide (n2o) emissions. here, the impact of swine manure on crop yield is reported.
result1: swine manure application reduced crop yields by 2.8% compared with synthetic n but was not statistically different (p = 0.08).
result2: NA
general_conclusion: the overall effect of swine manure application on crop yield is not significant.

search_strategy: a literature search was conducted using the scopus search engine, with search terms including “organic fertilizer,” “manure,” “compost,” or “meal,” and “yield” in the article title. the search was limited from 1980 through 16 july 2015 and returned 960 matches.
selection_criteria: 1) a non‐fertilized control (e.g., no synthetic fertilizer or organic amendment; this was the most common factor excluding studies from meta‐analysis because most studies compared organic amendments to n–p–k fertilized plots at rates typical for a specific crop and region, without including a non‐fertilized control); 2) at least one sole organic amendment treatment (e.g., no integration of synthetic fertilizer and organic amendment) to compare with the non‐fertilized control; 3) studies were also excluded if they were not published in the english language; 4) if they contained confounding experimental treatments (e.g., effect of compost on diseased crops); 5) did not include field‐based results (e.g., greenhouse or pot studies).
data_analysis: a hierarchical random‐effects model was fit to the data using the “metafor” package (r v. 3.1.3) with study considered as a grouping factor to account for studies containing several observations. in general, slight changes to mean effect sizes but not confidence intervals were observed using this approach compared to the non‐parametric bootstrapping method, which did not influence the conclusions of the study. non‐parametric bootstrap ci (95%) were calculated for mean response ratios of interest (i.e., crop type, amendment type and rate, soil organic matter content and texture, irrigation, and aridity index) using a first‐order normal approximation and 4999 iterations (“boot” package; r v. 3.1.3).
background: Organic soil amendments are increasingly promoted as a sustainable alternative to synthetic fertilizers and as a tool for building soil quality through improved chemical, physical, and biological properties. However, short‐term yield response to organic amendments is highly variable.
objective: 1) to develop a global estimate of first‐season crop yield response to organic amendments, and 2) to determine the effect of crop type, amendment characteristics, soil properties, cultural practices, and climate on the magnitude of this yield response.
result1: averaged across all studies, locations, crops, and amendment types and rates, crop yield increased by an average of 43±7% in the first season following organic amendment. organic amendments increased crop yield the first season after application in 96% of cases.
result2: NA
general_conclusion: organic amendment significantly increases crop yields, as compared to non- fertilised controls.

search_strategy: a comprehensive literature review was conducted using the isi web of science search tool with the search terms “poultry litter” for published data up to march 2016, yielding more than 6000 articles. a search of these records using the term “yield” resulted in 498 articles.
selection_criteria: 1) replicated experimental design (≥3 replications); 2) clear description of soil and poultry litter (pl) used; 3) have at least one pl treatment and is comparable against an inorganic fertilizer (if) treatment; 4) data containing means and standard deviation (or standard error).
data_analysis: estimation of weighted mean effect size using a random effect model. sensitivity analysis was conducted to test how robust the results are to the decisions and assumptions made in the analysis; therefore, leave-one-out sensitivity analysis was performed by iteratively removing one observation at a time to confirm that the findings were not driven by any single study. publication bias was analyzed.
background: Research has shown that poultry litter (PL) can be used as a nutrient source for crop production. However, yield responses often varied when compared with inorganic fertilizer (IF) depending on soil type, management conditions, and PL application practices.
objective: the objectives of this review were to: (i) use meta-analytic methods to summarize and quantitatively describe the effects of pl on crop production; (ii) compare crop yield with pl application to that of standard fertilization practices using if; and (iii) examine the effect of variables (e.g., repeated pl applications, tillage system, soil texture, time of pl application, as well as the application method) that were included in this ma to explain the variability of the response to crop productivity.
result1: overall, the average yield of all crops where pl was applied tended to have equal or slightly lower yields compared to when if was applied.
result2: no evidence of publication bias.
general_conclusion: overall, poultry litter application (pl) was comparable to mineral fertilisation. the efficacy of pl to benefit crop productivity is influenced by the soil and agricultural management conditions.
knowledge_gaps: future work is warranted to explore associations between poultry litter additions and improvements in soil organic matter and soil fertility.

search_strategy: studies published before march 2020 were searched for in the microsoft academic, google scholar, baidu scholar, and china national knowledge infrastructure databases. search terms related to maize production, organic fertilizer substitution, manure application, and n and c emissions were combined.
selection_criteria: 1) studies focused on maize production with substitution of mineral fertilizer with organic fertilizer, including animal manure (47%), compost (37%), commercial organic fertilizer (e.g., industrially processed, standardized poultry or livestock manure; 9%), digestate (5%), slurry (2%); 2) the amounts of applied organic material and the n content were clearly specified; 3) the mineral fertilizer treatment and “substitution treatments” (partial or full substitution of chemical with organic fertilizer) had identical total n rates, and phosphorus (p) and potassium (k) inputs were not major factors limiting maize growth; 4) the n application rates for each treatment were reported to allow calculation of the fertilization rates, defined as organic n input/total n applied; 5) field or lysimeter study, with articles reporting data from the same experiment excluded; and 6) experimental duration of at least 3 years with respect to the effects of organic fertilizer on soil properties (e.g., soc).
data_analysis: effect sizes were weighted by the inverse of the sampling variance. for studies where neither the standard deviation nor standard error were reported, the approach of bracken was applied to estimate standard deviations using in the “metagear” r (ver. 3.6.1) package. a random-effect model was employed for the meta-analysis, generated using the “metafor” r package.
background: Organic fertilizer is an effective substitute for mineral fertilizer that improves crop yield and is environmentally friendly. However, the effects of substitution often vary due to complicated interactions among the organic fertilizer substitution rate, total nutrient supply, and type of cropping system used.
objective: to quantitatively assess the effects of substituting organic fertilizers for mineral fertilizers on maize production, n and c emissions, and the soil organic carbon sequestration rate (socsr). we also evaluated the global warming potential (gwp) and net global warming potential (ngwp), considering the indirect effects of nh3 emissions and runoff/leaching. the responses of these variables to organic fertilizer substitution were evaluated according to the fertilization rate (low, optimal, or high), substitution rates, and treatment duration. the underlying causes of the different responses of these variables to substitution of chemical with organic fertilizer are discussed. here, results on maize production are reported.
result1: substitution of mineral fertilizer with organic fertilizer significantly increased maize yield (by 4.23%).
result2: the effect of the substitution of mineral fertilization with organic fertilizers on maize yield tended to increase with increasing n fertilization rate. while the low fertilization rate did not significantly enhance maize yield, the optimal fertilization rate significantly increased maize yield. the high fertilization rate significantly increased maize yield (4.83%).
result3: when mineral fertilization was substituted with organiz fertilizers, the long-term application (≥3 years) of organic fertilizer significantly increased maize yield (by 11.5%), whereas short-term application (<3 years) did not affect maize yield.
general_conclusion: organic fertiliser substitution significantly enhanced maize yield. the yield and environmental benefits of organic fertiliser substitution were higher with a high fertilisation rate. long-term organic fertiliser substitution further increased maize yield compared with short-term application.

search_strategy: an exhaustive literature search of studies investigating n2o emissions from grain cropping systems was conducted with isi-web of science for articles published before june 2014. because the first search produced a limited numbers of papers for enhanced efficiency fertilizers, cover crops and diversified rotations, we conducted a second search focusing on these practices in december 2015 to increase the size of the database and enable meta-analysis of these practices.
selection_criteria: 1) only studies conducted in field conditions that were at least one growing season in duration were included; 2) the authors included cover crop studies that measured n2o emissions from cover crop growth periods, cash crop growth periods or both.
data_analysis: it was performed an unweighted meta-analysis because roughly more than half of the studies did not report a measure of variance. bias-corrected 95% confidence intervals (95% cis) were generated through a bootstrapping procedure in metawin 2.0 (5000 iterations). the effect sizes was explored with categorical variables such as soil texture, fertilizer rates and manure forms and continuous variables such as manure ph and manure c:n ratios to examine how specific management regimes impact n2o emissions.
background: Understanding how agricultural management practices impact nitrous oxide (N2O) emissions is prerequisite for developing mitigation protocols.
objective: an extensive analysis of all management practices was conducted to assess the full range of options currently available for n2o mitigation. the trade off between n2o mitigation and yield outcomes in grain cropping systems was quantified. here, only results regarding the effect of organic fertilisers on n2o emissions are reported.
result1: the manure treatment did not detect significant differences in area-scaled n2o emissions compared to the control.
result2: when all studies comparing manures to n fertilizer were included in the analysis, regardless of differences in n additions, the percent change for n2o emissions using manure instead of fertilizers averaged 12% with a range of-9 to 38% (bootstrapping 95% ci).
result3: the average n2o emission from the manure treatment group was 3.8 kg n2o-n ha-1 year-1 compared to 3.4 kg n2o-n ha-1year-1 for the inorganic fertilizer treatment group.
result4: however, in 8 out of 23 studies, n additions from manure were greater compared to those from n fertilizer. removal of these pairs resulted in average n2o emissions of 4.8 kg n2o-n ha-1year-1from inorganic fertilizers and 4.2 kg n2o-n ha-1year-1from manures. the average percent change for n2o emissions using manure instead of fertilizers shifted from 11 to -3% (bootstrapping 95% ci-13 to 8%) indicating that the level n inputs was a significant driver for the manure effect on n2o in the full dataset.
general_conclusion: increased n2o emissions from manures compared to n fertilisers can be attributed to greater n additions in manure treatments rather than the use of manures per se. however, manure and n fertiliser interact with soil texture differently suggesting that fine-tuning n management to reflect ecosystems state factors is a necessary next step in n2o mitigation.

search_strategy: a wide review was performed which included every paper containing data on n2o emissions in mediterranean agroecosystems. articles were consulted on the isi web of knowledge database by simultaneously typing the words “nitrous oxide” or “n2o”, “emission”, and either the word “mediterranean” or the name of a country with territory in areas with a mediterranean climate. this search based on keywords was complemented with a search through the literature cited in the articles found.
selection_criteria: 1) the dataset was further narrowed down by restricting the data used to pairwise comparisons of field emissions from organic and synthetic fertilizers in order to examine them meta-analytically. weighted meta-analysis requires information on variance and the number of replications of each treatment; studies that did not report these data were therefore also excluded. these pairwise comparisons represent experiments where synthetic and organic fertilizers are compared under similar agro-climatic conditions and application rates.
data_analysis: individual effect sizes were pooled together into a common effect size following a random effects model; this is appropriate for situations in which individual studies are not projected to share a common effect size. this weighted mean effect size and its related statistical parameters were calculated using comprehensive meta-analysis software. the weighted mean effect sizes and their variances were transformed back in the presentation of the results.
background: There has been an increasing amount of research into the effects of using different types of fertilization on N2O emissions under Mediterranean climatic conditions, but the findings have sometimes been rather contradictory. Available information also suggests that water management could exert a high influence on N2O emissions.
objective: 1) to compare and contrast direct n2o emissions from the application of organic and synthetic fertilizers, describing the influence of agricultural practices and environmental factors; 2) to get an overview of indirect n2o sources related to fertilizer use, both upstream and downstream of the cropping system; 3) to identify options for mitigating n2o emissions, and their respective drawbacks, through the application of organic fertilizers in these agroecosystems and to detect the main gaps in currently available information.
result1: significantly lower n2o emissions for organic as opposed to synthetic fertilizers (23% reduction). when organic materials were segregated in solid and liquid, only solid organic fertilizer emissions were significantly lower than those of synthetic fertilizers (28% reduction in cumulative emissions).
result2: the emission factor (ef) is similar to the ipcc factor in conventionally irrigated systems (0.98% n2o-n n applied−1), but one order of magnitude lower in rainfed systems (0.08%).
result3: when organic fertilizers are applied at similar n rates to synthetic fertilizers, they generally make smaller contributions to the leached no3− pool.
result4: the most promising practices for reducing n2o through organic fertilization include: (i) minimizing water applications; (ii) minimizing bare soil; (iii) improving waste management; and (iv) tightening n cycling through n immobilization.
result5: the mitigation potential may be limited by: (i) residual effect; (ii) the longterm effects of fertilizers on soil organic matter; (iii) lower yield-scaled performance; and (iv) total n availability from organic sources.
general_conclusion: the available information suggests a potential of organic fertilisers and water-saving practices to mitigate n2o emissions under mediterranean climatic conditions, although further research is needed before it can be regarded as fully proven, understood and developed.
knowledge_gaps: 1) insufficient sampling periods; 2) high background emissions; 3) the need to provide n2o ef and yield-scaled ef; 4) the need for more research on specific cropping systems; and 5) the need for full ghg balances.

search_strategy: a detailed review of literature was carried out until june 13, 2014 with scopus (1960–2014) and cab abstracts (1910–2014) research databases using the key words listed in tables s1 combined with boolean operators. it retrieved 1064 papers published in peer-reviewed journals.
selection_criteria: 1) n2o fluxes were measured from agricultural soils for at least 30 d (modelling outputs excluded, grazing pasture and paddy soils excluded); 2) unamended soils that received no fertilizer/amendment addition were used as control; 3) soils were amended with organic by-products with or without synthetic fertilizers; 4) information on chemical properties of amendments and application rates was available to estimate the relative contribution of the applied materials  (e.g., total n input) to cumulative n2o fluxes; 5) only field experiment data was retained and excluded experiments done under controlled conditions such as disturbed soil and undisturbed soil column incubations; 6) studies without spatial replication or no replicates reported were excluded from the analysis; 7) three studies against the selected 38 used micrometeorological instrumentation and were excluded because not in a relatively large number to adequately sub-group the meta-analysis considering methodological aspects in n2o measurements.
data_analysis: meta-analysis was performed with the residual maximum likelihood (reml) approach which is appropriate for analysis of global meta-data related to soil n2o emissions and emission factors (efs). a linear mixed-effects model was performed using the “proc mixed” procedure of the sas software, version 9.2. the fertilizer type variable (ferticlass) was the fixed-effect component of the model. the unique study and site identifiers (idstudy, idsite), as well as ferticlass or fertitype, appeared in the random-effect component to account for the dependency of several effect sizes reported in the same study.
background: The variability in EF of agricultural soils receiving organic amendments (OAs) warrants more investigation to determine how key factors, such as the OA type and its properties, soil and climate conditions, modulate the EF responsible for soil N2O emissions.
objective: the aim of this study was to provide a comprehensive and quantitative analysis of a dataset containing 422 efs reported in 38 studies that measured soil n2o emissions after organic amendments addition in perennial and annual cropping systems.
result1: we propose a global emission factor for organic inputs of 0.57 ± 0.3% of n applied.
result2: emission factors were 2.8 times greater in fine- than in coarse-textured soils.
result3: the ipcc ef1 value was too high when considering the n2o contribution from agricultural soils amended with composts, but too low to represent the ef of n2o in agricultural soils receiving liquid manure (mostly pig slurry) combined with synthetic fertilizers.
general_conclusion: the analysis yielded a global emission factor (ef) for all organic sources, eforg, equal to 0.57% +-0.30%, i.e.; emissions are higher than when no fertilisation is applied.

search_strategy: an exhaustive literature survey of peer-reviewed publications was carried out using isi-web of science and google scholar for articles published before august 2011.
selection_criteria: 1) n2o and/or ch4 fluxes must have been measured under field conditions for the entire growing season (i.e. planting to harvest); 2) seasonal fluxes and the number of field replications had to be reported for both control and treatment plots; 3) growing conditions in the control and treatment plots had to be identical (except for the management practice being studied); 4) exact fertilizer n rates needed to be reported and the green manure treatment received the same total n rate as the control treatment.
data_analysis: studies were weighted by replication. they authors used metawin 2.1 to generate mean effect sizes and 95% bootstrapped cis (4999 iterations). to ease interpretation, the results for the analyses on ln r were back-transformed and reported as percentage change under management treatment in question relative to the control situation. treatment effects were considered significant if the 95% ci did not overlap with zero, and marginally significant if the 90% ci did not overlap with zero.
background: Flooded rice systems emit both methane (CH4) and nitrous oxide (N2O). Elevated CH4 emissions in rice systems can lead to a high global warming potential (GWP) relative to other crops, thus strategies to reduce greenhouse (GHG) emissions, particularly CH4, are needed. Altering water, residue (carbon) and fertilizer management practices are commonly suggested as options for mitigating GHG emissions in rice systems. While the effects of water and residue management have been reported on elsewhere, the impact of fertilizer management on GHG emissions has not been reviewed quantitatively.
objective: the objective was to analyze the peer reviewed literature to determine and quantify the effects of fertilizer management options on ghg emissions from rice systems in order to determine potential mitigation strategies for rice systems. the authors focused on the following areas: n management (rate, source, placement), the use of enhanced-efficiency n fertilizers (eenf), sulfate inputs, farmyard manure (fym) and green manure (grm). here, only results regarding the effect of farmyard manure on ghg emissions are reported.
result1: fym forming all or part of the total n rate increased ch4 emissions by 26% (95% ci: 12–47%) when compared to a treatment receiving only urea n at the same total n rate.
result2: this is important as the handling and processing of fym has been shown to strongly affect ch4 emissions.
result3: only three studies (6 observations) have evaluated the effect of fym on n2o emissions in rice systems through side-by-side comparisons. in these studies fym-n represented 25–100% of the total n rate. the authors found no significant effect on n2o emissions when fym was used instead of mineral n fertilizer.
general_conclusion: farmyard manure increased ch4 emissions by 26%, while it didn't have a significant impact on n2o emissions.
knowledge_gaps: since fym is an important input for many rice systems, a better understanding of how fym source, processing and application can affect ghg emissions is needed.

search_strategy: a systematic literature search approach into the search engines of google scholar, scopus, and web of science to identify relevant research articles for inclusion in the meta-analysis, to a cut-off date of december 31, 2019. the keywords ‘manure’ ‘animal manure’ ‘pig’ ‘swine’ ‘cattle’ ‘dairy’ ‘poultry’ ‘carbon dioxide or co2’ ‘methane or ch4’ and ‘nitrous oxide or n2o’ were used to search the publications.
selection_criteria: 1) experiments who had at least one pair of data (control and treatment) and calculated cumulative co2, ch4, and/or n2o emission fluxes; 2) clearly described experimental method with crop type and duration, and physiochemical properties of soil.
data_analysis: a random-effects meta-analysis model was used to examine the dataset. metawin 2.1 and openmee software were used to calculate the mean effect sizes of the dataset and 95% bootstrapped confidence intervals (cis) were generated using 4999 iterations. statistical results such as total heterogeneity (qt) in effect sizes among studies were also calculated using openmee software.
background: Globally, greenhouse gases (GHGs) emissions especially carbon dioxide (CO2), methane (CH4) and nitrous oxide (N2O) from the agricultural sector are increasing due to anthropogenic activities. Although, the application of animal manure to the agricultural soil as an organic fertiliser not only improves soil health and agricultural production but also has a significant impact on GHGs emissions, but the extent of GHGs emissions in response to manure application under diverse environmental conditions is still uncertain.
objective: the authors systematically compared the ghgs emissions of the soil under different animal manures, the quantity of manure, climate zone, soil ph, water filled pore space (wfps), soil texture, crop type, and crop duration.
result1: ch4 emissions were significantly increased by different types of manures (poultry, pig, cattle or n fertilisers) (lnrr = 2.31, 95%ci = 1.161 to 3.481) and different rates of manure application (lnrr = 1.495, 95%ci = 1.135 to 1.855). according to this meta-analysis, the application of poultry manure (lnrr = 2.605, 95%ci = 2.979 to 3.23) had higher impact on ch4 emissions compared to pig (lnrr = 1.248, 95%ci = 1.212 to 1.284), n fertilisers (lnrr = 1.2, 95%ci = 1.144 to 1.257) and cattle (lnrr = 0.741, 95%ci = 0.703 to 0.779) manure. manure at the rate of >320 kg n / ha (lnrr = 1.665, 95%ci = 1.609 to 1.7) or <120 kg n / ha (lnrr = 1.65, 95%ci = 1.578 to 1.723) had the maximum effect on ch4 compared to intermediate rate (lnrr = 1.182. , 95%ci = 1.156 to 1.209).
result2: n2o emissions were increased by different types of manures (poultry, pig, cattle or n fertilisers) (lnrr = 1.123, 95%ci = 1.004 to 1.241) and different manure application rates (lnrr = 0.862, 95% ci = 0.035 to 1.69). higher effect of manure was detected under higher rates of manure, i.e. > 320 kg n / ha (lnrr = 1.701, 95%ci = 1.603 to 1.799), compared to intermediate (lnrr = 0.308, 95%ci = 0.289 to 0.328) and lower (lnrr = 0.579, 95%ci = 0.475 to 0.684) application rates.
general_conclusion: the application of animal manure and n-mineral fertiliser significantly increased ch4 and n2o emission as compared to control treatment from soils.

search_strategy: peer-reviewed articles that reported n2o emission following manure application in field trials were searched in the web of science. literature prior to december 2017 with ‘manure’, ‘field’,and ‘n2o/nitrous oxide emission’ present in the title, keyword or abstract was collected.
selection_criteria: 1) studies were performed by field trial and with at least 3 replicates; 2) studies reported soil n2o emissions in both manure applied treatments and non-manure controls; and 3) at least one crop season was included at the same experimental site. if multiple growing seasons were available, each grow- ing season was considered as a separate observation. if multiple crops were cultivated at different periods in the same experimental site, each crop type was considered as one observation, as crop type contrib- utes greatly to changes in soil properties. if an experimental site included multiple measurements of n2o emission, only the final time point was chosen for this meta-analysis. when a treatment was applied as a mixed manure plus mineral fertilizer, the comparison was considered as one observation only if another treatment with the same mineral fertilizer application was set up as a control.
data_analysis: for studies not reporting the standard deviation, a value of 29.2% was assigned for n2o emission, which was the average value for the standard deviation in the dataset. metawin 2.1 software was used to calculate cumulative effect size using a random-effects model and weighted resampling method. the 95% confidence intervals (cis) were generated in metawin using a bootstrapping procedure with 4999 iterations. the cumulative effect size was significantly positive or negative at p < 0.05 if the 95% confidence interval did not overlap with zero.
background: The response of soil nitrous oxide (N2O) emission to manure application has been widely reported for laboratory experiments. However, the in-situ effects ofmanure application on soil N2O emission from field trials (i.e. real- world conditions) and related mechanisms are poorly understood at the global scale.
objective: 1) to investigate how manure application influences soil n2o emission fluxes and emission factors in field trials and to elucidate potential regulating mechanisms; and 2) identify important factors related to soil properties, manure characteristics and agricultural practices that regulate n2o emission fluxes following manure application. results from this study provide a scientific basis for developing strategies to mitigate soil n2o emission associated with manure application.
result1: manure application caused a significant increase in soil n2o emission (lnr = 1.03, 95% ci: 0.90–1.15), regardless of manure sources, n content, c content and c:n ratio. the overall n2o emission factor was 1.13% (of total n in manure) and higher than zero across all comparisons.
result2: the increase in n2o emission from raw manure (lnr = 1.31) was significantly higher than pre-treated manure (lnr = 0.84) (p < .05).
result3: manures with n contents of 5–20 g kg−1 resulted in lower n2o emission (lnr = 0.88) compared to manures with n content of ≤5 g kg−1 (lnr = 1.05) and > 20 g kg−1 (lnr = 1.38) (p < 0.05). the absolute emission factor increased as manure n content increased.
result4: manures with c content of 100–300 g kg−1 had significantly lower n2o emission (lnr = 0.69) compared to manures with c contents of <100 g kg−1 (lnr = 1.22) and > 300 g kg−1 (lnr = 1.74) (p < 0.05).
result5: manures with c:n ratio of 10–15 (lnr = 0.57) had lower n2o emission than manures with c:n of ≤5 (lnr = 1.17), 5–10 (lnr = 1.16) and 15–20 (lnr = 1.57) (p < 0.05).
general_conclusion: manure application increased soil n2o emission with emissions being affected by climate, agricultural practices, manure characteristics and some initial soil properties. compared with synthetic n fertilisers, manure application induced a similar net n2o emission, supporting the use of manure to achieve several beneficial effects, such as enhancement of soil nutrient levels, c sequestration, and soil physical properties. authors recommend application of pre-treated (i.e. composted or digested) manures with c:n ratios of 10–15 and c contents of 100–300 g c kg−1 to agricultural soils, to minimize n2o emission.

search_strategy: a systematic selection and review of all peer-reviewed scientific papers relevant to the objective of this study published till december 2019 was conducted, avoiding any publication bias by way of study or research group, regional focus, period of publication or crop attributes. the selection was made using isi-web of science, google scholar and the china knowledge resource integrated database (cnki) following the principles of i) identification of search terms based on key words used in relevant literature, ii) formulation of screening criteria, iii) data extraction, processing, and quality assessment and iv) data analysis using appropriate datasets. the keywords ‘nitrogen’, ‘nitrous oxide’, ‘n2o’, ‘emission factor’ and ‘sugarcane’, and their combinations were used for searching publications.
selection_criteria: 1) reports with soil n2o emissions measured for at least six months during the crop cycle from field-grown crops rather than in pots or soil columns; 2) studies with n2o emissions reported include both with and without n fertiliser treatments; 3) maximum n fertiliser use should be 600 kg n ha−1 yr−1, as rates of n above this level are seen only occasionally in commercial sugarcane production; 4) studies with replication; 5) n2o emissions were measured with manually operated or automatic chambers.
data_analysis: the robustness of the meta-analysis was determined by a sensitivity analysis of n2o emission response ratio (rr), which is the effect of applied fertiliser on n2o emissions. the authors performed two different procedures to maximise the robustness of meta-analysis: 1) a resampling procedure of bootstrapping (5000 iterations) to calculate means and 95% confidence intervals (ci) by spss 21.0; 2) the non-parametric procedure of kruskal-wallis one-way anova method with spss 21.0 to evaluate treatment effect for each category, and significance difference at a 5% level of probably.
background: Sugarcane is the second largest bioenergy crop in the world and it accounts for 80% of global sugar production. Grown mostly in wet and warm tropics with relatively high nitrogen (N) fertiliser input and crop residue retention, sugarcane production is a significant source of nitrous oxide (N2O) emission. Yet, a global evaluation of research on N2O emission from sugarcane crop is lacking.
objective: 1) to gain a better understanding of n2o emission in different sugarcane production systems by a quantitative analysis of all reported sugarcane n2o emission studies that meet the research and data quality criteria set in this study; 2) estimate the global sugarcane n2o emission factor (ef) based on the information published till dec 2019; and 3) determine crop production conditions that regulate n2o emission and identify factors or practices that help reduce n2o emission from sugarcane crop.
result1: the mean emission factors for organic amendments and synthetic fertilisers plus organic amendments were 1.19% (ci: 0.536–1.95), and 2.47% (ci: 1.79–3.15), respectively. use of combined synthetic fertilisers and organic amendments increased total and fertiliser-induced n2o emissions and ef by 63.0%, 169% and 127%, respectively, compared to the increases for sn application.
result2: among the different n fertiliser types used, sn + oa contributed the highest mean total n2o emissions (3.88; ci: 2.95–4.85 kg n2o-n ha−1 yr−1) followed by sn (2.38; ci: 1.92–2.87), eef (1.46; ci: 1.08–1.89) and oa (1.03; ci: 0.566–1.59).
general_conclusion: supplementing synthetic n fertiliser (sn) with organic amendments (oa) significantly increased mean n2o emission (~1.4-fold) and emission factor (~2.5-fold).
knowledge_gaps: more research is warranted to exploit the promising leads of eefs to improve sugarcane nue, soil health and environmental sustainability. gain a better understanding of the impact of organic amendments on n2o emission and soil health and use that knowledge to guide development of eef formulations and utilisation of mill by-products and other organic amendments.

search_strategy: papers were derived from the web of science.
selection_criteria: 1) field experiments were conducted for more than than 10 years. thus, those field experiments conducted less than 10 years and laboratory incubation studies were excluded; 2) chemical fertilizer treatment was n, p, k balanced application. thus the treatments of n or p or k application alone were not included in the data compilation; 3) gross rates of soil n transformations were measured using 15n pool dilution technique and 15 n tracing model; 4) no fertilizer application treatment was used as the control.
data_analysis: effect size for the response of variables gross rates of n transformations, soil properties, and crop yield were weighted and the variance of the natural log of the response ratio was calculated from the sample sizes and the standard deviations for the control and fertilization treatments. a fixed-effect model was used in our meta-analysis to determine whether long-term fertilization had a significant effect on the studied variables using metawin 2.1 software. 95% confidence intervals (ci) of the weighted effect size were generated using bootstrap resampling procedure with 9999 iterations.
background: Appropriate fertilizer managements are required to enhance crop yield, improve soil fertility, while minimize negative environmental impacts. It is important to take into account the effects of long-term organic or chemical fertilizer applications on gross rates of soil N transformations, which can provide an understanding of N dynamics in the different N fertilizer managements and help to optimize N fertilizer management.
objective: to explore if there is a general pattern of fertilizer application effects on gross rates of soil n transformations, to identify the mechanisms of fertilizer applications affecting soil n transformations, and to propose the appropriate fertilizer management for agricultural production. here the results for the effect of organic fertilization application on n2o emission are reported.
result1: significant positive effect of long-term fertilizer application on n2o emission compared to the control treatment.
result2: NA
general_conclusion: the stimulation of nitrification was related to high n2o emissions  and n leaching potential.
knowledge_gaps: other factors, such as soil type, cropping system, and climate, also probably affected the response of soil gross n transformation rates to long-term fertilization. however, these aspects due to the limited number of data in the present study were not discussed. in further studies, above-mentioned aspects should be investigated to comprehensively clarify the mechanisms of the effects of fertilization on soil n transformations.

search_strategy: a comprehensive literature search was conducted of peer- reviewed articles that reported n2o emissions following animal manure applications in agricultural soils in the web of science. ‘manure’, ‘nitrous oxide’, ‘n2o’, ‘nitrogen’, and ‘n’ were used as keywords to search for studies published prior to december 2015.
selection_criteria: 1) studies compared soil n2o emissions between manure applications, and synthetic n fertilization and/or no fertilization treatments in the same agricultural system and at the same experimental site.
data_analysis: estimation of weighted mean effect size and computation of confidence intervals using a bootstrap procedure. comparison of the effect sizes among the categorical groups through a framework similar to anova. test of the relationships between the effect sizes of n2o emissions and the n application rate, soil clay content, soil organic carbon (soc), soil c:n ratio, soil ph, and manure c:n ratio. all of the meta-analysis procedures were conducted using metawin 2.1 software.
background: Highly complex mechanisms associated with manuring regulate soil N2O production and consumption. However, the available research results on the impact of manuring on N2O emissions relative to synthetic N fertilizer have been contradictory.
objective: the objective is to quantitatively estimate the overall sign and magnitude of manuring effects on n2o emissions relative to synthetic n fertilizers in agricultural soils.
result1: on average, manure application significantly increased soil n2o emissions by 32.7% (95% ci: 5.1–58.2%) compared to synthetic n fertilizers.
result2: the effect sizes of manure application on n2o emissions were negatively correlated with soil clay content and soil ph (p < 0.01) but not with soil c:n ratio, soc, n addition rate, or manure c:n ratio.
result3: relative to synthetic n fertilizer, soil n2o emissions on average were increased by 22.9% (95% ci: 2.6–45.9%) and 70.7% (95% ci: 8.5 to 164.7%) from manure applications during short-term and long-term fertilization treatments, respectively, while the effect of long-term manure application treatment was not statistically significant
result4: compared to synthetic n fertilizer, cattle and poultry manure applications significantly increased soil n2o emissions by an average 28.7% (95% ci: 5.2–67.2%) and 45.4% (95% ci: 7.8– 159.2%), respectively. furthermore, soil n2o emissions increased by 41.6% (95% ci: 10.3 to 83.8%) for pig manure application and decreased by 21.4% (95% ci: – 37.2–16.8%) for fym application relative to synthetic n fertilizer while both effects were not statistically significant.
result5: compared with synthetic n fertilizer application, subsurface manure application significantly increased soil n2o emissions by 74.8% (95% ci: 6.0–104.2%), whereas no significant increase was found for surface manure application. the categorical group analysis indicated that manure preparation methods also significantly affected the effect sizes of manure application on n2o emissions relative to synthetic n fertilizer.
general_conclusion: manure application significantly increased n2o emissions compared to application of synthetic n fertiliser alone.
knowledge_gaps: the trade-offs between n2o emission and nh3 volatilization by manure application have not been well considered to date.

search_strategy: the literature searches were performed in 12 electronic bibliographic databases. in each database, an iterative process was used to refine the search strategy through testing of several search terms and incorporation of new search terms as new relevant studies were identified. a manual search was carried out for references that were cited in the identified studies.
selection_criteria: 1) studies must have reported measurement data of ch4 or n2o emission from swine manure land application to be included; 2) inclusion was not restricted by study size or publication type.
data_analysis: weighted paired t-tests were performed to compare the reported emissions from the land that applied swine manure with that from the control land (no n added) when data was available. a random-effect model was used to calculate weighted average metrics with 95% confidence intervals. studies with smaller standard deviations were given more weight. data across studies were analyzed statistically by anova using the mixed model procedure of sas.
background: Swine operations are important sources of GHG, primarily methane (CH4) and nitrous oxide (N2O).
objective: provide a systematic review of the literature on ghg emissions from swine manure land application through a meta-analysis that integrates results of individual previous studies.
result1: in both north american and european studies, n2o emission factors were below 1% in half of the studies and were above 1% in the other half of studies.
result2: the pooled n2o emission factors in north american studies and in european studies were 1.4% (95% ci, 0.7% to 2.2%) and 1.6% (95% ci, -0.3% to 3.5%) respectively.
general_conclusion: appling swine manure or applying commercial fertiliser with same n amount made no significant difference in n2o emissions from land. however, wide variations were observed in reported n2o emissions from land following swine manure application.

search_strategy: a literature search was conducted using web of science to find studies reporting a direct comparison between swine manure and synthetic n fertiliser in crop yield and/or n2o emissions. search terms included: “swine,” “pig,” “hog,” “manure,” “slurry,” “effluent,” “commercial,” “synthetic,” “mineral,” “urea,” “fertilizer,” “crop yield,” “fertilization,” and “production.” the search included only peer reviewed articles published before 1 june 2018.
selection_criteria: 1) replicated experimental design in field conditions; 2) comparisons made within the same cropping and management system; 3) no extreme conditions, such as flooding or major pest damage, occurred during the experiment; 4) only studies with approximately the same amount of plant-available n supplied from the fertiliser.
data_analysis: a random-effect meta-analysis model was applied assuming the effect sizes in the dataset are not intrinsically associated with each study. the random-effects model was applied separately for crop yield and n2o emissions, as well as each moderator variable.
background: Swine manure has potential for reuse as fertilizer on cropland and pastureland. Currently, producers may be hesitant to land apply swine manure because information regarding the impacts to crop production and environmental quality has been inconsistent.
objective: compare the effects of swine manure and synthetic fertilizer on both a measure of production, crop yield and a measure of environmental quality, nitrous oxide (n2o) emissions. here, the impact of swine manure on n2o emissions is reported.
result1: swine manure increased n2o emissions by 3.5% but variability was so high that no differences were found (p = 0.7).
result2: NA
general_conclusion: the overall effect of swine manure application on n2o emissions is not significant.

search_strategy: studies published before march 2020 were searched for in the microsoft academic, google scholar, baidu scholar, and china national knowledge infrastructure databases. search terms related to maize production, organic fertilizer substitution, manure application, and n and c emissions were combined.
selection_criteria: 1) studies focused on maize production with substitution of mineral fertilizer with organic fertilizer, including animal manure (47%), compost (37%), commercial organic fertilizer (e.g., industrially processed, standardized poultry or livestock manure; 9%), digestate (5%), slurry (2%); 2) the amounts of applied organic material and the n content were clearly specified; 3) the mineral fertilizer treatment and “substitution treatments” (partial or full substitution of chemical with organic fertilizer) had identical total n rates, and phosphorus (p) and potassium (k) inputs were not major factors limiting maize growth; 4) the n application rates for each treatment were reported to allow calculation of the fertilization rates, defined as organic n input/total n applied; 5) field or lysimeter study, with articles reporting data from the same experiment excluded; and 6) experimental duration of at least 3 years with respect to the effects of organic fertilizer on soil properties (e.g., soc).
data_analysis: effect sizes were weighted by the inverse of the sampling variance. for studies where neither the standard deviation nor standard error were reported, the approach of bracken was applied to estimate standard deviations using in the “metagear” r (ver. 3.6.1) package. a random-effect model was employed for the meta-analysis, generated using the “metafor” r package.
background: Organic fertilizer is an effective substitute for mineral fertilizer that improves crop yield and is environmentally friendly. However, the effects of substitution often vary due to complicated interactions among the organic fertilizer substitution rate, total nutrient supply, and type of cropping system used.
objective: to quantitatively assess the effects of substituting organic fertilizers for mineral fertilizers on maize production, n and c emissions, and the soil organic carbon sequestration rate (socsr). we also evaluated the global warming potential (gwp) and net global warming potential (ngwp), considering the indirect effects of nh3 emissions and runoff/leaching. the responses of these variables to organic fertilizer substitution were evaluated according to the fertilization rate (low, optimal, or high), substitution rates, and treatment duration. the underlying causes of the different responses of these variables to substitution of chemical with organic fertilizer are discussed. here, results on ch4 and n2o emissions are reported.
result1: substitution of mineral fertilizers with organic fertilizer had no effect on ch4 emissions. n2o emissions were decreased non-significantly (by 12.7%).
result2: ch4 emissions were not significantly affected by organic fertilizer substitution at any of the three fertilization rates.
result3: organic fertilizer substitution at the low rate significantly increased no2 emissions (by 33.1%). the decrease in n2o emissions tended to increase with increasing n fertilization rate. at the high fertilization rate, n2o emissions were significantly decreased by 71.7%.
result4: n2o emissions were promoted by long-term organic fertilizer substitution in comparison with short-term application.
general_conclusion: organic fertiliser substitution had no significant effect on ch4 emissions, whereas n2o emissions were decreased non-significantly during maize production.

search_strategy: studies published before march 2020 were searched for in the microsoft academic, google scholar, baidu scholar, and china national knowledge infrastructure databases. search terms related to maize production, organic fertilizer substitution, manure application, and n and c emissions were combined.
selection_criteria: 1) studies focused on maize production with substitution of mineral fertilizer with organic fertilizer, including animal manure (47%), compost (37%), commercial organic fertilizer (e.g., industrially processed, standardized poultry or livestock manure; 9%), digestate (5%), slurry (2%); 2) the amounts of applied organic material and the n content were clearly specified; 3) the mineral fertilizer treatment and “substitution treatments” (partial or full substitution of chemical with organic fertilizer) had identical total n rates, and phosphorus (p) and potassium (k) inputs were not major factors limiting maize growth; 4) the n application rates for each treatment were reported to allow calculation of the fertilization rates, defined as organic n input/total n applied; 5) field or lysimeter study, with articles reporting data from the same experiment excluded; and 6) experimental duration of at least 3 years with respect to the effects of organic fertilizer on soil properties (e.g., soc).
data_analysis: effect sizes were weighted by the inverse of the sampling variance. for studies where neither the standard deviation nor standard error were reported, the approach of bracken was applied to estimate standard deviations using in the “metagear” r (ver. 3.6.1) package. a random-effect model was employed for the meta-analysis, generated using the “metafor” r package.
background: Organic fertilizer is an effective substitute for mineral fertilizer that improves crop yield and is environmentally friendly. However, the effects of substitution often vary due to complicated interactions among the organic fertilizer substitution rate, total nutrient supply, and type of cropping system used.
objective: to quantitatively assess the effects of substituting organic fertilizers for mineral fertilizers on maize production, n and c emissions, and the soil organic carbon sequestration rate (socsr). we also evaluated the global warming potential (gwp) and net global warming potential (ngwp), considering the indirect effects of nh3 emissions and runoff/leaching. the responses of these variables to organic fertilizer substitution were evaluated according to the fertilization rate (low, optimal, or high), substitution rates, and treatment duration. the underlying causes of the different responses of these variables to substitution of chemical with organic fertilizer are discussed. here, results on n leaching and runoff are reported.
result1: substitution of mineral fertilizers with organic fertilizer significantly decreased n leaching and runoff (by 26.8%).
result2: substitution of mineral fertilizers with organic fertilizer decreased n leaching and runoff at all fertilization rates. the maximum decrease in n runoff and leaching (by 45.5%) was achieved at the optimal fertilization rate. at the high fertilization rate, runoff and leaching was significantly decreased by 22.1%.
result3: runoff and leaching were significantly decreased, by 47%, following long-term substitution of mineral fertilizers with organic fertilizer; this was significantly greater than the 11.2% reduction under short-term treatments.
general_conclusion: organic fertiliser substitution significantly reduced n losses.

search_strategy: a literature search (published per-reviewed papers, ph.d. and master thesis, or other studies either published or not) was carried out to retrieve information on experiments relevant for the meta-analysis. the focus of the search were soil or pot experiments reporting on agronomic or environmental performance, which included data on following response variables (i) crop yield, (ii) plant n uptake, (iii) n leaching, and (iv) gaseous n losses, i.e. nh3 losses, n2o losses. all types of process livestock manure n fertilisers were searched. the following search tools and sources were used: the web of science databases; the science internet browser (i.e. google scholar); the references of the selected studies; the contributions of neg, authors and other experts involved in the project.
selection_criteria: 1) experiments that assess in the same experimental conditions (e.g. same location, climate, soil and plant) agronomic or environmental performance data following a processed manure n fertiliser treatment, a haber-bosch derived and equivalent n (hbe n) fertiliser treatment, and a control treatment (without n fertiliser applied); 2) all studies that meet the abovementioned search criteria and have a minimum of three replicates were initially retained; 3) only studies where the processed manure application rates vary in between 50% and 200% of the hbe n fertiliser treatment were selected as linearity in plant responses to n fertilisation was not assumed outside the range; 4) no time frame, i.e. cut-off date, was applied in the selection criteria: 5) only studies in english or at least translated in english were considered so they can be scrutinized by all stakeholders. specific studies were discarded due to the 1) non-relevant climate conditions (e.g. tropical or subtropical climate or soil conditions), 2) lack of a focus on n fertilisation (e.g. assessment fertilising properties of p contained in processed manure), and 3) presence of possibly toxic non-agricultural residues in co-digestates (e.g. codigestion of manure and sewage sludge).
data_analysis: the meta-analysis was carried out using the 'meta' package with 'metacont' function as suggested by schwarzer et al. 2015 for continuous outcomes. the 'ratio of means' method was used along with the 'random effects model'. in addition, a refined variance estimator in the 'random effects model' was introduced: the so-called hartung-knapp method. the hartung-knapp is preferred over the standard dersimonian-laird method because it provides a more adequate 95% confidence interval for heterogeneous treatments. consequently, this method provides more conservative (wider) 95% confidence intervals.
background: Potential exists to reconcile on-going technological and market developments for the recycling of nutrients in a circular economy with the objective of protecting water bodies against pollution originating from livestock manure. Altogether, this report proposes a set of materials and use requirements to enable the safe use of manure-derived fertilisers in areas with water pollution by nitrogen, in amounts above the threshold established by the Nitrates Directive (91/676/EEC).
objective: the objective of this report is to help define those harmonised criteria that could allow nitrogen (n) fertilisers, partially or entirely derived from manure through processing, to be used in areas subject to the ceiling of 170 kg n/ha/yr prescribed in annex iii of the nitrates directive following otherwise identical provisions applied to n containing chemical fertilisers in the nitrates directive (91/676/eec), while ensuring the achievement the directive’s objectives and adequate agronomic benefits. such materials are referred to as recovered nitrogen from manure (renure) in this report. most candidate renure n fertilisers are rich in nh4+ as a result of the anaerobic digestion step that transforms organic n present in the manure into water-soluble nh4+, which can then be isolated through a solid-liquid separation and eventually be further concentrated (mineral n concentrates, air scrubbing).

search_strategy: a literature search (published per-reviewed papers, ph.d. and master thesis, or other studies either published or not) was carried out to retrieve information on experiments relevant for the meta-analysis. the focus of the search were soil or pot experiments reporting on agronomic or environmental performance, which included data on following response variables (i) crop yield, (ii) plant n uptake, (iii) n leaching, and (iv) gaseous n losses, i.e. nh3 losses, n2o losses. all types of process livestock manure n fertilisers were searched. the following search tools and sources were used: the web of science databases; the science internet browser (i.e. google scholar); the references of the selected studies; the contributions of neg, authors and other experts involved in the project.
selection_criteria: 1) experiments that assess in the same experimental conditions (e.g. same location, climate, soil and plant) agronomic or environmental performance data following a processed manure n fertiliser treatment, a haber-bosch derived and equivalent n (hbe n) fertiliser treatment, and a control treatment (without n fertiliser applied); 2) all studies that meet the abovementioned search criteria and have a minimum of three replicates were initially retained; 3) only studies where the processed manure application rates vary in between 50% and 200% of the hbe n fertiliser treatment were selected as linearity in plant responses to n fertilisation was not assumed outside the range; 4) no time frame, i.e. cut-off date, was applied in the selection criteria: 5) only studies in english or at least translated in english were considered so they can be scrutinized by all stakeholders. specific studies were discarded due to the 1) non-relevant climate conditions (e.g. tropical or subtropical climate or soil conditions), 2) lack of a focus on n fertilisation (e.g. assessment fertilising properties of p contained in processed manure), and 3) presence of possibly toxic non-agricultural residues in co-digestates (e.g. codigestion of manure and sewage sludge).
data_analysis: the meta-analysis was carried out using the 'meta' package with 'metacont' function as suggested by schwarzer et al. 2015 for continuous outcomes. the 'ratio of means' method was used along with the 'random effects model'. in addition, a refined variance estimator in the 'random effects model' was introduced: the so-called hartung-knapp method. the hartung-knapp is preferred over the standard dersimonian-laird method because it provides a more adequate 95% confidence interval for heterogeneous treatments. consequently, this method provides more conservative (wider) 95% confidence intervals.
