search_strategy: studies published before march 2020 were searched for in the microsoft academic, google scholar, baidu scholar, and china national knowledge infrastructure databases. search terms related to maize production, organic fertilizer substitution, manure application, and n and c emissions were combined.
selection_criteria: 1) studies focused on maize production with substitution of mineral fertilizer with organic fertilizer, including animal manure (47%), compost (37%), commercial organic fertilizer (e.g., industrially processed, standardized poultry or livestock manure; 9%), digestate (5%), slurry (2%); 2) the amounts of applied organic material and the n content were clearly specified; 3) the mineral fertilizer treatment and “substitution treatments” (partial or full substitution of chemical with organic fertilizer) had identical total n rates, and phosphorus (p) and potassium (k) inputs were not major factors limiting maize growth; 4) the n application rates for each treatment were reported to allow calculation of the fertilization rates, defined as organic n input/total n applied; 5) field or lysimeter study, with articles reporting data from the same experiment excluded; and 6) experimental duration of at least 3 years with respect to the effects of organic fertilizer on soil properties (e.g., soc).
data_analysis: effect sizes were weighted by the inverse of the sampling variance. for studies where neither the standard deviation nor standard error were reported, the approach of bracken was applied to estimate standard deviations using in the “metagear” r (ver. 3.6.1) package. a random-effect model was employed for the meta-analysis, generated using the “metafor” r package.
background: Organic fertilizer is an effective substitute for mineral fertilizer that improves crop yield and is environmentally friendly. However, the effects of substitution often vary due to complicated interactions among the organic fertilizer substitution rate, total nutrient supply, and type of cropping system used.
objective: to quantitatively assess the effects of substituting organic fertilizers for mineral fertilizers on maize production, n and c emissions, and the soil organic carbon sequestration rate (socsr). we also evaluated the global warming potential (gwp) and net global warming potential (ngwp), considering the indirect effects of nh3 emissions and runoff/leaching. the responses of these variables to organic fertilizer substitution were evaluated according to the fertilization rate (low, optimal, or high), substitution rates, and treatment duration. the underlying causes of the different responses of these variables to substitution of chemical with organic fertilizer are discussed. here, results on nitrogen use efficiency are reported.
result1: substitution of mineral fertilizer with organic fertilizer had no significant effect on nitrogen use efficiency.
result2: the effect of substitution of mineral fertilization with organic fertilizers on nitrogen use efficiency tended to increase with increasing n fertilization rate. the low fertilization rate had a negative impact on nitrogen use efficiency (−17.3%). the optimal fertilization rate compromised nitrogen use efficiency to some extent. the high fertilization rate significantly increased nitrogen use efficiency (8.77%).
result3: the duration of organic fertilizer application did not affect nitrogen use efficiency.
general_conclusion: organic fertiliser substitution had no significant effect on nitrogen use efficiency during maize production.

search_strategy: we collected data from relevant peer-reviewed publications. the publications were identified using the online database isi web of science, within the period 1997–2017. publications were searched using the keywords “organic amendment” and the results were refined using additional words—“long-term”, “yield”, “manure”, “compost”, “olsen p”, and “microbial biomass”. additionally, articles cited in review papers which had analysed data from long-term agricultural studies (≥ 10 years)  were also included in the dataset.
selection_criteria: 1) studies that reported crop yield, soil organic carbon, microbial biomass (mb) and/or plant-available p data for at least two types of treatments: (a) those that did not receive any fertiliser (‘nil control’); or (b) those where only inorganic npk fertiliser (if, ‘standard control’) was applied, and (c) where organic amendments (oa) with or without supplemental if was used. we defined oa as raw or composted materials derived from animals (e.g., manure), plant (e.g., straw) and municipal waste (e.g., sludge). the standard control did not always receive equivalent nutrient rates to those in oa and oa + if treatments; 2) crop yield data were included only for wheat, barley, corn, and rice grain in order to minimise differences in nutrient needs and rooting systems.
data_analysis: the meta-analysis was performed according to hedges et al. (1999) and cayuela et al. (2014) using metawin 2.0 software. the effect sizes (responses) of soil oc, mb, and olsen p were calculated  using a categorical random effects model, where the effect size is weighted by the inverse of the variance.
background: In recent years there has been a renewed interest in using organic amendments (OA) to agricultural soils as partial or full substitutes for inorganic fertilisers (IF) in order to manage nutrients more cost effectively, decrease our dependence on non-renewable resources (for example, P from phosphate rock), reduce and recycle waste that would otherwise be disposed to landfill, and increase soil organic matter.
objective: the present work aims to investigate the effect of oa and oa + if additions on soil nutrient fertility by carrying out a meta-analysis based on results from 132 long-lasting fertility trials (≥ 10 years) worldwide. in this study, the responses of crop yield—along with those of soil organic carbon (oc), size of mb, and plant-available p (i.e., olsen p)—to oa and oa + if relative to if alone (standard control) and no fertilisation (nil control) are determined. here results of the effect of oa and oa + if additions on soil microbial biomass are presented.
result1: the long-term application of oa and oa + mf caused an overall increase in the size of the soil microbial bioass, which was significant regardless of the control used. the relative increase was larger when comparing with the nil control (50 ± 7%; 95% ci) than with the standard control (30 ± 5%; 95% ci).
result2: climate was the only variable that had a significant influence on the variability of the mb responses for both standard and nil controls.
result3: years of application, application rate, oa type, initial soc, initial ph, soil order, soil texture had no significant influence on the variability of the mb responses.
general_conclusion: the long-term application of oa and oa + mf caused an overall increase in the size of the soil microbial biomass.

search_strategy: the meta-analysis was conducted using previously published peer-reviewed results identified using the online database isi web ofscience. in 2009, peer-reviewed studies were searched using the keywords microbial biomass and refined with words such as, soil carbon, organic, manure, compost, fertilizer and agriculture. the authors had two main pre-selected criteria in performing the search: that all of the peer-reviewed literature be based on field trials rather than laboratory or greenhouse studies and that results be published after 1990.
selection_criteria: they defined organic amendments as only those solid, raw or composted materials derived from animals. the analysis was also restricted to studies that reported soil microbial biomass (mb) for at least two types of treatments: (a) those that received only inorganic fertilizer (‘control’) and (b) those that received organic inputs with or without supplemental inorganic fertilizers.
data_analysis: the meta-analysis was performed according to hedges et al. (1999) and jablonski et al. (2002) using metawin 2.0 software. they used an unweighted approach. we used a procedure that allowed us to determine what experimental conditions influence the magnitude of the response to organic inputs relative to inorganic fertilizers. this procedure is similar to the partitioning of variance in anova where the total heterogeneity (q) for a group of observations is partitioned into within-group (qw) and between-group (qb) heterogeneity.
background: Soil microbial biomass (MB) facilitates key ecosystem functions such as soil aggregation and nutrient cycling and makes a substantial contribution to soil organic matter. While agricultural conversion drastically reduces MB, the use of organic amendments is an effective way to rebuild depleted MB. Yet, little is known about broad-scale, global controls over MB responses to organic inputs.
objective: the author conducted a meta-analysis of results published in the last 20 years on microbial carbon and microbial nitrogen responses to organic amendments relative to conventionally managed agricultural systems that receive only inorganic fertilizer applications. the primary objective was to develop a broad and predictive understanding of microbial biomass responses to organic amendments that encompasses a range of soil types, cropping systems and geographies.
result1: across all observations, organic amendment applications increased microbial carbon by 36% and microbial nitrogen by 27% compared to the control treatments receiving only inorganic fertilizer inputs.
result2: the variables that explained the greatest amount of variation in microbial carbon were the type of amendment added, the dry weight of the added amendment, and the amount of n applied, followed by climate, soil ph and rate of c input.
result3: in general, microbial n responses to organic amendments were more variable than microbial c.
general_conclusion: there is a robust and rapid microbial biomass response to even small and brief applications of organic amendments across a range of environments and agronomic practices.

search_strategy: peer-reviewed literature from 1996 to 2015.
selection_criteria: 1) study should be carried out in cropland (cereal crop, economic crop); 2) soil sampling should be conducted within the soil layer of 0–20 cm depth; 3) besides a control experiment with no fertilization (ck), the analytical data should be obtained from one of the four following fertilization regimes: inorganic nitrogen fertilizer only (nf, including the amount applied in kg n ha1 y1); inorganic nitrogen, phosphorus and potassium fertilizers (cf); organic fertilizer only (mf, including the amount applied in kg organic c ha1 y1); and organic fertilizer plus inorganic nitrogen, phosphorus and potassium fertilizers (mcf); 4) six kinds of organic fertilizer were considered and categorized as follows: animal manure (pig, cattle, chicken, horse), animal compost (pig, cattle, chicken, horse), cover crop (mulch, clover, legume, grain, grass, rye, vetch, oats), straw compost, straw, sludge (sewage, sugarcane) and waste (food, paper, biosolids).
data_analysis: publication bias was assessed a priori using funnel plot asymmetry under the r package metafor, and revealed no publication bias because the data fell within the expected 95% confidence interval.
background: Organic fertilizer applications that boost soil fertility and crop production are expected to enhance soil biodiversity, making ecosystems more resilient to stress. Numerous studies have compared biodiversity in soil receiving organic fertilizer to soil under other fertilizer regimes (inorganic fertilizers, unfertilized), yet the data were not analyzed systematically across studies.
objective: the study provides the first systematic and quantitative review of fertilization effects on soil nematode communities in cropland using a meta-analysis approach.
result1: total nematode abundance and diversity (h') were increased by all fertilization regimes, although species richness was greater in the mf fertilization regime and reduced in other regimes.
result2: species richness and total nematode abundance increased with greater organic c inputs.
result3: most of the organic materials applied to soils were animal manure/compost and straw/straw compost, and these increased the total number of nematode abundance.
result4: no effect was observed after organic fertilisation (both alone and combined with mineral fertilisation) for fungal-feeding nematode, plant-feeding nematode, enrichment index, structure index, species richness. no effect was observed for omnivore-predator nematode and shannon diversity after combined organic and mineral fertilisation and for maturity index after only organic fertilisation.
result5: negative effect was observed for maturity index after combined organic and mineral fertilisation.
general_conclusion: nematode species richness increased with the application of c-rich organic fertilisers.
knowledge_gaps: the underlying mechanisms that explain how c-rich and n-rich organic fertilizers control the species richness and composition of nematode assemblage are still not well understood – not only due to the diversity of organic amendments, but also due to the variety of soil environments.

search_strategy: the database isi web of science was used to search for primary literature that had been published prior to june 2019. the search terms were (“manure” or “poultry*” or “dairy*” or “swine*”), (“enzyme activity” or “enzyme activities”) and “soil*”.
selection_criteria: 1) the study involved application of manure to soil and the manure type was clearly stated; 2) control plots without manure application were included for comparison with the treatment that had received manure; 3) the literature investigated the activities of enzymes related to organic carbon (oc) or nutrient cycles; 4) the means, standard deviation (sd) and replicate numbers were reported.
data_analysis: the weighted mean response ratio was determined by using a random-effects model. during the categorical moderators' analysis, the significance of the heterogeneities between groups (qbetween) and within groups (qwithin) was applied by using the chi-square test. the meta-analysis was performed in metawin 2.1. spearman's correlation coefficients were calculated to analyze the relationships between the effect sizes of enzyme activities, soil organic carbon (soc), total nitrogen (tn), microbial c, microbial n and continuous explanatory variables.
background: Manure application mitigates land degradation and improves soil fertility. Despite the positive effects of manure on soil microbial indices, great variability in the response of soil biochemical properties after manure application  exists, especially for enzyme activities. A comprehensive overview of responses of soil biochemical properties depending on climate factors, management, soil, and manure characteristics is lacking.
objective: the authors generalized studies worldwide that report the effects of manure application on soil organic carbon (soc), total nitrogen (tn), microbial c and n and activities of seven enzymes. main objectives were to (1) comprehensively evaluate and quantify the effects of manure on soil biochemical properties, (2) verify the reliability of using the average extracellular enzyme activities as proxies of a specific substrate or nutrient acquisition and (3) clarify the influence of explanatory variables on manure impacts.
result1: microbial c significantly increased by 88 ± 6.3%.
result2: microbial n significantly increased by 84 ± 11%.
result3: manure application increased the activities of β-1,4-glucosidase (b-glu), dehydrogenase (deh), acid and alkaline phosphatase (acp and akp), n-acetyl-β-d-glucosaminidase (nag), urease (ure) and sulfatase (sul) by 147 ± 15%, 114 ± 10%, 39 ± 6%, 112 ± 12%, 58 ± 13%, 104 ± 8.7% and 228 ± 19%, respectively.
result4: all the enzyme activities showed either an increase or no change in response to the manure application for all conditions (i.e., climatic factors, soil properties, management and manure characteristics).
general_conclusion: activities of enzymes acquiring c-, energy-, n-, phosphorus- and sulfur were 1.3–3.3 times larger than those in soil without manure for all study durations included.

search_strategy: a total of 106 peer-reviewed literatures published between 2000 and 2016 listed in google scholar and the isi web of science were collected. through this search 599 measurements were identified from the 106 published literatures that included at least two of our targeted search terms: “alkaline phosphatases”, “acid phosphatases”, and either “manure”, “farmyard manure”, “straw”, “solid waste”, “compost” or “waste”.
selection_criteria: 1) if the interest data were only shown in figure or graph, both the means and the standard deviation (sd) were extracted by using the imagej 1.50i software and the standard errors (se) converted to sd; 2) if one research reported various independent experiments (e.g., three experiments at separate locations), each of experiment was considered as an independent observation into present dataset; 3) if one literature contained results from multiple sampling dates and soil depths, the data from the latest sampling time-point and the uppermost layer of soil were used for our database.
data_analysis: the mean effect-sizes and 95% confidence intervals (ci) were generated by building random-effect models with restricted maximum likelihood estimation in openmee software. data were weighted by using pooled variances. the rr and ci of treatments were back-transformed from lnrr values and all figures showing the weighted rr values were plotted in sigmaplot (version12.5). the rr results were shown as percentage changes based on the comparison between organic and mineral-only treatments.
background: Soil microorganisms may utilize phosphorylated compounds as a C source and in doing so mineralise organic P through the production and activities of extracellular enzymes. The mineralization of organic P is catalyzed by the extracellular presence of soil phosphatases produced principally by the soil microbiota, although plants can also exude acid phosphatases. There is currently no consensus regarding how phosphatase activities respond to organic amendments with activities reported to both decrease and increase across varying magnitudes.
objective: compare the effects of organic amendments versus mineral fertilizers on extracellular acid (acp) and alkaline (alp) phosphatase activities and soil c:n:p stoichiometry. here, only the results on phosphatase activities are reported.
result1: based on meta-analysis, organic amendments increased average extracellular acp and alp (phosphatase activities) by 22% and 53%, respectively, in comparison to the mineral-only fertilization.
result2: observed increases in activities were consistent with significant increases in soil organic carbon (c), total nitrogen (n) and available p contents, and microbial biomass c and n pools.
general_conclusion: organic amendments supported extracellular acp and alp activities, in comparison to the mineral-only fertilisation.

result1: overall there was a significant relative mean increase in olsen concentration of 60 ± 13% (95% ci) with oa and oa + mf application as compared with the standard control.
result2: the categorical variable that most consistently influenced the final olsen p concentrations was the type of oa, with those from animal origin having a relative mean increase of 93% in olsen p concentration as compared with standard controls. plant-derived oa had no significant effect as compared with their standard controls.

search_strategy: literature searches were conducted in scopus, targeting peer reviewed articles published online through july 2019. to obtain the papers listed, the authors used the keywords “almond or olive or citrus or vineyard or grapevine or orchard”, “and” combinations of the following items: “mediterranean climate”, “cover crop”, “intercropping”, “alley crop”, “multicrop”, “agroforestry”, “crop yield” and “soil”.
selection_criteria: 1) laboratory or greenhouse studies were excluded, and only studies performed in field conditions and carried out in a mediterranean climate were chosen; 2) when several papers included data from the same experiment, the longest study with the most soil and crop variables was chosen.
data_analysis: the authors decided to weight observations using the sample sizes to ensure statistical significance by keeping a sufficient sample size: studies with larger sample sizes were weighted higher during aggregation. for the uncertainty analysis, we reported the means and 95% confidence intervals (cis). the cis were constructed by non-parametric bootstrapping (nboot = 10 000). the bootstrapping was only carried out for treatments with n ≥ 8, as the bootstrap is unreliable when the sample size is too small. the effect of treatment was considered as significant if the 95% bootstrap ci did not overlap with zero.
background: Perennial crops, such as almond, olive, citrus or grapevines, represent ∼16% of the agroecosystems in the Mediterranean area, with great economic importance. Intensive tree cultivation in Mediterranean soils frequently causes land degradation by depletion of soil organic matter (SOM), erosion, and also, under irrigation farming, soil and water pollution.
objective: to assess the implication of fertilization in mediterranean orchards on soil nutrients, soil organic carbon and crop yield. here, results on soil nutrients are reported.
result1: organic fertilization was associated with a significant increase in soil-n compared to inorganic fertilization (wlog(rr) = 0.14).
result2: the use of organic fertilizers did not significantly affect soil p, with 50% of studies showing a positive effect, compared to inorganic fertilizers.
general_conclusion: the results of this meta-analysis highlighted the overall positive effects of organic fertilisation on soil nitrogen, with general increases compared to inorganic fertilisation.

search_strategy: the authors used the isi web of science and google scholar to exhaustively search papers published before march 2017. several terms (“soil nitrogen priming”, “nitrogen 15”, “soil 15n”, “added nitrogen interaction”, “labeled 15n fertilizer”, “nitrogen fertilization”, and “nitrogen mineralization”) were used to identify studies that compared mineralization or plant uptake of native soil n in control (no-fertilizer applied) and fertilizer treatments.
selection_criteria: 1) studies were required to have used 15n isotope tracers to separate unlabeled native soil n from labeled fertilizer n, and to report data for both fertilizer and control plots.
data_analysis: metawin (version 2.1) was used to calculate mean effect sizes and 95% confidence intervals (cis) by bootstrapping (9999 iterations). individual treatment effects were considered significant if their 95% cis did not overlap with zero. we used randomization tests in metawin to determine significant differences in treatment effects between study categories and treatment effects of mineralization vs. plant uptake of native soil n (p < 0.05).
background: Fertiliser input affect plant uptake of native soil nitrogen, yet the underlying mechanism remain elusive.
objective: assess the effect of fertiliser addition on mineralization and plant uptake of native soil nitrogen, testing for broad patterns across experiments performed to date.
result1: organic fertilizer tended to decrease native soil n mineralization by 99 kg n ha−1 year−1, though not significantly (p = 0.09).
result2: treatment effects of organic and inorganic fertilizers were not affected by soil texture or study location.
result3: with organic fertilizer, plant uptake of native soil n was greater than mineralization of native soil n (without plants) (179 vs. −99 kg n ha−1 year−1; p < 0.001).
general_conclusion: our findings demonstrate that fertiliser application consistently increased plant uptake of native soil n.
knowledge_gaps: results suggest complex interactions between fertilizer addition and microbial immobilization and mineralization of n, indicating the need for further study.

search_strategy: data were collected using google scholar and web of science to search for peer-reviewed literature on the topic of the effect of organic-c addition on microbial n immobilization.
selection_criteria: 1) the amount or the rate of n immobilization by soil microbes was reported; 2) microbial biomass n was reported; 3) identical management except organic-c input were performed for the control and the organic-c treatments; 4) the means and sample sizes of the chosen variables for both the control and the organic-c treatments could be directly or indirectly obtained from the literature.
data_analysis: the bootstrap resampling procedure of the software metawin (version 2.1) was used to generate the mean effect sizes (ln r) and bias-corrected confidence intervals (cis). heterogeneity statistics (qw) were obtained for each group of observations. significant chi-square values (p <0.05) indicated that the effects within a category were significantly heterogeneous. in addition, the relationship between microbial immobilization of nh4+and that of no3.
background: Through microbial N immobilization, surplus inorganic-N in soil can be incorporated into microbial biomass, reducing the risk of reactive N being lost to the environment. Increasing microbial N immobilization can potentially improve the synchrony between soil N supply and plant N uptake.
objective: this study aimed to perform a meta- analysis on the effect of organic-c quality on microbial n immobilization.
result1: the ln r of microbial n immobilization across all the observations was 0.717 (ci: 0.548–0.917), with wide variation from -0.154 to 1.125. organic-c addition significantly increased microbial n immobilization by 105% relative to unamended soil.
result2: overall, the differences in the ln r+of microbial n immobilization among different groups were not significant. these results indicate that the response of microbial n immobilization to organic-c addition may be not dependent on the c/ n ratio of organic materials in the short-term.
result3: the effect of the form of inorganic-n (ammonium [nh4+] or nitrate [no3-]) on the response of microbial n immobilization to organic-c addtion was not significant.
result4: the ln r for the experimental period decreased in the order of <30 d, 60–120 d, ≥120 d, and 30–60 d.
result5: glucose (classified as a labile compound) was more effective in stimulating microbial n immobilization than cellobiose and cellulose (classified as intermediately decomposable com-pounds). tannin and oxalic acid (classified as recalcitrant compounds) did not significantly affect microbial n immobilization.
general_conclusion: overall, the addition of organic-c increased significantly microbial n immobilization by 105% relative to unamended soil.

search_strategy: the database isi web of science was used to search for primary literature that had been published prior to june 2019. the search terms were (“manure” or “poultry*” or “dairy*” or “swine*”), (“enzyme activity” or “enzyme activities”) and “soil*”.
selection_criteria: 1) the study involved application of manure to soil and the manure type was clearly stated; 2) control plots without manure application were included for comparison with the treatment that had received manure; 3) the literature investigated the activities of enzymes related to organic carbon (oc) or nutrient cycles; 4) the means, standard deviation (sd) and replicate numbers were reported.
data_analysis: the weighted mean response ratio was determined by using a random-effects model. during the categorical moderators' analysis, the significance of the heterogeneities between groups (qbetween) and within groups (qwithin) was applied by using the chi-square test. the meta-analysis was performed in metawin 2.1. spearman's correlation coefficients were calculated to analyze the relationships between the effect sizes of enzyme activities, soil organic carbon (soc), total nitrogen (tn), microbial c, microbial n and continuous explanatory variables.
background: Manure application mitigates land degradation and improves soil fertility. Despite the positive effects of manure on soil microbial indices, great variability in the response of soil biochemical properties after manure application  exists, especially for enzyme activities. A comprehensive overview of responses of soil biochemical properties depending on climate factors, management, soil, and manure characteristics is lacking.
objective: the authors generalized studies worldwide that report the effects of manure application on soil organic carbon (soc), total nitrogen (tn), microbial c and n and activities of seven enzymes. main objectives were to (1) comprehensively evaluate and quantify the effects of manure on soil biochemical properties, (2) verify the reliability of using the average extracellular enzyme activities as proxies of a specific substrate or nutrient acquisition and (3) clarify the influence of explanatory variables on manure impacts.
result1: manure application significantly increased tn contents 33 ± 8.7% compared to soil without manure.
result2: NA
general_conclusion: manuring increased soil nutrient content.

search_strategy: papers were derived from the web of science.
selection_criteria: 1) field experiments were conducted for more than than 10 years. thus, those field experiments conducted less than 10 years and laboratory incubation studies were excluded; 2) chemical fertilizer treatment was n, p, k balanced application. thus the treatments of n or p or k application alone were not included in the data compilation; 3) gross rates of soil n transformations were measured using 15n pool dilution technique and 15 n tracing model; 4) no fertilizer application treatment was used as the control.
data_analysis: effect size for the response of variables gross rates of n transformations, soil properties, and crop yield were weighted and the variance of the natural log of the response ratio was calculated from the sample sizes and the standard deviations for the control and fertilization treatments. a fixed-effect model was used in our meta-analysis to determine whether long-term fertilization had a significant effect on the studied variables using metawin 2.1 software. 95% confidence intervals (ci) of the weighted effect size were generated using bootstrap resampling procedure with 9999 iterations.
background: Appropriate fertilizer managements are required to enhance crop yield, improve soil fertility, while minimize negative environmental impacts. It is important to take into account the effects of long-term organic or chemical fertilizer applications on gross rates of soil N transformations, which can provide an understanding of N dynamics in the different N fertilizer managements and help to optimize N fertilizer management.
objective: to explore if there is a general pattern of fertilizer application effects on gross rates of soil n transformations, to identify the mechanisms of fertilizer applications affecting soil n transformations, and to propose the appropriate fertilizer management for agricultural production. here the results for the effect of organic fertilization application on total n are reported.
result1: long-term fertilizer application significantly increased total n, and the highest mean effect size was observed in combination of organic and chemical fertilizers treatments.
result2: NA
general_conclusion: organic fertiliser alone or combination of organic and chemical fertiliser could not only improve crop yield, but also increase soil fertility and reduce the n losses potential.
knowledge_gaps: other factors, such as soil type, cropping system, and climate, also probably affected the response of soil gross n transformation rates to long-term fertilization. however, we did not discuss these aspects due to the limited number of data in the present study. in further studies, abovementioned aspects should be investigated to comprehensively clarify the mechanisms of the effects of fertilization on soil n transformations.

search_strategy: the study was conducted by an extensive meta-analysis of data extracted from literature on long term experiments (ltes) in europe, as well as from ltes held by the catch-c consortium partners from 10 european countries.
selection_criteria: not mentioned.
data_analysis: all statistical analyses were performed with the help of the package statgraphics centurion v. xvi. response rations (rr) frequency distributions were tested for normality and their descriptive statistics were calculated. a one-sample student t-test (2-tails) was used to identify which rr means were significantly different from 1 (p < 0.05). next, a multiple linear model with climate, soil type, sampling depth and duration of practice as a single nominal factor (without interactions) was used to evaluate if any of these factors affected the relative rr to a given management practice, and by how much. for this purpose, climate, soil texture and duration of practice were divided into four classes (“levels”) each, while three different depths of soil sampling were considered. a type iii wald statistics for maximum likelihood estimate of regres- sion was chosen. then, a t-test was used to separate means of single factors different at p < 0.05.
background: Organic fertilizers from animal wastes is known to represent viable options to substitute mineral N fertilizer.
objective: to verify the hypotheses that “best management practices” (including organic fertilisation) are not only effective in maintaining high yields, in reducing cultivation costs, and in mitigating climate change, but also contribute in improving chemical, physical and biological crop quality.
result1: farmyard manure application significantly increased soil total nitrogen and content of available (mineral) nitrogen.
result2: application of compost significantly increased soil total nitrogen and soil mineral nitrogen.
result3: slurry application (relative to mineral fertilizer) increased soil total nitrogen and soil mineral nitrogen significantly.
general_conclusion: long-term use of soil management practices as organic fertilisation with compost, farmyard manure, or slurry, influenced soil chemical quality indicators. both positive and negative effects were observed.

search_strategy: the selected publications were collected by searching the online reference database web of science (core collection) on 1 aug 2018 (timespan: 1988-2017).
selection_criteria: 1) the experiment had to be performed under field conditions, and experiments conducted in a laboratory or those where data were collected through modeling or remote sensing were excluded; 2) the study had to report the soc content (or soc stocks) directly before and after wetland cultivation; 3) the experiment had to be replicated, and the standard deviation (sd) was reported or could be calculated from the information provided; and 4) the experiment had to include a natural (or nearly natural) wetland as a control treatment, and the other treatments had to be in the vicinity (within ~10 km) of the control treatment or were converted from the control treatment.
data_analysis: the meta-analysis was conducted using the “metafor” package in r (version 3.5.1). the overall meta-estimates of soc changes were obtained from random effects meta-analysis models in which the calculated effect sizes were weighted with the inverse of their respective variances. mixed-effects models were fitted with each categorical variable as predictors (14 in total). a restricted maximum-likelihood estimator was established to estimate the degree to which the study variables could explain the effect size differences among the studies. for non-independent observations, e.g., measurements from the same site, a three-level meta-analysis model was used to correct for nonindependence by adding a random effect to the model at the level corresponding to the grouping variable. to determine the important influent factors that determine soc changes after wetland conversion, the “metafor” package in combination with the “glmulti” package was used to perform 2 model selection analyses: 1) all the categorical predictors except soil depth (13 in total) were included in the model at once to detect the most important predictors; and 2) the model selection analysis was performed by analyzing 5 categories (type of wetland change, previous wetland type, climatic conditions, wetland cultivation age and initial soc content) separately and selecting the most important predictor. for all the continuous variables (initial soc content, climatic conditions and soil physicochemical properties), a regression analysis was performed using sigma plot 11.0 to test their correlations with soc change.
scale: global: the studies were conducted in >20 countries, and the experimental sites were distributed worldwide.
background: Wetland cultivation has a profound effect on soil organic carbon (SOC) and global soil carbon cycles. However, the global patterns of the changes in SOC following wetland cultivation are still not well understood, especially with respect to the conditions under which SOC can increase in cultivated wetlands.
objective: to quantify the changes in soc comparing wetland cultivation and non-cultivated wetlands and identify the underlying mechanisms. here, results for peats are reported.
result1: significant positive effects on soc compared to cultivated wetlands were found for wetlands with peat soil (42.4%, p < .001).
result2: NA
general_conclusion: significant positive effects on soc compared to cultivated wetlands were found for wetlands with peat soil (42.4%, p < .001).
knowledge_gaps: in future studies, it will be important to conduct ecological experiments with uniform standards and criteria, and research on the effects of soil type and organic matter return on soc following wetland cultivation should be strengthened.

search_strategy: publications were selected for the meta-analysis by searching the web of science database (core collection) using a specific search string in 30st oct 2018 (timespan: 1988-2017).
selection_criteria: 1) the experiment had to be performed under field conditions, and those conducted in a laboratory or in which data were collected through modeling or remote sensing were excluded; 2) the study had to report the soc content (or soc stocks) directly before and after wetland restoration; 3) the experiment had to be replicated, and the standard deviation (sd) had to be reported or could be calculated from the information provided; and 4) the experiment had to include a control treatment (a natural wetland or a cultivated wetland). the restored wetlands had to be converted from control wetlands, and all treatments had to be adjacent to one another (within ~10 km).
data_analysis: the meta-analysis was conducted using the “metafor” package in r (version 3.4.1). the overall meta-estimates of soc changes were obtained from random effects meta-analysis models in which calculated effect sizes were weighted with the inverse of their respective variances. mixed-effects models were fitted with each categorical variable (16 in total) as predictors to evaluate the change in effect size relative to the different variables. a restricted maximum-likelihood estimator was established to estimate the degree to which the study variables could explain the effect size differences among the studies. for nonindependent observations, e.g., measurements from the same site at different soil depths or in different treatment years, a three-level meta-analytic model was used to correct for nonindependence by adding a random effect to the model at the level corresponding to the categorical variable. to identify the most important influential factors that determine soc changes among the various variables, the “metafor” package in combination with the “glmulti” package was used to perform model selection analyses.
background: Wetland restoration has been conducted worldwide due to the important ecological functions provided by wetlands. However, the global patterns of soil organic carbon (SOC) change following wetland restoration are not clear, which has limited the efficacy of the management of restored wetlands.
objective: to examine the soc dynamics following wetland restoration and the underlying mechanisms. specifically, the objectives of this study are to 1) evaluate the magnitude and direction of soc changes following wetland restoration, 2) obtain a better understanding of global patterns of soc dynamics following wetland restoration, 3) determine the most influential factors determining soc changes, and 4) provide theoretical support for managing and utilizing wetlands with the aim of increasing soc sequestration. here, the comparison between natural and restored wetlands with peat conditions is explored as "conservation" and the comparison between restored and cultivated wetlands is explored as "restoration".
result1: the soc in restored wetlands was significantly higher than that in cultivated wetlands when wetlands were identified as peatlands.
result2: the soc in restored wetlands did not significantly differ from that in natural wetlands when wetlands were identified as peatlands.
general_conclusion: wetland restoration facilitated soc sequestration when wetlands were peatlands. while soc in restored wetlands did not significantly differ from that in natural wetlands when wetlands were identified as peatlands.

search_strategy: a comprehensive search on the web of science database (accessed between january 2013 and july 2016) was conducted using the keywords: pristine peatlands, methane emissions, drainage, restoration, fens, bogs, mire, and northern peatlands. in an attempt to gain a comprehensive coverage, all references in the papers found in the web of science search were checked.
selection_criteria: only studies which covered at least one growing season and measured at weekly or more frequent intervals were selected.
data_analysis: drained peatlands: the data were tested, using paired t-tests on all paired sites where both natural (n = 42) and artificially drained (n = 61) (i.e., lower water table for using in agriculture, forestry or mining) peatlands had ch4 emission measurements. in addition, a t-test was performed to see whether there was a significant difference between drained fens (n = 26) and drained bogs (n = 35). the effects of different land use systems/vegetation cover (cropland [n = 4], grassland [n = 7], and woods [n = 29]) on drained peatland methane emissions were also tested using one-way anova. restored peatlands. the impacts of restoration system on ch4 emissions from peatlands were investigated. the management systems tested using paired t-test were as follows: rewetting (n = 16), and restoring by vegetation and rewetting (n = 16).
background: Northern peatlands constitute a significant source of atmospheric methane (CH4). However, management of undisturbed peatlands, as well as the restoration of disturbed peatlands, will alter the exchange of CH4 with the atmosphere.
objective: the aim of this systematic review and meta-analysis was to collate and analyze published studies to improve our understanding of the factors that control ch4 emissions and the impacts of management on the gas flux from northern (latitude 40° to 70°n) peatlands.
result1: a t-test shows that the difference in ch4 emissions between drained (n = 61) and natural peatlands (n = 42) is significant (t = 7.25, p < 0.001).
result2: drainage reduced the ch4 flux by, on average, 84% compared to the original emission values with a mean of 8.3 g c m−2 year−1.
result3: the effect of drainage is similar for all types of drained peatland regardless of the land use and vegetation cover.
result4: paired t-test showed that the change in ch4 flux due to rewetting was not statistically significant with mean flux before restoration being 3.0 ± 3.1 g c m−2 year−1 and after restoration being 4.2 ± 6.3 g c m−2 year−1 (p = .37) with a pooled standard deviation of 6.0.
general_conclusion: drainage significantly (p < .05) reduces the ch4 emissions, on average, by 84%. rewetting of drained peatlands increases the ch4 emissions, on average, by 46%, but the effect was not significant.
knowledge_gaps: uncertainty in ch4 changes over time is due to the limited long-term (>10 years) studies on drained northern peatlands. the published data are insufficient to identify why ch4 emissions from the different sites respond differently after rewetting.

search_strategy: the isi web of science database was used to conduct a literature search for papers published before october 2020 with query terms including ‘water table’, ‘carbon’, ‘methane’, ‘respiration’, ‘nee’, ‘primary production’, ‘drain’ and ‘peatland’. more papers were identified through the chinese cnki platform.
selection_criteria: 1) the study should measure at least water-table depth (wtd) and one flux of co2 or ch4 under both low- and high water-table treatments over the same time period in the same geographic region and have the same natural background and land use type; 2) studies that compare ecosystem responses under altered water table during different time periods, were not incorporated; 3) studies using laboratory peat columns, with synthetic/repacked soils, artificial additions (ameliorant, biochar or compost) or through incubations or have a treatment less than 1 month were also excluded.
data_analysis: the meta-analysis was conducted using the random-effect model (assuming that between-study variations are randomly distributed) and the inverse variance weighting scheme based on the extracted values of sd and sample sizes through the metafor package in r version 3.6.2. the between-study variance (heterogeneity, τ2) was quantified through the restricted maximum-likelihood method. the 95% ci was estimated as the wald-type (that is, normal) ci if the standardized residuals of observations are not strongly deviated from theoretical quantiles of a normal distribution. otherwise, authors applied a bootstrapping ci estimation. they randomly sampled 90% of the original datasets with replacement and estimated the mean effect 1,000 times. the 95% ci was calculated as the 2.5% and 97.5% quantiles of the 1,000 estimates in r 3.6.2. to test the robustness of conclusion towards an overall positive or negative response, authora conducted additional meta-analyses under alternative assumptions. first, they assessed whether the conclusions depended on how individual studies are weighted by applying the fixed effect model with weighting based on the number of replicates and with a uniform weighting. for studies with sample size not published (~20%), they used the average sample size from the database for corresponding gases. for the fixed effect model, they estimated the 95% cis of the mean response through 10,000 times bootstrapping using the bootes library. a significant asymmetry of the funnel plot indicates the bias in compiled studies, which tend to report more results with a significant response compared to studies without. an asymmetry test was conducted through the regtest function of the metafor package. publication bias was not detected in the combined effect of co2 and ch4 (p = 0.31). for co2 or ch4 alone, the funnel plot (p < 0.01) is significantly asymmetrical. publication bias was corrected through the trimfill function in metafor. these tests, the fixed effect models and correction of potential publication bias, pointed to consistent signs of the overall effects.
background: The balance between CO2 sinks and CH4 emissions determines the net climatic impact of peatlands, which remains unclear. This balance is highly sensitive to changes in hydrology, particularly the water-table position that regulates aerobic versus anaerobic conditions in the soil column and therefore the production and consumption processes of CO2 and CH4 in the soil profile.
objective: to quantify the direct impact of lowering the water table on peatland ghg emissions.
result1: overall, water-table increase induced a decrease in co2 emissions from respiration exceeding that of vegetation co2 uptake.
result2: the estimated mean value of changes in ch4 emissions 26 mgco2-eq m−2 h−1 (95% ci: 35, 20), reveals a significant increase of ch4  emissions or a decrease in the ch4 sink.
general_conclusion: this study reveals that despite increasing water-table increases global peatland ch4 emissions, decreased co2 flux outweights the climate benefits of increased ch4 in terms of global warming potential.

search_strategy: the data used in this study were drawn from peer-reviewed articles collected from the web of science with the following keywords: ts = (nee* or co2* or ch4* or n2o) and ts = (coastal wetland* or marsh* or mangrove* or freshwater wetland* or riparian wetland* or peatland* or fen* or bog) and ts = (land use* or agriculture* or cropland* or constructed wetland* or pasture* or aquaculture) with time span of 1950–2018.
selection_criteria: 1) the selected experiments were conducted in the field and included at least one type of natural wetland that was classified as natural coastal wetland, natural riparian wetland or natural peatland; 2) all converted land-use types were directly transformed from the natural wetlands, and land-use types that had undergone multiple land-use transitions, such as restored wetlands, were excluded; 3) the selected experiments were conducted at the same temporal and spatial scales in both the natural wetlands and converted land-use types ; 4) the selected studies provided data for at least one type of greenhouse gas flux.
data_analysis: the response ratio (rr) was used to evaluate the responses of ghg fluxes to lulcc. the weighting function was calculated based on the reciprocal of the variance in individual rrs.
background: Land-use/land-cover change (LULCC) often results in degradation of natural wetlands and affects the dynamics of greenhouse gases. However, the magnitude of changes in greenhouse gas emissions from wetlands undergoing various LULCC types remains unclear.
objective: the main objectives of this study were to quantify the effect of lulcc on greenhouse gas (ghg) emissions in natural wetland ecosystems (peatlands, in this case) and to detect the key environmental variables in relation to changes in ghg emissions and the potential resulting global warming potential effects since lulcc events.
result1: natural peatlands converted to pasture decreased net ecosystem co2 exchange.
result2: NA
general_conclusion: natural peatlands converted to pasture decreased net ecosystem co2 exchange.

search_strategy: the following databases were searched: 1) isi web of knowledge (inc. isi web of science and isi proceedings); 2) science direct; 3) directory of open access journals; 4) copac; 5) index to theses online; 6) agricola; 7) cab abstracts; 8) csa illumina/proquest; 9) scopus. searches of the following internet databases were performed: http://scholar.google.com and http://www.scirus.org (all journal and web sources). no time, language or document type restrictions were applied. websites of the following relevant specialist organisations, identified during the planning stages of the review, were also searched for relevant material.
selection_criteria: 1) relevant population(s): lowland peatland systems in temperate and boreal regions; 2) exposure/intervention: long-term rewetting or draining of peat or peat related soils. agricultural conversion of peat or peat-related soils. afforestation of peat or peat-related soils. agricultural or forestry management on peat or peat-related soils. natural experiments comparing areas of peat or peat-related soils in the same region with different long term (not seasonal or sporadic) hydrology; 3) types of comparator: control or no intervention or before-after comparisons; 4) types of outcome: amount of c or ghg stored in, sequestered or released from soils. other physical measures of c loss or gain from peat or peat-related soils, e.g. erosion, efflux of doc, subsidence and/or accumulation; 5) types of study: any primary study including measures of c or ghg storage, sequestration or release from peat or peat-related soils. studies that measured c or ghg storage, sequestration or release under laboratory conditions were excluded.
data_analysis: meta-analysis was performed in the statistics package r using the ‘metafor’ library using the rma function. this function is equivalent to a random effects meta-analysis; a mixed effects model when moderators are included. marginally significant test results (0.075>p >0.050) are reported for clarity, since thresholds for statistical significance are inherently arbitrary. the presence of significant heterogeneity was assessed using the test for residual heterogeneity (qe). the presence of potential publication bias was assessed for each intervention/exposure group by plotting study effect size against standard error. asymmetry in both axes of the plot may suggest publication bias and was tested for with egger’s z-test.
background: Peatlands constitute a substantial sink of atmospheric carbon dioxide (CO2) via photosynthesis and organic matter accumulation, but also release methane (CH4), nitrous oxide (N2O), and all global soil carbon (C), all of which are powerful greenhouse gases (GHGs). Lowland peats in boreo-temperate regions may store substantial amounts of C and are subject to disproportionately high land-use pressure. Whilst evidence on the impacts of different land management practices on C cycling and GHG fluxes in lowland peats does exist, these data have yet to be synthesised.
objective: the primary question of this review was: what is the impact of land management on ghg and c fluxes of boreo-temperate lowland peatland systems?
result1: no significant patterns in nee co2 release were identified across the three synthesised studies (all of which were from canada) for drained versus undrained peatlands.
result2: drained peatlands released, on average, 125 mg co2 m-2 h-1 (95% ci=6.71 to 243) more co2 through respiration than undrained peatlands, approximating to an annual difference of 11,000 kg co2 ha-1 (95% ci=0.588 to 21.3) resulting from drainage (p=0.038).
result3: drained peatlands may release 0.126 mg ch4 less than undrained peatlands per square metre per hour; equating to an approximate annual additional release of 11.0 kg ch4 ha-1 (95% ci = 22.3 to 0.263) and a 100-year global warming potential difference of 276 kg co2 equivalents ha-1, although this result is only marginally significant (p=0.055).
result4: drained peatlands were found to release, on average, 0.008 mg n2om-2 h-1 (95% ci=0.001 to 0.016) more relative to undrained peatlands (p=0.033).
result5: drier peat released 0.221 mg n2om-2 h-1 (95% ci=0.019 to 0.424) more than wet peat (p=0.032), corresponding to an approximate annual difference of 19.4 kg n2oha-1 (95% ci=1.66 to 37.1) and 5.77 tonnes of co2 equivalents ha-1. however, whilst the results are from three different studies, the data are collected from the same peatland area. furthermore, during the critical appraisal process, these studies were classified as unclear and high in their susceptibility to bias. the results should therefore be treated with caution.
general_conclusion: the results of the systematic review are broadly consistent, or at least do not generally conflict, with current understanding that lowland peat drainage is likely to lead to greater c loss (as co2 and/or doc), increased n2o emissions, and reduced ch4 emissions, and that these responses may, to varying degrees, be reversed by re-wetting and restoration.
knowledge_gaps: few inferences can currently be drawn from the literature regarding the size/ magnitude of effects of peatland agricultural activities in- cluding farming intensity, fertiliser use or irrigation, or of other lowland peat land-uses such as peat extraction or forestry. in consequence there is a need for additional well-designed primary measurement studies of lowland peats under a range of management regimes.

search_strategy:
studies were identifed through computerised searches of the following databases: english nature’s “wildlink”, jstor, isi web of knowledge, index to theses online (1970–2003). the search strategies used combined synonyms for moor burning with target habitat and
species terms. to enhance the search authors provided 52 recognised experts (individuals, organisations and current practitioners) in the field of upland ecology with the provisional short-list of articles and asked them to list any they thought we had missed. the bibliographies of articles accepted for full text viewing were also explored. authors of articles that did not present data that were inferred to exist from methodological descriptions, or that presented data that could not easily be extracted were contacted.
selection_criteria: 1) the study must have compared any form of burning with no burning as a variable; 2) the study must explore as outcome changes in floristic composition interpreted in terms of favourable condition as defined using the upland common standards monitoring (csm) tables.
data_analysis: data from the bog review was synthesised by “vote counting”.
background: Lack of systematic evaluation of the effectiveness of conservation practices has hindered advances in scientific management of biodiversity. Despite the research effort in UK upland plant ecology and the production of numerous reviews and management guidelines, there has been no formal, systematic evaluation of the evidence for the long-term eficiency of rotational burning in maintaining dry heathland vegetation diversity or the condition of wetter heathland vegetation from a conservation perspective.
objective: the objective was to evaluate the effectiveness of burning as a conservation intervention for uk sub-montane, dry dwarf shrub heaths (heath review) and blanket bog (bog review). specifically: 1) does rotational burning of uk sub-montane, dry dwarf-shrub heath maintain vegetation diversity? and 2) does burning degrade uk blanket bog? here, results for objective 2 are reported.
result1: overall, burning tends to promote the dominance of a few species (four data sets) or switch dominance from ericoids to graminoids (two data sets). in general, burning tends to increase the quantity of bare ground (four data sets) although two data sets show a minimal decrease in bare ground. and a decrease in abundance of key species as defined in the common standards monitoring was found in nine data sets. these three outcomes result in unfavourable condition after burning and are therefore, considered indicators of degradation.
result2: minor changes in floristic composition were found in two data sets. this outcome is “neutral” in terms of favourable condition.
result3: summarising, three data sets suggested that burning degrades blanket bog (resulting in failure of the common standar monitoring targets) three do not, whilst five present equivocal outcomes, apparently leaving the overall outcome somewhat equivocal. however, if methodological quality is considered, higher-quality randomised controlled trials suggest that burning does degrade blanket bog (two data sets) or has equivocal effects (three data sets).
general_conclusion: the bog review indicates that there are no consistent changes in floristic composition in response to burning. reviewers’ note: we labelled the results as uncertain due to the lack of statistical testing.
knowledge_gaps: the evidence-base for upland management by burning is insuycient to generate robust management recommendations highlighting the necessity for further work.

search_strategy: the database consisted no published and unpublished articles and reports written in finnish or english. published and unpublished reports were retrieved from the library of mtt agrifood research finland (jokioinen, finland). relevant published journal articles were found with key-word searches of the web of science database, and by searching the reference lists of previously published articles and narrative reviews. the english-language search terms consisted of ‘phosphorus’ together with one of the following: fertilizer, fertilization, cereal*, crop*, vegetable*, grass*, yield*.
selection_criteria: 1) the study had been carried out in finland; 2) the fertilizer used was single superphosphate containing 9% p, 20% calcium (ca) and 11% sulphur (s). for the overall database, p rates ranged from 6 to 100 kg/ha; mean 28 kg/ha; 3) the study had an appropriate control, i.e. fertilization with nitrogen (n) and potassium (k), but no p. n rates ranged from 15 to 200 kg/ha; mean 30 kg/ha,while k rates ranged from 30 to 150 kg/ha; mean 60 kg/ha; 4) the impact of p fertilization on the yields of either cereals, perennial grass mixtures or other crops had been assessed; 5) responses to p fertilization in terms of means of the treatment (= fertilized with pkn, xpkn) and control (= fertilized with kn, xkn) groups, corresponding standard deviations (spkn, skn) and sample sizes (npkn, nkn) were reported in the articles or reports in numerical or graphic form.
data_analysis: the meta-analysis was carried out using the meta win 2.0 statistical program. the log response ratios were combined across the studies using a weighting procedure. in testing, a mixed effects model was used, with the assumption that differences among studies within a class are due to both sampling error and random variation. bias-corrected 95% confidence intervals (cis) around the effect size were generated from 4999 iterations. to test the importance of the sources of variation in determining the sign and magnitude of the treatment effect, studies were subdivided into groups according to the explanatory variables, and between-group heterogeneity was determined using a x2-test statistic, qb.
background: Phosphorous (P) inputs into agricultural soils exceeded the P uptake by crops, leading to considerable annual surpluses (input–output) and substantial accumulation of P in agricultural soils. In Finland, the mean annual P surplus in agricultural soils has decreased from 35 kg/ha in the 1980s to about 8 kg/ha at present. From the agronomic point of view the amount of P lost annually from soils is generally low, but from the perspective of water quality very small annual inputs and changes in P concentrations may change the trophic status of a water body.
objective: the following questions are addressed: 1) is there a difference in yield responses to p fertilization between earlier (1927–1977) and more recent experiments (1977– 2007)?; 2) to what extent are yield responses to p fertilization determined by soil characteristics, such as soil groups, agronomic soil test p, or soil ph?; 3) how does the magnitude of yield responses to p fertilization differ between plant groups and/or cereal species?; 4) what is the impact of the cultivation zone (i.e. the length of the growing period) on yield responses to p fertilization?; 5) what is the impact of p fertilization on cereal yields in relation to productivity without p fertilization?; 6) what p fertilization rates give maximum yield increases? here, results for organic soils are reported.
result1: on organic soils, the yield increase with p fertilization was 15% compared to the control.
result2: NA
general_conclusion: the meta-analysis demonstrated that crop yields in p fertilised organic soils are 15% higher compared to no fertilised organic soils.

search_strategy: the authors conducted a literature search in september 2019 for all papers published over the past decade on greenhouse gases, nitrogen input and wetland ecosystems.
selection_criteria: 1) the control experiment was defined by no nitrogen input or atmospheric nitrogen deposition; 2) non-repetitive experimental studies were excluded; 3) non-experimental studies (such as modeling, meta-analyses, and reviews) were excluded.
data_analysis: the calculated mean effect size considered the confidence intervals (bootstrap cis, bootstrapping by 4999 iterations). if the bootstrap cis had nonzero overlap, the nitrogen input significantly influenced the greenhouse gas emissions. all of the standardized mean differences, the between-group heterogeneity, bootstrap cis and fail-safe number were counted using metawin 2.1.3 software.
background: Greenhouse gas emissions from wetlands are significantly promoted by global nitrogen input for changing the rate of soil carbon and nitrogen cycling, and are substantially affected by soil labile carbon and nitrogen conversely. However, the driving mechanism by which soil labile carbon and nitrogen affect greenhouse gas emissions from wetland ecosystems under global nitrogen input is not well understood.
objective: the authors used soil carbon dioxide emissions, methane emissions, nitrous oxide emissions, soil labile carbon and nitrogen, and soil microbial biomass to address the following questions: (i) how do the soil greenhouse gas emissions from wetland ecosystems fluctuate as a result of varying nitrogen input in terms of rates, compounds and environmental factors? (ii) what key factors affect soil greenhouse gas emissions as a response to nitrogen input? (iii) what is the major effect oflabile compounds on greenhouse gas emissions from wetland ecosystems under global nitrogen input? here, results for peatlands are reported.
result1: for peatland, nitrogen input significantly promoted n2o emission.
result2: for peatland, nitrogen input does not significantly affect ch4 emission.
general_conclusion: nitrogen input has a greater effect on n2o emission from peatlands than other wetlands while has no a significant effect on ch4 emission in peatlands.

search_strategy: the following databases were searched: 1) isi web of knowledge (inc. isi web of science and isi proceedings); 2) science direct; 3) directory of open access journals; 4) copac; 5) index to theses online; 6) agricola; 7) cab abstracts; 8) csa illumina/proquest; 9) scopus. searches of the following internet databases were performed: http://scholar.google.com and http://www.scirus.org (all journal and web sources). no time, language or document type restrictions were applied. websites of the following relevant specialist organisations, identified during the planning stages of the review, were also searched for relevant material.
selection_criteria: 1) relevant population(s): lowland peatland systems in temperate and boreal regions; 2) exposure/intervention: long-term rewetting or draining of peat or peat related soils. agricultural conversion of peat or peat-related soils. afforestation of peat or peat-related soils. agricultural or forestry management on peat or peat-related soils. natural experiments comparing areas of peat or peat-related soils in the same region with different long term (not seasonal or sporadic) hydrology; 3) types of comparator: control or no intervention or before-after comparisons; 4) types of outcome: amount of c or ghg stored in, sequestered or released from soils. other physical measures of c loss or gain from peat or peat-related soils, e.g. erosion, efflux of doc, subsidence and/or accumulation; 5) types of study: any primary study including measures of c or ghg storage, sequestration or release from peat or peat-related soils. studies that measured c or ghg storage, sequestration or release under laboratory conditions were excluded.
data_analysis: meta-analysis was performed in the statistics package r using the ‘metafor’ library using the rma function. this function is equivalent to a random effects meta-analysis; a mixed effects model when moderators are included. marginally significant test results (0.075>p >0.050) are reported for clarity, since thresholds for statistical significance are inherently arbitrary. the presence of significant heterogeneity was assessed using the test for residual heterogeneity (qe). the presence of potential publication bias was assessed for each intervention/exposure group by plotting study effect size against standard error. asymmetry in both axes of the plot may suggest publication bias and was tested for with egger’s z-test.
background: Peatlands constitute a substantial sink of atmospheric carbon dioxide (CO2) via photosynthesis and organic matter accumulation, but also release methane (CH4), nitrous oxide (N2O), and all global soil carbon (C), all of which are powerful greenhouse gases (GHGs). Lowland peats in boreo-temperate regions may store substantial amounts of C and are subject to disproportionately high land-use pressure. Whilst evidence on the impacts of different land management practices on C cycling and GHG fluxes in lowland peats does exist, these data have yet to be synthesised.
objective: the primary question of this review was: what is the impact of land management on ghg and c fluxes of boreo-temperate lowland peatland systems?
result1: farming intensity was not found to have a significant effect on n2o emission across the included studies.
result2: farming intensity had no significant effect on ch4 emission across the four included studies.
result3: no significant difference in ch4 emissions was identified between grazed and mown peat soils.
general_conclusion: farming intensity was not found to have a significant effect on n2o emission across the included studies. farming intensity had no significant effect on ch4 emission across the four included studies. no significant difference in ch4 emissions was identified between grazed and mown peat soils.
knowledge_gaps: few inferences can currently be drawn from the literature regarding the size/ magnitude of effects of peatland agricultural activities in- cluding farming intensity, fertiliser use or irrigation, or of other lowland peat land-uses such as peat extraction or forestry. in consequence there is a need for additional well-designed primary measurement studies of lowland peats under a range of management regimes.

search_strategy: a literature search of the web of science (1864–2015) and agricola (1927–2015) databases was performed in september 2015 using the key words “convolvulus arvensis,” “field bindweed,” “creeping jenny,” and “perennial morning glory.”
selection_criteria: selection criteria: (1) included studies were replicated field studies that assessed the relative efficacy of stand-alone or integrated weed management techniques taking place in annual cropping or perennial systems; (2) studies using herbicides were included only if the applied herbicide was approved for use, if it was applied within recommended rates and if the mecanism of action of the herbicide was known and classified; (3) studies have to report control/treatment comparisons that published quantitative response measurements for aboveground density, cover, biomass, frequency, survival, or percent control (measured from 0% to 100%) of c. arvensis.
data_analysis: non-treated control treatments were assigned as the treatment with the least management inputs. the mean, sample size, and standard deviation or standard error (when available) values were extracted for each response in each paper for a treated group and a non-treated group of convolvulus arvensis in annual or in perennial crops separately. each response ratio was weighted using sample sizes rather than standard deviation. bootstrapping methods were implemented with 1000 iterations to calculate a mean effect size and 95% confidence interval (ci) for each treatment category. the effect of integrated pest management compared to single control was estimated through an indirect comparison.
background: Field bindweed (Convolvulus arvensis L.) is a persistent, perennial weed species that infests a variety of temperate habitats around the globe.
objective: the objective of the study is to evaluate the efficacy of general management approaches and impacts on crop yield by conducting a series of meta-analyses using published studies focusing on c. arvensis management in annual cropping and perennial systems. here, the results regarding the impact of integrated management (combining at least two management techniques with or without herbicides) on crop yield are reported.
result1: integrated multitactic techniques, with or without herbicide use, resulted in improved crop yield compared to untreated control, while herbicide application only did not have a positive effect on crop yield relative to untreated controls.
result2: 95% confidence interval of non-herbicide integrated and herbicide effect overlapped, showing that non-herbicide integrated had a similar impact on crop yield than herbicide used alone.
general_conclusion: this meta-analysis shows that c. arvensis control using integrated management with herbicide improved yield compared to herbicide use alone, while non-herbicide integrated techniques and herbicide use alone had similar effect on crop yield.
knowledge_gaps: integrated management was studied less frequently (n=2 for herbicide integrated, n=8 non-herbicide integrated respectively) than herbicide alone (n =119).

background: Although stand-alone and integrated management techniques have been cited as viable approaches to managing Canada thistle [Cirsium arvense (L.) Scop.], it continues to impact annual cropping and perennial systems worldwide.
objective: the objectives of this study were to assess short- and long-term effectiveness of management techniques for controlling c. arvense in annual and perennial cropping systems and to determine whether and how management techniques for c. arvense control impact crop yield in annual cropping systems. here, the results regarding the impact of integrated management (combining at least two management techniques with or without herbicides) on on crop yield in annual crops are reported.

general_conclusion: integrated techniques (with herbicides) were more effective than solely applying herbicides for controlling of c. arvense in annual cropping systems, while its efficacy was uncertain in perennial cropping systems. integrated techniques (without herbicides resulted in a more efficient control of c. arvense than applying herbicides in perennial cropping systems, while the results were uncertain in annual cropping systems.

background: The primary management tactic for lepidopteran pests of cotton in the United States of America (USA) is the use of transgenic cotton that produces Bacillus thuringiensis Berliner (Bt) toxins. The primary target pests of this technology are Helicoverpa zea (Boddie) and Heliothis virescens (F.) in the eastern and central Cotton Belt of the USA. Concerns over the evolution of resistance in H. zea to Bt toxins and scrutiny of the necessity of Bt crops has escalated.
objective: the objective of this meta-analysis is to determine the impact of bt varieties on insecticides use, pest abundance and crop yield, compared to non-bt varieties in the usa. here the results regarding the impact of bt varieties on crop yield are reported.

general_conclusion: overall, the use of maize and cotton bt varieties improved crop yield, compared to non-bt varieties.

search_strategy: an extensive literature search was conducted to compile effect size estimates and associated vari- ables to perform a robust meta-analysis. searches were performed in agricola, the wiley online library, agris: fao, the sustainable agriculture and natural resource management knowledge base, the agriculture, life science and natural sciences database, and google scholar. search terms included ‘intercropping’, ‘conservation agriculture’, ‘companion planting’, ‘mixed planting’, ‘mixed farming systems’, alone or in combination with ‘africa’, and/or ‘development’.
selection_criteria: five pre-established criteria. the study had to provide information on (1) treatment means, (2) the standard deviation (sd), or the standard error of the means (se), the standard error of the difference (sed), least significant difference (lsd), or the variance, and (3) the number of treatment replicates (n). the study had to (4) include a randomized experimental design and (5) utilize control plots.
data_analysis: data were coded in two sets; s1 and s2. only the s2 data set contained studies that assessed ipm system. studies were only considered if the experimental design included more than one pest management technique and if at least one of the practices used in the system could be considered a biological or cultural control. information that was coded included the study identifier, study year, yield of ipm, and non-ipm treatments in kg/ha, whether or not the ipm system in the study was inclusive of intercropping practices (yes/no), ipm yield treatment sd (or some other measure of variation), country the study was conducted in, and descriptions of the ipm treatment combinations. the effect sizes (ratios) were combined via a random-effects model, which takes into account the between-study and within-study variation. the meta-analysis was run on the effect sizes for the calculated yield ratio of ipm/non-ipm treatment. subgroup moderators for these effect sizes included the inclusion or exclusion of intercropping practices in the ipm systems. publication bias was analysed.
background: There is a critical need for the adoption of agricultural practices that conserve natural capital and enhance crop yields. The sustainable intensification of agricultural systems requires more systemic approaches, such as conservation agricultural (CA), and integrated pest management (IPM).
objective: determine the (1) impact of intercropping systems on relative crop yield, ler, and gross income in africa, (2) effect of concurrent management factors that might influence intercropping system effects, such as the presence of a leguminous or root crops or the utilization of fertilizers, pesticides or minimum/no-till, and (3) efficacy of intercropping in reducing pest number and increasing yield when used in ipm systems. only the third objective is considered here.
result1: according to the ipm/no ipm effect size ratios, ipm systems increased yield by 20% and decreased the number of pests by 15% (p < .001).
result2: statistical heterogeneity was not significant for either effect size measure, but significant moderator differences were observed.
result3: yield within the ipm systems that integrated intercropping practices was, on average, 24% less than those that did not.
result4: moderator analysis of the ipm/no ipm ratio for effects on pest number revealed that ipm treatments inhibited 33–38% more weeds than pathogenic and macro-invertebrate pests (p = .001).
general_conclusion: integrated pest management increased crop yield
