fpid: water-saving irrigation practices in non-flooded lands
search_strategy:
google scholar (https://xueshu.soogle.top/), elsevier (science direct) (https:// www.sciencedirect.com/search), china national knowledge infrastructure (https://www.cnki. net/) and baidu scholar (https://xueshu.baidu.com/) were used to collect relevant previous
studies from 2001 to 2021 in this study. the key words included “subsurface drip irrigation” or “drip irrigation mode” or “irrigation method” or “buried depth of drip pipe” and “water use efficiency or water productivity” and “yield”.
selection_criteria: the following criteria were further used to screen these publications: 1) experiments were conducted in the open field and greenhouse (pot/rainproof experiments were excluded); 2) yield, iwp (yield/irrigation water applied) or wp (yield/crop evapotranspiration (et) or yield/total water applied by irrigation and rainfall)) data under subsurface drip irrigation (ssdi) and surface drip irrigation (sdi) must be paired; 3) the means, standard deviations (sd) and the number of replications (n) could be directly derived from the publication or could be calculated from the reported data.
data_analysis: because the heterogeneity among studies was greater than 50%, a random-effect model was adopted. stata/ic 15.1 and microsoft excel were used to conduct the meta-analysis.
background: The rapid population growth and economic development, climate change and irregular rainfall will inevitably intensify the competition of water resources, resulting in the reduction of agricultural irrigation water. In recent years, subsurface drip irrigation (SSDI), as an efficient water-saving irrigation technology, has been widely used in crop production, but its effects on crop yield, irrigation water productivity (IWP) and water productivity (WP) vary with field managements, climatic conditions and soil properties.
objective: a global meta-analysis was conducted to quantify the effects of subsurface drip irrigation (ssdi) on the yield, iwp and wp of crops, vegetables and fruits compared to surface drip irrigation (sdi), and identify the optimal application conditions (field managements, climatic conditions and soil properties) that increase yield, iwp and wp under ssdi systems, so as to further improve our understanding of the responses of crops to ssdi.
result1: generally, subsurface drip irrigation (ssdi) significantly increased the iwp and wp of crops, vegetables and fruits, with the percentage increases of iwp by 6.75% (95%ci: 6.13–7.36%) and wp by 3.97% (95%ci: 3.22–4.74%) across 358 and 187 comparisons compared to surface drip irrigation (sdi)
result2: NA
general_conclusion: subsurface drip irrigation significantly increased the irrigation wp and wp of crops, vegetables and fruits, with the percentage increases of irrigation water productivity by 6.75% (95%ci: 6.13–7.36%) and water productivity by 3.97% (95%ci: 3.22–4.74%) compared to surface drip irrigation.
knowledge_gaps: the responses of yield, irrigated water use efficiency and water use efficiency of crops, vegetables and fruits under sub-surface drip irrigation (ssdi) were evaluated in this meta-analysis. nevertheless, other factors such as the frequency of drip irrigation and fertilisation, seasonal temperature and precipitation also had influences on the results. future studies need to consider more factors affecting the application of ssdi. the data were not sufficient for the irrigation proportion group > 100% and soil ph < 7, so the results need to be further verified. besides, the authors only considered the responses of crops, vegetables and fruits under ssdi in this meta-analysis in recent 20 years, but the alfalfa and other grasses and studies before 2001 were not considered.

fpid: water-saving irrigation practices in non-flooded lands
search_strategy: the database of this meta-analysis arose from peer-reviewed articles published between 2000 and 2020 and referenced in scopus and web of sciences databases. the key words of the search of articles were: “maize or corn or mays” and “yield or productivity” and “irrigation or water” and “stress or deficit or shortage or drought) and ”stage or phase or step or level”.
selection_criteria: an article was selected when it meets the following selection criteria: (1) the results are from experiments on maize crop; (2) the article reports at least one of the three response variables (grain yield, actual crop evapotranspiration, and crop water productivity); (3) the article presents the standard deviations (sd) of the optimal irrigation (no stress) and di stress treatments, or the level of significance of the results, and the number of replicates. articles that reported data from pot experiments were excluded from this review.
data_analysis: this statistical meta-analysis was computed using the metafor package with r. this meta-analysis used a random effect model to merge the studies effect sizes, to compute the pooled effect sizes, and to access the trend of yield, wp and etc act under di stress across climates, growth stages, nitrogen, phosphorus and potassium fertilizer rates, soil textures, and crop cycle. the random effect model was used because the difference of variance between studies was statistically significant. we quantified the heterogeneity of true effect sizes between studies using the p-value associated with the heterogeneity test (q), and i2 statistics. meta-regression analysis was used to assess the relationship between response variable effect sizes and di stress at different maize growth stages.
background: Deficit irrigation (DI) has been implemented in arid regions to improve water productivity while maintaining or increasing crop yield.
objective: authors carried out a global scale meta-analysis to (1) quantify the response ratios of grain yield (gy), actual crop evapotranspiration (etc act) and water productivity (wp) under di stress. then, authors(2) examined the effects of nitrogen (n), phosphorus (p) and potassium (k) fertilizer rates, climate, soil texture, di application mode, and maize growing cycle on gy, etc act and wp.
result1: water productivity (wp) increased by 3%, 4% and 6% under nitrogen, phosphorus and potassium application, respectively.
result2: NA
general_conclusion: wue improved by 9% on heavy soils compared to both light and medium soils, indicating that heavy soils are more suitable for growing maize under deficit irrigation. the findings imply that deficit irrigation stress could be a promising strategy for water management in maize cropping systems while considering appropriate soil, growing stages, varieties and climate.
knowledge_gaps: 1) further studies may consider nutrient uptake associated with deficit irrigation stress. 2) future investigations should be geared towards improving the yield potential of early maturing maize varieties to reinforce their use under deficit irrigation stress.

fpid: water-saving irrigation practices in non-flooded lands
search_strategy: a comprehensive search for peer-reviewed literature published from january 1990 to january 2016 related to the effects of irrigation on wheat yields was performed. literature were searched in three databases: web of science, springerlink, and the china academic journal network publishing database using the terms including ‘irrigation,’ ‘wheat,’ and ‘china’.
selection_criteria: (1) comparisons between non-irrigation and irrigation practices; (2) at least one parameter of interest (grain yield, yield components, water productivity, and et) was reported; and (3) the experimental location was stated. studies that described only the relationship between irrigation and wheat yield without a non-irrigation practice, and those that did not provide clear descriptions of the experimental methods were rejected.
data_analysis: the natural log of the response ratio (irrigation/non-irrigation) was applied to represent the effect size in our meta-analysis. the weight of individual observations was calculated by replications, with weights = (n irrigation × n non-irrigation)/(n irrigation + n non-irrigation), where n irrigation and n non-irrigation are the number of replicates for irrigation and non-irrigation practices, respectively. bootstrapping procedures were conducted with a 95% confidence interval for weighted mean effect sizes using 4999 iterations.
background: Irrigation is a crucial measure for ensuring food security; however, the complex linkages among yield increases, water productivity, and greenhouse gas (GHG) emissions are unclear for irrigated wheat production in China.
objective: here a meta-analysis was conducted to determine the trade-offs among yield increase, water productivity, and ghg emissions in irrigated chinese wheat production systems.
result1: under irrigated systems, water productivity using irrigation did not increase, but rather decreased by 6%.
result2: water productivity in optimized irrigation amount systems increased by 11%, from 15.7 to 17.5 kg ha−1 mm−1. the high water productivity under optimized irrigation amount systems is similar to the 17.8 kg ha−1 mm−1 found with non-irrigated systems. irrigation-water productivity under optimized irrigation amounts increased by 50%, from 7.5 to 11.2 kg ha−1 mm−1.
result3: notably, compared with conventional irrigation periods, improved irrigation periods increased the irrigation-water productivity by 54%, and also led to a 6% increase in water productivity.
result4: compared with conventional irrigation amounts, the practice of using optimized irrigation amounts decreased the volume of irrigation water by 41%.
general_conclusion: compared with conventional irrigation amounts, optimised irrigation amounts and optimised irrigation period increased water productivity. optimised irrigation amounts and optimised irrigation period decreased irrigation water supply by 41% compared with conventional irrigation amounts.

search_strategy: the authors searched the peer-reviewed literatures for publications between 1980 and 2015 that reported on water in maize production using the web of science database and the china national knowledge infrastructure. different combinations of searching terms included “maize” or “corn” and “evapotranspiration (et)” or “seasonal water supply” and “irrigation” and “water use efficiency” or “water productivity” in the abstract or keywords were used for data extraction.
selection_criteria: the data had to be generated from field experiments, rather than pot experiments, experiments under rain-proof shelters or model simulations; the details of experimental sites had to be provided; and maize yield and seasonal water supply had to be documented or calculated based on published data; only irrigated maize were considered.
data_analysis: in this study, reports including deficit irrigation and tradition irrigation treatments from the 473 previous studies (1,028 paired measurements) were separately analyzed using the meta-analysis method to evaluate the general response of yield and wp to different deficit irrigation levels. authors used an unweighted resampling method based on a fixed-effects model, and corrected for bias, with 95% confidence intervals (cis) and a bootstrapping procedure. in addition, the available key factors from 473 studies including seasonal precipitation (n = 3,274), both seasonal irrigation amounts and precipitation amounts (n = 2,924), soil organic matter (n = 1,780), soil bulk density (n = 2.093), and soil ph (n = 2,172) were used to analyze how the yield and wp responded to those influencing factors. the authors performed pearson’s correlation analysis to identify these factors influencing maize yield and wp.
background: Detailed knowledge of the relationships between water productivityb (WP) and climate, soil characteristics and management practices is critical to determining how to close WP gaps at the global scale. However, a quantitative synthesis of the response of WP to all constraining factors and an understanding of the exploitable WP gaps at current production levels are still lacking.
objective: the authors conducted a meta-analysis of peer-reviewed studies to determine wp in different regions with irrigated maize production; evaluate the responses of wp and yield to climate, soil conditions and water management practices; quantify global wp gaps and yield gaps with limited and unlimited water supplies; and illustrate the potential benefits of improving wp for global maize supply and water consumption in the future.
result1: when deficit irrigation was >80%, wp increased by 7.1% with no loss of yield. in areas with 50–80% deficit irrigation, wp increased by 4.2–6.9%, but yield decreased by 10.5–20.2%.
result2: wp did not change significantly when 30–50% deficit irrigation was applied, but yield decreased sharply (−22%), compared to 50–60% deficit irrigation.
result3: deficit irrigation levels of <30% reduced both maize yield (−29%) and wp (−6.9%).
general_conclusion: the impacts of deficit irrigation on water productivity depend on deficit irrigation level. in this study, deficit irrigation at levels below 50% resulted in lower water productivity.
knowledge_gaps: 1) first, other field management practices may affect maize wp and yield, although those factors were difficult to investigate in the present analysis due to a lack of information from the individual studies. additionally, while critical soil and environmental factors were considered, other experimental variables which may affect maize and yield and wp were not provided in many studies, such as soil water supply, effective accumulated temperature, sunshine hours, soil texture, etc. 2) second, future research should focus on collecting measurements from farmers’ fields to generate more robust outcomes. 3) third, more effort are needed in evaluating potential wp under specific conditions or on smaller scales to minimize the current large uncertainties in global or regional estimates. 4) fourth, future climate change may affect maize yield and wp, although predicting these changes are complicated and general conclusions have not been made due to the intricate interactions of temperature, precipitation and co2. 5) greater attention in the future should be paid to field observations of wp in less-studied regions to minimize data biases.

fpid: water-saving irrigation practices in non-flooded lands
search_strategy: the search was conducted on google scholar and web of science using the different combinations of the following keywords: vegetable yield and deficit irrigation or moisture stress or water stress or drought stress. based on the availability of literature, eight major vegetable crops, potato (solanum tuberosum l.), tomato (solanum lycopersicum) l.), pepper (capsicum annuum l.), eggplant (solanum melongena l.), onion (allium cepa l.), cucumber (cucumis sativus l.), muskmelon (cucumis melo l.) and watermelon (citrullus lanatus l.) were identified for inclusion in the meta-analysis. thereafter, a thorough search was conducted for individual crops.
selection_criteria: should be an open-field or greenhouse plot study (pot studies were excluded), provided yield data for fi and dis; provided detailed information on irrigation criteria and di was given as a percentage of fi; provided information on soil texture of experimental site or percentage of sand, silt and clay particles in the soil; provided mean yield and sample size for individual irrigation levels.
data_analysis: the metaxl version 5.345 was employed to conduct the statistical analysis using the random effect model at a 95% confidence interval (ci). the possibility of any publication bias in the yield and wp data was examined using funnel plots46 and sensitivity analyses were performed to assess the influence of individual observations on mean effect sizes and corrected for biases. several distinct meta-analyses were conducted to assess the influence of different variables including, crop species, soil texture, production system (open-field or greenhouse), and climate on yield and wp effects under different di levels. any irrigation level or considered variables having less than two comparisons were excluded from the analysis. for each meta-analysis, fi (100%) was defined as control. a positive hedges’ g value indicated an increase in yield/wp for di over fi and a negative value indicated a reduction in yield/wp under di compared to fi. the significance of effect size is determined by the output ci.
background: Strategies promoting efficient water use and conserving irrigation water are needed to attain water security to meet growing food demands. This
objective: this meta-analysis study evaluated the effect of deficit irrigation (di) strategy on eight vegetables to provide a quantitative estimate of yield and water productivity (wp) responses
result1: the wp gains ranged from 8.1 to 30.1%, with 35–50%fi recording the highest benefits.
result2: NA
general_conclusion: positive effect of deficit irrigation on wue when 35 to 99% of full irrigation amount is applied, and no effect otherwise.

search_strategy: in february 2011, relevant published peer-reviewed articles on the impact of hydrological alterations on the biota in floodplain wetlands were searched using the electronic databases isi web of knowledge and scopus. no grey literature was used in this systematic review. possible bias resulting from this exclusion was verified.
selection_criteria: 1) relevant subject: community composition in any floodplain wetland. studies were included irrespective of habitat or spatial scale, except for experimental studies with a focus on micro scale processes; 2) types of intervention: human induced alteration of the natural flow regime, described in quantitative units; 3) types of comparator: undisturbed reference conditions in space or time (before-after or control- impact studies); 4) types of outcome: a quantitative comparison in terms of community composition (species richness, abundance or density).
data_analysis: for both metrics a random effect meta-analysis was used to derive a weighted mean for all datasets and test the global mean effect of flow regulation on the biodiversity of floodplains. publication bias was assessed by inspecting funnel plots of asymmetry along with formal regression tests. heterogeneity was assessed by inspection of forest-plots and formal tests of heterogeneity q and i2. the meta-analyses were performed with the ‘metafor’ package available in r 2.15.1 software.
background: Alteration of natural flow regime is considered a major threat to biodiversity in river flood- plain ecosystems. Measurements of quantitative relationships between flow regime change and biodiversity are, however, incomplete and inconclusive. This hampers the assessment of human impact on riverine floodplain wetlands in global biodiversity evaluations.
objective: to uncover and quantify any general patterns at the regional and global level, we systematically searched the scientific literature for existing datasets relating community composition to hydrological change.
result1: the analysis showed that on average, alteration of the natural flow regime has a negative impact on biodiversity in floodplain wetlands. the meta-analysis of all mean species abundance datasets results in a pooled effect size of 0.482 —a significant divergence from the no effect level (p < 0.0001).
result2: publication bias for mean species abundance was low (regression test, p>0.5), and the funnel plots showed no asymmetry. the high values for q and i2 indicated that the datasets did not share a common effect size (p(q)<0.0001
result3: when considering the datasets on species richness, the all-encompassing meta-analysis also showed a significant effect (p<0.01), with a pooled log-ratio of -0.140 (i.e. a 28 % reduction). there was no evidence for publication bias and, in contrast to the species abundance, there was no evidence for heterogeneity (p(q)>0.1); the low values for q and i2 indicated that the variance in effect size values was not higher than expected from natural variation and the studies might share a common ‘true’ effect size.
general_conclusion: the meta-analysis showed that alteration of a natural flow regime reduces the mean species abundance by more than 50 % on average, and species richness by more than 25 %. impact on species richness and abundance tends to be related to the degree of hydrological alteration.

search_strategy: the authors conducted a systematic literature search to identify potentially relevant publications containing information about the effectiveness of wetland restoration, the performance of restored wetlands, and the rate and timeframe of recovery. eligible publications included published and gray literature that contained information regarding the ecological recovery of restored wetlands in the northern gulf of mexico (limited to the usa). no restriction on publication year was placed. search was not restricted to english language publications, but no relevant non-english publications were found during the search. authors searched 11 relevant databases using the database aggregator service proquest. the authors performed a keyword search of these databases in december 2013, using different structured combinations of eight different basic search statements. then, the authors updated our literature search in april 2017 to identify additional relevant studies published between 2014 and early 2017.
selection_criteria: 1) the study evaluated a marsh or wetland restoration action (in 2014, we included the following restoration techniques: wetland creation, thin-layer sediment addition, marsh terracing, sediment and fresh-water diversions, canal backfilling, or other coastal marsh restoration methods; in 2017, only wetland creation and thin-layer sediment addition were included); 2) the restored marsh or wetland was located in the northern gulf of mexico; 3) in the same year, the author(s) measured at least one ecological parameter (e.g., soil, vegetation, fish, wildlife) in a restored marsh or wetland, and in one or more natural marshes that could serve as reference sites; 4) the restored site included one treatment over an ecologically relevant area (on the order of acres) and did not represent a small-scale experiment.
data_analysis: all computations were done in sas version 9.3; in particular, proc mixed was used to fit the random effects meta-analysis. the authors tested a number of characteristics as covariates to understand what factors could be driving both variance and observed effects. covariates included geographic location, size of restored site, marsh type (fresh, brackish, or saline), landscape position, active vegetation vs. passive vegetation recovery, and sand content of sediment used in restoration. the authors created funnel plots by plotting the estimated ln rr against the inverse of its within-study se.
background: The extent to which ecological properties of restored coastal wetlands in the northern Gulf of Mexico recover to natural wetland conditions has not been synthesized.
objective: the authors addressed the following three questions: 1) does wetland restoration in the northern gulf of mexico result in the convergence of multiple wetland properties to reference site conditions? 2) are there differences in the degree and rate of convergence for different metrics of vegetation condition or different soil properties? 3) does the degree of convergence for particular metrics depend on salinity (also characterized as wetland type), position of sampling locations within the wetland, or on characteristics of the restoration?
result1: the mean rr for the vegetation cover response group began at age zero at − 1.1274 (se = 0.202, not shown), meaning restored values were 68% less than reference values, and crossed the zero (equality) line at approximately 5 years following restoration.
result2: vegetation cover was 50% lower at restored sites compared to reference sites over the first 5 years of restoration.
result3: the mean rr for the aboveground biomass response group (including aboveground biomass, productivity, and stem density) began at age zero at 0.284 (se = 0.110, not shown), meaning restored values were 33% greater than reference values, had a negative slope, and crossed the zero (equality) line at approximately 17 years following restoration.
general_conclusion: mean recovery trajectories for vegetation cover indicated that mean values for restored sites reached reference site conditions within 30 years following restoration. aboveground biomass was 25% higher at restored sites compared to reference sites over the first 5 years of restoration.

search_strategy: the authors identified papers by conducting a keyword search in 12 databases available through the service proquest using a standardized set of relevant search terms. then, they conducted an author-based literature search where we included the authors identified in the keyword search with four or more publications; we also included three additional authors who appeared three times in the keyword search and who wrote papers we previously found relevant. lastly, they identified additional papers using online search engines (e.g., google scholar, louisiana state university electronic thesis and dissertation library), accessing individual digital libraries, and reviewing previously collected papers.
selection_criteria: the authors reviewed the papers identified during the literature searches for relevant data on nekton density of coastal habitats in the northern gom.
data_analysis: the othe authors fitted a weighted linear mixed model with the random effects of a study (i.e., literature reference) and record (i.e., observation) within a study, a fixed effect of categorical age (since restoration began), and weights equal to the inverses of the sums of the variances of response ratio and random effects. the random effects were tested using likelihood ratio tests (χ2 with 1 degree of freedom). authors calculated 95% cis for the mean at each age.
background: While the goal of many coastal habitat restoration projects is to achieve functional equivalency to reference sites, evaluation of restoration success is typically performed on site-specific scales, which can restrict the applicability of lessons learned to other sites. Thus, characterizing general trends in how restored sites compare to reference sites across locations, habitat types, and key taxonomic groups would be useful for restoration planners and practitioners in the northern Gulf of Mexico region charged with designing, implementing, and monitoring coastal restoration in the coming decades.
objective: the authors conducted a systematic literature review and meta-analysis to evaluate regional trends in nekton utilization of restored and reference marshes in the northern gulf of mexico.
result1: for marsh habitat samples, mean densities of total nekton at restored sites were smaller than at paired reference sites, both during the "early" period following restoration and the "late" period.
result2: results for total crustaceans in marsh habitats were similar to total nekton, with mean densities at restored sites 35.6% of reference locations (95% ci: 16.6–76.7%) during the early period and 71.3% of reference locations (95% ci: 42.7–119.2%) during the late period.
result3: mean relative densities of fish at marsh habitat sites were highly variable and somewhat lower at restored sites during both time periods.
general_conclusion: a generally increasing trend in total nekton and total crustacean densities was observed over the first 15 years following restoration; mean densities at restored sites were comparable to paired reference locations by approximately year 13. findings from this study indicate that marsh restoration may not consistently result in nekton production similar to that ofnatural sites, particularly in the earlier years following restoration when baseline ecosystem processes are developing.

search_strategy: thompson isi’s web of science was used to search for relevant peer-reviewed journal articles. in addition, authors screened all papers in aquatic botany and wetlands from 2006 to 2008 to improve the keywords used in the literature search. authors searched thomson isi’s web of science bibliographic database in march 2010, and retained all papers published to december 2009. the search was run as a single combination string of “environment” and “flow” and “plant” and “plant response” not “exclude”.
selection_criteria: exclusion criteria: 1) were not primarily about wetland plants (e.g. were concerned with fish, invertebrates or waterbirds); 2) papers simply described the vegetation and did not explore a causal relationship; 3) their focus was a process like methane or co2 flux, heavy metal pollution, or wastewater treatment.
data_analysis: the eco evidence method was used for the systematic review. in eco evidence, each study is assigned a weight based on its inferential strength (study design and replication). studies that better control for confounding [e.g. before-after, control-impact (baci) models] are given more weight than less rigorous designs. the default study weights in eco evidence were originally set using an expert consultation process. although the study weights can be altered by the user if there is justification for doing so, the default values were used. the primary assessment relies on the comparison of the sum of study weights in favour of the hypothesis against the sum of weights for those that refute the hypothesis (no response or a response opposite to that predicted). eco evidence uses a threshold to determine whether or not there is support for a cause–effect relation. the default threshold value of 20 points (summed across multiple studies) was originally derived from the same expert consultation process used to derive the default study weights. like the study weights, this threshold value may be altered by the user, but we used the default value of 20.
background: Changes to the natural flow regime caused by river regulation adversely affect wetland plant communities. A natural flow regime is important for maintaining the ecological integrity of rivers and their floodplains. Environmental flow allocations must have a solid scientific basis, since they may face political or legal challenges. However, iIt is often claimed that we have relatively little knowledge of ecological responses to flow alteration.
objective: to analyze the literature for evidence of causal relationships between components of wetland water regimes (waterlogging, inundation, depth, duration, frequency, timing) and their effects on plant establishment, growth, reproduction, assemblage composition and diversity. authors used the following sequence of questions: is there any effect of individual water regime components on individual wetland plant responses? if yes, then is the effect consistent, or are there inconsistent results between different studies caused by differences among taxa, wetland types, etc.? if no, is this because the studies did not detect an effect (either because there was none or because of limitations of experimental design); or because there is insufficient information in the literature, indicating a research gap?
result1: while the evidence was not consistent enough to support the hypothesis that waterlogging increases wetland plant establishment, the opposite hypothesis of decreased establishment was rejected. similarly, while there was not support for the hypotheses that increasing inundation, water depth and flood duration decrease plant establishment, the hypotheses of opposite effect was also rejected.
result2: regarding inundation, the response for total biomass was inconsistent. authors did not find support for the hypothesis that increasing water depth decreases total biomass, but did reject the opposite hypothesis of increased biomass. the evidence did not support the hypothesis that plant growth is increased in waterlogged substrates versus inundated, but the opposite hypothesis of decreased growth was also rejected. the evidence for effects of flood duration on the growth of wetland plants was inconsistent.
result3: the evidence for a relationship between increased inundation and reproductive output was inconsistent. there was evidence to support a negative effect of increasing water depth on the reproductive output of wetland plants. authors rejected the hypothesis in both directions that increased inundation duration affects reproductive output.
result4: authors found support for the hypotheses that inundation decreases plant diversity. they did not find support for the hypotheses that increasing water depth and flood duration decrease plant diversity, but were able to reject the opposite hypotheses of increased diversity. the hypothesis in both directions that flood frequency affects plant diversity was also rejected.
general_conclusion: overall, results show that increases in the magnitude of water regime components are related to negative effects on plant characteristics. within this, the strongest set of results related inundation depth to negative impacts on nearly all plant characteristics. waterlogging (as opposed to complete inundation) was generally related to improvements in plant characteristics, but there was insufficient evidence to test several hypotheses. a large number of hypotheses showed inconsistent effects of water regime components, reflecting the diversity of responses of different plant taxa, wetland types, and study methods. reviewers’ note: we labelled the results as uncertain due to the lack of statistical testing.
knowledge_gaps: authors were unable to find sufficient evidence to test 10 of the hypotheses, and are confident that these represent true knowledge gaps that can only be filled by future targeted research.

search_strategy: relevant journal articles were found by using key-word searches in web of science database and by looking through the reference lists of previous narrative reviews. the following combinations of english language search terms were used: phragmites australis or common reed, and either cut*, burn*, grazing, manage*, bird*, insect*, invertebrate*, vegetation, plant* or conservation.
selection_criteria: 1) the study has been made in europe; 2) the method of reed management used has been either harvesting, mowing, burning or grazing; 3) the study had an appropriate control (unmanaged stands); 4) impact of reedbed management on either plants, invertebrates and/or birds have been assessed; 5) responses to treatments in terms of means of the experimental (mannaged) and control (unmanaged) groups, corresponding standard deviations and sample sizes have been reported in numerical or graphical form in the article.
data_analysis: the meta-analysis was carried out by using the meta win 2.0 statistical program. the log response ratios were combined across studies using the mixed effects model, which assumes that differences among studies within a class are due to both sampling error and random variation. bias-corrected 95% confidence intervals (ci) around the effect size were generated from 4999 iterations. to test the importance of different sources of variation in determining the sign and magnitude of the treatment effect, authors subdivided studies into groups on the basis of the selected explanatory variables and examined between-group heterogeneity using a x2-test statistic, qb.
background: Common reed (Phragmites australis) is a tall grass species of great economic and ecological importance that is widely distributed in European wetlands. It often forms extensive stands known as reedbeds. Reedbeds represent an important habitat for plants, birds and invertebrates including many rare and vulnerable species. On the other hand, reedbed represents the early stages of succession from open water to woodland. Without management a reedbed will gradually dry out, becoming colonised by other grasses and tall herbs eventually developing into scrub and woodland. In addition, reedbeds are annually harvested for thatching material in several western and central European countries.
objective: to summarize the available evidence regarding the impact of reed management on wildlife in europe. the following questions were addressed: 1) what is the impact of management on the performance of re-growing reed? 2) what is the impact of reed management on plants, invertebrates, and bird species associated with reedbeds? 3) how do the type of reed management, its timing and the duration of management period affect wildlife? 4) do habitat, water salinity and the type of vegetation modify the effects of management on wildlife? here, results for objectives 2, 3 and 4 are reported.
result1: reed management reduced other plant stem height, while no effects on stem density or aboveground biomass have been observed. abundance and richness of other plants increased by 160%, although this increase was not statistically significant, probably due to the small number of studies (95% ci [-27%; 702%], n = 5).
result2: reed management significantly decreased invertebrate species richness (-30%, 95% ci [-51%; -10%], n = 2) and abundance (-20%, 95% ci [-35%; -0.5%], n = 161), and harvesting, burning and grazing had a similar effect on their abundance (qb = 2.3, d.f. = 2, p = 0.318). overall, colleoptera abundance and density decreased with reed management while araneae abundance and density were not affected by reed management.
result3: reed management reduced the number of birds by 60% as compared to unmanaged sites (95% ci [-73%; -41%], n = 19), and both harvesting and burning of reed affected number of birds to the same extent (qb = 0.98, d.f. = 1, p = 0.322). similarly, other explanatory variables such as habitat (qb = 0.95, d.f. = 1, p = 0.329), water salinity (qb = 0.26, d.f. = 1, p = 0.607), vegetation (qb = 0.80, d.f. = 1, p = 0.372) and the duration of the management period (qb = 2.18, d.f. = 1, p = 0.140) did not modify the negative effect of reed management on number of bird species. there was no effect of reed management on nesting success (-2%, 95% ci [-6%; 16%], n = 4) or laying date (20%, 95% ci [-11%; 21%], n = 2).
general_conclusion: plant species richness increased by 90% in managed stands in fresh water marshes, but not in saline water marshes. overall, reed management had a significant negative impact on invertebrate community, but the duration of management was an important factor determining the magnitude of the effect. short-term management (1–2 years) had no effect on invertebrates, whereas management for longer period significantly reduced invertebrate abundance. reed harvesting and burning reduced abundance of passerine birds by about 60%. therefore, the optimal reed management regime to preserve number of birds and invertebrates in reedbeds could be a rotation of short-term management (1–2 years).

search_strategy: the original data base (moreno-mateos et al. (2012)) was constructed after a reference search conducted on 22 december 2010 in the scientific data base isi web of science – sci-expanded. the terms used were ‘(wetland* or floodplain*or peatland* or marsh* or mangrove*) same (restor* or creat* or re-creat* or rehabilit*)’.
selection_criteria: 1) studies of wetlands under natural hydrological regimes, planted with native species, and in which no allochthonous substrates were imported during the restoration or creation activities.; 2) articles must compare measurements of structural components and biogeochemical processes in restored or created and reference wetlands at a known age.
data_analysis: linear mixed-effects models were used to evaluate whether the selected restoration and creation approaches and the environmental factors generated a significant response on restored and created wetlands separately for biotic assemblage structure and biogeochemical functionality. in addition, ‘time since restoration or creation started’ was taken as a continuous fixed factor. the study was included as a random factor in the model. authors applied a backward elimination procedure in which non-significant terms (p < 0.05) were removed in order of decreasing p-value. only main effects were included excluding interactions. bias-corrected 95% bootstrapping confidence intervals based on 999 permutations were used. rosenthal fail-safe number, the publication bias (through exploring funnel plots), and plotted standardized effect sizes against the normal quantiles to inspect the fit of the results to a normal distribution were checked.
background: Current efforts to restore and create ecosystems require greater understanding of ecosystems’ responses to commonly used physical and biological intervention approaches to overcome ecological and technological limitations.
objective: 1) do recovery trajectories of wetlands affected by different restoration and creation approaches differ significantly?; 2) if so, which interventions yield better results in enhancing biotic assemblage structure and biogeochemical functions?;  3) do biophysical setting (regional climate, hydrogeomorphology, and area of the restored or created wetland) and the nature of the anthropogenic perturbations at play in the pre-restoration state affect the performance of the varying restoration and creation approaches? here, results for biotic assemblages are reported.
result1: after 5 years of restoration or creation efforts, no approach, including surface modification or flow re-establishment alone, or either one of them combined with revegetation, was significantly different from the others (i.e. bootstrap confidence intervals overlapped) in regard to the recovery trajectories of biotic assemblage structure.
result2: in cold climates, the recovery completeness of the biotic assemblage structure of wetlands restored or created using surface modification and revegetation combined was significantly lower (n = 54; 63 +/- 13%) than in temperate climates (n = 102; 90 +/- 6%) and surprisingly lower, and almost significantly, (n = 26; 82 +/- 6%), than in wetlands restored or created in cold climates where surface modification was used alone.
result3: non-significant differences of the biotic assemblage structure were found between tidal and depressional wetlands in relation to the restoration or creation approach used.
result4: although the linear mixed-effects model showed significant effects of the pre-restoration anthropogenic perturbation type on biotic assemblage structure of restored wetlands, no clear differences were found among restored wetlands for this set of variables, regardless of the perturbation category, nor whether they were intentionally revegetated or not during restoration.
general_conclusion: wetlands where surface modification and flow re-establishment were used followed similar recovery trajectories regardless of whether they were revegetated or not.
knowledge_gaps:
results highlight the urgent need to increase our understanding of the long-term effects of restoration and creation actions in our aim to engage in large-scale ecosystem management strategies for wetlands. besides, although the original selection of studies included wet
land ecosystems from all over the world, most were located in the usa.

search_strategy: a systematic literature search for peer-reviewed publications was conducted in web of science. to compile the database of the recovery of native faunal communities after spartina removals, the following query was used: ts = (invas*or alien or nonnative or nonnative or exotic or introduced) and ts = (spartina or cordgrass or ricegrass) and ts = (salt marsh*or estuar*or coastal marsh*or coastal wetland*) and ts = (restor*or remov*or control*or eradicate*). all published records from january in 1980 to august in 2018 were collected, and the publications included in the review by gallardo et al., (2016) were also identified.
selection_criteria: 1) published native faunal responses to spartina species invasions or removals (i.e., diversity, abundance, and fitness metrics; and 2) replicated studies with treatment and control, where mean values and statistical variations were presented and which statistically compared the responses of native faunal communities between the control and treatment (i.e., uninvaded vs. invaded; before- invasion vs. after- invasion; unremoved vs. removed; before- removal vs. after- removal) by field observations or experimental manipulations.
data_analysis: for spartina removal studies, mean lnrrs and 95% cis on each variable of native fauna in different taxonomic groups, removal measures, and removal time (i.e., time since invader removals) were estimated. random- effect models were used. the heterogeneity was estimated using the q statistics. all meta- analyses and statistical analyses were performed using r 3.5.3. two methods were conducted to test whether there were publication biases in our meta- database. we first graphed the funnel plots for each effect size metric, and then examined funnel plot asymmetry using visual inspection and egger's test. second, rosenberg's fail- safe number was used to examine the robustness of effect size estimates to publication bias. all funnel plots of the variables showed a symmetrical shape both by visual inspections and egger's tests (p > 0.05). moreover, large rosenthal's fail- safe numbers (greater than 5n + 10) were also observed in all funnel plots. thus, the potential effects of publication biases on results of meta- analyses were negligible.
background: Coastal ecosystems worldwide are being threatened by invasive plants in the context of global changes. However, how invasive plants influence native faunal communities and whether native faunal communities can recover following the invader removals/ controls across global coastal ecosystems are still poorly understood.
objective: to quantitatively evaluate the displacement of coastal faunal communities caused by spartina species invasions, as well as their recovery following the invader removals with different measures, based on peer- reviewed scientific literatures. here, results on the effect of removal treatments are reported.
result1: the majority of removal measures showed a significant positive impact on native fauna. specifically, removal measures such as mowing, herbi- ciding, and uprooting/inversion significantly improved the diversity of native fauna. similarly, the abundance of native fauna was significantly increased by these measures of herbiciding and tilling/breaking roots, and the fitness was significantly increased through native plant replacement. importantly, it was noted that removal through constructing a cofferdam to waterlog spartina combined with mowing (i.e., waterlogging +mowing) had a significant negative impact on native faunal communities, despite no significant negative effect on their diversity.
result2: differential effects of removal time on native fauna for each removal measure were observed.
general_conclusion: analyses revealed that invader removals were overall beneficial for native faunal communities to recover from the displacement caused by spartina invasions, but this recovery process depended on specific removal measure and time. although invasive plant removals could restore native faunal communities, future functional restorations of invaded ecosystems should take the legacy effects of invasive species on native communities into account.

search_strategy: the isi web of science database was used with no restriction on the publication date. the following search term combination was used: (((ecosystem or environment*) and (service* or function*)) and (("environment* flow*") or ("flow* releas*") or ("dam releas*") or ("flood* pulse") or ("restor* flow") or ("recover* flow") or ("enhanc* flow")) and (stream* or instream* or wetland* or lake* or river*)). the preliminary search results was refined to focus on the following subject areas: (environmental sciences or ecology or water resources or marine freshwater biology or geology or plant sciences or engineering or fisheries or zoology or biodiversity conservation).
selection_criteria: 1) the paper report quantitative measures of one or more variables relating to the provision of one or more ecosystem services or to biodiversity, in the context of an assessment of the implementation of environmental flow releases; 2) studies that focused on frameworks, methodology, models, simulations, and scenario analysis, as well as on theoretical hydro-ecological responses were excluded.
data_analysis: authors confirmed the normality of the distribution of ecosystem services using the kolmogorov–smirnov test and confirmed the homogeneity of variance using levene’s test. where the values were normally distributed and homoscedastic, significant differences among the results were tested using one-way analysis of variance (anova). when the anova showed a significant difference, tukey’s honest significant difference (hsd) test was used to identify which pairs of values differed significantly. ecosytem services that differed significantly from zero were also identified by means of the t test. all statistical analysis was performed using version 20.0 of the spss statistical software.
background: Environmental flow releases are a tool for wetland restoration, but there has been no systematic evaluation of their success.
objective: to determine whether releasing environmental flows could maintain or promote biodiversity and increase ecosystem services, and which strategies were most effective. specifically, to answer three main questions: 1) what are the magnitudes of the environmental flow releases that have been conducted around the world?; 2) have these releases maintained or significantly promoted biodiversity and the delivery of ecosystem services?; 3) which flow release strategies were most effective? here, results for objective 2 are reported for biodiversity.
result1: overall, environmental flow releases generaly maintained biodiversity.
result2: NA
general_conclusion: authors found that environmental flow releases maintained biodiversity.
knowledge_gaps: small sample sizes. bility. the effect sizes of environmental flow release projects for biodiversity and ecosystem services are significantly and positively correlated in rivers, but not in other wetlands. challenges for future research include encouraging more researchers to obtain data on cultural ecosystem services and finding ways to identify and understand the factors responsible for the high degree of variation in the results of the flow releases.

search_strategy: the authors systematically searched the research literature to identify quantitative studies of the effects of ecological restoration on biodiversity and es of non-marine aquatic and semi-aquatic degraded wetlands. the authors searched the isi web of knowledge database, as it provides access to peer-reviewed studies. the authors searched studies published between 1970 and 2010 using the following string of search terms: (riparian or river* or lake or mangroves or marsh or stream or wetland) and (restor* or re-creat* or rehabilitat* or forest* or reforest* or afforest* or plant* or recover*) and ((ecosystem or environment) and (service or function*)). preliminary search results were filtered to include only the following isi-defined subject areas: ‘‘agriculture’’, ‘‘biodiversity and conservation’’, ‘‘environmental sciences and ecology’’, ‘‘fish- eries’’, ‘‘forestry’’, ‘‘marine and freshwater biology’’, ‘‘plant sciences’’, ‘‘water resources’’, and ‘‘zoology’’.
selection_criteria:
1) studies had to focus on at least one estuarine, lacustrine, palustrine, or riverine wetland; as well as report the following information: 2) quantitative assessment of passive restoration (i.e. natural regeneration) or active restoration in terms of variables related to biodiversity and/or to the supply of one or more wetland es consistent with the framework of the millennium ecosystem assessment, according to which biodiversity underpins all es; 3) comparison of restored wetland with either degraded or natural wetland;
4) sample size of the reported data and at least a variance estimate of such data.
data_analysis: the authors performed separate analyses to compare restored and degraded wetlands and to compare restored and natural wetlands. response ration (rr) calculations and statistical analyses were performed using metawin v2.1. to assess the statistical significance of differences in rr effect sizes among groups or the significance of deviations of effect sizes from zero, the authors used the conservative test of the bias-corrected 95% bootstrapping confidence intervals (ci) based on 999 permutations. to assess the risk of publication bias towards positive results and larger sample sizes in our included studies, the authors generated funnel plots, which indicated that such bias was unlikely to affect the results of the comparisons between restored and degraded wetlands or between restored and natural wetlands.
background: Wetlands are valuable ecosystems because they harbor a huge biodiversity and provide key services to societies. When natural or human factors degrade wetlands, ecological restoration is often carried out to recover biodiversity and ecosystem services (ES). Although such restorations are routinely performed, we lack systematic, evidence-based assessments of their effectiveness on the recovery of biodiversity and ES.
objective: to address the following four questions: 1) how much biodiversity and 2) how much of ecosystem services (es) levels can be recovered through wetland restoration; 3) whether biodiversity and es recovery correlate, and 4) whether the effectiveness of biodiversity and es recovery depends on context, including ecosystem type, cause of degradation, restoration action, experimental design, and restoration age. here, results for biodiversity are reported
result1: restoring degraded wetlands enhanced biodiversity by 19%; and biodiversity in restored wetlands did not significantly differ from that in natural wetlands. restoration significantly enhanced the diversity of vertebrates (+53%), vascular plants (+45%), and terrestrial (+17%) and aquatic (+15%) invertebrates, but it had no significant effect on macroinvertebrate diversity. restored and natural wetlands showed similar diversity of vascular plants, aquatic invertebrates, macroinvertebrates and protists. in contrast, these two types of wetlands differed significantly in the diversity of non-native vascular plants, which was 44% lower in restored wetlands, and in vertebrate diversity, which was 37% higher in restored wetlands.
result2: NA
general_conclusion: the meta-analysis strongly supports the idea that ecological restoration increases biodiversity in degraded wetlands, thereby benefiting the human communities that interact with and depend on them. the detailed effects of restoration depend heavily on context factors, emphasizing the need for habitat-specific planning and assessment of restorations.

search_strategy: the authors conducted a systematic literature search to identify potentially relevant publications containing information about the effectiveness of wetland restoration, the performance of restored wetlands, and the rate and timeframe of recovery. eligible publications included published and gray literature that contained information regarding the ecological recovery of restored wetlands in the northern gulf of mexico (limited to the usa). no restriction on publication year was placed. search was not restricted to english language publications, but no relevant non-english publications were found during the search. authors searched 11 relevant databases using the database aggregator service proquest. the authors performed a keyword search of these databases in december 2013, using different structured combinations of eight different basic search statements. then, the authors updated our literature search in april 2017 to identify additional relevant studies published between 2014 and early 2017.
selection_criteria: 1) the study evaluated a marsh or wetland restoration action (in 2014, we included the following restoration techniques: wetland creation, thin-layer sediment addition, marsh terracing, sediment and fresh-water diversions, canal backfilling, or other coastal marsh restoration methods; in 2017, only wetland creation and thin-layer sediment addition were included); 2) the restored marsh or wetland was located in the northern gulf of mexico; 3) in the same year, the author(s) measured at least one ecological parameter (e.g., soil, vegetation, fish, wildlife) in a restored marsh or wetland, and in one or more natural marshes that could serve as reference sites; 4) the restored site included one treatment over an ecologically relevant area (on the order of acres) and did not represent a small-scale experiment.
data_analysis: all computations were done in sas version 9.3; in particular, proc mixed was used to fit the random effects meta-analysis. the authors tested a number of characteristics as covariates to understand what factors could be driving both variance and observed effects. covariates included geographic location, size of restored site, marsh type (fresh, brackish, or saline), landscape position, active vegetation vs. passive vegetation recovery, and sand content of sediment used in restoration. the authors created funnel plots by plotting the estimated ln rr against the inverse of its within-study se.
background: The extent to which ecological properties of restored coastal wetlands in the northern Gulf of Mexico recover to natural wetland conditions has not been synthesized.
objective: the authors addressed the following three questions: 1) does wetland restoration in the northern gulf of mexico result in the convergence of multiple wetland properties to reference site conditions? 2) are there differences in the degree and rate of convergence for different metrics of vegetation condition or different soil properties? 3) does the degree of convergence for particular metrics depend on salinity (also characterized as wetland type), position of sampling locations within the wetland, or on characteristics of the restoration?
result1: the mean rrs for the soil organic carbon increased during the first 15 years following restoration toward values similar to those at reference sites.
result2: NA
general_conclusion: on average, soil organic matter was 92% lower at restored sites during the first 15 years of restoration compared to reference sites.

search_strategy: authors searched in web of science and google scholar for published literature on invasive grasses using search terms in the title, abstract, and keywords.
selection_criteria: 1) papers that conducted pairwise comparisons between an invaded state and either an uninvaded control or a managed treatment (i.e., variables were measured with and without the invasive grasses)
data_analysis: all analyses were performed in the statistical computing environment r, ver. 3.6.2. authors used randomizations to analyze data. this permutational approach effectively generates a bespoke null distribution for each response variable with the resulting mean of permuted hedges’ g centered at zero, which can then be used to quantify the probability of our observed hedges’ g values if there was no true difference between systems where invasive grasses are absent and present. null distributions were generated using 10,000 permutations and mean observed hedges’ g was used as the critical effect size for each response variable separately.
background: It remains unclear how severely invasive grasses alter ecosystem functions and whether alterations persist after invasive grass removal, limiting our ability to determine if management practices are truly sufficient to fully restore ecosystems.
objective: to quantify ecological alterations and the efficacy of management following the invasion of spartina alterniflora and phragmites australis, two common and pervasive invaders in coastal wetlands. specifically to: 1) assess the effects of invasive perennial grass species on ecosystem functioning (e.g., nutrient cycling) and communities (e.g., abundance), 2) determine if effects of invasive perennial grasses differed across components of habitat (i.e., soil or water) or between organism types (i.e., invertebrates, microbes, and plants), and 3) compare the extent of invasive perennial grass impacts between habitat types. here, results for abiotic c fluxes are reported.
result1: c fluxes measured from soil and water were generally elevated in invaded systems relative to managed (i.e., invasive removal) areas.
result2: NA
general_conclusion: management practices may not adequately promote recovery from invasion, but more data are needed to fully assess management efficacy.
knowledge_gaps: most invasive plant literature focuses on quantifying the scale of the invasions rather than developing tangible solutions tied to ecological responses and outcomes. although several studies and meta-analyses have compared management techniques of invasive species, a broader understanding of management efficacy in conjunction with ecosystem response is still lacking. the geographical scope of this meta-analysis is limited largely to the northeastern united states and eastern china. although these findings have important implications, these results are limited in scope, preventing additional analyses quantifying the effectiveness of frequently used management techniques (e.g., herbicide, prescribed fire, livestock grazing, and mechanical removal).

search_strategy: the data used in this study were drawn from peer-reviewed articles collected from the web of science with the following keywords: ts = (nee* or co2* or ch4* or n2o) and ts = (coastal wetland* or marsh* or mangrove* or freshwater wetland* or riparian wetland* or peatland* or fen* or bog) and ts = (land use* or agriculture* or cropland* or constructed wetland* or pasture* or aquaculture) with time span of 1950–2018.
selection_criteria: 1) the selected experiments were conducted in the field and included at least one type of natural wetland that was classified as natural coastal wetland, natural riparian wetland or natural peatland; 2) all converted land-use types were directly transformed from the natural wetlands, and land-use types that had undergone multiple land-use transitions, such as restored wetlands, were excluded; 3) the selected experiments were conducted at the same temporal and spatial scales in both the natural wetlands and converted land-use types ; 4) the selected studies provided data for at least one type of greenhouse gas flux.
data_analysis: the response ratio (rr) was used to evaluate the responses of ghg fluxes to lulcc. the weighting function was calculated based on the reciprocal of the variance in individual rrs.
background: Land-use/land-cover change (LULCC) often results in degradation of natural wetlands and affects the dynamics of greenhouse gases. However, the magnitude of changes in greenhouse gas emissions from wetlands undergoing various LULCC types remains unclear.
objective: the main objectives of this study were to quantify the effect of lulcc on greenhouse gas (ghg) emissions in natural wetland ecosystems and to detect the key environmental variables in relation to changes in ghg emissions and the potential resulting global warming potential effects since lulcc events.
result1: the lulcc types across all natural wetlands decreased net ecosystem co2 exchange, with significant (p < .05) effects of natural coastal wetlands converted to constructed wetlands and natural riparian wetlands converted to drained wetlands or to pasture.
result2: all lulcc types (except for aquaculture ponds relative to natural coasta wetlands) decreased the fch4, with significant (p < .05) effects of drained wetlands and croplands relative to natural riparian wetlands.
result3: natural riparian wetlands converted to cropland stimulated fn2o across the natural wetlands, while natural riparian wetlands converted to pasture decreased n2o emissions.
general_conclusion: the lulcc types across all natural wetlands decreased net ecosystem co2 exchange ch4 emnissions (except for aquaculture ponds relative to natural coasta wetlands). natural riparian wetlands converted to cropland stimulated fn2o across the natural wetlands, while natural riparian wetlands converted to pasture decreased n2o emissions.

search_strategy: a broad spectrum of the following online literature databases were searched to identify relevant articles and reports: isi web of knowledge (wok), science direct-agricultural and biological sciences section, blackwell synergy, ingentaconnect, directory of open access journals, copac, scirus (all journal sources), scopus, index to theses online, digital dissertations online, agricola, cab abstracts, english nature’s ‘wildlink’, centre for ecology and hydrology (ceh) online database, jstor, conservationevidence.com and conserveonline. in addition, further general internet searches using www.alltheweb.com and http://scholar.google.com/ (google scholar beta) were undertaken for the identification of further articles and unpublished (grey) literature. searches were completed for each of the search terms four times (standard search, pdf files only, doc/txt files only, and xls/excel files only). the first 50 ‘hits’ of each search were assessed for their relevance against the study inclusion criteria. the websites of the following statutory bodies and non-governmental organisations were inspected for further relevant material including pertinent grey literature or unpublished datasets: us fish & wildlife service, the nature conservancy, english nature, scottish natural heritage, countryside council for wales, uk joint nature conservation committee, uk department of environment, food and rural affairs, national trust (uk), environment & heritage service northern ireland, and various individual state environment/agricultural departments in the usa and australia. all searches were conducted during the first quarter of 2006.
selection_criteria: 1) subject of control/eradication intervention: one or more of the following spartina species: s. alternifolia (smooth or ‘atlantic’ smooth cordgrass) +hybrids, s. anglica (common or ‘english’ cordgrass), s. densiflora (chilean cordgrass), s. patens (saltmeadow cordgrass), and s. x townsendii (townsend’s cordgrass); 2) interventions: one or more of the following control/eradication management interventions: hand pulling and manual excavation, mechanical excavation and dredging, mowing, crushing and mechanical smothering, covering or blanketing, flooding or draining, salinity adjustments and herbicide (aerial, boat or ground application methods) and any combination of the above methods; 3) outcome measure of the study: either a measure of change in cover, density, frequency, biomass or a measure of any plant characteristic (e.g. height of plant, leaf elongation); 4) types of study: any randomised block design, control trial, site comparison or before and after time series experiment was accepted through to the final review analysis.
data_analysis: separate meta-analyses were undertaken for each of the management interventions (irrespective of spartina species), and then reanalysed for each species individually. cohen’s d effect sizes were calculated for each study where the mean, number of replicates and standard deviation was known. standardized mean difference, dersimonian–laird (random effects) pooled effect d+ meta-analysis was used to combine the effect sizes across all studies. prior to each of the meta-analyses, heterogeneity was assessed by the use of forrest plots and formal tests of heterogeneity ‘i2’ (the percentage of variation across studies that is due to heterogeneity rather than chance). publication bias was also assessed using funnel plots of asymmetry along with formal tests, to see the effect of the inclusion and exclusion of grey literature and non-english language studies.
background: Spartina species (cordgrasses) have been introduced to the estuaries around Europe, USA, Australia, New Zealand and Asia as a coastal management tool to stabilise mud banks, and through accidental introductions. Though important in their native settings, these non-native species are highly aggressive in their new environment, and frequently become the dominant plant species in areas they invade. Various methods are in use or are currently being trialled for use in the control and/or eradication of invasive Spartina species.
objective: to identify and critically appraise all primary sources of experimental evidence, whether published or ‘grey’ literature, in order to evaluate, using of meta-analysis, the effectiveness of the various management interventions used to control or eradicate spartina spp.
result1: 2,2-dpa did not significantly reduce the density of s. alterniflora (d+ = -0.708; 95% ci = -1.550 to 0.133; p = 0.099). amitrole–t applications did not significantly reduce s. alterniflora densities (d+ = -0.577; 95% ci = -1.404 to 0.250; p = 0.01715). diurin was found to be the least effective of all those assessed within the review (d+ = -0.034; 95% ci = -1:024 to 0.956; p = 0.9462). aerial application of glyphosate did not significantly reduce the density of s. alterniflora (d+ = -0.812; 95% ci = -5.175 to -3.551; p = 0.7153). however, groundsprayed glyphosate did significantly reduce s. alterniflora density (d+ = -3.065; 95% ci = -4.144 to -1.986; p < 0.0001). the use of 1–5% wetter or surfactant with the glyphosate application improved the impact (d+ = -6.240; 95% ci = -8.988 to -3.492; p <0.0001). imazapyr application significantly reduced s. alterniflora densities (d+ = -3.208; 95% ci = -3.889 to -2.527; p <0.0001). the addition of a surfactant/wetting agent greatly increased imazapyr effectiveness (d+ = -5.768; 95% ci = -7.354 to -4.181; p <0.0001). paraquat did not significantly reduce the density of s. alterniflora (d+ = -0.794; 95% ci = -1.630 to 0.041; p = -0.0623).
result2: the addition of a wetting agent (mixture b) with the glyphosate application, significantly reduces the density of s. anglica (d+ = -0.789; 95% ci = -1.567 to -0.011; p = 0:0468).
result3: cutting alone, achieved significant reductions in the density of s. alterniflora (d+ = -4.853; 95% ci = -9.093 to -0.614; p = 0:0248). however, in s. anglica, densities non-significantly increased over a year’s follow-up (d+ = -0.594; 95% ci = -0.765 to 1.952; p = 0.3918). the use of cutting and then dalapon application significantly reduced the density of s. alterniflora (d+ = -8.002; 95% ci = -11.081 to -4.923; p <0.0001) and also significantly reduced the density of s. anglica (d+ = -3.826; 95% ci = -5.021 to -2.630; p <0.0001). the use of cutting and then glyphosate application non-significantly increased the density of s. anglica (d+ = -0.249; 95% ci = -1.003 to 1.501; p = 0.6967). cutting and smothering has been used against s. anglica, and significantly reduced its density (d+ = -4.307; 95% ci = -5.799 to -2.814; p <0.0001).
result4: the use of mechanical tracked vehicles or specially adapted rollers to crush s. alterniflora provided significant declines in s. alterniflora densities (d+ = --1.951; 95% ci = -3.033 to -0.870; p <0.0004). the addition of glyphosate, applied up to 6 weeks after the crushing event provides a highly significant reduction in s. alterniflora densities (d+ = -3.806; 95% ci = -5.967 to -1.645; p <0.0006). the use of disking to control s. alterniflora through a shredding action, also has the added value of crushing the plants due to the tracks of the mechanical vehicles that are used to administer this control methodology (d+ = -4.535; 95% ci = -8.371 to -0.700; p <0.0205). the use of machines to work the substrate to improve its structure and drainage (tilling) achieved the best control of s. alterniflora densities of all mechanical control methods (d+ = -5.108; 95% ci = -9.804 to -0.413; p <0.033).
result5: the use of ungulates (hoofed grazing animals) was not effective in reducing the densities of s. alterniflora (d+ = -0.702; 95% ci = -2.679 to 1.275; p = 0.4865).
general_conclusion: the effectiveness of glyphosate and imazapyr herbicides at reducing s. alterniflora differ greatly depending upon application method and whether surfactant or wetting agents are used. cutting combined with smothering is highly effective at reducing s. anglica densities, but its efficacy has not been established for other spartina spp. cutting alone increases densities of s. anglica and s. townsendii, while reducing s. alterniflora densities. biological control, while in its infancy, has the potential to significantly reduce s. anglica densities, while against s. alterniflora it might be of benefit as part of an integrated programme.

search_strategy: relevant journal articles were found by using key-word searches in web of science database and by looking through the reference lists of previous narrative reviews. the following combinations of english language search terms were used: phragmites australis or common reed, and either cut*, burn*, grazing, manage*, bird*, insect*, invertebrate*, vegetation, plant* or conservation.
selection_criteria: 1) the study has been made in europe; 2) the method of reed management used has been either harvesting, mowing, burning or grazing; 3) the study had an appropriate control (unmanaged stands); 4) impact of reedbed management on either plants, invertebrates and/or birds have been assessed; 5) responses to treatments in terms of means of the experimental (mannaged) and control (unmanaged) groups, corresponding standard deviations and sample sizes have been reported in numerical or graphical form in the article.
data_analysis: the meta-analysis was carried out by using the meta win 2.0 statistical program. the log response ratios were combined across studies using the mixed effects model, which assumes that differences among studies within a class are due to both sampling error and random variation. bias-corrected 95% confidence intervals (ci) around the effect size were generated from 4999 iterations. to test the importance of different sources of variation in determining the sign and magnitude of the treatment effect, authors subdivided studies into groups on the basis of the selected explanatory variables and examined between-group heterogeneity using a x2-test statistic, qb.
background: Common reed (Phragmites australis) is a tall grass species of great economic and ecological importance that is widely distributed in European wetlands. It often forms extensive stands known as reedbeds. Reedbeds represent an important habitat for plants, birds and invertebrates including many rare and vulnerable species. On the other hand, reedbed represents the early stages of succession from open water to woodland. Without management a reedbed will gradually dry out, becoming colonised by other grasses and tall herbs eventually developing into scrub and woodland. In addition, reedbeds are annually harvested for thatching material in several western and central European countries.
objective: to summarize the available evidence regarding the impact of reed management on wildlife in europe. the following questions were addressed: 1) what is the impact of management on the performance of re-growing reed? 2) what is the impact of reed management on plants, invertebrates, and bird species associated with reedbeds? 3) how do the type of reed management, its timing and the duration of management period affect wildlife? 4) do habitat, water salinity and the type of vegetation modify the effects of management on wildlife? here, results for objective 1 are reported.
result1: the effect of reed management on stem density of re-growing reed was significantly positive (28%, 95% ci [12%; 45%], n = 16). no difference between the effects of type of reed management (harvesting, burning, grazing and mowing) on stem density was found (qb = 2.3, d.f. = 3, p = 0.570).
result2: there was significant difference between the effects of various types of reed management on stem height: reed burning significantly shortened stem height while reed harvesting did not (qb = 5.9, d.f. = 1, p = 0.015).
result3: neither stem diameter (-3.3%, 95% ci [-14%; 7%], n = 12) nor aboveground biomass of re-growing reed were affected by reed management (8.8%, 95% ci [-17%; 29%], n = 10). also, no differences between the effects of type of reed management on these parameters were observed (for diameter: qb = 0.69, d.f. = 2, p = 0.749; for biomass: qb = 0.37, d.f. = 1, p = 0.659).
result4: other explanatory variables such as habitat, water salinity, vegetation, the time ofmanagement and the duration of management period did not alter the effect of reed management on the performance of re-growing reed (p > 0.05).
general_conclusion: reed management modifies the structure of re-growing reed stands: reed stems were shorter and denser in managed sites than in unmanaged sites. however, harvesting does not have an impact on aboveground biomass.

search_strategy: the authors systematically searched the research literature to identify quantitative studies of the effects of ecological restoration on biodiversity and es of non-marine aquatic and semi-aquatic degraded wetlands. the authors searched the isi web of knowledge database, as it provides access to peer-reviewed studies. the authors searched studies published between 1970 and 2010 using the following string of search terms: (riparian or river* or lake or mangroves or marsh or stream or wetland) and (restor* or re-creat* or rehabilitat* or forest* or reforest* or afforest* or plant* or recover*) and ((ecosystem or environment) and (service or function*)). preliminary search results were filtered to include only the following isi-defined subject areas: ‘‘agriculture’’, ‘‘biodiversity and conservation’’, ‘‘environmental sciences and ecology’’, ‘‘fish- eries’’, ‘‘forestry’’, ‘‘marine and freshwater biology’’, ‘‘plant sciences’’, ‘‘water resources’’, and ‘‘zoology’’.
selection_criteria:
1) studies had to focus on at least one estuarine, lacustrine, palustrine, or riverine wetland; as well as report the following information: 2) quantitative assessment of passive restoration (i.e. natural regeneration) or active restoration in terms of variables related to biodiversity and/or to the supply of one or more wetland es consistent with the framework of the millennium ecosystem assessment, according to which biodiversity underpins all es; 3) comparison of restored wetland with either degraded or natural wetland;
4) sample size of the reported data and at least a variance estimate of such data.
data_analysis: the authors performed separate analyses to compare restored and degraded wetlands and to compare restored and natural wetlands. response ration (rr) calculations and statistical analyses were performed using metawin v2.1. to assess the statistical significance of differences in rr effect sizes among groups or the significance of deviations of effect sizes from zero, the authors used the conservative test of the bias-corrected 95% bootstrapping confidence intervals (ci) based on 999 permutations. to assess the risk of publication bias towards positive results and larger sample sizes in our included studies, the authors generated funnel plots, which indicated that such bias was unlikely to affect the results of the comparisons between restored and degraded wetlands or between restored and natural wetlands.
