background: Wetlands are valuable ecosystems because they harbor a huge biodiversity and provide key services to societies. When natural or human factors degrade wetlands, ecological restoration is often carried out to recover biodiversity and ecosystem services (ES). Although such restorations are routinely performed, we lack systematic, evidence-based assessments of their effectiveness on the recovery of biodiversity and ES.
objective: to address the following four questions: 1) how much biodiversity and 2) how much of ecosystem services (es) levels can be recovered through wetland restoration; 3) whether biodiversity and es recovery correlate, and 4) whether the effectiveness of biodiversity and es recovery depends on context, including ecosystem type, cause of degradation, restoration action, experimental design, and restoration age. here, the results for non-native vascular plants are reported.
result1: restored and natural wetlands differed significantly in the diversity of non-native vascular plants, which was 44% lower in restored wetlands.
result2: NA
general_conclusion: restored and natural wetlands differed significantly in the diversity of non-native vascular plants, which was 44% lower in restored wetlands.

search_strategy: the isi web of science database was used with no restriction on the publication date. the following search term combination was used: (((ecosystem or environment*) and (service* or function*)) and (("environment* flow*") or ("flow* releas*") or ("dam releas*") or ("flood* pulse") or ("restor* flow") or ("recover* flow") or ("enhanc* flow")) and (stream* or instream* or wetland* or lake* or river*)). the preliminary search results was refined to focus on the following subject areas: (environmental sciences or ecology or water resources or marine freshwater biology or geology or plant sciences or engineering or fisheries or zoology or biodiversity conservation).
selection_criteria: 1) the paper report quantitative measures of one or more variables relating to the provision of one or more ecosystem services or to biodiversity, in the context of an assessment of the implementation of environmental flow releases; 2) studies that focused on frameworks, methodology, models, simulations, and scenario analysis, as well as on theoretical hydro-ecological responses were excluded.
data_analysis: authors confirmed the normality of the distribution of ecosystem services using the kolmogorov–smirnov test and confirmed the homogeneity of variance using levene’s test. where the values were normally distributed and homoscedastic, significant differences among the results were tested using one-way analysis of variance (anova). when the anova showed a significant difference, tukey’s honest significant difference (hsd) test was used to identify which pairs of values differed significantly. ecosytem services that differed significantly from zero were also identified by means of the t test. all statistical analysis was performed using version 20.0 of the spss statistical software.
background: Environmental flow releases are a tool for wetland restoration, but there has been no systematic evaluation of their success.
objective: to determine whether releasing environmental flows could maintain or promote biodiversity and increase ecosystem services, and which strategies were most effective. specifically, to answer three main questions: 1) what are the magnitudes of the environmental flow releases that have been conducted around the world?; 2) have these releases maintained or significantly promoted biodiversity and the delivery of ecosystem services?; 3) which flow release strategies were most effective? here, results for objective 2 are reported for sediment regulation.
result1: the effect size value for sediment regulation had 95% confidence intervals of (0.033, 2.15), and hence was significantly greater than 0 (p< 0.05).
result2: NA
general_conclusion: authors found that environmental flow releases remarkably increased sediment regulation.
knowledge_gaps: small sample sizes. bility. the effect sizes of environmental flow release projects for biodiversity and ecosystem services are significantly and positively correlated in rivers, but not in other wetlands. challenges for future research include encouraging more researchers to obtain data on cultural ecosystem services and finding ways to identify and understand the factors responsible for the high degree of variation in the results of the flow releases.

search_strategy: authors searched in web of science and google scholar for published literature on invasive grasses using search terms in the title, abstract, and keywords.
selection_criteria: 1) papers that conducted pairwise comparisons between an invaded state and either an uninvaded control or a managed treatment (i.e., variables were measured with and without the invasive grasses)
data_analysis: all analyses were performed in the statistical computing environment r, ver. 3.6.2. authors used randomizations to analyze data. this permutational approach effectively generates a bespoke null distribution for each response variable with the resulting mean of permuted hedges’ g centered at zero, which can then be used to quantify the probability of our observed hedges’ g values if there was no true difference between systems where invasive grasses are absent and present. null distributions were generated using 10,000 permutations and mean observed hedges’ g was used as the critical effect size for each response variable separately.
background: It remains unclear how severely invasive grasses alter ecosystem functions and whether alterations persist after invasive grass removal, limiting our ability to determine if management practices are truly sufficient to fully restore ecosystems.
objective: to quantify ecological alterations and the efficacy of management following the invasion of spartina alterniflora and phragmites australis, two common and pervasive invaders in coastal wetlands. specifically to: 1) assess the effects of invasive perennial grass species on ecosystem functioning (e.g., nutrient cycling) and communities (e.g., abundance), 2) determine if effects of invasive perennial grasses differed across components of habitat (i.e., soil or water) or between organism types (i.e., invertebrates, microbes, and plants), and 3) compare the extent of invasive perennial grass impacts between habitat types. here, results for some abiotic nutrients are reported.
result1: results for the anayses of other abiotic nutrients comparing managed and invaded wetlands were not significant.
result2: after 11–20 years, soil c and n in restored and created wetlands are still significantly lower by 51.7% and 50.3%, respectively, than those in natural wetlands. the soil c and n in restored wetlands recovered faster than in created wetlands. furthermore, the soil c in restored organic flat and created depressional wetlands recovered more rapidly than in restored and created hydrologically open wetlands (riverine and tidal), respectively
general_conclusion: management practices may not adequately promote recovery from invasion, but more data are needed to fully assess management efficacy.
knowledge_gaps: most invasive plant literature focuses on quantifying the scale of the invasions rather than developing tangible solutions tied to ecological responses and outcomes. although several studies and meta-analyses have compared management techniques of invasive species, a broader understanding of management efficacy in conjunction with ecosystem response is still lacking. the geographical scope of this meta-analysis is limited largely to the northeastern united states and eastern china. although these findings have important implications, these results are limited in scope, preventing additional analyses quantifying the effectiveness of frequently used management techniques (e.g., herbicide, prescribed fire, livestock grazing, and mechanical removal).

search_strategy: the authors conducted a systematic literature search to identify potentially relevant publications containing information about the effectiveness of wetland restoration, the performance of restored wetlands, and the rate and timeframe of recovery. eligible publications included published and gray literature that contained information regarding the ecological recovery of restored wetlands in the northern gulf of mexico (limited to the usa). no restriction on publication year was placed. search was not restricted to english language publications, but no relevant non-english publications were found during the search. authors searched 11 relevant databases using the database aggregator service proquest. the authors performed a keyword search of these databases in december 2013, using different structured combinations of eight different basic search statements. then, the authors updated our literature search in april 2017 to identify additional relevant studies published between 2014 and early 2017.
selection_criteria: 1) the study evaluated a marsh or wetland restoration action (in 2014, we included the following restoration techniques: wetland creation, thin-layer sediment addition, marsh terracing, sediment and fresh-water diversions, canal backfilling, or other coastal marsh restoration methods; in 2017, only wetland creation and thin-layer sediment addition were included); 2) the restored marsh or wetland was located in the northern gulf of mexico; 3) in the same year, the author(s) measured at least one ecological parameter (e.g., soil, vegetation, fish, wildlife) in a restored marsh or wetland, and in one or more natural marshes that could serve as reference sites; 4) the restored site included one treatment over an ecologically relevant area (on the order of acres) and did not represent a small-scale experiment.
data_analysis: all computations were done in sas version 9.3; in particular, proc mixed was used to fit the random effects meta-analysis. the authors tested a number of characteristics as covariates to understand what factors could be driving both variance and observed effects. covariates included geographic location, size of restored site, marsh type (fresh, brackish, or saline), landscape position, active vegetation vs. passive vegetation recovery, and sand content of sediment used in restoration. the authors created funnel plots by plotting the estimated ln rr against the inverse of its within-study se.
background: The extent to which ecological properties of restored coastal wetlands in the northern Gulf of Mexico recover to natural wetland conditions has not been synthesized.
objective: the authors addressed the following three questions: 1) does wetland restoration in the northern gulf of mexico result in the convergence of multiple wetland properties to reference site conditions? 2) are there differences in the degree and rate of convergence for different metrics of vegetation condition or different soil properties? 3) does the degree of convergence for particular metrics depend on salinity (also characterized as wetland type), position of sampling locations within the wetland, or on characteristics of the restoration?
result1: the mean rrs for soil total n response groups increased during the first 15 years following restoration toward values similar to those at reference sites.
result2: NA

search_strategy: a search of published studies was conducted via isi web of science for 1900–2019 employing four different search strings.
selection_criteria: 1) the inlet water had to originate from drainage systems transporting water from agricultural fields, and must not be mixed with water from other sources such as streams; 2) based on the köppen-geiger climate classification system, the sites had to be located in oceanic (cfb, cfc) or continental (dfa, dfb, dfc, dfd, dsc) climates, where the conditions for denitrification are often suboptimal. thus, climate zones with dry winters (letter w) were excluded; 3) the study had to be a field study with sites exposed to ambient temperature and with a surface area larger than 10 m2; 4) the study had to include a mass balance for either nitrate—n, total phosphorus (tp) or total suspended solids (tss) for at least one drainage season, whose length depended on the climate region.
data_analysis: the average nitrate and tp removal efficiencies of mitigation measures treating agricultural drainage water were quantified using meta-analysis. prior to the analysis, the assumption of normality was tested visually (q–q plot, histogram) and by the shapiro–wilk test, and where the assumptions were not fulfilled this is mentioned in the result section. meta-analysis was only conducted for a mitigation measure if sufficient data were available, i.e. data from more than two sites originating from different studies. the meta-analysis was performed in r software 3.6.1 using the r package ‘meta’. the effect size of each study was expressed as the raw removal efficiency. each effect size was weighted, and a higher weight was given to studies with small standard error and large sample size, as these were regarded as more precise. the summary effect was calculated based on the effect sizes and their weight, using a random effect model, which allow the true mean to vary between studies, as the selected studies differed in design, materials and methods.
background: Mitigation measures treating drainage water before it enters streams hold a high potential for reducing nitrogen and phosphorus losses from agricultural areas.
objective: assess the efficiency of nitrate removal from drainage water induced by free water surface constructed wetlands.
result1: free water surface significantly reduced nitrate loading by 41% within a range from − 8 to 63%. the ci varied from 29 to 51%.
result2: the funnel plot did not indicate major biases, as the studies were more or less evenly scattered.
result3: the heterogeneity of the selected sites was rather high (i2 = 96%).
result4: the average total phosphorus removal efficiency of fws was 33%, ranging from − 103 to 68% (ci: 19 to 47%, pi: − 2 to 69%).
result5: the removal efficiencies did not follow a normal distribution; the data were skewed to the left due to net release of tp from multiple sites. the funnel plot showed an asymmetrical scatter of sites, as sites with tp release had much higher se. as expected, the heterogeneity was rather high, and t2 (226%) was much lower than σ2 (838%). the subset data analysis for tp removal reported a slightly higher removal (35%) than the initial data; however, σ2 was still very high as the included studies reported both removal and release of tp.
general_conclusion: the results showed that free water surface wetland significantly reduced the nitrate loss from drainage systems, but variation in the reported removal efficiencies was large. the results showed that free water surface wetland significantly reduced the phoshorus loss from drainage systems, but variation in the reported removal efficiencies was large.

search_strategy: searches for literature were made in isi web of science, georef and geobase, scopus, agricola, asfa, academic search, biological abstracts, wiley online library, directory of open access journals and sciencedirect. no particular time, document type or language constraints were applied. grey literature was searched for using the search engine google where simplified search strings were used. in addition, the websites of relevant specialist organisations were also searched. generally, the first 100 hits were examined in the searches using google and on specialist websites.
selection_criteria:
1) relevant study: secondary or tertiary treated domestic wastewater, urban storm water, stream/river water, freshwater aquaculture effluents, and runoff from agricultural fields were considered in the study. untreated wastewater was not considered since it is not permissible to discharge such water into the environment in most european countries. industrial or agricultural wastewater can vary considerably in composition, and was therefore also excluded. farmyard runoff was in most cases classified as agricultural wastewater, and thus excluded, since it is often mixed with untreated parlour washings and silage/farmyard manure effluents, among other things; 2) types of intervention: creation or restoration of wetlands; 3) the comparator has to be no intervention (inlet conditions
can serve as control); 4) types of outcome: included outcomes are mass removal of total nitrogen (tn) or total phosphorus (tp) from the water body per unit wetland area and year. removal efficiency of tn or tp (% of load); 5) to be included in the review, it is a prerequisite that the wetland is established in field conditions and exposed to the ambient climate. this means that laboratory and greenhouse studies were excluded and that each study must cover at least one complete annual cycle; 6) in order to reflect realistic conditions the wetland must be of a reasonable size. while typical microcosm studies were excluded, mesocosm studies were included since they potentially provide valuable information on the variability of the outcomes based on true replicates. a cut-off wetland size of 1 m2 was applied; 7) climate: studies conducted in snow climates, warm temperate climates, and equatorial climates with one dry season were included; 8) to be included the studies must have taken all removal processes into account.
data_analysis: the studies with true or temporal replication (n = 39) were subjected to meta-analyses, using random effects models. to examine how the removal of nitrogen of phosphorus was influenced by effect modifiers (hydraulic loading rate, concentrations of nitrogen and phosphorus in the inflow to the wetlands, type of wetland, type of inflow, climate zone, average air temperature, and wetland area) all included studies (n = 93) were subjected to meta-regression by response surface analyses various regression models. publication bias was analysed (in the present case publication bias was not considered as a major concern).
background: A widely used method to reduce the input of nutrients to freshwater and marine environments is to allow water to pass through a created or restored wetland. However, the large variation in measured nutrient removal rates in such wetlands calls for a systematic review.
objective: the objective of this review is to quantify observed removal rates of nutrients (nitrogen and phosphorus) in created or restored wetlands, and to examine the distribution of these rates and quantify the variation between different studies.
result1: the overall average summary effect represents a median tp removal ratio (r) of about 0.54, which can be recalculated to a median tp removal efficiency of 46 %, with a 95 % confidence interval of 37 to 55 %.
result2: the removal efficiency of total phosphorus was correlated with total phosphorus concentrations at the inlet, hydraulic loading, wetland area, and air temperature. the total phosphorus removal rate was positively correlated with concentration at inlet and hydraulic loading rate. in contrast, the total phosphorus removal rate was negatively correlated with wetland area, especially for wetlands smaller than 2*10^4 m2.
result3: the overall average summary effect represents a median tn removal ratio (r) of about 0.63. this means that the median tn load reduction, or removal efficiency, is 37 %, with a 95 % confidence interval of 29 to 44 %.
result4: removal efficiency of total nitrogen in wetlands was positively correlated with average annual air temperature and negatively correlated with hydraulic loading rate. the model fit was better if interaction effects between these variables were allowed. the total nitrogen removal rate was positively correlated with the inflow concentration and was also found to be positively correlated with hydraulic loading.
general_conclusion: restored and created wetlands remain appropriate and potentially sustainable ecological engineering approaches for removing nutrients from treated wastewater and urban and agricultural runoff.
knowledge_gaps: most studies are from europe and north america; the size distribution of included wetlands may also be biased; most studies of nutrient removal in wetlands have been made during the years following wetland restoration or creation.

search_strategy: authors searched web of  science in april 2015,  using  the  following  query:  ts  =  (top-  down*  or  herbivor* or grazing* or predat* or consumer* or trophic  cascade*)  and  ts  =  (salt  marsh*  or  mangrove*  or  coastal  wetland*  or  coastal  marsh*)  and  ts = (plant* or vegetation* or mangrove* or grass* or forb* or shrub*). 28  other  published  and  unpublished studies that were known to be relevant were included.
selection_criteria: 1) paper examined the effects of herbivores, omnivores, or predators (including parasitoids) on plants in observational studies and field or laboratory experiments (studies of omnivores or predators without examining their effects on plants or herbivory were excluded); 2) measured the effects of consumers on variables related to plant demography, growth, chemistry, or diversity;  3) reported mean values of the data with sample sizes and some measure of variance (e.g., standard deviations/errors) in both consumer present and absent treatments.
data_analysis: using random- effects models, authors first estimated mean g∗c and 95% confidence intervals (95% cis) on each plant demographic and growth variable available for salt marsh and mangrove studies, respectively. heterogeneity was estimated using the q statistic, a measure of weighted squared deviations, and mean effect sizes are considered significant if their 95% cis do not overlap zero. all analyses were conducted using r 3.1.2 and its metafor package.
background: Rapid, global, anthropogenic alteration of food webs in ecosystems necessitates a better understanding of how consumers regulate natural communities.
objective: to test the following hypotheses: 1) herbivores generally affect the demography, growth, and chemistry of plants in salt marshes and mangroves; 2) herbivores decrease the strength of plant competition and increase plant diversity; 3) predators and omnivores generate trophic cascades and thereby enhance plant performance by suppressing herbivore abundance and grazing rate; 4) consumer control of coastal vegetation is generally observed independently of study methodologies.
result1: livestock increased plant density and had no effect on plant reproduction.
result2: livestock decreased above-ground biomass and plant height, while had no effetc on plant cover.
general_conclusion: analyses show that salt marsh herbivores, including insects, snails, crabs, waterfowl, small mammals, and livestock, generally and often strongly suppress plant survival, aboveground biomass, and height, while their effects on plant density, belowground biomass, reproduction, and cover are more variable. the results confirm the top-down effects of large-bodied herbivores such as livestock and geese.
knowledge_gaps: a greater understanding of the impacts of trophic cascades, top predators and predator diversity in coastal wetlands is sorely needed. then, experimental studies on the impact of global change on consumer control in coastal wetlands have been lacking. a variety of global change drivers have been forecasted to impact the functioning and stability of coastal wetlands, and one possible impact mechanism is altered consumer control of vegetation. last, future studies are needed to examine whether and to what extent the effects of consumers on coastal vegetation scale up to affect the functioning of coastal wetlands. finally, more studies should be conducted on other types of consumers, including parasites and fungal path- ogens, and in understudied regions.

search_strategy: keyword searches in scopus and web of science were used to identify peer-reviewed literature quantifying the effects of livestock grazing on the ecosystem properties of salt marshes. authors retrieved papers published from 1950 to november 2015 containing the terms (saltmarsh* or “salt marsh*” or salt-marsh or “salt meadow” or “coastal marsh”) and (graz* or herbivor* or livestock or cow* or cattle or sheep or horse* or deer) in their title, abstract or keywords. additionally, the doctoral thesis repository ethos was searched in november 2015 for phd theses containing these terms.
selection_criteria: 1) studies must have measured an ecosystem property on a grazed and ungrazed area of salt marsh; 2) only ungulate grazers were considered. 3) both observational and experimental studies were included, as were those that replicated the effects of livestock by clipping or trampling.
data_analysis: a weighted meta-analysis, by inverse of variance, was used to calculate an overall average effect of grazing for every ecosystem property (ep) that had mean and variance values from ≥3 separate publications. for each ep, a random effects, multilevel linear model was used to combine individual effect sizes to estimate an overall mean effect with 95% ci. models were fitted with a restricted maximum likelihood (reml) structure using the rma.mv function within the metafor package in r. study (i.e. publication) nested within site was included as a random factor to account for non-independence of multiple entries extracted from the same study, and multiple studies conducted at the same site. in addition, funnel plots were examinated to assess publication bias.
scale: global: 89 single studies (75 in eu; 12 in america, 2 in asia)
background: How livestock affect the structure and functions of sensitive coastal ecosystems has hitherto lacked synthesis. Grazing-induced changes in salt marshes have the potential to alter the provision of valuable ecosystem services, such as coastal protection, blue carbon and biodiversity conservation.
objective: to investigate how livestock alter soil, vegetation and faunal properties in salt marshes. stocking density, grazing duration, grazer identity, continent and vegetation type were also analysed as potential modifiers of the grazing effect. here, the results for biodiversity are reported.
result1: biodiversity responses depended on focal group, with positive effects of grazing on vegetation species richness, but negative effects on invertebrate richness. grazing reduced the abundance of herbivorous invertebrates, which may affect fish and crustaceans that feed in the marsh. overall vertebrate abundance was not affected.
result2: the majority of the vertebrate data were extracted from studies on bird abundance (85% of entries) and goose abundance in particular (62%).
result3: all measures of above-ground plant material (canopy height, cover, above-ground biomass) were decreased by grazing.
result4: for most properties, no bias was evident from visual assessment of funnel plots. the exceptions were plant richness, that showed bias towards reporting of negative effects in smaller, less precise studies (those with a larger standard error). this indicates that the true effects on plant richness may be more positive than the values calculated here. and plant cover, that showed bias towards reporting of negative effects in smaller, less precise studies (those with a larger standard error). this indicates that the true effects on plant cover may be more positive than the values calculated here.
general_conclusion: authors found that livestock grazing affected 11 of the 21 ecosystem properties tested, spanning soil, vegetation and faunal response variables.

search_strategy: authors searched for peer-reviewed articles published before may 2021 from the institute for scientific information (isi) web of science and china national knowledge infrastructure (cnki) databases. the search strings were: (“nitrogen deposition” or “nitrogen addition” or “nitrogen enrichment” or “nitrogen loading” or “nitrogen fertilization” or “nitrogen application” or “nitrogen elevated” or “nitrogen supply”) and (methane or ch4) and (uptake or oxidation or emission or flux).
selection_criteria: 1) only in situ n addition experiments were selected, the laboratory incubation studies were excluded; 2) soil ch4 flux was measured using the static chamber method and gas chromatography technique; 3) the measurement duration of soil-atmosphere interface ch4 flux should be at least one growing season or an entire year; 4) for studies involving factorial experiments, only data from control and solely n addition treatments were selected; 5) means, sample size and standard deviation (sd) of control and n treatments were reported or could be calculated from the information provided in the publication.
data_analysis: to test whether hedges’ d significantly differed from zero, authors assessed bias-corrected 95% bootstrap confidence interval (ci) overlapping zero based on 999 iterations. hedges’ d calculations and meta-analyses were conducted with metawin v2.1 software. between-group q statistical test (expressed as qm value) was applied to compare the heterogeneity of the weighted effects size of the different groups for each categorical variable listed above. significant chi-square values (p < 0.05) indicated that the effects within a category were significantly heterogeneous. random forest modelling was used to identify relative importance of the categorical and continuous variables in influencing the responses of soil-atmosphere exchange of ch4 flux to n addition. random forest modelling was conducted by using ibm spss modeler 18.0. additionally, rank correlations (kendall’s tau rank correlations and spearman’s rank correlation) between the standardized effect size and the standardized variance were used to test the publication bias within each variable. an alternative method for testing publication bias was to calculate the rosenberg’s fail-safe number (n). both rank correlations analysis and fail-safe number suggested that all of the variables were without publication bias.
background: Reactive nitrogen (N) addition may profoundly impact the global CH4 budget through its substantial effects on soil CH4 uptake and emission. However, the magnitude and direction of soil CH4 uptake and emission rates in response to N addition on a global scale are still unclear.
objective: to investigate the effects of n addition on soil ch4 uptake and emission rates in various upland and wetland ecosystems. here, results on carbon sequestration for wetlands are reported.
result1: n addition did not significantly affect soil organic carbon (soc) content in wetland ecosystems.
result2: NA
general_conclusion: n addition did not significantly affect soil organic carbon (soc) content in wetland ecosystems.

search_strategy: the authors conducted a literature search in september 2019 for all papers published over the past decade on greenhouse gases, nitrogen input and wetland ecosystems.
selection_criteria: 1) the control experiment was defined by no nitrogen input or atmospheric nitrogen deposition; 2) non-repetitive experimental studies were excluded; 3) non-experimental studies (such as modeling, meta-analyses, and reviews) were excluded.
data_analysis: the calculated mean effect size considered the confidence intervals (bootstrap cis, bootstrapping by 4999 iterations). if the bootstrap cis had nonzero overlap, the nitrogen input significantly influenced the greenhouse gas emissions. all of the standardized mean differences, the between-group heterogeneity, bootstrap cis and fail-safe number were counted using metawin 2.1.3 software.
background: Greenhouse gas emissions from wetlands are significantly promoted by global nitrogen input for changing the rate of soil carbon and nitrogen cycling, and are substantially affected by soil labile carbon and nitrogen conversely. However, the driving mechanism by which soil labile carbon and nitrogen affect greenhouse gas emissions from wetland ecosystems under global nitrogen input is not well understood.
objective: the authors used soil carbon dioxide emissions, methane emissions, nitrous oxide emissions, soil labile carbon and nitrogen, and soil microbial biomass to address the following questions: (i) how do the soil greenhouse gas emissions from wetland ecosystems fluctuate as a result of varying nitrogen input in terms of rates, compounds and environmental factors? (ii) what key factors affect soil greenhouse gas emissions as a response to nitrogen input? (iii) what is the major effect oflabile compounds on greenhouse gas emissions from wetland ecosystems under global nitrogen input? here, results for wetlands (salt marshes, freshwater marshes, estuaryies and alpine wetlands) are reported.
result1: nitrogen input increased greenhouse gas emissions for all types of wetlands, except for the alpine wetland, which had significantly decreased methane emission (smd = -1.41, bootstrap cis = -2.14 to -0.74).
result2: NA
general_conclusion: nitrogen input significantly promoted methane and nitrous oxide emissions from wetlands.

search_strategy: one hundred and nine publications that contained 313 observations across north and south america, europe and asia were selected for our analysis.
selection_criteria: 1) the authors included studies in which control and treatment sites experienced same climatic, soil and vegetation conditions. therefore, some studies examining n enrichment effects along n deposition gradients were not included; 2) although n2o emission from leguminous crops may be considerable, the authors could not estimate n2o response ratio caused by biological n fixation because there is no non-n fixation control treatment. the application of organic n fertilizers, such as animal manures, also increases c supply. the effects of added c and n on ghg emissions could not be separated. therefore, those studies that examined organic fertilizers were excluded from this analysis; 3) publications which did not report experimental error were not included in the analysis. in total, six response variables, nee, ec, soc, ch4 emission, ch4 uptake and n2o emission, were included to characterize the effects of n addition on the ghg flux.
data_analysis: the n effect on a response variable was considered significant if the 95% ci did not overlap 1. for each categorical group (ecosystem type, n addition level, chemical form of n addition and experimental condition) of each response variable (nee, ec, soc, ch4 emission, ch4 uptake and n2o emission), total heterogeneity among group (qt) can be partitioned into within group heterogeneity (qw) and between group heterogeneity (qb), such that qt =qw +qb, where q-statistic has a chi-square distribution.
background: Anthropogenic nitrogen (N) enrichment of ecosystems, mainly from fuel combustion and fertilizer application, alters biogeochemical cycling of ecosystems in a way that leads to altered flux of biogenic greenhouse gases (GHGs).
objective: the authors report the results of a meta-analysis that quantitatively synthesizes the available research on changes in ghg flux (co2,ch4 or n2o) from n addition in multiple terrestrial ecosystems, including agricultural crop, forest, grassland, wetland, tundra, heathland and desert. authors investigated whether the direction and magnitude of ghg flux differs by: 1) ecosystem type; 2) the level of n loading; 3) chemical species of n addition; 4) experimental condition.
result1: overall, n addition, ranging from 10 to 562 kg n ha-1 year-1, had no significant effect on nee for non-forest natural ecosystems.
result2: n addition, ranging from 30 to 400 kg n /ha /year, significantly increased ch4 emission by an average of 95% when averaged across grassland, wetland and anaerobic agricultural system.
result3: overall, ch4 uptake was significantly reduced by an average of 38% under n addition, ranging from 10 to 560 kg n ha)1 year)1. the mean ch4 uptake decreased by 0.016 ± 0.004 kg ch4-c ha)1 year)1 for non-agricultural ecosystems (n =23) per 1 kg n ha)1 year)1 added to the ecosystem. the mean response ratios of ch4 uptake were < 1 for all ecosystem types, but this inhibition was not significant for grasslands and drained wetlands.
result4: nitrogen addition, ranging from 10 to 562 kg n ha)1 year)1, significantly increased n2o emission by an average of 216% across all ecosystems.
general_conclusion: overall, n addition had no significant effect on nee, but significantly increased ch4 and n2o emissions.
knowledge_gaps: ecosystems, such as wetland and tundra, have significant influences on global ghg budget, but our understanding on how n addition affects ghg balance in those ecosystems is insufficient. measurements from those underrepresented regions and ecosystems are needed to fill the data gap.

search_strategy: peer-reviewed publications were searched using web of science to build a compiled database, which included the responses to p addition of different variables related to plant biomass production, plant n and p concentrations, and soil available n and p concentrations.
selection_criteria: 1) measurements and data were only collected from field manipulative experiments of p addition that conducted in natural terrestrial ecosystems; 2) the examined variables were plant biomass production at the community level, plant n and p concentration, and soil n and p concentration; 3) when data from the same site were presented in multiple publications, a single measurement from the latest sample date was used to meet the statistical assumption of independence among observations.
data_analysis: using the metawin software 2.1, the authors calculated the variables such as the mean, the response ratio, where standard deviation (s) or standard error, and sample size for each observation were extracted to calculate the rr, the variance, the weighting factor, the weighted response ratio, and the 95% confidence interval of rr++ for the purpose of statistic tests. total heterogeneity among group (qt) was partitioned into within-group heterogeneity (qw) and between group heterogeneity (qb). to examine whether n addition will stimulate p limitation, the authors compare the effect size of p addition between the groups of with or without n addition. t-test was used to test the statistic differences. the authors used the linear regression methods to analyze the relationships of biomass response ratios with the response ratios of soil p availability, leaf p concentration, soil and plant n : p ratios. the regression analysis was conducted with the spss software, and the graphs were drawn with the sigmaplot software.
background: Nitrogen (N) and phosphorus (P), either individually or in combination, have been demonstrated to limit biomass production in terrestrial ecosystems. Field studies have been extensively synthesized to assess global patterns of N impacts on terrestrial ecosystem processes. However, to our knowledge, no synthesis has been done so far to reveal global patterns of P impacts on terrestrial ecosystems, especially under different nitrogen (N) levels.
objective: the authors conducted a meta-analysis of results from field experiments on responses of aboveground (agb) and belowground biomass production (bgb) to manipulative p addition under ambient and enriched n conditions. the specific questions this synthesis addressed were as follows: 1) what are the global patterns of the responses of terrestrial biomass production, plant and soil n and p concentrations, and n : p ratios to p addition? 2) whether p limitation is enhanced under increased n loading? 3) whether the p- induced increase in ecosystem biomass production is correlated with changes in soil p availability, leaf p concentration, or n : p ratio?
result1: p addition increased plant p concentration in wetland.
result2: NA
general_conclusion: p addition increased plant p concentration in wetland.

search_strategy: the authors conducted a literature search, last updated in october 2019, using the web of science (thomson reuters) search engine. studies investigating the effect of agricultural practices on soil nematodes. studies should include nematode data and evaluate the effects of at least one of the four main agricultural practices (manipulation of plant diversity, pesticide use, tillage, fertilization) or those of different types of agricultural systems (“system”) on the nematode community. here we report only data regarding organic farming systems as compared to conventional systems.
selection_criteria:
(1) data should be available in the articles either in table or in graphical forms. in the case of graphics, the programme getdata graph digitizer (version 2.26 http://getdata-graph-digitizer.com/), was used to extract data from figures.
(2) nematode data should be a measurement of the abundance of nematode trophic groups, that is bacterial feeding (bf), fungal feeding (ff), omnivores and predators (op) and plant feeding nematodes (pf), and/or nematode diversity and/or nematode indices. diversity indices were taxonomic richness (s) and shannon diversity (h′). nematode indices were the maturity index (mi), plant-parasitic index (ppi), structure index (si), enrichment index (ei), and nematode channel ratio (ncr). studies had to report at least one of the abovementioned nematode parameters to be included in this synthesis.
(3) studies needed to evaluate the effect of the conversion of conventional agriculture to organic agriculture. conventional systems use pesticide, mineral fertilizers and tillage. organic agriculture does not use synthetic pesticide and mineral fertilizers. tillage is used for weed management.
(4) the samples should be collected from the topsoil layer (soil depth between 0 and 30 cm maximum).
(5) studies needed to report means (x ̅), standard deviations (sd) or standard errors (se) and sample size (n, number of true replications) of nematode variables in control and treatment groups. when sd, se or sample size were missing, articles were discarded as these data are required to compute the effect size. a total of 103 articles, i.e. 30% of articles, met these inclusion criteria and were used in the meta-analysis, corresponding to a total of 1338 unique observations (control + treatment, fig. 2).

search_strategy: literature searches of the web of science and cab direct online databases were conducted using the combination of search terms “monensin”, “methane”, and “cattle”, or “cow”. the period covered was 1970 to 2011.
selection_criteria: 1) to include a control treatment group that did not receive monensin; 2) to be conducted in vivo using cattle; 3) to include measured ch4 production as an outcome.
data_analysis: separate meta-analyses were conducted for quantifying overall antimethanogenic effects of monensin in dairy cows, beef steers, and both dairy cows and beef steers using the metafor package (version 1.6–0) in r (version 2.12.2). heterogeneity of the monensin effects were estimated using random effect models. due to significant heterogeneity (>68%) in both dairy and beef studies, the random effect models were then extended to mixed effect models by including fixed effects of dry matter intake (dmi), dietary nutrient contents, monensin dose, and length of monensin treatment period. values of each explanatory variable were first centered on their means and then regressed individually against mean differences (md). the meta-analytic models were fitted using the rma function in the metafor package. full mixed-effect models carrying all explanatory variables having effects (p < 0.10) when fitted individually were then fitted using the maximum likelihood (ml) method. reduced models were formed via stepwise elimination of variables. the parameter estimates of the final model were obtained by fitting the model using the reml method. forest and funnel plots were constructed. publication bias was were assessed using egger’s regression test for funnel plot asymmetry.
background: Monensin is a widely used feed additive with the potential to minimize methane (CH4) emissions from cattle. Several studies have investigated the effects of monensin on CH4, but findings have been inconsistent.
objective: to conduct meta-analyses to quantitatively summarize the effect of monensin on methane (ch4) production (g/d) and the percentage of dietary gross energy lost as ch4 in dairy cows and beef steers.
result1: monensin showed a potential (p = 0.065) to reduce methane (ch4) production in dairy cows by 6 g/d with dry matter intake (dmi) and dietary ether extract (ee) content have significant independent effects on ch4 production.
result2: feeding monensin in a diet with average neutral detergent fiber (ndf) content (379 g/kg of dm) significantly (p < 0.001) reduced ch4 emissions from beef steers by 19 g/d.
result3: dietary gross energy lost as ch4 decreased with monensin in dairy cows.
result4: none of the selected explanatory variables had a significant effect on the monensin effect on dietary gross energy lost as ch4 in beef steers.
general_conclusion: overall, monensin had stronger anti-methanogenic effects in beef steers than dairy cows, but the effects in dairy cows could potentially be improved by dietary composition modifications and increasing the monensin dose.

search_strategy:
the search strategy of the systematic review was based on the pico: population, intervention, comparator, and outcome. the following terms were used respectively for population: bovine or “beef cattle” or “dairy cattle” or steer* or cow* or calf* ; and for intervention: tannin* or “condensed tannin” or “hydrolyzed tannin” or phytochemicals or tannins* or "tannic acid" or tannin* or “plant extract” or chestnut or quebracho or acacia or sainfoin or “natural feed additives”. search for manuscripts in english, spanish and portuguese were carried out from august to december 2018 in scopus (elsevier,
1960–2018), web of science (clarivate analytics, 1945–2018), pubmed (1940–2018), sciencedirect (elsevier, 1960–2018) and cab- abstracts (thomson reuters, 1910–2018). the references were exported to endnote web (thomson reuters, new york, usa) to organize and remove duplicates.
selection_criteria:
the population considered calves, heifers, steers, cows lactating and/or gestating cows and dairy calves. the intervention was represented by the inclusion of tannin in cattle diets. the comparator was considered as animals undergoing the same treatment with or without intervention. two previously trained reviewers independently assessed the publications by analyzing the title, abstract, and keywords of each
abstract. the inclusion criteria for research selection was: (1) it was primary study; (2) evaluate the effects of tannins in the feeding of cattle; and (3) evaluate at least one of the response variables (scfa, n-nh3, dmd or ch4). randomized and non-randomized studies were included. manuscripts
data_analysis: the mean difference (md) between treated and control groups and a 95 % confidence interval (95 % ci) was considered. assuming that there were experimental differences in the studies designs. the q cochran test (chi square heterogeneity test) and i2 were calculated based on the outcome. the magnitude of i2 was considered low (25 %), moderate (50 %), or high (75 %) heterogeneity (higgins et al., 2003). stata v. 14.0 (stata corp., texas, usa) was used in all statistical analyses. differences were considered significant when p < 0.05, and trends were discussed when 0.05 ≤ p < 0.1.
background: Numerous studies have proven the beneficial activity of tannins with important actions in ruminal fermentation. However, data in the scientific literature are inconsistent since they do not consider aspects inherent to the composition of tannins and their interaction in the rumen with different types of diets.
objective: a systematic review protocol was designed to identify studies that evaluated the effect of the use of tannins on performance and rumen fermentation in beef and dairy cattle. this paper presents part of the results obtained, referring only to the effects of tannins on the total production of short-chain fatty acids (scfa) and ammonia nitrogen concentration (n-nh3), dry matter digestibility (dmd), and methane production (ch4) from beef and dairy cattle, considering the source (natural or extract), type (ct, ht, or blend), total tannin concentration (in the source) and dose.
result1: no effect of tannins on ch4 production was found (i2 = 64.1 % - moderate). methane production was higher in animals receiving tannins (p = 0.025) when the total concentration of tannins in the source was greater than 500 g/kg ms (i2 = 17.1 %).
result2: the production of ch4, when added doses of tannins between 11 and 20 g/kg ms, was reduced by 4 % (p = 0.005; i2 = 44.5 % - moderate)
result3: no difference was observed in tannins coming from plant or from extract.
general_conclusion: no effect of tannins on methane production was found in dairy and beef cattle.

search_strategy: a literature search was conducted on the public databases web of science™ and pubmed®. the following keywords were used to search titles and abstracts: chicken(s), broiler (s), ross, cobb, reduce(d) protein diets, reduce(d) cp, low protein, low cp, levels of cp, and protein dilution.
selection_criteria: to be included in the data set, the trials had to use diets formulated with the same levels of digestible lysine (diglys) and apparent metabolizable energy (ame) or nitrogen-corrected ame (amen) within each trial. trials were removed if the daily lys intake of the control broilers deviated by more than 20% from the recommended lys intake, which is derived from hauschild et al. (2015). only trials using fast-growing strains (ross 308 or cobb 500) were considered, and the bird performance in the control treatment was required to be at least 90% of the genetic potential of the breeder’s guidelines. in addition, feed composition, experimental conditions (bird variety, sex, age, ambient temperature, etc.), and growth performance had to be detailed.
data_analysis: the effect ofcp on the variables of interest was studied in both databases using minitab® (2021) to conduct a multivariate analysis with the trial as a random effect. the linear model was used when the quadratic effect was not significant. the effect of cp was studied for several datasets. finally, to ensure the quality of the cp response models, the normality of residuals, the independence of the error, and the homogeneity of the variance were tested. effects were considered significant at a p-value< 0.05 and trends at a p-value< 0.10.
background: In broilers, the effects of crude protein (CP) reduction on animal performance are heterogeneous. This could limit the use of this strategy in commercial farms despite its potential to improve the sustainability of production.
objective: the objective of this meta-analysis was to study the effect of lowering dietary cp in fast-growing broilers with a focus on growth performance.
result1: in the gen-database, the decrease in dietary cp content led to a linear (p< 0.001) and quadratic (p< 0.001) decrease in average daily feed intake (adfi) and adg. in contrast, in the aacon-database (with amino acid control), the dietary cp content did not affect adfi and adg.
result2: NA
general_conclusion: the decrease in dietary crude protein content without aminoacid control led to a decrease in average daily feed intake and average daily gain in broilers. however, no effect was observed when low crude protein diet include amino acid control.

search_strategy: the studies included in the analysis were those cited in isi web of science database until february 2019 with the keywords ‘soil organic carbon’ or ‘soil organic matter’ and ‘no-till’, ‘no tillage’ or ‘zero tillage’ or ‘direct seeding’.
selection_criteria: (a) experiments of no-till lasting more than 5 years, which were used to reduce the instabilities at the beginning of the experiment; (b) the duration of conventional tillage and no-till were the same; (c) measured thick- ness of soil layers was not less than 30 cm; and (d) reduced tillage and minimum tillage practices were excluded and only continuous no-till (i.e. complete absence of tillage) was selected.
data_analysis: to include as many studies as possible, studies were weighted by sample size: w=ncnt∕(nc+nt), where w refers to the specific weight of a given pair of data, and nc and nt are sample sizes for the control and no-till respectively. given that studies differed in sample sizes, more weights are given to large sample sizes. resampling methods (e.g. bootstrapping) were used to cal- culate bias-corrected 95% confidence intervals (cis) around the mean effect size. if the 95% ci of the effect size for a variable did not overlap with zero, the effect of restoration on the variable was considered significant.
background: Conservation agriculture has been shown to have multiple benefits for soils, crop yield and the environment, and consequently, no-till, the central practice of conservation agriculture, has rapidly expanded. However, studies show that the potential for carbon (C) sequestration in no-till farming sometimes is not realized, let alone the ability to maintain or improve crop yield.
objective: global analysis of no-till-induced changes of soil c and crop yield
result1: relative to local conventional tillage, arid regions can benefit from no tillage.
result2: relative to local conventional tillage, arid regions can benefit the most from conservation agriculture.
general_conclusion: there was a positive effect of no-tillage or conservation agriculture on crop yied in arid region but negative effect in humid regions.

search_strategy: a comprehensive search was conducted for peer-reviewed publications on the effect of ca on crop yields compared to ct in sub-saharan africa using the online databases isi web of science (thomson reuters) and scopus (elsevier). the following search terms were used (an asterisk being a replacement for any ending of the respective term): ‘conservation agriculture’, ‘zero till*’, ‘no till*’, ‘reduced till*’, ‘minimum till*’, ‘direct seeding’, or ‘direct drill*’ in combination with ‘yield’ and ‘africa’ or a country from the list of all countries of sub-saharan africa (excluding south africa and lesotho) in the publication title, abstract or keywords. the database searches were augmented with searches of library resources for relevant papers from citations in retrieved papers. the last search was done in december 2019.
selection_criteria: studies from the retrieved publications were screened and had to meet the following defined basic selection criteria to be included in the meta-analysis. first, studies report crop yields from field experiments in which a ct treatment is compared with a (partial) ca treatment using statistical methods. second, the effect of no- or reduced tillage must be tested with the ca treatment. third, the experiments must be conducted under rain-fed field conditions in a specified location in sub-saharan africa. fourth, the mean, sample size and standard deviation of crop yields must be directly reported as numerical or graphical data or can be calculated from the reported data. standard deviations were calculated from standard errors, coefficients of variation, 95% ci or least significant differences in cases where they were not reported in the papers. for some observations, the least significant difference was estimated as the smallest difference between the mean values of treatments that were still significant. data from the same study that were reported in more than one publication were not repeated to avoid double counting; instead, the data from the most recent publication were used. observations were excluded from the analysis when only average crop yields over seasons or sites were presented. if more than one form of tillage was assessed in a study, we selected the ct treatment that represented the greatest soil disturbance. studies were rejected if crop management practices other than those related to the three ca principles (rt, m and ir) differed between ca and ct treatments, with the exception of weed management. tillage in ct systems helps with the control of weeds, and its absence in ca systems often implies the use of herbicides and/or additional mechanical weeding. in total, 87 publications were selected, giving 992 ca-to-ct yield comparisons.
data_analysis: individual response ratios were weighted by the reciprocal of their respective estimated variances as a measure of study quality; that is, observations with low variance were considered more reliable and received a higher weight in the meta-analysis. as expected, the on-farm trials had a significantly (p < 0.0001) higher variance, thus smaller weight, than on-station trials. the model parameters were estimated by the restricted maximum likelihood approach. estimated mean response ratios were considered statistically different from zero (that is, the ca yield is significantly different from the ct yield) if their 95% ci did not overlap zero; the cis were calculated by multiplying the standard error by the 95% point of the student’s t-test distribution corresponding to the number of degrees of freedom. paired student’s t-tests on the logarithmic difference of response ratios between two subgroups of studies were performed to determine whether the ca-to-ct yield ratios differed significantly between the two groups.
background: Conservation agriculture (CA) has become a dominant paradigm in scientific and policy thinking about the sustainable intensification of food production in sub-Saharan Africa. Yet claims that CA leads to increasing crop yields in African smallholder farming systems remain controversial.
objective: here we present the results of a comprehensive meta-analysis of crop yields under ca in sub-saharan africa. more specifically, our meta-analysis aimed to elucidate crop yield responses to ca and the agro-environmental and management conditions that favour positive crop responses. the latter, in particular, can contribute to a more effective targeting of investments in ca research and development in africa, and thereby to increase crop production and food availability as part of a broader strategy to achieve sustainable food security.
result1: maize yields under no- or reduced tillage alone were not significantly (p > 0.05) different from yields under conventional tillage. however, ca with mulching (conservation tillage + mulching) had a significantly positive effect on maize yields (3.9%, ci: [2.5, 5.3], p < 0.0001). when all three ca principles are implemented (conservation tillage + mulching + rotations or intercropping), the effect more than doubled (8.4%, ci: [6.1,10.8], p < 0.0001)
result2: NA
general_conclusion: conservation farming systems (conservation tillage applied in parallel to mulching and to crop rotations or intercropping) had a significantly positive effect on maize yields, compared to conventional tillage without mulching.
knowledge_gaps: more observations from long-term studies are clearly needed to establish whether a relationship exists between increased crop yields, improved soil quality and the duration of the practice of ca.

search_strategy: the on-station data were archived from 143 original peer-reviewed publications and 13 proceedings/book chapters/reports through the web of science and google scholar search, libraries and personal communications (supplementary note). the on-farm original data (published/unpublished) were obtained from researchers on a personal contact basis as well as using open access data. in on-farm data, trials conducted in a given year in a specific location and soil type under a single cropping system with similar management practices (ca sublevels) were identified (or referred to) as a single study. the peer-reviewed publications dealing with the effects of zero tillage in relation to the ct practice were searched, using the web of science (elsevier) indexing service, with keywords ‘tillage’, ‘conservation’, ‘zero tillage’, ‘no-tillage’, ‘cropping system’, ‘crop’, ‘residue’, ‘yield’, ‘water use’, ‘cost’, ‘economics’, ‘methane’, ‘carbon dioxide’, ‘nitrous oxide’ and ‘global warming potential’ in different combinations in the article abstract. proceedings/book chapters/reports were included, and non-english language publications were excluded.
selection_criteria:
1. field experiments with side-by-side comparisons of ca and ct practices

2. ca practices falling within the three options described in table 1

3. studies conducted in the same location and same soil type with the same crop management practices in ca and ct options

4. studies that used the same methods of measurements in ct and ca options

5. studies that reported yield data
data_analysis: NA
background: Agriculture’s contribution to the Sustainable Development Goals requires climate-smart and profitable farm innovations. In the past decade, attention has been given to conservation agriculture as a ‘sustainable intensification’ strategy, although a lack of evidence-based consensus on the merits of conservation agriculture prevails in the context of intensive smallholder farming in South Asia.
objective: although numerous on-station and on-farm studies have been carried out during the past two decades to evaluate ca in south asia, a systematic synthesis of evidence is lacking. to clarify the regional potential of ca as a full package or combination of its components in south asia, this study presents a comprehensive meta-analysis on data from on-station (1996–2016) and on-farm (2010–2014) studies in south asia’s dominant cereal-based cropping systems.
result1: compared with conventional practice, ca had 4.6% higher grain yield, which was very similar to pey.
result2: on-station crop yields increased by 11.1% and on-farm by 4.7%.

search_strategy: the authors comprehensively searched the peer-reviewed literature for publications investigating the effects of no-till in relation to the other two conservation agriculture principles on cropyields fromjan 1980 to may 2013 using scopus (elsevier). search terms included ‘tillage’, ‘no till’, ‘zero till’, ‘direct drill*’, or ‘conservation ag*’ in the article title and ‘yield’ in the article title, abstract, or keywords.
selection_criteria: this search produced a total of 2,471 publications, which were screened on the basis of the following criteria: (1) studies had to represent field experiments containing side-by-side comparisons of no-till and conventional tillage practices; (2) no-till treatments consisted of zero tillage immediately before crop establishment for a given growing season (that is, reduced tillage treatments such as strip-tillage were rejected); (3) crop yields were reported; (4) location of the experiment was stated; (5) management information regarding at least one other conservation agriculture principle was available (that is, residue management or crop rotation); and (6) confounding effects between treatments were absent (that is, differences in residue management, seeding rates, fertilizer rates, etc. were determined to be negligible). conference proceedings and non-english language publications were excluded. studies were rejected if it was unclear from reading the experimental methods whether factors other than tillage differed between treatments with the exception of herbicides (the absence of tillage as a weed control strategy generally requires changes in herbicide management under no-till). owing to the large size of the database, particular attention was given to avoiding data duplication (for example, when different studies reported the same data). thus, if it was unclear whether a publication contained duplicate data, it was rejected.
data_analysis:
the authors calculated the natural log of the response ratio (the ratio of no-till to conventional tillage yields) as the effect size in the meta-analysis. because within-study variance measures for mean yields were
available for less than a few percent of studies, individual observations were weighted by replication. bootstrapping procedures were used to generate 95% confidence intervals for weighted mean effect sizes using 4,999 iterations. between-group heterogeneity was assessed using randomization procedures based on 4,999 replications.
background: Conservation agriculture represents a set of three crop management principles that has received strong international support to help address this challenge, with recent conservation agriculture efforts focusing on smallholder farming systems in sub-Saharan Africa and South Asia.However, conservation agriculture is highly debated, with respect to both its effects on crop yields and its applicability in different farming contexts.
objective: here, the authors synthesized current scientific evidence at a global scale to assess crop yields under no-till in relation to implementation of the other two conservation agriculture principles, residue retention and crop rotation.
result1: overall, the authors found that no-till negatively impacts crop yields by 5.7%. importantly, the negative impacts of no-till are minimized when both of the other conservation agriculture principles are also applied (-2.5%) (no till + residues retention + crop rotation vs conventional till + residues retention + crop rotation). the largest yield declines occur when no-till is implemented alone (-9.9%) or with only one other conservation agriculture principle (-5.2 and -6.2% for residue retention and crop rotation, respectively).
result2: the analysis shows that no till significantly enhances yields (7.3%) under rainfed agriculture in dry climates when the other two conservation agriculture principles are also implemented. yet, the reverse is true when no-till is applied alone (-11.9%). furthermore, yields decrease with no-till regardless of whether the other principles are applied in humid climates.
result3: regardless of whether the other two conservation agriculture principles are implemented, no till reduces yields in the first few years following adoption. however, the yield decline in initial years is minimized when all three principles are applied compared with one principle (-3.0% versus -11.4%, respectively). moreover, despite no-till yields in all categories becoming comparable with conventional tillage in the medium term, after 10+ years yields begin to decline when only no-till is implemented.
result4: when considering the relative importance of crop rotation versus residue management practices in enhancing yield of no-till systems, this meta-analysis does not provide evidence that one principle regulates productivity more than the other. across all observations, the individual effects of residue retention and crop rotation reduce the negative impacts of no-till by 4.8 and 3.8%, respectively, although differences between categories are insignificant. however, in dry climates these principles each have a much stronger effect on rainfed crop yields, reducing yield losses by 10.1 and 11.0%, respectively.
general_conclusion: to help close the yield gap with conventional tillage, these findings suggest that instead of implementing no-till as the first step towards conservation agriculture in cropping systems where residue retention and crop rotation are absent (and anticipating that these two principles will follow in time), the primary focus should be on implementing no-till systems that already employ the other two principles.

search_strategy: an extensive literature search was conducted to compile the studies on ca practices in south asian region using google scholar, scopus and science direct till the end of nov 2019. the keywords used in different combinations in searching the peer-reviewed literature were zero tillage, minimum tillage, reduced tillage, conservation agriculture, crop yield, crop residue, mulch, rotation, carbon sequestration, soil health, greenhouse gas emission, water use, rice, wheat, maize, cotton, indo-gangetic plains, india, pakistan, nepal and bangladesh.
selection_criteria: (1) studies had to be field experiments containing side-by-side comparisons of no-till (zero tillage or/and minimum/reduced tillage) and conventional tillage practices; (2) c-sequestration, ghg emission, water use, costs and returns were reported; (3) the location of the experiment was stated. the database was further screened and finalized using the criteria of lundy et al. (2015): (1) studies for which crop rotation information was available; (2) duration of the experiment was reported; (3) information on crop residue management practices was stated (retention of >30% of crop residue/soil cover).
data_analysis: all equations were estimated using the mixed model in stata 14.2 to test the null hypothesis that no change in carbon sequestration between ca practices and conventional tillage. the null hypothesis of the constant variance of carbon sequestration potential across the experiment locations was tested using the white test and the breusch–pagan test of heteroskedasticity. further, akaike information criteria (aic) was used to select a better-fitted model. variance inflation factors (vifs) were used for detecting multicollinearity in the data-set.
background: Agriculture plays a key role in ensuring food and livelihood security in South Asia. However, this region is vulnerable to climate change which is likely to impact the livelihoods of millions of marginal and small holders. Agriculture is not only impacted by climate change but also one of the major contributor to global warming in South Asia. As compared to the traditional practices, Conservation Agriculture (CA) practices help mitigate the impact of climate change through a reduction in carbon emission and conservation of natural resources.
objective: this study attempts to synthesize the results of various studies on ca in the framework of meta-analysis. the study assesses the impacts of ca on carbon sequestration, water use, ghg emission and economic benefits. the impacts were further investigated in relation to the different practices of ca, crops cultivated, cropping systems and soil characteristics. the study is confined to south asia and the meta-analysis was done with respect to factors influencing its impacts, so as to better target the technology.
result1: carbon sequestration was found significantly higher in the ca practices (9.5–16.30%) as compared to the conventional tillage. though each ca practice has a positive effect on carbon sequestration, much sizable carbon sequestration of 4.60 mg ha−1 (16.30%) is achieved by the adoption of all the ca practices altogether (no-tillage along with crop rotation & mulching/soil cover/crop residue). thus, the combination of all the three elements of ca is crucial to secure a sizable magnitude of carbon sequestration.
result2: NA
general_conclusion: carbon sequestration was found significantly higher in the conservation agriculture and much sizable carbon sequestration of 4.60 mg ha−1 (16.30%) is achieved by the adoption of all the conservation practices altogether (no-tillage along with crop rotation & mulching/soil cover/crop residue).
