search_strategy: a literature search was undertaken during 2014 (updated 31st march 2015), searching for keywords soil carbon; soil organic matter; conservation agriculture; zero tillage; reduced tillage; and either indo-gangetic plains or sub-saharan africa.
selection_criteria: in general only papers that included information on soil c stocks (as opposed to soil c concentration) were selected, though in some cases soc stock could be calculated from the published data on soc concentration and soil bulk density. in a few cases, where an experiment had continued for at least 5 years but the authors only quoted soc concentrations, an assumed bulk density value (based on published bulk density data for similar soils in the region) was used to estimate stock.
data_analysis: the statistical analysis used adopts the between-study variation to assess the overall levels of effects and variability and to examine the differences between the different ca practices. one approach would be to treat the practices as being a random sample from a population, i.e. a large number of possible practices. this would enable the effects from the different practices to be assessed in a random effects model in the reml framework. this leads to estimates that shrink towards the overall mean and to smaller standard errors. it was found that the spread of values within each category was quite large, especially in ssa and this caused the reml procedure to not converge. it was considered appropriate to use the same kind of analysis for the two regions and so the treatment categories were treated as fixed effects. while the nominal descriptions of the ca practices are similar for the two regions, they generally refer to different cropping systems so the data from the two regions were analysed separately. the effect of including the random effect for authorship was statistically significant for both regions.
background: Conservation agriculture (CA), comprising minimum soil disturbance, retention of crop residues and crop diversification, is widely promoted for reducing soil degradation and improving agricultural sustainability. It is also claimed to mitigate climate change through soil carbon sequestration
objective: ca comprises three principles, namely: 1. zero or reduced tillage as opposed to inversion ploughing, thus minimising soil disturbance. 2. maintenance of soil cover by retaining crop residues, as opposed to burning or removing them, or growing a green manure over crop during periods when the soil would otherwise be bare. 3. introduction of diversified and economically viable crop rotations instead of practicing monoculture. the first aim of this paper is to quantify the impact of ca practices on soil organic c (soc) stock through a meta-analysis of data from two tropical regions that are important for global food security. the second aim is to critically interpret the measured changes in soil c under ca practices to assess the extent to which they genuinely contribute to climate change mitigation as opposed to a redistribution of organic c within the landscape or soil profile; this aspect is lacking in many previous assessments. the third aim is to quantitatively compare any climate change benefits through soil c sequestration under ca with other mitigation measures such as improved management of nitrogen (n) fertilizers.
result1: in the literature reviewed from ssa there were only four publications where the full set of ca principles were applied simultaneously (i.e. reduced tillage, residue retention and crop diversification), though two of these included data from multiple sites.
result2: the predicted annual rate of soc increase for the full set of ca principles of 1.01 mg c ha−1 yr−1, with a standard error of 0.39 mg c ha−1 yr−1.
general_conclusion: the predicted annual rate of soc increase for the full set of conservation agriculture principles is of 1.01 mg c ha−1 yr−1, with a standard error of 0.39 mg c ha−1 yr−1.
knowledge_gaps: there are severe methodological constraints to making meaningful comparisons of soc stock between flat planting (often used with ca in the region) and ridge and furrow systems which are conventional practice in several parts of ssa, especially malawi. in these situations it is difficult to draw unequivocal conclusions about the impact of ca practices on soc and almost certainly contributed to the diversity of results at some sites (ngwira et al., 2012, thierfelder et al., 2013a). the situation is further complicated when attempting to make comparisons between treatments under realistic conditions in farmers' fields.

search_strategy: database: isi web of knowledge from january 2003 to may 2009. search of literature that correlated bird species diversity with plantations with the terms plantation∗ + bird∗.
selection_criteria: the authors selected only articles that compared bird richness or abundance between natural habitats and plantations with different structural complexity. of the 60 publications considered, 38 were conducted in tropical and subtropical broadleaved forests and 14 were carried out in temperate broadleaf and mixed forests. three studies were conducted in mediterranean environments.
data_analysis: assessment of bird responses at the assemblage level in all types of plantations regardless of the commodity cultivated. for each case, they registered how the bird assemblage responded to  structural complexity within the plantation, in terms of increases or decreases in mean and total richness and abundance. to evaluate the consistency of the responses, data were analyzed  with a sign test both for the plantation–plantation and for the forest–plantation responses. increases in bird richness or abundance in more complex habitats were regarded as a positive response.
background: Plantations with a well developed understory or multiple vegetation strata ought to support more species than plantations that are structurally simple.
objective: to assess the responses of bird abundance and richness to habitat complexity in forests and structurally complex and simplified plantations. here we focus on complex plantations (agroforestry).
result1: bird richness and abundance were significantly higher in structurally complex plantations than in structurally simple ones.
result2: NA
general_conclusion: structural complexity within plantations enhanced the avifauna assemblage and promoted increased bird species richness and abundance. management practices that allow or promote structural complexity and understory growth should be promoted to aid in conserving biodiversity.
knowledge_gaps: no data available for europe. test the relationship between biodiversity and (resources provided by multiple vegetation layers in understory vegetation in plantations, to help determine the proximal factors behind such enhancement. solid evidence that complex plantations adapted to support some biodiversity maintain their yields and profitability.

search_strategy: the literature published between 1989 and 2011 was investigated using the following electronic databases: cab abstracts, biological abstract, scopus and google scholar. titles, abstracts and keywords were searched using these keywords: agroforestry parkland, dehesa, grassland production, grazed woodlands, herbaceous production, montado, paddock trees, pasture understory, pasture yield, savanna, scattered tree, silvopastoral system, tree-grass.
selection_criteria: data collection was limited to experimental plots that included exclusively an unimproved herbaceous layer (i.e. unfertilized, nonirrigated, not sown with genetically improved varieties) to avoid possible confounding effects of agricultural inputs with that of tree environment. data collection was restricted to results in which means, variance (standard deviation, standard error, or confidence intervals), and sample size (i.e. total number of repetitions) were reported directly as numerical or graphical data in the paper, or were made available to us through personal communication with the authors. data were considered only if pasture yield estimates for a specific year was available together with precipitation (mm) for the same year.
data_analysis: the effect size is defined as hedge g (standardised difference).  g is adjusted with the small-sample correction factor. first, a simple random effects model was used to test the overall effect of trees on pasture yields. a mixed-effects model was then performed by including tree functional group and annual precipitation as moderators. significant differences between groups were explored using contrasts. mixed-effects models were built for each group including precipitation as a moderator. moderators were tested using between-groups heterogeneity (qm), which estimates the amount of heterogeneity in effect sizes that is explained by a given moderator while controlling for others. a plot of the effect sizes against sample size (not shown) revealed a funnelshaped distribution of the data points (z = −0.273, p = 0.785), as would be expected in the absence of publication bias.
background: Scattered trees in agricultural landscapes are declining worldwide due to intensive land use and are often perceived by farmers as having negative impacts on agricultural production. Large-scale assessments in different biomes of agricultural yield in scattered tree ecosystems remain rare.
objective: this study addressed the following key questions: (1) what is the overall effect of scattered trees on pasture yield across different biomes and species? (2) does the effect of scattered trees on pasture yield differ between different tree functional groups? (3) does decreasing annual rainfall influence the effects of scattered trees on pasture yield? (4) are the latter interactions mitigated among tree functional groups?
result1: overall, tree overstorey had a neutral effect on total herbaceous aboveground biomass, with a non-significant (n = 73, z = −1.268, p = 0.205) mean effect size of −0.39 and 95% ci ranging from −1.00 to 0.21.
result2: the tree functional groups had a significant effect on effect sizes (qm = 21.44, d.f. = 3, p < 0.0001). the effect size was negative and significant for eucalyptus (g = −2.49 +- 1.97, p = 0.0135), positive and near-significant for n2-fixing (g = 1.73 +-1.91,p = 0.076), and near zero and non-significant for deciduous (g = 0.16 +- 0.61, p = 0.838) and evergreen oak (g =−0.37+-1.66, p = 0.666). mean effect sizes were ordered among groups as: n2-fixing > deciduous = evergreen oak > eucalyptus.
result3: annual precipitation had no significant effect on effect size across all tree functional groups when these were taken together (qm = 0.30, d.f. = 1, p = 0.584).
result4: linear mixed-models within each tree functional group revealed significant effect of annual precipitation for the eucalyptus (qm = 12.16, d.f. = 1, p = 0.0005) and n-fixing (qm = 9.04, d.f. = 1, p = 0.0026) groups.
result5: a positive linear relationship (r2 = 0.35) between effect size and annual precipitation was found for the eucalyptus group, while a negative linear relationship (r2 = 0.61) was found for the n2-fixing group.
general_conclusion: the meta-analysis provides evidence that the net effect of trees on pasture yield was nul across the four studied tree functional groups, i.e. pasture yield beneath and outside the canopy of scattered trees did not differ.

search_strategy: literature search was conducted using isi web of science, focusing on literature published up to october 2013 reporting the effects of agroforestry on invertebrate pests (insects, mitesand nematodes), plant diseases (fungi, bacteria and virus) and/or weeds. we considered both sequential and simultaneous agroforestry systems. sequential systems include improved fallows, relay cropping with trees and rotational woodlot systems where a piece of land is deliberately planted with fast-growing nitrogen-fixing trees. simultaneous systems include scattered trees in crop land, often known as parkland agroforestry, alley cropping, cereal-tree inter-cropping and multi-strata agroforestry. the literature search was conducted using 20 terms describing agroforestry interventions and 10 terms describing response variables.
selection_criteria: papers that presented data on any of the following variables were considered: (1) pest abundance, (2) proportion of plant damage due to pests and diseases, (3) abundance of natural enemies, (4) diversity of natural enemies, (5) proportion of pests predated or parasitized and (6) weed abundance. a study had to fulfil the following criteria: (1) the study was conducted at the plot, field or farm scale, (2) a measure of pest control was reported for both a control treatment (i.e. the crop grown without the agro-forestry intervention or under low levels of shade) and for one or more treatments subjected to either agroforestry interventions, or higher shade levels, and (3) the same crop was grown in both treatment and control.
data_analysis: the mean values of pest abundance, plant damage, natural enemy abundance, and weed abundance for the treatment and control groups were recorded from all studies. rr is defined as the ratio of the treatment mean to the corresponding control mean for each study. log(rr) was analyzed using a mixed-effect model without weighting. the effect of moderator variables (i.e. annual vs. perennial crops, above vs.belowground organisms, parasitic vs. non-parasitic weeds) were tested using a mixed modelling approach, allowing for random variation in effect sizes within groups (i.e. between studies within groups) and fixed differences between groups. publication bias was analyzed.
background: Evidence is mounting that agroforestry influences other ecosystem services delivered by biodiversity, such as pest control. However, quantitative reviews of the effects of agroforestry on pest control are still lacking.
objective: the objective of this meta-analysis was to investigate the effects of agroforestry practices on the abundance of invertebrate pests, weeds, diseases, natural enemies, and crop damage. this study also assesses whether (1) agroforestry practices affects pests differently in annual vs. perennial crops, (2) whether above and below-ground organisms were differently affected by agroforestry, and (3) if agroforestry practices reduce both parasitic and non-parasitic weeds.
result1: weeds were significantly less abundant under agroforestry compared to control cropland. agroforestry significantly reduced non-parasitic weeds and had a marginally significant positive effect on control of parasitic weeds.
result2: natural enemies of pests were significantly more abundant under agroforestry. overall, plant damage due to pests and plant diseases was significantly reduced by agroforestry, but pest abundance was not significantly affected. however, the significant reduction of both pest abundance and plant damage was observed for perennial crops, whereas agroforestry had no effect in annual crops.
result3: there was no difference between above and belowground pest abundance and plant damage.
result4: the majority of studies (7 out of 11) showed no effect of agroforestry on enemy diversity and the response of predation and parasitism was mixed, with 3 of the 7 studies showing no effect and the remainder split evenly between positive and negative effects.
result5: potential publication bias for plant damage due to pest and disease.
general_conclusion: this meta-analysis indicates that agroforestry generally benefits most aspects of natural pest control.
knowledge_gaps: most of the studies testing how agroforestry practices affect pest control were done in either coffee or maize (>80%of studies). thus, it is possible that the results are partly dependent on the crop types studied. only two studies explored the impact of agroforestry on plant diseases, and the impact on a large number of important invertebrate pests and naturalenemies remain unknown. the trials had been done mainly in western and eastern africa and in central and south america (36 studies).

selection_criteria: the systematic literature mapping sought to include all scientific publications that provide quantitative data comparing agroforestry with an alternative land use system in a european study area and using indicators that assess biodiversity and ecosystem services. 53 articles selected (31 silvopastoral, 13 silvoarable, 7 mixed).

background: Agroforestry has played an important role in Europe in the past, and traditional agroforestry practices, such as wood pasture and grazed or intercropped orchards, are still practised widely in Europe. During the 20th century, the area of many European agroforestry systems decreased while the remaining agroforestry practices are vulnerable. In 2005, the European Union provided opportunity for national and regional governments to financially support the establishment of new agroforestry systems.
objective: the study aimed at answering the following research questions: 1) does european agroforestry enhance biodiversity and ecosystem services relative to conventional agriculture or forestry (natural and planted forest)?; 2) which species groups and which categories of ecosystem services are most supported by agroforestry?; 3) what differences arise among different kinds of agroforestry (e.g. silvoarable systems, silvopastoral agroforestry)?; 4) do biophysical system properties such as temperature and precipitation drive inter-site differences? here, only results regarding biodiversity are reported.
result1: for agroforestry (all types) the responses were poisitive but not significant, relative to agricultural and pasture land.
result2: significantly positive effects of agroforestry (all types) compared to all other land uses were observed for the mediterranean and pannonian biogeographical regions; the effects of agroforestry in the continental, alpine and boreal regions were not significant.
result3: a positive trend of agroforestry (all types), compared to all other land uses was revealed in all the taxa, but the effect was only significant for birds
result4: silvopastoral agroforestry compared to all other land uses showed significant benefits in biodiversity. silvoarable and mixed systems showed increases, however non statistically significant.
general_conclusion: for agroforestry (all types) the responses were poisitive but not significant, relative to agricultural and pasture land.
knowledge_gaps: when analyzing the overall results, the fragmented structure of the primary data should be taken into account, especially when focusing on trade-offs between ecosystem services. subgrups of data were sometimes poor, to estimate small confidence intervals.

result1: when compared to forestry, agroforestry had a significant positive effect on soil fertility/nutrient cycling.

result3: benefits were observed for the mediterranean and pannonian biogeographical regions; the effects of agroforestry in the continental, alpine and boreal regions were not significant.
result4: when compared with agricultural land and pastureland, agroforestry had non-significant effects on soil fertility/nutrient cycling.
general_conclusion: when compared with forestry, agroforestry had a significant positive effect on soil fertility/nutrient cycling. in comparison with pastureland and agricultural land, no significant differences were reported.
knowledge_gaps: when analyzing the overall results, the fragmented structure of the primary data should be taken into account, especially when focusing on trade-offs between ecosystem services.

search_strategy: data were acquired by searching existing peer-refereed literature published between 1950 and 2015, using the web of science and google scholar with search terms such as carbon sequestration, carbon storage, carbon stocks, the different greenhouse gases (ch4 and n2o), and types of agroforestry. number of papers selected: 56  on net rates of change of biomass and/or soil carbon (c) stocks + 15 on net changes in the emissions of methane (ch4) and nitrous oxide (n2o)
selection_criteria: studies that reported annual biomass increments (above-ground, below-ground or total biomass), soil c sequestration rate or annual ch4 and n2o emissions in field measurements, or provided enough information from which annual sequestration rates and emission rates of non-co2 greenhouse gases could be estimated through unit conversions and/or extrapolation of given data.
data_analysis: from the collected data of biomass and soil c sequestration rates in agroforestry and the net difference in soil ch4 and n2o emission rates between agroforestry and adjacent agricultural lands, mean responses and 95% confidence intervals were calculated. to determine the relationship between either above-ground or total biomass c sequestration rates and soil c sequestration rates, a pearson correlation analysis was used.
background: In spite of the recognized potential of C sequestration in agroforestry and the many valuable individual studies that have been carried out, there have been few comprehensive and quantitative summary reports of net C sequestration rates and net changes in overall GHG emissions under various types of agroforestry.
objective: 1)summarise c sequestration rates and net ghg emissions across available studies; 2) discuss the underlying mechanisms and drivers of responses; and 3) identify knowledge gaps and highlight future research questions.
result1: the data showed high variability in net c sequestration rates in both biomass and soils depending on the type of agroforestry, with reported c increments ranging from 0.3 to 7.7 t c ha-1 y-1 in biomass, and 1.0 to 7.4 t c ha-1 y-1 in soils.
result2: the highest reported soil c sequestration rates of more than 8 t c ha-1 y-1, were for the first year after agroforestry establishment. averaged across all observations, soil c sequestration rates were about 2 t c ha-1 y-1 in youngest stands that gradually diminished with time since stand establishment.
result3: overall, type 1 agroforestry stands (at an average age of 14 years) sequestered 7.2  +/- 2.8 t c ha-1 y-1, with biomass and soil c sequestration contributing about 70% and 30% of that increment, respectively.
result4: soils under agroforestry oxidised 1.6 +/- 1.0 kg ch4 ha-1 y-1 and emitted 7.7 +/- 3.3 kg n2o ha-1 y-1
result5: comparing agroforestry and adjacent agricultural lands, only minor differences in net ch4 and n2o emissions were found, with no clear overall direction of change.
general_conclusion: overall, agroforestry was estimated to contribute to mitigating 27 +/- 14 t co2 equivalents ha-1 y-1 at least for the first 14 years after establishment, compared to arable land or pasture.

result1: soils under agroforestry had a net negative ch4 emission (i.e. uptake by ch4 oxidation) of −1.6 ± 0.5 kg ch4 ha−1 y−1, and net n2o emission of +7.7 ± 1.7 kg n2o ha−1 y−1 .
result2: the largest ch4 uptake was reported for improved fallow systems (–3.2 ± 0.5 kg ch4 ha−1 y−1), and improved fallow, shaded perennial-crop systems, and riparian buffers had the largest n2o emissions of 9–10 kg n2o ha−1 y−1; shifting cultivation and tree plantations had quite low emissions of little over 1 kg n2o ha−1 y−1.
result3: comparing agroforestry and adjacent agricultural lands, only minor differences in net ch4 and n2o emissions were found, with no clear overall direction of change. differences in emissions between agroforestry and agriculture were: −0.1 ± 1.4 kg ch4 ha−1 y−1 and −2.7 ± 10.6 kg n2o ha−1 y−1.
result4: soil n2o emissions were observed to be reduced under shifting cultivation, tree plantations on arable land and riparian buffers, with one observation from a riparian buffer giving a dramatic reduction in n2o emissions by almost 30 kg n2o ha−1 y−1
result5: combining c sequestration in biomass and the soil with changes in net emissions of ch4 and n2o emissions, it was estimated that a shift to agroforestry can mitigate 27.2 ± 13.5 t co2 eq ha−1 y−1. the contribution of  ch4 and n2o emissions reductions to this figure is relatively small (around 10%).
general_conclusion: overall, agroforestry was estimated to contribute to mitigating 27 +/- 14 t co2 equivalents ha-1 y-1 at least for the first 14 years after establishment.
knowledge_gaps: soil ch4 and n2o emissions in some agroforestry types had to be determined from a limited number of observations and estimated values should be updated as additional results from future studies will become available. estimated values for n2o are particularly uncertain, and uncertainty bounds based on the existing information range from possible quantitatively important positive to negative fluxes.

search_strategy: to investigate the effect of hedgerows and trees on crop yield, a double research question was defined: i) what is the spatial extent of the influence of the trees on crop yield and ii) what is the impact of tree-crop interaction on crop yield? potentially relevant papers were searched on the isi web of knowledge and sciencedirect. search terms were: trees, tree row, agroforestry, hedgerow, alley cropping, intercropping, woody edge, woody field margin, crop yield and productivity. several combinations of these terms were searched.
selection_criteria: first, candidate papers were selected on title and abstract, meeting following conditions: i) data from areas with temperate climate, ii) actual field data are used (modelling studies are excluded), iii) true controls are present allowing yield comparison with and without tree-influence, iv) yield data are linked to the distance from the trees and v) interaction with arable crops, not with pasture. we focused on arable crops because we expect the effect of trees to be better measurable in crops compared to pasture. when necessary, the authors were contacted and asked to provide more information on the experimental setup or data statistics.
data_analysis: the authors used meta-regression and non-linear mixed models to analyze data. they performed a traditional meta-regression with the metaphor package in r, weighting ln(r) by the inverse of standard deviations. a mixed-effects model accounted for non-independence between studies.
background: The meta-analysis utilizes various statistical models, including traditional meta-regression and non-linear mixed models, to analyze data on tree height and hedgerow scenarios. It addresses the impact of study design on results, emphasizing the importance of standard deviations and the structure of data in ecological research.
objective: the main objectives of the meta-analysis are to investigate the spatial extent of tree influence on crop yield and the impact of tree-crop interaction on crop yield. the analysis includes both meta-regression and non-linear mixed models to compare results.
result1: hedgerows require 0.1 ha minimum surface, with a weighting factor of two, reducing efa requirement to 2.5%. alley cropping requires 5% of arable land, with a weighting factor of one.
result2: NA
general_conclusion: tree-crop interactions can enhance crop yield but require specific data for optimization. the economic analysis indicates that without greening payments, hedgerows and alley cropping are not economically attractive for farmers. the study suggests that policy support and adjustments in payment levels based on ecological benefits could enhance the viability of these agroforestry practices.
knowledge_gaps:
need for comprehensive studies on the long-term ecological impacts of hedgerows and alley cropping on biodiversity.

exploration of indirect benefits from greening measures, such as soil quality improvement through wood chip utilization.

evaluation of different weighting factors for greening options to enhance ecological value and competitiveness.

search_strategy: the literature search strategy included databases with specific search terms for various ecosystem services. searches were updated until june and july 2016, identifying studies based on titles and abstracts. key studies were retained for analysis based on criteria like region and empirical data availability.
selection_criteria: the selection criteria for the studies included in the meta-analysis were based on title and abstract retention, reference checking, and author searching. specific studies were chosen for various analyses related to natural pest control, carbon stock, and nutrient interception.
data_analysis: the authors used various statistical methods, including mixed models and meta-analysis, to analyze data on crop yield and nutrient interception. they applied criteria like aic, bic, and log-likelihood for model selection, comparing models with and without outliers.
background: The meta-analysis compares mixed models and traditional methods for analyzing hedgerows (HR) and grass strips (GS) in ecological studies. It highlights the importance of including study statistics, such as population size and variance, to ensure accurate results.
objective: the main objectives of the meta-analysis include evaluating the effectiveness of hedgerows (hr) and grass strips (gs) in intercepting nitrogen (n) and phosphorus (p), as well as assessing soil sediment interception. specific studies were selected for each analysis based on available statistics.
result1: the agroforestry practices of hedgerows (hr) and grass strips (gs) show a trade-off between crop yield and regulating ecosystem services. while hr reduces crop yield by 29% near the hedgerow, it increases soil carbon stock by 22%. gs enhances predator diversity and reduces aphid density.
result2: NA
general_conclusion: carbon sequestration is significant in agroforestry systems, aiding climate mitigation.
knowledge_gaps:
limited understanding of the interaction effects between hedgerows (hr) and grass strips (gs) on various crop types.

insufficient empirical data on nitrogen (n) and phosphorus (p) interception across different environmental conditions.

need for standardized methodologies in assessing the effectiveness of hr and gs in natural pest control.

selection_criteria: studies included field data, and each study site had an agroforestry system and adjacent cropland or pasture control plots. modeling studies and reviews were excluded.
data_analysis: effect sizes were calculated and formal meta‐analyses was conducted in r with the ‘rom’ function in the ‘metaphor’ package. individual effect sizes weighted according to their sds. mixed models were used to study the effect of covariates.
scale: global. 6 continents and 16 countries, ranging from temperate to tropical climatic zones. most of the studies were in asia and in tropical areas.
background: Although there are various estimates of C stocks in agroforestry, the results are highly divergent, and some studies do not have control plots for comparison, making it difficult to accurately evaluate C sequestration potential in agroforestry.
objective: the objectives are: 1) quantify c stocks (both aboveground and soil c) in soils in four agroforestry systems compared with adjacent agricultural control plots under various soil and climatic conditions; 2) evaluate the effects of agroforestry characteristics, such as tree age, soil properties, and depth on soil c stocks; and 3) to identify knowledge gaps regarding the main processes and mechanisms in agroforestry for short‐, medium‐, and long‐term c accumulation in agroforestry.
result1: mean soil c stocks (1‐m depth) in agroforestry were 126 mg c·ha−1, which is 19% higher (with statistical significance) than that in cropland or pasture.
result2: homegardens had 30% more soil c stocks than had controls, which was higher than those of other af systems. silvopasture has similar or even higher tree density than have alley cropping and windbreaks, but it had the lowest increase or even had no changes in soil c stocks.
result3: across all age classes, increased soil c stocks in agroforestry were reduced with tree age, indicating the highest changes in the younger trees (younger than 10 years)
result4: soil c stocks in agroforestry were similar across climatic zones.
result5: agroforestry systems have much higher increases in aboveground c stocks than in soil c, especially in silvopastures. aboveground c was correlated with tree density and growth rate, which was higher in agroforestry systems such as homegardens, windbreaks, and silvopastures. tree management in the alley cropping system, such as pruning, might limit the biomass accumulation in stems, while increasing soil c stocks.
general_conclusion: all four main agroforestry systems—alley cropping, windbreaks, silvopastures, and homegardens—sequestered significantly more c than did cropland (or pasture).
knowledge_gaps: the following important knowledge gaps regarding c sequestration in af were identified: (a) quantitative assessment of c inputs and stocks in various parts of af systems, with special focus on deep soil c and its dependence on tree species and their age; (b) optimization of the area allocated to trees and crops within each af system to reach maximal c sequestration, increase yield, maximize ecosystem services, and improve environmental conditions; and (c) development of new remote sensing approaches to distinguish af from the background of forests, plantations, and gardens and to quantify the af area.

search_strategy: peer reviewed studies were selected through the isi-web of knowledge, google scholar, and scopus. the searches were performed using several words related to agroforestry systems and carbon sequestration (or the same terms in spanish or portuguese). the terms were used separately or in combination with each other. the reference lists of the published reviews on the topic were also searched for eligible studies through snowballing.
selection_criteria: 1)above ground carbon sequestration per year (mg c ha−1yr−1) or total carbon storage per hectare (mg c ha−1) before and after implementation of the agroforestry system; 2) soil carbon sequestration per year (mg c ha−1yr−1) or total carbon storage per hectare (mg c ha−1) before and after implementation of the agroforestry system (covering soil carbon only and not tree roots); 3) land use before and after the implementation of the agroforestry system; 4) time since implementation of the agroforestry system (age of the agroforestry system in number of years); 5) climate; 6) country. selected papers: 40 for above-ground carbon + 46 for soil carbon
data_analysis: the mean above ground and soil carbon sequestration was calculated for each agroforestry system in the six world regions identified. in addition, the mean, minimum, and maximum were calculated. a more detailed analysis was undertaken for agroforestry systems implemented in tropical climates because soil and above ground carbon was more often reported in these studies. the calculations were undertaken with ibm spss statistics 24. to better understand the changes with respect to time since implementation, forest plots were created using microsoft excel 2010 and the r statistical platform (r core team,2017). to identify the factors, a set of general linear mixed models (glmm) were fitted. the potential covariates tested were: the effect of time after conversion, climate, continent, land use before change, current agroforestry system, and land use change (type of change)
scale: global (africa, asia, australia, europe, latin america, and north america).
background: Climate change mitigation and food security are two of the main challenges of human society. Agroforestrysystems, defined as the presence of trees on external and internal boundaries, cropland, or on any other available niche of farmland, can provide both climate change mitigation and food.
objective: 1)identify agroforestry systems implemented in different regions of the globe; 2) quantify the sequestration potential of different agroforestry systems and; 3) understand the factors influencing carbon sequestration.
result1: difference in above-ground carbon sequestration is higher under transition from degraded land to improved fallows (12.8 tc ha−1 yr−1, sd1 = 5.4, n = 14), cropland to improved fallows (9.4 tc ha−1 yr−1, sd = 5.2, n = 5), and grassland to woodlots (8.3 tc ha−1 yr−1, sd = 5.2 n = 17)
result2: difference in soil carbon sequestration is higher under transition from grassland to silvopastoral (4.4 tc ha−1 yr−1, sd = 0.86, n = 9), underutilised land to homegarden (3.8 tc ha−1 yr−1, sd 1.54, n  19), and cropland to improved fallow (1.9 tc ha−1 yr−1, sd = 1.9, n = 17)
result3: there are also negative (but non-significant) absolute changes in soil organic carbon under transition from cropland to woodlot (−0.5 tc ha−1 yr−1, sd = 2.57, n = 10), and grassland to agrisilvicultural (−0.8 tc ha−1 yr−1, sd = 0.98, n = 5).
result4: the most common agroforestry systems found in the literature on above ground carbon sequestration were shadow systems (n = 40) and woodlots (n = 34). fig. 1b shows that the most common agroforestry systems found in the literature on soil carbon sequestration were agrisilvicultural systems (n = 52) and shadow systems (n = 24).
result5: absolute means of above ground and soil carbon sequestration rates are, on average, higher in tropical climates (around 5 tc ha-1 y-1), where above ground carbon sequestration is higher in improved fallows and boundary planting and soil carbon sequestration is higher in silvopastoral systems and home-gardens.
general_conclusion: this study found that transition to agroforestry leads to net carbon storage in the system. this change is very clear for above ground carbon. results for soil carbon sequestration were not so consistent, even though a positive increment in carbon was observed in most cases. large differences in soil carbon sequestration values among the land use systems can result from biophysical and socio-economic characteristics of the system and/or methodological issues.
knowledge_gaps: most studies report on systems in tropical climates (n = 133 for above ground carbon and n = 88 for soil carbon). only few studies directly reported the land use before the agroforestry system implementation, and this often had to be inferred from the information provided in the case study description. statistical information such as the variance or the inventory design or sample size was also omitted in the great majority of studies. another factor that can affect quality of the analysis is the homogenisation of soil depths to 0–30 cm. this analysis only provides information on absolute change in soil and above ground carbon sequestration, and not on other green house gas emissions (e.g. nitrous oxide, methane).

search_strategy: the databases used included google (http://google.com), google scholar web of science, scirus, and scopus. search terms were run in separate or limited combinations, depending on the requirements, or limitations, of the database used. in addition, we identified scientific articles, books, and reports by consulting published studies, including major review articles.
selection_criteria: papers were rejected because they did not address a biodiversity issue or did not take place in the terrestrial ecosystem of the mediterranean basin. among the studies reviewed, some were excluded from the systematic review, due to their lacking information necessary for the analysis (e.g., sample size, mean or standard deviation of species richness). all studies included in the review used quantitative methods in their analyses. if a study considered more than one taxon, more than one parameter (e.g., diversity and abundance), or more than one measure of comparison, we treated them as independent studies, resulting in the inclusion of 154 papers.
data_analysis: we found 18 studies that provided suitable data for conducting a meta-analysis of species richness for the different taxonomic groups in terrestrial ecosystems with dense or open vegetation, allowing comparisons. the heterogeneity of the effect sizes was estimated using the q-statistic. all meta-analyses were conducted using metawin 2.0. the effect sizes were analyzed using a random effects model. the output of each statistical test consisted of the mean effect size for the analysis with an accompanying bias-corrected bootstrapped 95% ci and a total heterogeneity statistic (q). a two-way anova was also performed to examine the effects of habitat type and taxa and their interaction on the species richness of biodiversity indicators.
background: Global land-use change has caused declines in biodiversity through the direct loss of habitats, degradation of soil and water, overexploitation of native species, and the introduction of exotic species, leading to the degradation and unsustainable use of 60% of the ecosystem services examined during the Millennium Ecosystem Assessment. While there is clear experimental evidence of the linkage between biodiversity loss and the deterioration of ecosystem functions, the structure (shape and strength) of this relationship remains contentious.
objective: to performe a quantitative assessment of the relationship between biodiversity measurements and landscape characteristics in agrosylvopastoral systems of the mediterranean basin.
result1: as open and closed habitats often represent very different biological environments, the analyses were conducted separately. the estimated mean effect size was significantly different from zero (open habitats: e++ = 2.98, 95% ci = −4.47 to 8.67, bias-corrected ci 1.97 to 2.20; closed wooded habitats: e++ = −0.21, 95% ci = −5.06 to 4.64, bias-corrected ci -2.93 to −2.42), indicating that open habitats have fewer species than other closed wooded habitats.
result2: with respect to taxon type, plants, birds, and invertebrates represent the most useful indicators when evaluating biodiversity in mediterranean environments, even though these groups have different spatial requirements. the estimation of species richness depends on its ecological importance, as well as on the design of the study.
result3: herbaceous plants represent most taxa in agroecosystems, making them a key group for conserving biodiversity. as a result, plants had the highest species richness in comparison to other taxa. in managed woodlands, plants had the highest average species richness, whereas birds had the lowest.
general_conclusion: open agrosylvopastoral habitats have fewer species than other closed wooded habitats.
knowledge_gaps: the selection of inappropriate indicators of species richness in biodiversity studies might negatively affect overall biodiversity conservation. stronger focus should be placed on how to manage forests, inappropriate farming practices, and the livestock more effectively most of the studies included in the current review provided insufficient information on study conditions and details, or were poorly replicated or pseudoreplicated, which is common for biodiversity studies.

search_strategy: collected data on soil infiltration rate from peer-reviewed papers published in both chinese and english language journals from 1999 to 2016. papers in chinese were collected from the china national knowledge infrastructure (cnki) database and those in english from isi-web of science and google scholar.
selection_criteria: 1)studies had to report at least one of variables including soil initial infiltration rate and steady infiltration rate before and after land use change; 2) means and sample sizes had to be reported; 3) any studies lacking replication was not considered; 4) land use change could be represented by two different land use types, as long as they locate in adjacent sites.
data_analysis: a fixed-effects model option was employed  in metawin 2.1 for calculation of grouped effect sizes except in instances where the results of homogeneity test were statistically significant (p < 0.05), in which case a random effects model was used. confidence intervals (cis) on the weighted effect size were generated using bootstrapping (9999 iterations). publication bias was quantified by egger's regression test.  trim-and-fill analysis was also conducted to test the robustness of these results which existed publication bias.

result1: soil initial and steady infiltration rates of agroforestry were 70.28% and 84.17% higher than that of cropland, respectively.

search_strategy: the research articles on afs used for the analysis were selected from peer-reviewed publications found in isi web of science and google scholar, based on a search with keywords (alone or in combinations): agroforestry/ specific agroforestry system, soil organic carbon (soc) stock, c sequestration, soil c stock, and soil c pool.
selection_criteria: only those reports that included data on soil c stocks were included. soil c concentration or stock per unit land area (mg c ha−1 or equivalent). paired sites were chosen for further analysis.
data_analysis: weighted response ratio for each category was calculated from the rr of individual pairwise comparisons. analyses were performed with the packages metafor and ggplot2 and r version 3.4.0. random effect models are considered where the heterogeneity of true effect size among studies arises from random variation around the mean effect sizes of population studies.  if sd (standard deviation) values were missing from a study, other variance measures like standard error (se) of means were used to calculate the sd, or error bars of the figures were used for sd estimation. the overall coefficient of variance (cv), without the missing sd, was generated and then multiplied with the means of missing sd to obtain the imputed sd. meta-regression (anova) was performed, to assess the relationship between the moderator variables or covariates.
scale: global. arid and semiarid (asa), lowland humid tropics (lht), mediterranean (med), temperate (tem). 30 countries (asia, africa, north america, latin america, and europe)
background: Tree-based land-use systems such as agroforestry are reported to have the potential to enhance C sequestrationboth above and below ground. The importance of managing such systems through appropriate agroecological (carbon) farming methods is increasingly being recognized as a promising strategy for enhancing soil carbon sequestration.
objective: the objective of this study was to undertake a statistically rigorous, quantitative assessment of the scattered results on soil organic carbon (soc) stocks reported under various agroforestry systems, in comparison with those in agricultural, forestry, and pasture systems in different agroecological regions around the world through a meta-analytical approach.
result1: the conversion of cropland to agroforestry significantly increased soc stocks at 0–15, 0–30, 0–100, but not at 0–60 and > 100 cm.
result2: comparison of afs vs. non-agroforestry cropland showed that, in general, percentage in soc% stock increased under afs across all agroecological regions and depth classes. the silvoarable systems in the med regions showed the lowest soc% (1.4%).
result3: no significant differences were observed in the conversion from pasture/grassland to agroforestry (0–15, 0–30, 0–100, 0 ≥ 100 cm), while a significant increase was observed at 0–60 cm. soc stocks were found significantly reduced when pasture/grassland were converted into agrisilvicultural systems (0–100 cm), probably due to the lack of perennial grasses.
result4: comparing afs vs. pasture showed varying trends in soc% stock improvements across different agroecological regions and depth classes, especially in the tropics. within the 0–20 cm depth class, the highest soc% stock was noted under silvopastoral systems in lht regions (151.6%). in the top soil (0–20 cm), the asa region showed higher soc% stock across agrisilviculture (+15%), agrosilvopasture (+12.8%) and a higher soc stock of +89.4% in the silvopasture systems. in the lht region, soc stocks were lower under all afs practices; the silvopasture systems within med region too reported lower soc% stock (–9.2%) in the top soil.
result5: the comparison of afs vs. forest showed a general trend line of lower soc% stock under afs across most agroecological regions and depth classes, with the exception of multistrata systems in lht region that reported higher soc% (12.6% and 20.4%) up to a depth of 40 cm and 60 cm respectively. in the 0–100 cm depth, afs vs. forest reported higher soc% stock under multistrata systems and agrosilvopasture, while agrisilviculture had a decline (–26.8%; lht). in the med region, silvopasture showed a higher soc% by 56.1% over forest within 0–100 cm.
general_conclusion: the conversion from agriculture to agroforestry increased soc stocks in most of the cases. significant increases were also observed in the transition from pasture/grassland to agroforestry in the top layers, especially with the inclusion perennial in the systems, such as in silvopasture and agrosilvopastoral systems. the conversion from forest to agroforestry lead to losses in soc stocks in the top layers, while no significant differences were detected when deeper layers were included.
knowledge_gaps: the δsoc%stock for afs vs. uncultivated lands comparison had low numbers of data points and did not show any consistent trend. some studies do not report the important parameters such as soil bulk density, and the methods followed in sampling and analysis of soils and computation of data. also the database for the conversion of forest plantations to afs had observations only from a few studies.

search_strategy: a literature survey of peer-reviewed publications was carried out using isi-web of science, cab direct, and google scholar (google inc., mountain view, ca, usa). the first step was the identification of the potential studies to be included in the analysis through the examination of the abstract, using agroforestry, c sequestration, soil c sequestration, soil c stock, soil c pool, and their combination their combination, as keywords for the search.
selection_criteria: to be included, studies had to contain information about soil c concentration or stocks per unit land area (i.e. mg of c/ ha or in other appropriate equivalent), for both non-agroforestry and agroforestry land uses.
data_analysis: the effect of agroforestry on soc stock was quantified by calculating the natural log of the response ratio using metawin 2.0. a randomeffects model was used for analysis of all data sets, based on the assumption that random variation in soc stocks occurred between observations. mean effect size for each observation was calculated with 95% confidence intervals (cis) generated by a bootstrapping procedures. to facilitate the interpretation of effect size, it was transformed as percentage change.
scale: global (mostly located in northern, central, and southern america, africa, and asia).
background: Within human driven land use change, agricultural and forestry practices have the potential to mitigate CO2 concentration through C sequestration, allowing the land acts as a sink for C. Soil plays an important role in C sequestration, being able to store 1.5–3 times more C than in vegetation. The adoption of specific land management practices, such as the implementation of trees and permanent vegetation, could significantly boost their C sequestration potential.
objective: the main objective of this paper was to investigate the effects of agroforestry on soil organic carbon (soc) stocks by summarizing the data from literature using meta-analytical techniques.
result1: full dataset (with forest and uncultivated/other land-uses included): agroforestry revealed a significant and positive effect on soc stocks at 0–30 and 0–100 cm depths. reduced dataset (including only agriculture, pasture/grassland, forest plantation): the significant positive effect of agroforestry was observed at all depths, except for 0 ≥ 100 cm.
result2: the conversion of agricultural land to agroforestry significantly increased soc stocks at 0–15, 0–30, 0–100, but not at 0–60 and > 100 cm.
result3: among agroforestry systems, positive significant increases of soc stocks were observed in the change from agriculture to agrisilviculture (0–15, 0–30, 0–100 cm), agriculture to agrosilvopastoral systems (0–60, 0–100 cm), and agriculture to silvopasture (0–100 cm).
result4: no significant differences were observed in the conversion from pasture/grassland to agroforestry (0–15, 0–30, 0–100, 0 ≥ 100 cm), while a significant increase was observed at 0–60 cm. soc stocks were found significantly reduced when pasture/grassland were converted into agrisilvicultural systems (0–100 cm), probably due to the lack of perennial grasses.
general_conclusion: the conversion from agriculture to agroforestry increased soc stocks in most of the cases. significant increases were also observed in the transition from pasture/grassland to agroforestry in the top layers, especially with the inclusion perennial in the systems, such as in silvopasture and agrosilvopastoral systems.
knowledge_gaps: the database for forest plantations had observations only from a few studies. the lack of standardized methodologies certainly influences findings, in particular heterogeneity, which might bias outcomes. inconsistency across the studies is noticeable in wide confidence intervals. the available database is unfortunately limited. the adoption of consistent standards in agroforestry research will increase the precision of future studies.

search_strategy: the literature search included databases such as isi—web of knowledge, google scholar, and scopus. keywords used were ""biomass or soil"" combined with various terms related to carbon stocks and agroforestry systems. data were collected from 50 studies on biomass c storage and 72 on soc stock changes.
selection_criteria: the selection criteria for studies included in the meta-analysis were: estimation of soil organic carbon (soc) stocks or necessary data to calculate them, biomass carbon stocks, previous land use, measurement depth, time frame of land use change, and location or climate data of study sites.
data_analysis: the authors used statistical methods including mean ± standard deviation (sd) and 95% confidence intervals (ci) to analyze data on soil organic carbon (soc) stocks and biomass storage rates across various land use changes. analyses were performed using r software at a significance level of <0.05.
background: The meta-analysis examines soil organic carbon (SOC) stocks in agroforestry systems, highlighting issues with reference systems and missing data on previous land use. It synthesizes findings from 72 studies, providing coefficients for SOC storage and emphasizing the need for localized data for accurate carbon accounting.
objective: the main objectives of the meta-analysis are to estimate soil organic carbon (soc) stocks and biomass carbon storage in agroforestry systems resulting from various land use changes (lucs). key research questions focus on the impacts of transitioning from cropland, forest, grassland, and plantation to agroforestry. the main variables considered in the meta-analysis as moderators include: climate region; tree density (number per hectare); aboveground biomass (abg) storage rate (tc per hectare per year); belowground biomass (blg) storage rate (tc per hectare per year).
result1: agroforestry practices generally increase soil organic carbon (soc) stocks when converting croplands to agroforestry systems, though some studies report soc loss. conversion from grassland to agroforestry shows variable results.
result2: NA
general_conclusion: agroforestry practices generally increase soil organic carbon (soc) stocks when converting croplands to agroforestry systems, though some studies report soc loss. conversion from grassland to agroforestry shows variable results.
knowledge_gaps:
need for more comprehensive studies on carbon sequestration in diverse agroforestry systems.

exploration of the long-term impacts of land use changes on soil organic carbon (soc) stocks.

assessment of the effectiveness of different agroforestry practices in various climate regions.

search_strategy:
literature survey: conducted a comprehensive search using isi web of science to identify studies on the roles of scattered trees in biodiversity.

data analysis: employed response ratios (rr) to measure effect sizes and percentage of similarity indices to compare community compositions.

sampling methods: used standardized sampling techniques across studies to ensure comparability of data on abundance and richness.
selection_criteria:
the selection criteria for the studies included in the meta-analysis were:

studies must evaluate the roles of scattered trees in both natural and disturbed environments.

studies should use the same sampling method for treatments being compared.

only studies reporting abundance or species richness of individual species or groups were included.
data_analysis: the authors used response ratios (rr) to measure effect size, linear mixed-effect models for abundance analysis, and the percentage of similarity index for community composition comparisons. they accounted for potential biases and non-independence in their datasets.
background: The meta-analysis highlights the ecological significance of scattered trees, which are crucial for supporting biodiversity in various landscapes. It reveals that areas near scattered trees have higher species richness and abundance compared to open areas, emphasizing the need for their conservation in management practices.
objective: aim was to to quantify relationships between scattered trees and the species richness, abundance and composition of vertebrates, arthropods and plants.
result1: scattered trees have a neutral effect on the abundance of biological communities compared to open areas. they support similar levels of biodiversity as habitat patches, indicating they do not significantly reduce pasture biomass. overall, they are important for maintaining biodiversity in landscapes.
result2: NA
general_conclusion: scattered trees have a neutral effect on the abundance of biological communities compared to open areas. they support similar levels of biodiversity as habitat patches, indicating they do not significantly reduce pasture biomass. overall, they are important for maintaining biodiversity in landscapes.
knowledge_gaps:
the influence of scattered trees on species abundance and distribution patterns needs further exploration in various landscapes.

future research should quantify the ecological roles of scattered trees across different taxonomic groups.

conservation and management strategies must explicitly incorporate scattered trees as key biodiversity elements.

search_strategy: publications were searched in web of science. to minimise the risk of publication bias, both peer-reviewed and non-peer-reviewed literature, including theses and reports (british library ethos thesis search) and personal communications were sourced.
selection_criteria: 1. a measure of abundance or activity density of invertebrate herbivores/pests, natural enemies or pollinators, and/or a measure of conservation biological control of animal pests and/or pollination were recorded; 2. studies were undertaken in a temperate region, defined as latitude> 40° north or south; 3. a silvoarable system, for this purpose defined as trees or shrubs incorporated into an arable field, was compared with an arable control, with the respective arable components comprising annual crops. to minimise the risk of publication bias, we sourced both peer-reviewed and non-peer-reviewed literature, including theses and reports.
data_analysis: the significance of effects for herbivore/pest and natural enemy abundances were analysed in a mixed-effects meta-analysis model, using the rma.mv function of the metaphor package version 2.1-0 (viechtbauer, 2010) within r version 3.5.2 (r core team, 2018). as multiple data points were extracted from some individual studies, study id was included as a random effect.
scale: temperate region, defined as latitude> 40° north or south (canada, france, turkey, uk and usa)
background: Global crop demand is rising rapidly, and is forecasted to increase by 100110% from 2005 to 2050. The intensification of arable production in temperate regions has driven declines in biodiversity and associated ecosystem services, such as pest control and pollination. There is a strong and growing pressure to move towards more sustainable intensification of production, through harnessing natural processes to sustain productivity rather than relying on pesticides and managed pollinators. Agroforestry has been proposed as a winwin opportunity for productivity and environmental protection.
objective: 1) collate and analyse studies of pollinators, pests and their natural enemies in temperate silvoarable systems, specifically in terms of their potential contribution to pest control and pollination ecosystem services; and 2) develop a framework for future research to predict the factors which influence variation in results, with the aspiration of driving forward a unified research agenda. here we report only results on pests control and natural enemies of pests.
result1: relatively to pollinator abundance the effect sizes ranged from 1.17 to 2.55, indicating beneficial effects on pollinator populations in silvoarable systems compared with arable controls, but study replication was low.
result2: one study also reported higher california poppy phytometer seedset by a factor of 4.5 in agroforestry compared with arable systems.
general_conclusion: pollinators were more abundant in silvoarable than arable systems, but study replication was low. the study lacks of full statistical analysis.
knowledge_gaps: study replication was low for pollinators. only three studies, in the uk and canada, reported abundances of pollinating insects in silvoarable systems and arable controls. the analysis focused on invertebrates as data about others taxa was missing.

objective: 1) collate and analyse studies of pollinators, pests and their natural enemies in temperate silvoarable systems, specifically in terms of their potential contribution to pest control and pollination ecosystem services; and 2) develop a framework for future research to predict the factors which influence variation in results, with the aspiration of driving forward a unified research agenda. here we report only results on pests control and natural enemies of pests.
result1: invertebrate herbivore/pest abundances were lower in the silvoarable compared with arable systems, with a back-transformed mean effect size of 0.89.
result2: the abundance of natural enemy of pests was significantly higher in silvoarable compared with arable systems, with a mean effect size of 1.24.
result3: the abundance of arthropod herbivores/pests was significantly lower in the silvoarable than arable systems, with a mean effect size of 0.75.
result4: slug abundance was higher in the silvoarable than arable systems, with effect sizes of 1.12 to 1.53 across two studies.
general_conclusion: evidence was found for significantly enhanced natural enemy populations and significantly suppressed arthropod herbivore populations in silvoarable systems, but molluscan pests were more numerous in the two available studies, compared with arable.
knowledge_gaps: number of studies available for slugs was low. pests of the tree component has been scarsely studied. the analysis of pooled numbers of captures/observations does not take diversity into account, as only two of the studies report on diversity of functional groups. there was a strong bias towards systems with alley widths of around 12m. more research is needed to quantify subsequent effects on pest control service outcome. evidence of crop damage by invertebrate pests is very limited, and only two studies have attempted to establish a link between pest control and yield of the arable component. griffiths et al. (1998) recorded higher slug damage to a pea crop in a uk silvoarable system compared with an arable control, with damage level positively correlated to slug captures. however, yield was not measured. in turkey, akbulut et al. (2003) observed a lower level of crop damage from invertebrates in silvoarable plots, accompanied by higher yield of beans but lower yield of maize, relative to arable. other studies have simultaneously sampled cereal yields and invertebrates in silvoarable systems, finding lower yields in silvoarable compared with arable in conventional systems (burgess et al., 2003), and the opposite result in organic systems (varah, 2015), but disentangling the effect of pest control or pollination on yield from other factors, notably tree-crop interactions such as shade, is problematic.

search_strategy: the literature search utilized ebsco discovery service, focusing on english peer-reviewed field experiments up to 2015. keywords included ""infiltration rate"" and ""crop,"" yielding approximately 700 studies, with 89 ultimately included after applying specific criteria.
selection_criteria:
the selection criteria for the studies included in the meta-analysis were:

no-till: included if experiments had a no-till treatment compared to conventional or reduced tillage.

cover crop: included if there was a control with no cover crop present.

crop rotation: included if there was a control of continuous cropping with at least one additional crop in rotation.
data_analysis: the authors used a linear mixed model to analyze data, calculating means and standard errors for different agricultural practices. they calculated response ratios (lrr) comparing experimental and control treatments, applying a weighting factor based on study replications. a sensitivity analysis and publication bias evaluation were also performed.
scale: global, including temperate (majority of the data)
background: The meta-analysis examines how different agricultural practices affect soil infiltration rates, highlighting the benefits of continuous root presence and soil cover. It suggests that practices like cover crops and perennial systems improve soil structure and hydrology, influencing water entry into the soil.
objective: the main objective of the meta-analysis is to assess the effects of agricultural management practices on infiltration rates. it also examines how these effects are influenced by factors like soil texture, climate, and study duration. the main variables considered in the meta-analysis as moderators include: soil texture (percent sand, silt, clay); climate; study location; study length (years of treatment); tillage descriptions (within no-till); inclusion of cover crops (within no-till); number of crops in rotations; crop residue management (removed or maintained)
result1: the analysis indicates that introducing perennials and cover crops significantly improves soil infiltration rates.
result2: the context indicates that practices with continuous roots and soil cover, like perennials and cover crops, positively influence infiltration rates. conversely, crop and livestock systems show a negative trend compared to crop-only systems. longer experiments did not consistently yield significant changes.
general_conclusion: the analysis indicates that introducing perennials and cover crops significantly improves soil infiltration rates.
knowledge_gaps:
limited research on practices like perennials and crop-livestock systems, despite their potential benefits.

need for more complex, long-term studies evaluating combined management practices for better understanding.

insufficient detail on environmental and management factors in existing studies, hindering meta-analysis utility.

search_strategy: search strategy: the systematic search included terms like ""silvopasture,"" ""production,"" ""forage,"" and excluded terms such as ""tropical"" and specific plant species. a total of 862 records were identified, with 22 articles included in the quantitative synthesis after screening.
selection_criteria:
the selection criteria for the studies included in the meta-analysis were:

studies must report productivity data of forages or livestock in silvopastures and open pastures.

studies must report productivity data of trees in silvopastures or conventional silvicultural systems.

excluded studies did not include appropriate control comparisons or were from tropical regions.
data_analysis: the authors used a systematic review following the prisma methodology. they analyzed abstracts and keywords, extracted production data, and compared land equivalent ratios (lers) of silvopastures to open pastures or forests. metrics included tree height, forage yield, and livestock productivity, with standard errors calculated from standard deviations.
background: The meta-analysis focuses on silvopasture, defined as integrating trees, livestock, and improved pasture plants. It aims to compare productivity in silvopastures versus open pastures and forests. The review follows PRISMA methodology, analyzing peer-reviewed studies to assess productivity metrics and control treatments in temperate regions.
objective: the main objective of the meta-analysis is to compare the productivity of forages and livestock in open pastures and silvopastures, including timber and non-timber forest products. the review focuses on temperate silvopastures and requires studies to report productivity data for both forages and trees.
result1: silvopasture systems show improved forage productivity compared to traditional pastures.
result2: livestock performance, including weight gains, is often higher in silvopasture systems.
general_conclusion: silvopasture practices significantly improve productivity by 42–55% compared to conventional systems. they enhance environmental benefits, such as reduced nutrient loss and improved water quality, while sequestering more carbon and increasing biodiversity, making them socially and environmentally sustainable.
knowledge_gaps:
financial implications of silvopasture systems need further exploration due to their high productivity.

more research is required on the ecological benefits of agroforestry systems, particularly regarding biodiversity and ecosystem services.

the impact of tree planting configurations on livestock productivity in silvopastoral systems warrants additional investigation.

search_strategy: an extensive literature search was conducted in scopus, google scholar, science direct, and web of science. keywords included ""agroforestry and nutrient loss,"" ""water and soil losses in agroforestry,"" and ""agroforestry and herbicides and pesticides."" the review covered literature published in english over the past 40 years.
selection_criteria: the authors selected studies based on six indicators related to erosion and nutrient loss reduction in agroforestry. they included literature published in english over the past 40 years, focusing on the reduction of fertilizer and pesticide loss, and extracted critical data from 83 case studies across 33 countries.
data_analysis: the authors used one-way analysis of variance (anova) with a tukey test for multiple comparisons to assess differences in water efficiency, soil, and nutrient losses among agroforestry practices. they also employed regression models to identify relationships between buffer slopes and reduction effectiveness of runoff and losses.
scale: global, including temperate (majority of the data)
background: The meta-analysis examines agroforestry's role in reducing erosion and nutrient loss, analyzing 83 case studies from 33 countries over 40 years. Key indicators include runoff, soil erosion, organic carbon loss, and nutrient losses (N, P, K). It highlights agroforestry's effectiveness in mitigating agricultural pollution.
objective: the main objective of the meta-analysis is to evaluate the effectiveness of agroforestry systems in reducing runoff, soil erosion, organic carbon loss, and nutrient losses (n, p, k). key research questions focus on the extent of these reductions across different agroforestry practices and their site-dependent variability.
result1: agroforestry practices generally have a positive effect on reducing runoff, soil, and nutrient losses compared to conventional agricultural systems, with reductions averaging 58%, 65%, 9%, 49%, and 50%, respectively. however, they do not reach the efficiency of forest ecosystems. further research is needed for specific agroforestry systems.

search_strategy: the literature search included peer-reviewed articles reporting carbon stocks in agroforestry systems (afs) using isi web of science and google scholar up to april 3, 2019. keywords used were combinations of terms related to agroforestry and carbon. the search yielded 2,415 publications.
selection_criteria: the selection criteria for studies included in the meta-analysis were: (a) field data reporting carbon stocks in agroforestry systems (afs) with adjacent cropland or pasture as control; (b) afs must be tree-based; and (c) carbon stock data must be extractable from the text, tables, or figures.
data_analysis: the authors used structural equation modeling (sem) with continuous predictors as fixed effects and ""study"" as a random effect. they employed akaike information criterion (aic) for model selection and conducted analyses in r software, utilizing the ""piecewisesem"" and ""lme4"" packages.
background: The meta-analysis examines carbon accumulation in agroforestry systems (AFS) over 141 studies, highlighting the impact of tree species diversity, age, and climate. It compares AFS to sole land uses, revealing an average increase of 46.1 Mg/ha in tree biomass carbon.
objective: the main objectives of the meta-analysis are to examine how carbon (c) accumulation in biomass and soil components of agroforestry systems (afs) varies across climatic zones and to investigate the relationship between changes in soil organic carbon (soc) stock and biomass c.
result1: agroforestry practices, particularly those with multiple tree species, significantly enhance biomass carbon (c) sequestration. the impact on soil organic carbon (soc) varies by tree age and regional climate, with tropical zones achieving quicker soc peaks compared to temperate zones.
result2: NA
general_conclusion: agroforestry practices, particularly those with multiple tree species, significantly enhance biomass carbon (c) sequestration. the impact on soil organic carbon (soc) varies by tree age and regional climate, with tropical zones achieving quicker soc peaks compared to temperate zones.
knowledge_gaps:
investigate how carbon stock accumulation in different components of agroforestry systems varies over time, influenced by factors like tree age and density.

explore the role of previous land use history on long-term carbon storage in agroforestry systems.

examine the processes by which deep-rooted trees modify soil organic carbon inputs in agroforestry systems.

search_strategy:
literature review: analyzed 37 publications to summarize effects of grazing and other management practices on soil and plant metrics.

meta-analysis: employed random effects meta-analysis modeling to assess management practices' influence on soil properties and plant metrics.

data compilation: compiled 399 soil observations and 64 plant community observations across california's ecosystems.
selection_criteria:
the selection criteria for studies included in the meta-analysis were:

soil observations across at least three sites for composite metric-management pairs.

two sites for composite plant metrics to include compost amendments.

inclusion of all management practices regardless of literature support, with qualitative descriptions for limited evidence.
data_analysis: the authors used random effects meta-analysis modeling to assess the influence of management practices on soil properties and plant metrics, utilizing log response ratios (lnrr) as the effect size. they also examined how soil texture and aridity moderated these responses across studies.
background: The meta-analysis evaluates the impact of rangeland management practices on soil and plant metrics in California. It synthesizes evidence on practices like silvopasture and compost application, aiming to inform ecosystem service enhancement and carbon sequestration efforts amid varying environmental conditions.
objective:
the main objectives of the meta-analysis are to assess the influence of management practices on soil and plant metrics in california rangelands, particularly focusing on four practices: silvopasture, prescribed grazing, compost application, and riparian restoration. the research questions include evaluating the effects of these practices on soil properties and plant dynamics. the main variables considered as moderators in the meta-analysis include:

soil texture

aridity

soil properties (e.g., nitrogen, phosphorus, carbon, compaction)

plant-related metrics (e.g., species richness, forage quality)

management practices (e.g., silvopasture, prescribed grazing, compost application, riparian restoration)
result1: agroforestry practices, particularly oak presence, significantly enhance soil fertility metrics.
result2: silvopasture establishment improves soil properties and plant-related metrics.
result3: riparian restoration contributes to improved soil health.
result4: oak establishment requires further research on soil property changes over time.
general_conclusion: the agroforestry practices studied show mixed effects on soil fertility, forage productivity, and herbaceous species richness. oaks enhance soil fertility, but their impact on forage dynamics remains inconsistent. future research should focus on oak regeneration and the relationship between soil properties and plant metrics.
knowledge_gaps:
quantify changes in soil properties with oak establishment, focusing on shorter time scales (< 5 years).

improve oak regeneration and success of silvopasture projects in california's future climate.

investigate patterns in forage productivity and the impact of oaks on forage quality for livestock systems.

selection_criteria: the selection criteria for the studies included in the meta-analysis were: (1) addressing agroforestry practices, (2) publication of data, and (3) publication after the year 2000.
data_analysis: the authors used several statistical methods for data analysis, including random forest (rf) models for assessing the influence of predictor variables on carbon sequestration rates. they calculated root mean squared error (rmse) and squared regression coefficient (r²) for prediction accuracy, and applied pairwise wilcoxon rank sum tests with bonferroni correction for multiple comparisons.
